DR. JAMIL Anaphylaxis Anaphylaxis is a severe, systemic, life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction to an allergen, which is characterised by rapid and massive release of histamine and other mediators.  Overview Key Facts  Anaphylaxis is a severe, systemic, life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction to an allergen, which is characterised by rapid and massive release of histamine and other mediators.  Type I immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated hypersensitivity reaction (the Gell–Coombs Classification).  Clinical features include:  bronchospasm  angioedema  laryngeal oedema  urticaria  increased vascular permeability  cardiovascular collapse (anaphylactic shock).  Incidence is increasing, up to 7 : 100 000 population admitted to hospital annually with anaphylaxis.  Diagnosis is mostly clinical; further investigation to identify triggers may be warranted in the long term.  The condition is a medical emergency; management should follow the ABCDE approach.  Mainstay of treatment:  intramuscular (IM) adrenaline  fluid resuscitation  IM/intravenous (IV) chlorphenamine may be given once the patient is stabilised following adrenaline administration  hydrocortisone (although still recommended by NICE, is no longer recommended by the resuscitation council following a 2021 update)  bronchodilators (salbutamol) added for wheeze.  Following emergency treatment, all patients should be offered two adrenaline autoinjectors and referral for further specialist advice and management.  With prompt treatment, the overall prognosis is good; however, there are approximately 20 deaths annually due to anaphylaxis. Epidemiology  It is difficult to calculate the true incidence of anaphylaxis, but it is estimated that approximately 1 : 1 333 people living in

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI England will have an anaphylactic reaction within their lifetime.  Incidence is rising within the United Kingdom (UK), with up to 7 : 100 000 cases being admitted to hospital annually according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE).  More prevalent in children and adults < 30.  More prevalent in women than men.  Increased risk in those who have a personal or close family history of atopic disease (eg asthma or eczema).  Estimated 20 deaths per year in the UK relating to anaphylaxis. Aetiology  IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to an allergen which the patient has been previously exposed to.  It is a type I reaction.  Common precipitants include:  food substances (peanuts, shellfish, eggs etc.)  drugs (penicillin, radiological contrast media, anaesthetics)  others (latex, venom). Pathophysiology  Exposure to allergen leads to formation of IgE.  IgE binds to mast cells and basophils.  Re-exposure to allergen causes the release of antiinflammatory mediators from these cells.  Mediators:  histamine  leukotrienes  neutrophil/eosinophil chemotactic factors  neutral proteases  platelet-activating factor (PAF).  Pathology  Increased vascular permeability results in:  oedema (larynx, eyelids, tongue and lips)  bronchospasm (wheeze)  urticaria  increased mucosal secretions.  Clinical Presentation  Rapid onset symptoms include:  itching

DR. JAMIL  wheezing  diarrhoea and vomiting  urticaria  sweating  angioedema (swelling, especially of the facial features).  Severe/Life-threatening features include:  laryngeal obstruction (stridor/poor respiratory effort)  cyanosis  hypotension  tachycardia. Urticaria on the abdomen of a child: Angioedema affecting the face (especially eyelids):

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  hereditary angioedema  carcinoid syndrome  phaeochromocytoma  anaphylactoid reaction (direct release of mediators from inflammatory cells without involving antibodies, usually drug-related response, eg to acetylcysteine)  pure angioedema with no obvious trigger may be angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor sideeffect.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis of acute anaphylaxis is clinical and based on characteristic findings from the history and examination.  Anaphylaxis is a likely diagnosis if all three of the following criteria are met, according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE):  sudden and rapid onset of symptoms  life-threatening problems with airway, breathing or circulation  skin and/or mucosal changes (may be absent in approximately 20% of reactions).  The diagnosis is supported by the patient’s exposure to a known allergen.  Following emergency treatment, further testing may be undertaken to confirm the diagnosis.  timed blood samples measuring mast cell tryptase (one sample to be taken as soon as possible following emergency treatment and the second 1–2 hours after the initial symptom onset  patients may be asked to attend an allergy clinic to have their baseline mast cell tryptase levels measured.  Management Pharmacological  Intramuscular (IM) adrenaline - can be repeated after 5 minutes if airway, breathing or circulatory compromise persists.  Intravenous (IV) chlorphenamine may be given once patient is stabilised following initial resuscitation  Hydrocortisone, although still recommended by NICE, is no longer recommended as part of management of anaphylaxis following an update from the resuscitation council guides in 2021.  Emergency management (ABCDE):  ensure patient’s airway is secure; give 100% O2 (15 L non-rebreathe mask)

DR. JAMIL  remove the triggering allergen (if known and still present)  raise the patient’s legs to help improve circulation  give adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (eg 0.5 ml of 1 : 1 000); repeat every five minutes if needed (until blood pressure, pulse and respiratory function improve)  give chlorphenamine 10 mg IV once stabilised  hydrocortisone 200 mg IV - recommended by NICE,NOTE no longer a part of resuscitation council guidelines (2021)  IV infusion NaCl (titrate against blood pressure, eg 500 ml in 15 minutes) up to 2 L  if there is wheeze present, add in bronchodilators and treat as for asthma; consider ventilatory support  if the patient is still hypotensive, escalate further; consider intensive care unit (ICU).  Biphasic Reactions  Patients may experience a recurrence of symptoms within 72 hours of the initial episode without further allergen exposure (after initial anaphylaxis has completely recovered).  It is important to inform patients of this risk following an anaphylactic reaction.  These reactions are managed in the same way as anaphylaxis.  Patient Follow-up  In adults (and young people > 16 years), 6–12-hour observation post-emergency treatment.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  In children < 16 years, admit to hospital under paediatric medical team.  Offer a referral to a specialist allergy service where they can investigate, diagnose, monitor and provide ongoing management of (and patient education about) suspected anaphylaxis.  Offer two adrenaline injectors as an interim measure until they attend a specialist allergy appointment. It is important to explain how and when to use these.  Offer information about anaphylaxis (signs and symptoms, risk of biphasic reaction, what to do if it occurs, patient support groups and allergen avoidance).  Prognosis  With prompt treatment, the overall prognosis is good, with fatality rates estimated to be < 1%.  Approximately 20 deaths per year occur as a result of anaphylaxis; the risk of death is higher in patients with coexisting asthma.  Patients with previous reactions are at a higher risk of recurrence (allergy is lifelong).  Recurrence rates of anaphylaxis are also related to the risk of exposure to the allergen and the quality of management provided.  Other Resus council anaphylaxis algorithm:

DR. JAMIL Angioedema Angioedema is subdermal, subcutaneous or submucosal tissue inflammation that can occur with or without urticaria.  Overview Key Facts  Angioedema is subdermal, subcutaneous or submucosal tissue inflammation that can occur with or without urticaria.  It can cause life-threatening upper airway obstruction.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  The most common locations are the eyes and mouth.  The cause determines the classification, associated clinical features, management and prognosis.  If quickly progressing, the treatment is intravenous (IV) or intramuscular (IM) chlorphenamine plus hydrocortisone plus hospital admission.  Prognosis depends on whether there is a treatable secondary cause. Epidemiology  Lifetime prevalence approximately 10%.  The most common cause is idiopathic.

DR. JAMIL Aetiology  The aetiology of angioedema influences its classification: Type Detail  Allergic Common triggers:  food (eg nuts, dairy, eggs, fish)  drugs (eg penicillin, vaccines, NSAIDs)  insect bites  latex  radiology contrast Adverse drug reaction (non-allergic)  Most common is from ACE inhibitors; most cases seen in African–Caribbean patients Hereditary (aka ‘HAE’ hereditary angioedema) Caused by many possibilities Most common inherited cause is from mutations of the SERPING1 gene which encodes C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH); this is inherited by autosomal dominance There are two main mutations that occur:  I – low levels C1-INH  II – impaired C1-INH function  Idiopathic  Possible link to autoimmunity  Acquired C1-INH deficiency  Often secondary to connective tissue disorders (eg lupus) or lymphoma are seen Pathophysiology  Similar pathophysiological processes in urticaria and angioedema:  angioedema is a process of oedema below the dermis (skin/mucosa)  urticaria is a process of oedema occurring above the dermis.  Histamine (released during the complement cascade) and bradykinin (released from tissue damage) are key proinflammatory factors involved in the development of angioedema.  C1-INH is a protein C1 inhibitor, coded for by the SERPING1 gene, of which abnormalities are inherited in an autosomal dominant nature. Problems with C1-INH disrupt the physiological inhibition of the complement cascade.  ACE inhibitors (the most common cause of non-allergy, drugrelated angioedema) increase bradykinin by inhibiting its degradation (causing arteriole dilatation).  The difference in whether the angioedema is histamine or bradykinin mediated can be seen in some clinical features. Histamine-led processes tend to also cause urticaria and the swelling tends to be more superficial. If a bradykinin increase

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI is the main factor, normally there is neither urticaria nor itching as the dermis is less involved.  Clinical Presentation  Angioedema co-exists with urticaria in approximately 40–85% of cases.  Indicators of potential upper airway compromise – worsening angioedema, shortness of breath or ‘panic’.  Chronic and recurrent forms might be preceded by an infection or stress.  Main features of angioedema:  red or skin-coloured swelling  non-pitting  painful  tender to touch  not normally itchy  common sites:  lips  tongue  oropharynx  genitals  periorbital region. Urticaria  Itchy, white papule/plaque surrounded by erythema.  The ‘weals’ may join-up. Presentation factors by angioedema type  Allergic Likely acute onset to allergen trigger Urticaria present Swelling more superficial  Adverse drug reaction History of ACE-inhibitor use Delayed onset, after medication start Urticaria not present  Hereditary angioedema (HAE) Can be serious as often involves laryngeal oedema When GI mucosa affected – abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea Urticaria not normally present  Idiopathic Chronic, relapsing in nature May have urticaria or not

DR. JAMIL  Acquired C1-INH deficiency GI mucosa involved – abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea Known lymphoma or connective tissue disorder  Acquired angioedema secondary to lymphoma affecting the upper lip and face:  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  anaphylaxis  other causes of ‘oedema related’ airway compromise, eg epiglottitis  similar skin lesion appearance may exist in conditions such as lymphoedema, erythema multiforme, contact dermatitis and cellulitis  similar abdominal symptoms from another cause, eg ‘food poisoning’.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is normally based on clinical history and examination.  Key to physical examination:  airway assessment  extent of oedema  full skin inspection for weals/urticaria.  Key points of clinical history:  urticaria coexistence

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  past episodes  trigger assessment (including onset time from exposure)  family history  associated autoimmune disease  previous anaphylaxis  GI symptoms.  Response to antihistamine medication may aid assessment into the cause of the angioedema.  Investigations are not essential but might help determine cause and categorisation.  Investigations might include:  bloods, eg full blood count (FBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), auto-antibodies  urinalysis  allergy testing, eg skin-prick testing  for hereditary angioedema (HAE) – first, the C4 level is measured and if low the C1-INH level is measured  skin biopsy to confirm diagnosis and cause.  Management  Treatment depends on the cause, duration and frequency of the angioedema.  Mild symptoms may not need treatment.  There is a clear difference in treatment choice depending on whether the process causing the angioedema is bradykinin or histamine/mast-cell mediated. Likely to respond to  Antihistamines  Glucocorticoids HAE (bradykinin and histamine) ✗ ✗ Allergic (histamine) ✓ ✓ ACE-inhibitor induced (bradykinin) ✗ ✗ Non-pharmacological  Patient information is especially important, including information about the risk of airway compromise and when/how to seek help.  If there are concerns that anaphylaxis or airway compromise may occur, such as via allergic causes, consider supplying the patient with an ‘EpiPen’ or other emergency treatment.

DR. JAMIL  Consider advising trigger avoidance.  Referral to a dermatologist/immunologist; especially if cause unknown or allergen difficult to identify.  Airway compromise should be a concern if angioedema is rapidly progressing. Treatment is supportive with oxygen, venous access and early anaesthetic/intensivist involvement. Pharmacological  If the angioedema is quickly developing, but without anaphylaxis:  IV/IM chlorphenamine + hydrocortisone + admission.  If C1-INH is not an aetiological factor, medications often include:  non-sedating antihistamines (for even up to six weeks)  NSAIDs.  If not helping, treatments like those for HAE, eg tranexamic acid or a short course of oral corticosteroids (eg standard dosing of prednisolone 40 mg OD for seven days). Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Angioedema is life-threatening if it impacts airway patency. In the United Kingdom, 2008, it caused the deaths of five people.  It has a big impact on life if it is recurrent and has occurred over a long period of time.  Prognosis may depend on whether there is a treatable secondary cause.  With angioedema caused by ACE inhibitors, episodes may occur long after drug cessation.  Other  Anaphylaxis is a generalised, systemic hypersensitivity response causing, airway, breathing and circulatory difficulties. It is often combined with changes such as angioedema and urticaria. Anticoagulant Overdose Anticoagulant overdose is a serious medical emergency that can lead to excessive bleeding and is typically managed with specific reversal agents to counteract the effects of the anticoagulant medication. Pathophysiology Overdose: tricyclic antidepressants Pharmacology  TCAs are absorbed quickly into the digestive tract and are metabolised in the liver (first pass) relying on CYP450.  They are renally excreted.  They are protein-bound, they have a long half-life, > 24 hours (eg amitriptyline approximately 31–46 hours).  TCAs inhibit neuronal noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake. They can block sodium channels and histamine/cholinergic muscarinic receptors. They also act as antagonists on alpha-1 receptors.  TCAs are also sometimes called MARIs (monoamine reuptake inhibitors) with the same peripheral antimuscarinic effects of this class.  GI absorption may decrease with overdose due to their antimuscarinic effect.  The drug levels may further increase in respiratory or metabolic acidosis resulting from an overdose, as the acid will unbind the TCA from protein.  Possible causes of acidosis from overdose are due to respiratory depression and seizures or tissue hypoperfusion increasing lactate.  The more serious complications of overdose are cardiac. This is thought to be due to massive electrolyte changes.  Postural hypotension in overdose due to TCA antagonistic effect on alpha-1 receptors decreasing peripheral vascular resistance and myocardial contraction ability.  Neurological symptoms and drowsiness resulting from overdose could be due to a toxic increase in neurotransmitters, sodium channel blockade and antimuscarinic effect of TCAs.  Drowsiness also can be due to histamine blockade.  As with all overdose cases, individual pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic factors may play a role into why some people have more serious consequences than others at the same dose.

Anti-Emetics Nausea is an unpleasant sensation of the need to vomit, often accompanied by autonomic symptoms (pallor, cold sweat, salivation, tachycardia).  Overview Key Facts  Nausea is an unpleasant sensation of the need to vomit, often accompanied by autonomic symptoms (pallor, cold sweat, salivation, tachycardia).  Vomiting is the forceful ejection of stomach contents through the mouth.  People may experience nausea for a number of reasons including fear/anxiety, pain, systemic upset, metabolic disruption, alcohol intake, motion sickness, gastrointestinal irritation/stretch or raised intracranial pressure.  Nausea and vomiting are controlled by the chemoreceptor trigger zone and the vomiting centre within the brain/brainstem.  The features or pattern of nausea and vomiting can be useful in determining the cause.  Anti-emetic medication should be considered if symptoms are distressing or causing complications and conservative measures have failed or are inappropriate. Epidemiology  Nausea and vomiting are said to occur in:  43% of people with AIDS  30% of people with end-stage renal disease

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  17% with advanced heart disease  50–70% of people with advanced cancer  up to 70% of patients approaching the end of life  up to 80% of pregnant women; around 35% of these women have clinically significant symptoms. Aetiology  People may feel nauseous or vomit for a number of reasons including:  fear  pain  systemic infection  motion sickness/middle ear issues  alcohol intake  gastroenteritis/gastritis  pregnancy  post-operatively.  Palliative care patients may experience nausea and/or vomiting specifically including:  bowel dilatation due to obstruction and/or constipation  liver capsule stretch from metastatic disease. Pathophysiology  Nausea is an unpleasant sensation of the need to vomit, often accompanied by autonomic symptoms (pallor, cold sweat, salivation, tachycardia).  Vomiting is the forceful ejection of stomach contents through the mouth – caused by contraction of the diaphragm and abdominal muscles alongside relaxation of the stomach, oesophageal sphincter and pylorus (reverse peristalsis).  Vomiting may be triggered by:  chemoreceptor trigger zone  vomiting centre (in the brainstem – co-ordinates vomiting process). Causes Mechanisms Leading to Nausea and Vomiting  Chemical:  drugs  metabolic  toxins  Cytotoxic drugs cause vagal receptor and vomiting centre stimulation  Chemicals/toxins stimulate receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone

Benzodiazepine Overdose Despite prescriptions of benzodiazepines by general practitioners (GPs) falling, increased use of illicitly manufactured benzodiazepines has increased the fatality rate in England in the last decade.  Overview Key Facts  Despite prescriptions of benzodiazepines by general practitioners (GPs) falling, increased use of illicitly manufactured benzodiazepines has increased the fatality rate in England in the last decade.  Benzodiazepines act as a central nervous system (CNS) depressant.  Benzodiazepines enhance the activity of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) on GABA-A receptors, which has an inhibitory effect on the CNS.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  If alcohol or other CNS depressants have also been ingested, toxicity is increased.  Flumazenil, the antidote for benzodiazepine toxicity, is a competitive antagonist at the GABA-A receptor.  Common signs and symptoms include drowsiness, dysarthria, ataxia and nystagmus.  Less common signs and symptoms include hypotension, bradycardia, coma, respiratory depression, rhabdomyolysis and hypothermia.  Diagnosis is usually based on the history and clinical examination findings.  Computed tomography (CT) head imaging is required in patients presenting with CNS depression of unknown cause.  Flumazenil is the antidote:  for patients who have taken benzodiazepines only and require mechanical ventilation  contraindicated if a patient has also taken medications that may cause seizures (such as tricyclic antidepressants)  use with caution in patients who have a history of head injury, convulsions, long-term benzodiazepine use (using flumazenil as an antidote may induce seizures due to sudden benzodiazepine withdrawal) or uncertainty as to whether a mixed overdose has been taken  should never be used as a diagnostic test in people with symptoms of CNS depression.  Activated charcoal may be given within one hour of toxic dose.  Treatment is otherwise supportive.  Fatalities caused by the use of benzodiazepines alone are uncommon and usually occur when other drugs or alcohol have also been consumed. Epidemiology  There were 5740 deaths related to benzodiazepines in England between 2006 and 2015. Of these, only 3.6% were caused by benzodiazepines alone.  Despite prescriptions of benzodiazepines by GPs falling, increased use of illicitly manufactured benzodiazepines has increased the fatality rate in England in the last decade.  Opioid use is commonly associated with benzodiazepine use and this combination results in an increased risk of fatal outcomes. Aetiology  Overdose with suicidal intent.  Accidental overdose, especially in patients with dependence on and tolerance to benzodiazepines.  Use of illicit benzodiazepine preparations.  Benzodiazepines may be mixed with other drugs, such as heroin.

JAMIL Pathophysiology  Benzodiazepines act as a CNS depressant.  Benzodiazepines enhance the activity of GABA on GABA-A receptors, which has an inhibitory effect on the CNS.  The GABA-A receptor is a ligand-gated chloride-selective ion channel and benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators, amplifying the effects of GABA on the receptors.  If alcohol or other CNS depressants have also been ingested, toxicity is increased.  Flumazenil, the antidote for benzodiazepine toxicity (which should only be used in specific circumstances), is a competitive antagonist at the GABA-A receptor.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms are rarely life-threatening if benzodiazepines are taken alone. If alcohol or other CNS depressants have also been ingested, toxicity is increased.  Common signs include:  drowsiness  dysarthria  ataxia  nystagmus.  Less common signs include:  hypotension  bradycardia  coma (usually short and self-limiting, but may be prolonged in older patients)  respiratory depression (more common if underlying chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)  rhabdomyolysis  hypothermia.  If benzodiazepines have been injected intra-arterially, this may lead to limb ischaemia.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  alcohol intoxication  stroke  opiate toxicity  barbiturate overdose  ethylene glycol poisoning  encephalitis.

JAMIL Beta-Blocker Overdose Beta-blocker overdose is a potentially life-threatening condition that can result in symptoms such as low blood pressure, slowed heart rate, and cardiac complications, requiring immediate medical intervention and supportive care.  Overview Key Facts  Beta-blockers are competitive inhibitors of catecholamines.  Beta-blockers may be either selective (target beta 1 receptors) or non-selective (target beta 1 and beta 2 receptors).  Beta-receptor inhibition results in decreased production of intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).  Some beta-blockers, such as propranolol and labetalol, have ‘membrane stabilising effects’; they also inhibit cardiac myocyte sodium channels, prolonging QRS duration and impairing cardiac conduction.  Symptoms and signs of beta-blocker overdose include bradycardia, hypotension, prolonged QT or widened QRS (may lead to ventricular tachyarrhythmias), central nervous system (CNS) depression, hypoglycaemia, respiratory depression and bronchospasm.  Hydrophilic beta-blockers such as atenolol and bisoprolol are less likely to cross the blood-brain barrier and cause neurological symptoms than highly lipid-soluble beta-blockers such as propranolol.  Calcium-channel blocker overdose is the main differential but usually presents with hyperglycaemia rather than hypoglycaemia.  The diagnosis is clinical; beta-blocker overdose should be considered in all patients presenting with hypotension, bradycardia and/or hypoglycaemia.  Patients usually require ICU-level care and treatment includes:  gastric lavage if presentation is within 1 hour of a large overdose  intravenous (IV) glucagon (for severe hypotension and cardiogenic shock)  IV sodium bicarbonate (if wide QRS or hypotension unresponsive to fluids)  atropine for symptomatic bradycardia  high-dose insulin (with dextrose) to increase myocardial contractility  fluid resuscitation  treat other symptoms as necessary depending on clinical presentation.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  In the event of cardiac arrest, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should continue for at least 1 hour as a good neurological outcome is still possible.  Prognosis is worse in older patients and those with underlying cardiorespiratory disease. Epidemiology  Propranolol is often prescribed to patients with migraines, anxiety or depression who are at increased risk of overdose.  There was a 33% increase in deaths caused by propranolol overdose in the United Kingdom (UK) between 2012 and 2017, with 52 deaths occurring in 2017. Pathophysiology  Beta-blockers are competitive inhibitors of catecholamines.  Beta 1 receptors:  predominantly found in the heart, increasing heart rate and contractility  also induce renin release from the kidneys, leading to increased blood pressure.  Beta 2 receptors:  relaxation of smooth muscles (for example, beta 2 agonists such as salbutamol cause relaxation of smooth muscle in the airways resulting in bronchodilatation)  stimulate glycogenolysis.  Beta-receptor inhibition results in decreased production of intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).  Some beta-blockers are ‘cardioselective’ and more specific for beta 1 receptors (atenolol, bisoprolol, metoprolol), causing a reduction in heart rate, blood pressure and myocardial oxygen demand.  Some beta-blockers are ‘non-selective’ and act on beta 1 and beta 2 receptors (propranolol, sotalol and labetalol), causing cardiac effects, inhibiting relaxation of smooth muscles and inhibiting glycogenolysis causing hypoglycaemia.  Some beta-blockers, such as propranolol and labetalol, have ‘membrane stabilising effects’; they also inhibit cardiac myocyte sodium channels, prolonging QRS duration and impairing cardiac conduction.  Glucagon, used in the treatment of severe beta-blocker overdose, produces an increase in heart rate and blood pressure by bypassing blocked beta receptors and activating adenylyl cyclase. This promotes the formation of cyclic AMP from ATP. Cyclic AMP exerts a direct stimulant effect on the heart.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms include:  bradycardia  hypotension:

DR. JAMIL  severe cardiovascular compromise is more common in older patients and those with underlying ischaemic heart disease.  prolonged QT interval (usually sotalol) or widened QRS (usually propranolol) leading to ventricular tachyarrhythmias  neurological symptoms:  drowsiness  confusion  seizures  hallucinations  coma.  hypoglycaemia  respiratory depression  bronchospasm.  Hydrophilic beta-blockers such as atenolol and bisoprolol are less likely to cross the blood-brain barrier and cause neurological symptoms than highly lipid-soluble beta-blockers like propranolol.  Symptoms may vary between different beta-blockers.  The half-lives of different beta-blockers also vary widely, so it is important to establish exactly which beta-blocker has been taken.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  calcium-channel blocker toxicity:  usually presents with hyperglycaemia as opposed to hypoglycaemia or euglycaemia seen in beta-blocker overdose  carbamazepine toxicity  digoxin toxicity  clonidine toxicity  cocaine toxicity  meningitis  torsade de pointes.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is clinical.  Beta-blocker overdose should be considered in patients presenting with hypotension, bradycardia and/or hypoglycaemia.  It may also present with widened QRS, long QT or ventricular tachyarrhythmias.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Investigations should include:  serial 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG)  bloods for full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, magnesium, calcium, creatine kinase and troponin (to look for myocardial ischaemia).  A full toxicology screen should be performed.  Management  Patients usually require ICU-level care.  ABCDE assessment (early intubation may be required).  Consider activated charcoal if patient presents within 1 hour of a large overdose.  IV sodium bicarbonate if:  QRS >120 ms (high risk of dangerous tachyarrhythmias)  hypotension not responsive to fluids.  Correct electrolyte abnormalities as necessary.  Serial ECGs should be performed.  Fluid resuscitation:  may require inotropes or vasopressors to maintain blood pressure.  Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia:  may also require dobutamine, isoprenaline or temporary pacing.  IV glucagon can be used in cases refractory to fluid resuscitation and atropine.  High-dose insulin:  in severe toxicity, may increase myocardial contractility  should be given with dextrose and glucose, and potassium should be closely monitored.  Treat seizures, agitation or delirium as necessary.  Bronchospasm may be treated with nebulised bronchodilators and steroids.  Prognosis  In the event of cardiac arrest, CPR should continue for at least 1 hour as a good neurological outcome is still possible.  Prognosis is worse in older patients and those with underlying cardiorespiratory disease.

DR. JAMIL Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Carbon monoxide is produced by the incomplete combustion of fuels when insufficient oxygen is present. It is colourless, tasteless and odourless.  Overview Key Facts  Carbon monoxide is produced by the incomplete combustion of fuels when insufficient oxygen is present. It is colourless, tasteless and odourless.  There are approximately 40 deaths per year in England and Wales due to carbon monoxide poisoning.  Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin with approximately 240 times the affinity of oxygen, reducing the capacity of blood to carry oxygen, leading to tissue hypoxia.  Chronic exposure to low levels of carbon monoxide may produce flu-like symptoms and is often misdiagnosed.  Acute exposure may initially cause non-specific flu-like symptoms and then progress to neuropsychiatric symptoms.  Onset of neuropsychiatric symptoms may be delayed for as long as 40 days.  The classic ‘cherry red’ skin colour is a sign of extremely severe poisoning and rarely seen in practice.  Diagnosis should include a thorough history of possible sources of exposure and a full neurological examination.  A blood gas sample should be taken for carboxyhaemoglobin concentration and may also show metabolic acidosis.  Carbon monoxide pulse oximetry and carbon monoxide breath analysis may also be used.  Management should involve an ABCDE approach. The main treatment is high-flow oxygen and supportive treatment for symptoms.  Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is not routinely recommended in the United Kingdom (UK).  10–15% of people with severe poisoning may develop longterm complications, particularly neurological sequelae. Epidemiology  There are approximately 200–250 hospital admissions and 40 deaths per year in England and Wales as a result of carbon monoxide poisoning.  The actual incidence is probably much higher as mild poisoning can cause non-specific symptoms and maybe unrecognised or misdiagnosed.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI Aetiology  Carbon monoxide is produced by the incomplete combustion of fuels when insufficient oxygen is present. It is colourless, tasteless and odourless.  Mechanisms of poisoning include:  a car engine is run in a garage with inadequate ventilation  a fire is lit with a blocked chimney  a gas oven is used for heating  a barbeque is lit inside  inhalation from a house fire.  At-risk groups include:  children: they are more sensitive to harmful effects  older people: they are less able to physiologically compensate for hypoxia  pregnant women and fetus: a fetus has a higher affinity for carbon monoxide and also takes longer to eliminate it; maternal exposure may cause fetal or neonatal death, pre-term birth, neurological effects, congenital malformations and sudden infant death  people with underlying health conditions – particularly anaemia (where oxygen-carrying capacity is already reduced) and cardiovascular disease (as the cardiovascular system has a high oxygen demand and is particularly sensitive to hypoxia). Pathophysiology  Carbon monoxide forms carboxyhaemoglobin when it binds to haemoglobin.  Carboxyhaemoglobin takes a few hours to dissociate from haemoglobin.  Carbon monoxide exposure is particularly dangerous because it binds to haemoglobin with approximately 240 times the affinity of oxygen, reducing the capacity of blood to carry oxygen.  The result is an inadequate supply of oxygen to tissues, which causes tissue hypoxia.  Carbon monoxide dissolves in plasma and causes direct tissue injury.  Normal concentration of carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood is:  1–2% in non-smokers  5–10% in smokers.  Severe symptoms may be seen with concentrations >20%.  Clinical Presentation  Chronic exposure to low levels of carbon monoxide may produce flu-like symptoms and is often misdiagnosed.

DR. JAMIL  Acute exposure may initially cause non-specific flu-like symptoms, including:  headache  nausea and vomiting  weakness  tachypnoea.  These symptoms may be followed by predominantly neurological symptoms, including:  confusion  dizziness  ataxia  syncope  agitation  seizures  low Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score  onset of neuropsychiatric symptoms (such as memory loss, personality change and parkinsonism) may be delayed after exposure.  Other symptoms include:  respiratory failure  myocardial ischaemia  hypotension  cerebral oedema (in severe cases).  The classic ‘cherry red’ skin colour is a sign of extremely severe poisoning and rarely seen in practice.  Differential Diagnosis  It may mimic any condition that presents with flu-like symptoms, so is often misdiagnosed.  It is sometimes mistaken for cyanide poisoning.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is often missed as symptoms can be non-specific.  History should include the following questions:  do other people in the household also have symptoms?  do symptoms improve when out of the house?  are heating and cooking appliances well-maintained?  is a carbon monoxide alarm installed?  Examination:  full neurological examination, including fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhages in patients who have lost consciousness

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  cognitive assessment (eg mini-mental state examination).  Blood gas sample for carboxyhaemoglobin concentration – may also show metabolic acidosis.  Carbon monoxide pulse oximetry.  Breath analyser:  measure carbon monoxide concentration (and convert to carboxyhaemoglobin concentration)  used in smoking cessation clinics  may produce a normal reading if the patient has been away from the source of carbon monoxide for a period of time  interpretation in smokers is difficult as carbon monoxide will be raised.  Management  ABCDE assessment.  Administer high-flow oxygen (consider high-flow nasal cannulae which can deliver oxygen at up to 60 l/min).  Bloods should be taken for full blood count, urea and electrolytes, troponin, creatine kinase and blood gas analysis.  12-Lead electrocardiogram (ECG) (treating accordingly if arrhythmias, bradycardia or tachycardia).  Intravenous fluids and management of hypotension; may need ICU-level care (vasopressors and inotropes).  May require sodium bicarbonate if metabolic acidosis persists despite fluid resuscitation and oxygen therapy.  Further management should be centred around the patient’s clinical condition (eg may need treatment for cerebral oedema or seizures).  Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) is not routinely recommended in the UK.  Prognosis  Between 10–15% of people with severe poisoning may develop long-term complications, particularly neurological sequelae such as memory problems and parkinsonism.  The onset of complications is more common in people aged over 40 years and may be delayed for up to 40 days. Chemotherapy Chemotherapeutic drugs are drugs used to treat cancer by affecting specific mechanisms underlying cell proliferation.

DR. JAMIL  Overview Key Facts  Chemotherapeutic drugs are drugs used to treat cancer by affecting specific mechanisms underlying cell proliferation.  Chemotherapy of cancer is complex and prescribing should be confined to oncology specialists.  Chemotherapeutic agents are broadly classified into two major types:  cycle-specific: they are effective throughout the cell cycle  phase-specific: they are effective during a part of the cell cycle.  They can be used in a variety of settings:  primary treatment, for example for lymphoma  neoadjuvant treatment, eg to reduce tumour bulk before surgery (especially colorectal)  adjuvant therapy, which is usually for the prevention of recurrence (commonly colorectal and breast)  palliation, which is usually in advanced disease  maintenance treatment, eg in leukaemia.  Chemotherapeutic drugs include:  alkylating agents  antimetabolites Name of agent Method of action Com Alkylating agent Classic alkylating agents form covalent bonds with biomolecules such as proteins and hence inactivate enzymes involved in DNA production and protein synthesis  Non-classic alkylating agents interrupt normal DNA functions by causing cross-linkage of DNA strands  Cisplatin for testicular, ovarian, lung and bladder cancers  Antimetabolites  Interfere with purine or pyrimidine synthesis and therefore, DNA synthesis   5-Fluorouracil is commonly used for colon cancer under the FOLFOX regimen  Palmar plantar syndrome and cardiotoxicity

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  antibiotics  vinca alkaloids  taxanes  topoisomerase inhibitors.  Delivery of chemotherapy takes many shapes and forms, with doses based on body surface area and affected primarily by hepatic metabolism and renal excretion.  Commonly, chemotherapy is given intravenously or orally, however certain cancers may lend themselves to strategies such as intravesical (eg for TCC of the bladder) or intra-arterial (eg for HCC), amongst other methods.  Side effects are common and can be grouped into acute (related to dose) and chronic (related to the duration of the treatment).  General side effects relate to the nature of its impact on cell proliferation, thereby being toxic to normally proliferating cells (ie bone marrow, GI epithelium, hair follicles).  This leads to the common side effects of chemotherapy including myelosuppression (neutropenia and anaemia), nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and hair loss.  Most chemotherapeutics are teratogenic.  It is possible that tumours may eventually become resistant to individual chemotherapeutic agents. mmon agents and uses Side effects Cyclophosphamide for lung, breast and ovarian cancers Haemorrhagic cystitis, pulmonary interstitial fibrosis Kidney failure, ototoxicity, and peripheral neuropathy Methotrexate for breast and lung cancer  Hepatic failure, pulmonary fibrosis

DR. JAMIL Antibiotics  Anthracycline antibiotics have complex, not fully understood mechanisms, but are thought to intercalate into DNA strands and produce free radicals   Non-anthracycline antibiotics act by intercalation, free radical production, and/or alkylation  Bleomycin for testicular and H&N cancers   Mitomycin C for breast, bladder, pancreatic and gastric cancer  Kidney failure, stomatitis, rash, alopecia Vinca alkaloids Act by inhibiting mitosis, by preventing spindle formation They are M-phase specific  Taxanes  Act by inhibiting mitosis through stabilisation of microtubules  Topoisomerase inhibitors  Inhibit topoisomerase I, which is an enzyme involved in DNA replication  Cyanide Poisoning  Overview Key Facts  Hydrogen cyanide may be found in fumes from building fires, cigarettes, plastic combustion and car exhausts.  It is also produced in the production of plastic, paint and nylon and in the processes of ore extraction, electroplating, printing, dying and photograph development.  Smoking is considered to be the greatest source of exposure to hydrogen cyanide for the general population.  Cyanide inhibits oxidative phosphorylation disrupting aerobic metabolism and resulting in cellular hypoxia, lactic acidosis and a switch from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism.  The central nervous system (CNS) is particularly severely affected due to a high oxygen requirement and limited utilisation of anaerobic respiration.  Cherry red skin and ‘bitter almond’ odour on a patient’s breath are often named as characteristic features but are actually not commonly seen.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI Doxorubicin for breast, small cell lung cancer, and bladder cancer  Congestive cardiac failure amongst general chemotherapy side effects Pneumonitis and pulmonary fibrosis, rash Vincristine for lymphoma, neuroblastoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma  Highly vesicant, neuropathy and bronchospasm Paclitaxel for ovarian, lung and breast cancers  Sudden total alopecia, myalgia, and peripheral neuropathy Irinotecan for colorectal cancer  Cholinergic syndrome and profuse, life-limiting diarrhoea  Symptoms of mild poisoning include nausea, dizziness, hyperventilation and drowsiness.  Moderate poisoning may cause seizures, vomiting, hypotension and a reduced level of consciousness.  Severe poisoning may lead to coma, respiratory failure, cardiovascular compromise, cyanosis and cause fixed dilated pupils.  Features of chronic exposure to cyanide are predominantly neurological and neuropsychiatric, including parkinsonian-type symptoms resulting from CNS demyelination.  The main differential diagnosis is carbon monoxide poisoning, but patients usually recover on moving from the toxic environment and with high-flow oxygen and it is not usually associated with seizures.  Blood cyanide concentration will give a definitive diagnosis, but treatment should not be delayed if poisoning is suspected and the test is not immediately available.  Blood gases classically show a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap.  Treatment depends upon the severity of poisoning:  mild poisoning: intravenous (IV) sodium thiosulphate  moderate poisoning: IV hydroxocobalamin  severe poisoning: IV hydroxocobalamin and/or IV sodium thiosulphate.

DR. JAMIL  Gastric lavage may be considered if the patient presents within 1 hour of ingestion.  Treatment is otherwise supportive and involves oxygen therapy, management of hypotension and treatment of metabolic acidosis with sodium bicarbonate.  If dermal or eye exposure, the patient should be decontaminated and then treated for systemic toxicity as necessary.  Patients most commonly either recover completely or die from acute exposure. Long-term sequelae are rarely reported but may include parkinsonism, confusion and intellectual impairment. Epidemiology  Industry workers are at greater risk of exposure to hydrogen cyanide, although levels in industrial workplaces are closely monitored to protect employees.  Smoking is considered to be the greatest source of exposure to hydrogen cyanide for the general population.  Cyanide is highly toxic by ingestion, inhalation, and dermal and eye exposure. Aetiology  Hydrogen cyanide may be found in:  smoke from building fires or cigarettes  fumes from plastic combustion  car exhaust fumes  some foods when unprocessed or ground:  apricot kernels  wild ‘bitter’ almond kernels  fumigants  metal cleaning products.  Hydrogen cyanide is also used in the production of plastic, paint and nylon and in the processes of ore extraction, electroplating, printing, dying and photograph development. Pathophysiology  Cyanide inhibits oxidative phosphorylation by binding to the enzyme cytochrome C oxidase and disrupting aerobic metabolism and the production of ATP.  This results in:  cellular hypoxia  a switch from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism  lactic acidosis.  The CNS is particularly severely affected due to a high oxygen requirement and limited utilisation of anaerobic respiration.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation Cherry red skin and ‘bitter almond’ odour on a patient’s breath are often named as characteristic features but are actually not commonly seen.  Acute Exposure Severity of Poisoning Signs and Symptoms Mild:  Lactate < 10 mmol/l  Blood cyanide concentration < 1 mg/l  Nausea  Dizziness  Hyperventilation  Drowsiness Moderate:  Lactate 10–15 mmol/l  Blood cyanide concentration 1–3 mg/l  Reduced Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score  Vomiting  Seizures  Hypotension Severe:  Lactate 15 mmol/l  Blood cyanide concentration > 3 mg/l  Coma  Cardiovascular compromise  Respiratory failure  Fixed dilated pupils  Cyanosis  Myocardial ischaemia  Cardiac arrhythmias  Pulmonary oedema  Chronic Exposure  Features of chronic exposure to cyanide are predominantly neurological and neuropsychiatric.  Patients may develop demyelinating lesions in the brain which may present with parkinsonian-type symptoms.  Optic neuropathy has also been reported.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  carbon monoxide poisoning:  patients improve rapidly when removed from their environment and treated with high-flow oxygen  seizures are rare, as opposed to cyanide poisoning  carbon monoxide does not affect pupillary response.  salicylate overdose.  organophosphate poisoning.

DR. JAMIL  tricyclic antidepressant overdose.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood cyanide concentration:  gives a definitive diagnosis, but not widely or rapidly available  treatment should not be delayed while awaiting test results if there is clinical suspicion of cyanide poisoning.  Venous or arterial blood gas:  raised lactate (usually > 7 mmol/l)  metabolic acidosis  raised anion gap.  Management  ABCDE assessment.  Give oxygen.  Consider gastric lavage within 1 hour of ingestion in moderate or severe toxicity; activated charcoal is an alternative if gastric lavage is not possible.  Treatment depends upon the severity of poisoning:  mild poisoning: IV sodium thiosulphate  moderate poisoning: IV hydroxocobalamin  severe poisoning: IV hydroxocobalamin and/or IV sodium thiosulphate.  IV fluids: may require vasopressors or inotropes if resistant hypotension.  Metabolic acidosis that persists despite fluids and correction of hypoxia can be treated with IV sodium bicarbonate.  If dermal or eye exposure, the patient should be decontaminated and then treated for systemic toxicity as necessary.  Prognosis  Rapid treatment is essential, as exposure to cyanide can lead to death within minutes to hours.  Patients most commonly either recover completely or die from acute exposure. Long-term sequelae are rarely reported but may include parkinsonism, confusion and intellectual impairment. Digoxin Overdose Digoxin is indicated for the treatment of mild-to-moderate heart failure and for rate control in atrial fibrillation or flutter.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Digoxin is indicated for the treatment of mild-to-moderate heart failure and for rate control in atrial fibrillation or flutter.  Overdose can be acute, chronic, intentional or accidental.  Patients aged > 55 years are more commonly affected but toxicity can occur in older and younger patients.  It most commonly presents with gastrointestinal (nausea and vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain) or central nervous system (lethargy, confusion) features.  Toxicity can occur even at normal serum levels (0.5–0.9 ng/ml); therefore the diagnosis is made on clinical and electrocardiogram (ECG) findings.  Arrhythmia is the most dangerous manifestation of digoxin toxicity.  Digoxin-specific antibody (Fab) fragments are the most effective and safest treatment of digoxin toxicity.  There are usually no long-term complications for those patients treated appropriately, provided they do not develop end-organ hypoperfusion-related damage prior to treatment. Epidemiology  Digoxin use, and therefore toxicity, is decreasing due to its inferiority to other heart failure medications.  Patients age > 55 years are more commonly affected but toxicity can occur in older and younger patients. Aetiology  Acute:  suicide attempt  medication dosing error  poisoning with malicious intent.  Chronic:  chronic overmedication of digoxin  decreased renal clearance  other conditions increasing susceptibility to digoxin toxicity – hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia

DR. JAMIL  P-glycoprotein inhibition via drugs such as verapamil, diltiazem, amiodarone, ketoconazole, erythromycin.  Digoxin is dependent on P-glycoprotein for elimination and therefore, anything that inhibits this increases the risk of accumulation of digoxin. Pathophysiology  Digoxin directly inhibits the Na+/K+ATPase pump, increasing intracellular sodium and reducing intracellular potassium.  This rise in sodium reduces the activity of the Na+–Ca2+ exchanger that normally extrudes calcium from inside the cells.  This leads to the positive ionotropic action and increased heart contractility.  Other electrolyte disturbances, such as abnormal sodium, potassium and magnesium levels, increase this toxicity by further depressing the Na+/K+-ATPase pump.  Digoxin also increases vagal tone, resulting in decreased conduction through the sinoatrial node (SAN) and atrioventricular node (AVN).  The adverse effects of digoxin are often due to its narrow therapeutic window.  Clinical Presentation  The clinical features of digoxin overdose can be classified into cardiac and non-cardiac features.  Cardiac:  SA and AV block  premature ventricular contractions (bigeminy and trigeminy on ECG)  PR prolongation  ST depression.  Non-cardiac:  gastrointestinal:  nausea  vomiting  diarrhoea.  visual – blurred or yellow vision

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  central nervous system:  weakness  dizziness  confusion  apathy  malaise  headache  depression  psychosis.  haematological – thrombocytopenia and agranulocytosis  gynaecomastia (due to its oestrogenic activity).  Differential Diagnosis  Overdose of beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers and alpha agonists (such as clonidine) can present in a similar way to digoxin toxicity.  It is helpful to check capillary blood glucose as hyperglycaemia is a prominent feature of calcium channel blocker overdose and can help distinguish the presentation from alternative differentials.  Clonidine overdose tends to lead to greater central nervous system (CNS) and respiratory depression and miosis, than is seen with digoxin toxicity.  Other differentials might include sick sinus syndrome, hypothermia, hypothyroidism, myocardial infarction and hyperkalaemia from other causes.  Diagnosis/Investigation  If there is any clinical suspicion of toxicity, it is important to check serum digoxin levels.  Digoxin levels are only truly reflective after the distribution is complete (4–6 hours after the last dose) so a second sample may be needed.  An ECG and bloods for electrolytes and renal function should be done in such patients.  Take particular note of other medications that increase the serum digoxin level:  amiodarone  diltiazem  verapamil  trazodone  carvedilol  proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)  macrolides

DR. JAMIL  tetracycline  trimethoprim.  Digoxin toxicity is a clinical diagnosis that relies in part on ECG findings. Serum digoxin concentration is usually greater than the therapeutic range (0.5–0.9 ng/ml) but can be normal.  At therapeutic levels, the ECG typically shows PR prolongation and scooped ST segment.  In toxicity, typical ECG findings include increased automaticity (premature ventricular contractions), AV nodal blockade and slowed ventricular response.  Serum potassium level is a helpful marker of prognosis but also reflects the severity of digoxin toxicity.  Patients with hyperkalaemia are more at risk of digoxin toxicity and dysrhythmias. Acute digoxin toxicity can in itself cause hyperkalaemia by inhibition of Na+/K+-ATPase pump.  Note that routine monitoring of digoxin levels is not recommended.  Management  All patients with suspected digoxin toxicity should be assessed using the ABCDE approach.  The patient should be placed on cardiac monitoring immediately. Pharmacological  The treatment of any significant cardiac arrhythmia secondary to digoxin toxicity is digoxin-specific antibody (Fab) fragments. Such decisions are usual made in conjunction with a toxicologist.  When Fab fragments are not immediately available, symptomatic bradycardia can be treated with atropine and hypotension with intravenous fluid. Be cautious of fluid replacement in those with decompensated heart failure.  Fab fragments are highly effective and safe in the management of digoxin toxicity.  Fab fragments should not be given solely based upon serum digoxin levels, but rather directed by the presence of clinical manifestations described above.  It is recommended that Fab fragments be given to those patients who have:  life-threatening or haemodynamically unstable arrhythmia  hyperkalaemia  evidence of end-organ dysfunction from hypoperfusion.  The use of activated charcoal (AC) should be viewed as an adjunctive treatment and not a primary therapy. AC effectiveness relies on early presentation, and should ideally be administered within the first few hours of ingestion.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Electrolyte disturbances need correction. Exercise caution in the treatment of hyperkalaemia associated with digoxin toxicity – calcium gluconate can be fatal if administered in this setting, leading to the so-called ‘stone heart’.  Prognosis  In acute toxicity, the degree of hyperkalaemia correlates with mortality.  Those presenting with acute toxicity and have serum potassium ≥ 5.0 mmol/l, who remain untreated and/or undiagnosed, have a mortality rate of 50%.  There are no long-term complications of poisoning in patients treated appropriately for digoxin toxicity, as long as anoxic brain injury, myocardial infarction and terminal arrhythmias have not occurred prior to treatment.  Other  The National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommendation for the prescription of digoxin:  loading dose 250–750 μg once daily for seven days  a clinical response is usually seen within 1 week; therefore patients should be reviewed at seven days and their heart rate and pulse rate checked  the usual maintenance dose is 125–250 μg daily; this should be adjusted according to clinical response and also renal function  seek specialist advice for those who are elderly and have renal impairment; the dose will need reducing. Drug-Induced Liver Injury Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) can cause acute and chronic liver disease.  Overview Key Facts  Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) can cause acute and chronic liver disease.  DILI can be idiosyncratic (not predictable) or intrinsic (predictable dose-related hepatoxicity, eg paracetamol overdose).  Early diagnosis of DILI and removal of the offending agent is essential for the prevention of chronic liver disease or liver failure.  Pre-existing liver disorder and family history of liver disorder act as major risk factors in drug DILI.

DR. JAMIL  Side-effects associated with drugs also cause DILI and may require discontinuation after recognition.  The most common hepatotoxic drug is paracetamol. Epidemiology  Women are more susceptible to developing liver disorders such as hepatitis and are more prone to acute liver failure than males.  The most common hepatotoxicity is due to paracetamol overdose, ie 57%.  In the United Kingdom (UK) the frequency is 2.3–2.4 per 100 000. Aetiology  Acetaminophen.  Halothane-induced DILI usually occurs after multiple exposures (anaesthetic agent).  Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).  Isoniazid (antibacterial-drug-induced liver damage).  Penicillins and cephalosporins.  Sulfonamide.  Ketoconazole (antifungal).  Thiazolidinedione (oral hypoglycaemic).  Ezetimibe (lipid-lowering drug).  Herbal medicines (Kava root, antidepressant). Pathophysiology  DILI may be the result of direct toxic effect from the administered drug or its metabolite.  Injury may result from immune-mediated mechanisms.  A number of drugs are lipid-soluble and are processed in the liver and are excreted in bile or urine.  The first step of drug metabolism is:  phase I reaction and is catalysed by enzymes of the hepatic cytochrome p450 cytochrome system  intermediate bioactive agents produced in this step interact with cellular organelles (eg mitochondria) leading to hepatocyte damage and dysfunction.  DILI may result due from drug-induced inhibition of the mitochondrial respiratory system, which results in the proliferation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and depletion of ATP.  ROS proliferation, ATP depletion and the above-mentioned mitochondrial damage contribute a major part to induce hepatotoxicity.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation  Lethargy, malaise and nausea.  Lack of appetite.  Pruritus, in advanced liver damage.  Jaundice.  Abdominal pain, similar in nature to acute cholecystitis.  Increased levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), which reflect hepatocyte destruction.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses may include:  jaundice  acute cholecystitis  acute viral hepatitis  liver cancer  liver abscess  fatty liver  Wilson’s disease  hepatic cirrhosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  History regarding drug administration and the start of symptoms.  Drugs that are known to have liver toxicity usually evoke clinical features within hours to a few days.  Immune-mediated toxic effects may take weeks to manifest the toxic effects.  Ultrasound abdomen for liver texture and to exclude acute cholecystitis.  Alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) are measured by performing liver function tests.  Very high levels of paracetamol can elevate liver enzymes above 20 000–25 000 IU/l.  Computed tomography (CT) scan to exclude liver cancer, only if indicated on ultrasound.  Management Non-pharmacological  Monitoring in pre-existing cases of liver disorders.  The majority of cases of DILI are acute illnesses.

DR. JAMIL  The majority of cases do not require hospitalisation; cessation of hepatotoxic agent relieves the symptoms and the liver heals within a few weeks.  Patient education. Surgical  Very severe cases that lead to acute liver failure may require hepatic transplant.  Prognosis  Prognosis is generally very good if DILI is identified and the causative agent is stopped. Drug-Induced Rashes Drug eruptions occur after exposure to a drug.  Overview Key Facts  Drug eruptions occur after exposure to a drug.  These eruptions are on a spectrum of severity.  They result in response to an immunological mechanism.  Drug induced reactions include:  anaphylaxis and angioedema  urticaria  exanthem-like  fixed drug eruptions  drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)  acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP)  toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) and Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS).  Severe cutaneous adverse reactions include SJS/TENs and DRESS.  Exanthematous drug eruption is the most common type of eruption, usually characterised by a morbilliform or maculopapular eruption which may become confluent.  Erythema nodosum is where red, tender, round nodules develop on the shins and can be triggered by the oral contraceptive pill.

Dyskinesia And Dystonia Dystonia is a syndrome of sustained muscle contractions causing twisting and repetitive movements.  Overview Key Facts  Dystonia is a syndrome of sustained muscle contractions causing twisting and repetitive movements.  Dystonias can be congenital, acquired or idiopathic.  Dyskinesia is uncontrolled and involuntary movements of the face, arms, legs or trunk.  Dystonia and dyskinesia are movement disorders that commonly occur in Parkinson’s disease.  Diagnosis is mainly clinical. Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI Gynaecomastia Gynaecomastia is defined as an increase in male breast tissue.  Overview Key Facts  Gynaecomastia is defined as an increase in male breast tissue.  The causes of gynaecomastia can be broadly divided into physiological, pathological and pharmacological (3 Ps); however, in many patients, no sole cause is identified.  Management aims to reduce pain and improve cosmetic appearance.  Treatment is reassurance, especially if physiological, and removal of the precipitating cause, or treatment for other more serious aetiologies.  Direct treatment in non-resolution – androgen-modifying drugs or surgery (eg mastectomy or liposuction).  If gynaecomastia is due to increased male oestrogen, the patient has a resulting higher lifetime risk of breast cancer. Epidemiology  Epidemiological analysis depends on the cause of gynaecomastia:  approximately 50% of men have some degree of pubertal gynaecomastia  approximately 1 in 10 men are affected when using spironolactone. JAMIL Pathophysiology  The pathophysiology can be summarised by saying that gynaecomastia is caused by an imbalance between oestrogen and testosterone, with the latter being in relative or direct deficit.  Typical histology shows ductal proliferation and epithelial hyperplasia with potential inflammation, oedema and fibrosis.  Clinical Presentation  Gynaecomastia can be:  unilateral or bilateral, regardless of the cause  painful, or not  completely asymptomatic.  Examination findings – it is firm and extends from the nipple in a concentric manner.  Differential Diagnosis  Pseudo-gynaecomastia (due to adipose tissue alone).  Diagnosis/Investigation  The first step is to exclude male breast cancer (eg through examination and potential 2-week wait referral), followed by further assessment into the cause.  Examination of the chest area and potentially of the genitalia and axillae is needed.  Other examinations to consider – respiratory, abdominal and neurological.  Key clinical history – medications, recreational drug use, ‘red flags’ (ie for lung, brain and gastrointestinal cancer), other risk factors, any abnormality in sexual differentiation/secondary sexual characteristics.  Investigations to consider:  bloods – urea and electrolytes (U&Es), liver function tests (LFTs), thyroid function tests (TFTs), oestrogen/testosterone levels, luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), human chorionic gonadotrophin, sex hormone-binding globulin, prolactin, α-fetoprotein.

Surgical/other  Mastectomy or liposuction in the case of non-resolution and associated cosmetic concerns.  Prophylactic chest radiotherapy might be considered in those with prostate cancer due to the start of anti-androgen treatment.  Prognosis  Most cases of gynaecomastia are reversible by eradication of the causative factor, with a higher likelihood if the onset is recent.

JAMIL  Pubertal gynaecomastia is usually self-limiting within 0.5–1.5 years.  If gynaecomastia is due to increased male oestrogen, the patient has a resulting higher lifetime risk of breast cancer.  Other  ‘Mammogenesis’ (breast growth) is mainly stimulated by prolactin, oestrogen, progesterone and prolactin.  Physiological increase of aromatase (key in oestrogen production) occurs naturally with advancing age in men. Thus, increasing oestrogen levels, accompanied by possible gynaecomastia, as men age is normal.  Hyperprolactinaemia can result in gynecomastia and is often associated with hypogonadism. Aside from pregnancy being a physiological cause in women, it can also be present in newborns or in high-stress situations. Prolactin is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. It is mainly regulated by the dopamine that is produced by the hypothalamus. It stimulates lactation. The presence of prolactin inhibits hypothalamic gonadotropin hormone-releasing hormone (GnRH) secretion and the effects of luteinising hormone (LH) on the gonads, thus reducing testosterone levels.  Testosterone directly inhibits and oestrogen stimulates breast growth.  Dopamine antagonists (including many antipsychotics, eg chlorpromazine, sulpiride and flupentixol; spironolactone; opioids; and many anti-emetics, eg domperidone and metoclopramide) lead to prolactin increase by disrupting the inhibitory action of dopamine in the pituitary.  Hypothyroidism might cause increases in sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), which reduces the levels of bodily free testosterone.  Chronic liver disease is thought to cause gynaecomastia through reduced hepatic oestrogen removal, increases of SHBG in liver damage, or as a side-effect of using spironolactone diuretics in the management of the disease process. Immunosuppressive Drugs Immunosuppressive drugs suppress the immune system activity and are used in the management of autoimmune conditions, inflammatory diseases and in patients with organ transplants.  Overview Key Facts  Immunosuppressive drugs suppress the immune system activity and are used in the management of autoimmune conditions, inflammatory diseases and in patients with organ transplants.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Immunosuppression can increase the risk of severe infection and malignancy.  Therapeutic drug monitoring is required for some immunosuppressive drugs, eg tacrolimus.  Some of the autoimmune disorders managed with immunosuppressant agents include:  rheumatoid arthritis  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  Addison’s disease  Crohn’s disease  multiple sclerosis  Graves’ disease.  Immunosuppressive drugs used in organ transplantation are broadly categorised into – calcineurin inhibitors, antiproliferative agents, mTOR inhibitors and steroids. The mechanism of action (MOA) of these different drug classes  Calcineurin inhibitors:  these agents reduce immunity by reducing the production of IL-2 (interleukin-2) and T-cell proliferation as a result of inhibition of calcineurin when these agents bind to immunophilins, intracellular proteins.  examples include ciclosporin and tacrolimus.  Antiproliferative agents:  these drugs act by cytokine-induced T-lymphocyte cell proliferation and activation which achieves immunosuppression as a result  examples include mycophenolate mofetil, mycophenolate sodium and azathioprine.  mTOR inhibitors:  these inhibit antibody production; they bind to the immunophilin FK-binding protein-12 (FKBP-12) to create an immunosuppressive reaction cascade; as a result, cytokine-driven T-cell proliferation is suppressed resulting in overall immunosuppression  examples include sirolimus, everolimus, etc.  steroids:  these agents cause immunosuppression by sequestration of CD4+ T lymphocytes in the reticuloendothelial system and by inhibiting the transcription of cytokines  examples include prednisolone, budesonide, etc.

Iron Poisoning Iron toxicity is one of the leading causes of poisoning deaths in children younger than 6 years and can be taken as an intentional overdose in adults.  Overview Key Facts  Iron toxicity is one of the leading causes of poisoning deaths in children younger than 6 years and can be taken as an intentional overdose in adults.  Adult iron tablets may look like sweets so children sometimes ingest them in large quantities.  Cellular toxicity impairs oxidative phosphorylation and causes mitochondrial dysfunction leading to cellular death and anaerobic metabolism.  Common symptoms include vomiting, diarrhoea and upper and lower gastrointestinal bleeding.  Severe cases can lead to metabolic acidosis and multiorgan failure.  Diagnosis is made by visualisation of iron pills on X-ray and elevated serum iron levels.  Mainstay of treatment is iron-chelating therapy and fluid resuscitation.  Complications include gastric outlet obstruction and renal or liver failure.  Prognosis is good if therapy is initiated without delay. Epidemiology  Most common in the United Kingdom (UK) in children under 5 years and in young people aged between 15 and 20 years. Aetiology  In children, the risk of ingestion increases with the availability of iron-containing products, eg multivitamins.  Adult iron tablets may look like sweets so children sometimes ingest them in large quantities.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI Pathophysiology  Ingested iron can have corrosive effects on the gastrointestinal mucosa.  Cellular toxicity can also occur and impair oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial dysfunction causing cellular death and anaerobic metabolism.  Iron toxicity affects the liver largely, but can also affect the heart to cause myocardial siderosis if iron overload is chronic.  As excessive iron has both corrosive and cellular toxicity, it can often cause metabolic acidosis.  This happens as a result of hypoperfusion due to volume loss from vomiting/diarrhoea, vasodilatation and negative inotropic effects of iron, which all subsequently cause lactic acidosis.  Clinical Presentation Stages or phases of iron poisoning  Stage 1 or gastrointestinal phase  Occurs within 6 hours of exposure  Nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain  Upper and/or lower gastrointestinal bleeding  Hypovolaemia or shock  Stage 2 or latent phase  6–12 hours after ingestion  GI symptoms may resolve  Metabolic abnormalities predominate including hypotension, metabolic acidosis and coagulopathy  Stage 3 or shock and metabolic acidosis  Metabolic acidosis and cardiovascular symptoms including organ failure  CNS symptoms such as coma may also occur  Most deaths occur during stage 3 which can start from 6 hours all the way to 2 days post-ingestion  Stage 4 or hepatotoxicity  12–96 hours after iron ingestion  Elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin levels with coagulopathy  Hypoglycaemia as well as liver dysfunction  Stage 5 or bowel obstruction  2–8 weeks after iron ingestion  Presents with symptoms of gastric outlet obstruction due to scarring  Vomiting, abdominal pain

DR. JAMIL  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  other toxicities – paracetamol, alcohol, arsenic, mercury, salicylate, colchicine  diabetic ketoacidosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Serum iron levels above 500 μg/dl require aggressive management.  An abdominal X-ray may reveal radiopaque pills.  Glucose – elevated (hepatic dysfunction may cause hypoglycaemia in later stages).  Full blood count – anaemia from blood loss.  Liver function tests – hepatic dysfunction.  Renal profile – establish electrolyte abnormalities and acidosis.  Management  Mild gastrointestinal symptoms with serum concentration < 500 μg/dl ⇢ observe only.  Intravenous (IV) volume resuscitation.  IV deferoxamine ⇢ binds ferric iron ⇢ promotes urinary excretion ⇢ indications:  Severe symptoms – altered mental status, hemodynamic instability, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea.  Anion gap metabolic acidosis.  Serum iron concentration > 500 μg/dl.  Significant number of pills on radiograph.  Hemodialysis and liver transplant can be needed in severe cases that do not respond to therapy and develop renal and liver failure, respectively.  Prognosis  Severe toxicity can cause death.  Patients are unlikely to come to harm if they are asymptomatic 6 hours post-ingestion.  Other  Complications:  hepatic necrosis  coagulopathy  coma  cardiogenic shock  gastrointestinal perforation or obstruction.

JAMIL  Acute symptoms may resolve with interventions, but neurological and cardiovascular toxicities are often irreversible.  Long-term monitoring required as lead can be present in bone for many years after exposure. Epidemiology  Major risk to children (especially those aged 18–24 months) in developed countries is from inhalation of lead-based paints and soil and dust that has been contaminated with lead-based paints.  In adults, the exposure largely is occupation from battery manufacturing, radiator repairs or exposure to old lead paint.  Increased risk in patients who live in old housing with poorly maintained paint surfaces. Aetiology  Inhalation or ingestion of lead particles leads to toxicity.  Sources of exposure include:  deteriorating paint surfaces  occupational exposure, eg heavy construction, battery production  bullet firing ranges  folk medications, eg azarcon, greta  lead-contaminated water  toys  fetal exposure. Pathophysiology  Smaller lead particles are better absorbed.  Lead particles compete with minerals such as zinc and calcium to cause problems with mitochondrial function, neurotoxicity and haem-dependent processes.  Lead mainly binds to red blood cells but can be found in plasma if levels are very high (> 60 μg/dl).  > 90% of lead is stored in the bone which provides a long-term storm of lead to target tissues even after exposure had ended.  Toxicity is targeted at multiple systems:  renal – potent toxic to proximal renal tubules causing Fanconi syndrome  cardiovascular – hypertension, coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease  neurodevelopmental – notably in children.  Clinical Presentation  Children – cognitive impairment, behavioural changes, headache, agitation, loss of appetite, constipation, somnolence.

Lithium Toxicity Lithium is primarily a mood stabiliser mainly used in bipolar affective disorder but also in recurrent depression and in cases of aggressive or ‘self-harming’ behaviours.  Overview Key Facts  Lithium is primarily a mood stabiliser mainly used in bipolar affective disorder but also in recurrent depression and in cases of aggressive or ‘self-harming’ behaviours.  Modern usage of lithium for mood disorders (since the 1950s) has produced well-established treatment protocols.  Correct dosage of lithium is based on routine blood tests to produce a typical therapeutic window of 0.4–1 mmol/l (carried out 12 hours post dosage).

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Toxicity of lithium occurs in levels > 1.5 mmol/l, but this can slightly vary between individuals.  Clinical features of lithium toxicity include nausea and vomiting, drowsiness, ataxia and tremor; levels > 2 mmol/l can result in seizures, coma and death.  There is no specific antidote for lithium toxicity. Treatment is supportive. Options include rehydration, forced diuresis and haemodialysis.  Patients should be counselled regarding the importance of correct treatment and monitoring compliance as well as the signs/symptoms to look for in case of toxicity. Aetiology  Toxicity can occur due to poor monitoring, poor compliance, overdose or changes in body sodium (eg iatrogenic, ‘fad diets’, dehydration, or illness, rarely Addison’s disease).  Medications which increase toxicity risk:  typical antipsychotics (eg haloperidol)  diuretics (especially thiazides)  calcium channel blockers (less common - may cause ataxia/ confusion)  non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs  ACE inhibitors  carbamazepine  selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.  Two types of lithium salt preparations exist – carbonate and citrate. There is no dose equivalence with these forms.  Lithium is prescribed by brand name as different preparations can differ not only in salt type but also bioavailability. Pathophysiology  Lithium is processed in the body similarly to sodium (ie gastric absorption, renal excretion).  Dehydration causes renal sodium reabsorption which in turn increases lithium reabsorption and blood lithium levels.  Diuretics can reduce lithium renal clearance (eg levels can increase as much as fourfold with loop diuretics).  Clinical Presentation  Levels > 1.5 mmol/l – symptoms can be grouped into two categories – ‘gastrointestinal’ and ‘CNS’ Gastrointestinal CNS ↑ Anorexia Nausea Diarrhoea Muscle weakness Drowsiness Ataxia Coarse tremor Muscle twitching
