Liver Enzyme Induction The main site of drug metabolism in the body is the liver. The lungs, kidneys and bones are minor sites of drug metabolism.  Overview Key Facts  The main site of drug metabolism in the body is the liver. The lungs, kidneys and bones are minor sites of drug metabolism.  The main drug metabolism site is the microsomal system of the liver.  Liver enzymes such as aspartate transaminase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), gammaglutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) and microsomal liver enzymes can be induced naturally or by external factors or drugs.  Liver microsomes are a main source of the drug metabolising enzymes, including cytochrome P450.

DR. JAMIL  Cytochrome P450 the most important microsomal enzyme in drug metabolism.  Most drug-initiated enzyme induction occurs due to the action of the drug resulting in the increase of cytochrome P450.  An intermediate metabolite of the drug can also increase the secretion of cytochrome P450.  Cytochrome P450 can be induced by pollutants in the environment, such as cigarette smoking and alcohol, etc.  When more cytochrome P450 is released, drug metabolism occurs at a faster rate and it is ultimately excreted from the body through urine. Enzyme induction increases the speed of biotransformation 2–4 times.  There are two main types of enzyme induction – selective and non-selective. Clinical effects of liver enzyme induction  Therapeutic failure occurs because the enzyme induction will decrease the overall duration of action of a particular drug by fast pacing the biotransformation process.  For example, failure of oral contraceptive when someone is simultaneously taking rifampicin for tuberculosis.  Drug toxicity can also occur because of toxic metabolite formation at an accelerated rate due to enzyme induction.  For example, when rifampicin and paracetamol are utilised simultaneously, toxic metabolites (N-acetyl-pbenzoquinone imine of paracetamol and rifampicin’s toxic metabolite) will accumulate and cause their toxic effects due to excessive enzyme induction.  Tolerance of the drug may decrease due to liver enzyme induction when the drug is excreted rapidly out of the body, which implies that more dose of the drug will be required to reach the required therapeutic level.  For example, carbamazepine (through autoinduction – the drug is itself inducing the enzymes which are affecting its own duration of action).  Liver enzyme induction can result in disease.  For example, the use of anti-epileptic drugs increases the breakdown of vitamin D because of enzyme induction which ultimately leads to osteomalacia.  Variable response of a drug in an individual can occur due to enzyme induction. For example, the variable response of a drug with varying quantity of alcohol consumption. Therapeutic application of liver enzyme induction  Phenobarbitone is used in the treatment of neonatal jaundice by conjugating bilirubin, which can then be excreted along with bile. This effect is achieved due to liver enzyme induction. Examples of drug-inducing liver enzymes:  Phenobarbitone

JAMIL  disulfiram  sodium valproate Long QT Syndrome Long QT syndrome is characterised by a prolonged QT interval on the ECG and it increases the risk of sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachyarrhythmias.  Overview Key Facts  Long QT syndrome is characterised by a prolonged QT interval on the ECG and it increases the risk of sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachyarrhythmias.  Prolonged QTc is defined as QTc > 440 ms in men and > 460 ms in women, but as a generic guide > 450 ms:  a QTc > 500 predisposes patients to develop torsades de pointes.  Long QT syndrome can be congenital (eg Romano–Ward syndrome) or acquired (secondary to drugs or electrolyte imbalances).  Many patients with long QT syndrome will be asymptomatic; it may be detected as an incidental finding on electrocardiogram (ECG).  Usually managed by correcting the cause, avoiding predisposing medications and prevention of arrhythmias by medication or pacemaker/implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD).  The Schwartz score is used for the diagnosis of long QT syndrome. This takes into consideration clinical and ECG features to determine the likelihood of a patient having an inherited long QT syndrome.  Treatment involves avoiding activities that may trigger an arrhythmia (eg stress), use of beta-blockers or ICD insertion for patients at high risk of cardiac arrest.  Prognosis is usually good if treated and prevented. If left untreated, there is a 50% chance of death within 15 years. Epidemiology  Long QT syndrome affects 1:2000 to 1:5000 people, more commonly affecting women. Aetiology Congenital causes (account for 90–95% of cases)  Romano–Ward syndrome (autosomal dominant):  LQT1 – most common subtype of Romano–Ward syndrome:

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  usually triggered by swimming.  LQT2 – 2nd most common subtype of Romano–Ward syndrome:  usually triggered by stress/emotional event or auditory stimulus.  LQT3:  patients often suffer cardiac events while sleeping at night.  Jervell and Lange–Nielson syndrome (autosomal recessive):  associated with sensorineural deafness in both ears.  Anderson–Tawil syndrome:  presentation triad:  prolonged QT interval  periodic paralysis  characteristic facial and skeletal abnormalities.  Timothy syndrome:  features:  prolonged QT  syndactyly  structural heart abnormalities  features of autism spectrum disorder. Acquired causes – drugs  Antiarrhythmic drugs:  amiodarone  sotalol  procainamide.  Antipsychotics:  haloperidol.  Antidepressants:  citalopram.  Antibiotics:  erythromycin  trimethoprim.  Antihistamines:  terfenadine.  Antifungals:  ketoconazole  fluconazole. Acquired causes – electrolyte abnormalities

Pathophysiology  The QT interval represents depolarisation and repolarisation of the ventricles.  Prolonged QT means it takes a longer time for repolarisation and a longer action potential, which in turn can lead to arrhythmias:  eg torsades the pointes – after depolarisations occur before the cells have fully repolarised because of the prolonged time thus leading to arrhythmias.  Clinical Presentation  Many patients with long QT syndrome will be asymptomatic. It may be detected as an incidental finding on ECG.  Cardiac syncope may be associated with palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath and cyanosis.  Differential Diagnosis  Differntial diagnoses include:  Brugada syndrome  vasovagal syncope  seizures  torsades de pointes  hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Long QT syndrome is commonly unknown until a cardiac event has happened (syncope or cardiac arrest) or a seizure. Otherwise, it is diagnosed by measuring the QT interval length on a 12-lead ECG.  QT interval is measured from the beginning of QRS complex to end of T wave.  QTc is the QT interval divided by the square root of the RR interval.  Long QT interval:

If left untreated, there is a 50% chance of death within 15 years. Methaemoglobinaemia Methaemoglobinaemia occurs when red blood cells have excessive methaemoglobin (MetHb >1%). MetHb cannot bind oxygen and is unable to deliver oxygen to tissues.  Overview Key Facts  Methaemoglobinaemia occurs when red blood cells have excessive methaemoglobin (MetHb >1%). MetHb cannot bind oxygen and is unable to deliver oxygen to tissues.  It is an important but uncommon cause of hypoxia and is reversible.  Patients commonly present with cyanosis not matching their level of clinical presentation, symptoms related to low oxygen levels (fainting, lightheadedness), chocolate-coloured blood and hypoxia that does not improve with supplemental oxygen.  Methaemoglobinaemia can be congenital or acquired:  the most commonly acquired cause is from toxins and drugs

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  the most common congenital cause is cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency.  The gold standard investigation is checking MetHb levels in the blood.  The mainstay of treatment is supportive oxygen and methylene blue which reduces ferric iron to ferrous iron:  if this is contraindicated then ascorbic acid is used, or other supportive treatment such as hyperbaric oxygen therapy or exchange transfusion.  The prognosis is usually determined by the amount of endorgan damage that is caused by hypoxia. If MetHb levels reach 70%, mortality rates are very high. Epidemiology  The epidemiology is not well known.  It is more common in infants < 4 months as they are more susceptible, with fetal haemoglobin more likely to be oxidised and lower levels of NADH reductase.  Congenital methaemoglobinaemia (cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency) is more common in Navajo, Puerto Ricans, Athabaskan people from Alaska and Yakutsk people of Siberia.  Acquired methaemoglobinaemia in people with glucose-6phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is more common in Mediterranean and African people. Aetiology Congenital  Cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency.  Pyruvate kinase deficiency:  reduced NADH production  NADH is a cofactor for cytochrome b5 reductase.  Haemoglobinopathy (haemoglobin M disease):  alters the structure of globin units:  tyrosine replaces histidine which allows oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+  limits the ability of reducing enzymes. Acquired  Toxins are the most common cause:  toxins can oxidise or produce oxygen to convert Fe2+ to Fe3+  local anaesthetics  aniline dyes  benzene derivatives  chloroquine  nitrites  metoclopramide

JAMIL  antibiotics (dapsone)  sulphonamide  smoke.  Diet.  Stress:  sepsis.  Fetal haemoglobin oxidises more easily:  more common in premature infants  level of NADH reductase increases with age; there are low amounts when young. Pathophysiology  Red blood cells (RBCs) are made up of haemoglobin which transports oxygen around the body:  tetramer of four globins, each containing a haem group  haem:  iron held in porphyrin ring  iron binds oxygen  each haemoglobin unit can carry four oxygen molecules  ferrous and ferric iron states  majority of iron is Fe2+ or ferrous ion:  Fe2+ is functional and can bind oxygen.  ferrous ion (Fe2+) can be oxidised to its ferric state (Fe3+)  Fe3+ is not functional and unable to bind oxygen  results in a left shift of the oxygen-dissociation curve  increased oxygen affinity of haemoglobin  less oxygen available to tissues.  haemoglobin with Fe3+ is methaemoglobin (MetHb).  Having more MetHb in the body results in:  haemoglobin carries less oxygen  oxygen release at tissues is impaired causing more hypoxia.  RBCs are exposed to oxidative stresses which normally cause ferrous ions to be converted to ferric ions:  this is usually maintained at < 1% by protective pathways that reverse the oxidation  protective pathways:  cytochrome b5 reductase pathway:

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  removes 95–99% of MetHb produced in normal circumstances.  NADPH MetHb reductase:  the minor role is to remove MetHb  uses glutathione and G6PD to reduce MetHb to haemoglobin.  Clinical Presentation  Patients commonly present with the following symptoms:  MetHb <10% of total Hb:  unlikely to have symptoms.  MetHb 10–20% of total Hb:  cyanosis.  MetHb 20–30% of total Hb:  presyncope  headache  tachycardia  anxiety.  MetHb 30–50% of total Hb:  confusion  dizziness  tachycardia  tachypnoea  tiredness.  MetHb 50–70% of total Hb:  seizures  arrhythmias  respiratory depression  coma.  MetHb > 70% of total Hb:  death.  One should be suspicious of methaemoglobinaemia if the patient appears clinically well but is cyanotic or if the SpO2 is low and does not improve with oxygen.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  heart failure  sulfhaemoglobinaemia  argyria.

Investigations  Blood sample which appears brown and does not oxidise when exposed to air.  Urine samples may be discoloured.  Arterial blood gas (ABG) sample:  may include MetHb or need to be requested  normal PaO2 (or raised if on oxygen) but reduced SaO2.  Co-oximetry.  Pulse oximetry (less accurate than co-oximetry).  MetHb = gold standard investigation.  Full blood count:  Hb levels.  ECG:  rule out differentials or arrhythmias.  Potassium cyanide:  can distinguish MetHb from sulfhaemoglobin.  Chocolate-coloured blood:

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Management  Patients who are at low risk may not need active treatment, but supportive treatment only.  Patients require active treatment if:  MetHb > 30%  MetHb < 30% and symptomatic.  Other considerations include:  evidence of tissue hypoxia (eg end-organ damage)  co-morbidities  haemoglobin levels  chronic or acute methaemoglobinaemia. Non-pharmacological  Supportive treatment:  ABCDE approach  remove any reversible causes/toxins  oxygen  observe and monitor MetHb levels.  Active treatment:  if pharmacological treatment fails:  consider exchange transfusion  consider hyperbaric oxygen. Pharmacological  Supportive treatment:  intravenous (IV) dextrose.  Active treatment:  methylene blue:  reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+  1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes  if the first administration fails, discuss with National Poisons Information Service and consider further dose.  ascorbic acid:  if methylene blue is contraindicated, eg G6PD deficiency.  Prognosis  Patients with methaemoglobinaemia usually have a good outcome if it is detected and treated promptly. Methanol Poisoning Methanol is found in paint, paint thinners, antifreeze, car windscreen wash, varnishes and illegally distilled alcoholic drinks. It may be absorbed following ingestion, inhalation or dermal exposure.  Overview Key Facts  Methanol is found in paint, paint thinners, antifreeze, car windscreen wash, varnishes and illegally distilled alcoholic drinks. It may be absorbed following ingestion, inhalation or dermal exposure.  Methanol is metabolised in the liver by zero-order kinetics.  Methanol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde and then to formic acid, which is the primary cause of toxic effects. Only 3% of methanol is converted to carbon dioxide and water for exhalation or excreted unchanged in the urine.  Initial symptoms such as ataxia, nystagmus, drowsiness and dysarthria may mimic alcohol intoxication. However, patients may be asymptomatic for up to 24 hours following ingestion.  Symptoms are predominantly neurological (headache, confusion, vertigo, seizures and coma) and visual (blurred vision, ‘snow-field’ vision, photophobia optic disc/retinal oedema and permanent blindness).  Diagnosis is made from history and examination, bloods for methanol concentration and arterial blood, which may initially show a raised osmolar gap only and later progress to metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap.  It is important to note that patients with severe poisoning may have a normal pH and normal anion gap at presentation.  Fomepizole is the preferred antidote:  a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing the conversion of methanol to formaldehyde.  Ethanol may also be used if fomepizole is not available:  ethanol competes with methanol for metabolism, reducing the formation of toxic metabolites.  Gastric lavage may be considered if the presentation is within 1 hour of poisoning.  Treatment is otherwise supportive and includes sodium bicarbonate if there is persistent acidosis despite intravenous (IV) fluids, treatment of hypotension and haemodialysis in cases of severe poisoning.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Ingestion of as little as 10 ml methanol may result in blindness and 30 ml may result in death.  Poor prognostic features include coma, seizures, persistent acidosis, renal failure and bradycardia. Epidemiology  Children are at risk of accidental poisoning and products containing methanol should be kept out of reach.  There have been several outbreaks of methanol poisoning around the world involving ‘bootleg liquor’, which has not been properly distilled.  ‘Home-brewed’ liquor may also increase the risk of accidental methanol poisoning. Aetiology  Methanol may be absorbed following ingestion, inhalation or dermal exposure.  Methanol is found in:  paint  paint thinners  antifreeze  car windscreen wash  varnishes  illegally distilled alcoholic drinks. Pathophysiology  The primary site for the metabolism of methanol is the liver.  Methanol is metabolised by zero-order kinetics.  Methanol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde and then to formic acid.  Approximately 3% of methanol is converted to carbon dioxide and water for exhalation or excreted unchanged in the urine, but it mostly accumulates.  Formic acid is the primary cause of the raised anion gap metabolic acidosis, blindness and end-organ damage seen in methanol poisoning.  Fomepizole (used in the treatment of methanol poisoning) is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing the conversion of methanol to formaldehyde.  Ethanol may also be used in the treatment of poisoning as it competes with methanol for metabolism, reducing the formation of toxic metabolites.  Clinical Presentation  Initial symptoms may appear within 30 minutes of ingestion and mimic alcohol intoxication:  ataxia

DR. JAMIL  dysarthria  drowsiness  nystagmus.  Patients may be asymptomatic for up to 24 hours following ingestion, especially if alcohol has also been consumed.  Symptoms and signs of toxicity include:  neurological:  headache  confusion  vertigo  seizures and coma (severe toxicity).  visual (tend to correlate with severity of toxicity):  blurred vision or ‘snow-field’ vision  photophobia  optic disc and retinal oedema  permanent blindness (severe toxicity).  gastrointestinal:  nausea and vomiting  abdominal pain  pancreatitis.  metabolic:  metabolic acidosis:  patients may have a normal pH and normal anion gap at presentation, but the osmolar gap will be raised.  increased anion gap  increased osmolar gap.  Differential Diagnosis  Initial symptoms may mimic alcohol intoxication.  Other causes of metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap include:  carbon monoxide poisoning  cyanide poisoning  ketoacidosis (diabetic, alcoholic, starvation)  metformin  uraemia  ethylene glycol, propylene glycol  iron  lactic acidosis

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  salicylates.  Diagnosis/Investigation  A thorough history may reveal the diagnosis.  Initial examination may elicit symptoms similar to acute intoxication with alcohol.  Blood tests:  methanol concentration:  sample should be taken at least two hours after ingestion  do not delay treatment while waiting for results.  arterial blood gas (ABG):  may initially show a raised osmolar gap only and later progress to metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap.  full blood count (FBC)  liver function tests (LFTs)  urea & electrolytes (U&Es, including bicarbonate and chloride)  glucose  full toxicology screen (including salicylates, paracetamol and ethanol)  amylase (if the patient has severe abdominal pain).  Management  ABCDE assessment.  Consider gastric lavage if presenting within one hour of poisoning.  Early administration of fomepizole or ethanol to reduce the further production of toxic metabolites:  fomepizole is the preferred antidote (does not need regular monitoring or cause symptoms of intoxication like ethanol)  if fomepizole is not immediately available, ethanol can be given followed by fomepizole when available.  Treatment with an antidote may need to continue for several days.  Intravenous (IV) folinic acid for 48 hours.  IV fluids (may need a referral to ICU for treatment with vasopressors or inotropes).  IV sodium bicarbonate if metabolic acidosis persists despite initial supportive treatment.  Indications for haemodialysis:

JAMIL  methanol concentration > 500 mg/l  visual disturbance or features of CNS toxicity  severe metabolic acidosis  severe electrolyte imbalance  renal failure  deterioration despite initial treatment.  Prognosis  Ingestion of as little as 10 ml methanol may result in blindness and 30 ml may result in death.  Poor prognostic features include coma, seizures, persistent acidosis, renal failure and bradycardia.  Patients who survive severe poisoning may be left with permanent extrapyramidal symptoms. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome occurs as a complication of treatment with antipsychotic drugs or withdrawal of dopamine agonists.  Overview Key Facts  Neuroleptic malignant syndrome occurs as a complication of treatment with antipsychotic drugs or withdrawal of dopamine agonists.  Can be life-threatening and is a diagnosis of exclusion.  Symptoms/signs include muscle rigidity, autonomic instability, hyperthermia and altered mental state.  Treatment consists of supportive measures and ceasing the responsible drug.  The mortality reported to be between 8% and 9%, and the risk of recurrence as high as 30%. Epidemiology  Estimated incidence of 0.02–3% making it relatively uncommon.  May be more common in men.  Risk factors include pre-existing structural abnormalities in the brain, older age and catatonia.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI Aetiology  Caused by a quick reduction in dopamine/dopamine agonist availability at postsynaptic receptors.  Risk factors include dopamine disorders, eg Parkinson’s disease, structural brain abnormalities and potentially genetics. Pathophysiology  Pathophysiology not well established but dysfunction/imbalance of dopamine thought to be implicated.  Acute reduction in dopamine causes muscle rigidity, autonomic dysfunction and impaired thermoregulation.  Clinical Presentation  Altered mental state – confusion, delirium.  Muscle rigidity – lead-pipe rigidity or hypertonia generally.  Autonomic dysfunction – tachycardia, diaphoresis, tachypnoea, urinary incontinence.  Hyperthermia.  Psychiatric history.  DSM-5 diagnostic criteria:  major criteria (must all be present):  exposure to dopamine blocker  muscle rigidity  hyperthermia.  Other criteria (> 2 must be present):  diaphoresis  dysphagia  tremor  incontinence  altered level of consciousness  mutism  tachycardia  elevated or labile blood pressure  leukocytosis  elevated creatine kinase (CK).  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  sepsis  drug abuse

DR. JAMIL  catatonia  serotonin syndrome  mania  malignant hyperthermia  heatstroke  metabolic conditions, eg caused by dehydration, hyponatraemia  brain infarcts  normal pressure hydrocephalus  brain tumours  autoimmune encephalitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a clinical diagnosis. Investigations should be performed to exclude other differential diagnoses.  Full blood count – elevated WCC.  Creatine kinase (CK) – elevated.  Basic metabolic panel – usually normal.  Computed tomography (CT)/Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain – usually normal.  Myoglobin levels and urinalysis – myoglobin can be present.  Urine culture – usually normal.  Blood culture – usually normal.  Lumbar puncture – usually normal.  Toxicology screen – usually normal.  Chest X-ray – usually normal.  Management  Withdrawal of antipsychotic medication – reintroduction of antipsychotic drugs should be delayed for at least two weeks.  Supportive therapy – fluids, correction of electrolyte imbalances.  Pharmacological therapy – lorazepam (for agitation and catatonia), dantrolene (for hyperthermia and muscle rigidity), bromocriptine or amantadine.  Electroconvulsive therapy (case reports showing effective in refractory cases; however often impractical to perform).  Prognosis  Mortality reported to be between 8% and 9%.  Risk of recurrence as high as 30%.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Reintroduction of medication should be postponed until at least two weeks after symptoms/signs have resolved and should be done under very close monitoring.  Complications:  sepsis  acute kidney injury (AKI)  rhabdomyolysis  pulmonary embolism  aspiration pneumonia  cognitive deficits  permanent neurological disability  worsening of psychosis. Opiate Toxicity Opiate toxicity results from an overdose of opioid drugs, causing symptoms such as respiratory depression and altered mental status.  Overview Key Facts  Opioids account for about 70% of all fatal prescription drug overdose.  Common causes include intentional overdose or therapeutic drug error.  Opioids act at mu, kappa and delta-opioid receptors and can cause severe respiratory depression which is the major cause of mortality.  Key signs are central nervous system (CNS) and respiratory depression, miosis and apnoea.  Diagnosis is clinical. Other investigations such as ECG, serum glucose and urine toxicology are ordered to rule out other potential causes.  Differential diagnosis must include other drug overdoses such as alcohol, acetaminophen, benzodiazepines and hypoglycaemic agents.  The goal of naloxone therapy is a respiratory rate above 12 breaths/minute and oxygen saturation of above 90%.  Patients should be monitored for re-sedation and repeat antidote dose.  Opioid withdrawal and naloxone toxicity are common clinical problems faced during the management of acute opioid overdose.

DR. JAMIL Epidemiology  Opiate toxicity and abuse have become an increasing problem worldwide.  Opioids account for about 70% of all fatal prescription drug overdose.  Risk factors include:  age less than 45 years  psychiatric disorder  opioid abuse/addiction history  legal history  hepatic or renal failure. Aetiology  Intention overdose or suicide attempt.  Therapeutic drug error.  Unintentional overdose in patients using prescribed opioids.  Complications of substance abuse in those using illicit or prescription opioids. Pathophysiology  Opioids act at mu, kappa and delta-opioid receptors:  mu – analgesia, sedation, respiratory depression, gastrointestinal (GI) dysmotility, miosis, diuresis, dysphoria  kappa – analgesia, miosis, diuresis, dysphoria  delta – analgesia, inhibits dopamine release, cough suppression.  Most deaths occur after opioid injection due to potent effects from significant first-pass hepatic metabolism.  In overdose, mu receptors cause respiratory depression and apnoea.  Clinical Presentation  Vital signs:  bradycardia – best predictor of opioid toxicity is respiratory rate of less than 12 breaths/minute  hypotension  decreased respiratory rate  hypothermia.  Neurological:  altered mental status  seizures  coma.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Decreased GI motility, decreased bowel sounds.  Miosis, except meperidine and propoxyphene.  Dramatic response to naloxone.  Track marks on arms/legs.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  overdose of another substance, eg ketamine, antipsychotics, clonidine, GHB/GBL  alcohol intoxication. Drugs that can cause coma other than opioids Distinguishing feature Drugs  Normal pupils and bowel sounds  Antipsychotics  Ethanol  Methanol  Ethylene glycol Isoniazid ⇢ seizures  Isopropanol  Sedative-hypnotic agents  Serum concentration  Barbiturates  Carbamazepine  Ethanol Lithium ⇢ tremors, hyperreflexia  Carbon monoxide  Hypoglycaemic agents  Nystagmus  Phencyclidine  Prominent cardiovascular findings  Beta-blockers  CCBs Prolonged QRS and ⇡HR  Tricyclic antidepressants  Diagnosis/Investigation  Opioid toxicity is a clinical diagnosis; therefore routine urine toxicology is not required:  a positive urine toxicology report will only confirm recent use, not active toxicity.  ECG – abnormal, eg prolonged QRS, signs of myocardial ischaemia.  Therapeutic trial of naloxone – reversal of overdose signs.  Serum glucose to rule out hypoglycaemia.  Serum creatinine kinase levels to rule out rhabdomyolysis.

DR. JAMIL  Management  If the respiratory rate is ≥ 12 breaths/minute and O2 saturation > 90% on room air ⇢ observe, monitor and reassess frequently.  If the respiratory rate is less than 12 breaths/minute or O2 saturation is less than 90% ⇢ administer naloxone (intravenous (IV) or intramuscular (IM)).  Repeated doses of naloxone are given until clinical response is seen.  Goal of treatment is adequate ventilation, NOT normal mental status.  Gastric decontamination or hemodialysis is never indicated in opioid toxicity.  Give sodium bicarbonate in loperamide overdose.  Cardiac monitoring is needed in case of toxicity with loperamide or methadone.  Prognosis  Excellent prognosis with timely naloxone administration and appropriate ventilation.  Poorer prognosis in patients who suffer from significant hypoxia or aspiration of gastric contents.  Other Rapid review: opioid toxicity Risk factors  Substance abuse  Chronic opioid use  Hospitalised patients (especially post-op)  Hepatic or renal insufficiency Clinical features  Vital signs: ⇣ RR and shallow breaths ⇢ best indicator of intoxication and a frequent cause of mortality bradycardia, hypotension ⇢ histamine release  hypothermia (or normothermia) ⇣ Mental status, seizures, sedation, coma ⇣ Bowel sounds Miosis (normal/enlarged if coingestions) ⇢ meperidine and propoxyphene do not cause miosis Diagnosis ABGs ⇢ respiratory acidosis  Hypoglycaemia  CK, chest X-ray

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI Evaluate for other drugs ⇢ acetaminophen ECG ⇢ prolonged QTc with methadone, loperamide Management  Naloxone  ABC and ventilation QTc >500 msec ⇢ continuous cardiac monitoring Loperamide ⇢ sodium bicarbonate  Complications:  hypoxia  aspiration  acute respiratory distress syndrome  opioid withdrawal  naloxone toxicity. Organophosphate Poisoning Organophosphates are most commonly found in insecticides and can be absorbed by ingestion, inhalation or dermal contact.  Overview Key Facts  Organophosphates are most commonly found in insecticides and can be absorbed by ingestion, inhalation or dermal contact.  Organophosphates may also be used as chemical weapons and are known as ‘nerve agents’.  Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase which usually breaks down acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction.  Acetylcholine accumulates and exerts its action on muscarinic and nicotinic receptors and in the central nervous system (CNS).  Systemic features of inhalation or ingestion include sweating, hypersalivation, bronchoconstriction, miosis, fasciculations, muscle weakness, increased respiratory secretions, respiratory depression, seizures and coma.  Delayed effects may develop after the systemic symptoms seem to have settled, namely neuromuscular dysfunction leading to respiratory failure. This is known as ‘intermediate syndrome’.  Diagnosis is centred around clinical features and a history of exposure.  Bloods for erythrocyte and plasma cholinesterase activity should confirm the diagnosis, but treatment should not be

DR. JAMIL delayed while awaiting the result if clinical features are present.  Decontamination and PPE (personal protective equipment) procedures should be followed as per local guidelines.  Management in cases with severe symptoms includes atropine, which is used to block the action of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors.  Atropine is given with pralidoxime chloride.  Tidal volume and strength of neck flexor muscles should be monitored regularly.  Management is otherwise supportive and patients often require care in ICU.  The primary cause of death is respiratory failure. Epidemiology  It is thought that organophosphate poisoning accounts for approximately 300 000 deaths per year. Aetiology  Organophosphates are most commonly found in insecticides and can be absorbed by ingestion, inhalation or dermal contact.  Organophosphates may also be used as chemical weapons and are known as ‘nerve agents’:  contact with very low concentrations may be fatal  examples include sarin and novichok. Pathophysiology  Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, which usually breaks down acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction.  Acetylcholine accumulates and exerts its action on muscarinic and nicotinic receptors and in the CNS.  Increased action of acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors leads to:  hypersalivation  miosis  sweating  bradycardia  excess bronchial secretions  diarrhoea.  Increased action of acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors leads to:  muscle fasciculations  muscle paralysis.  Clinical Presentation  Acute ingestion may cause:

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  vomiting and diarrhoea  retrosternal burning due to irritation  laryngeal oedema and airway obstruction.  Acute inhalation may cause:  upper airway irritation  chest tightness  difficulty in breathing.  Systemic features of inhalation or ingestion include:  abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea  sweating  hypersalivation  chest tightness  miosis  fasciculations  muscle weakness  bronchoconstriction  increased respiratory secretions  respiratory depression  seizures and coma  ECG changes (AV block, long QT, bradycardia, peaked T waves, ventricular arrhythmias)  glycosuria and hyperglycaemia (severe cases)  fever.  Delayed effects may develop after the systemic symptoms seem to have settled and 1–4 days after exposure, namely neuromuscular dysfunction leading to respiratory failure. This is known as ‘intermediate syndrome’ and it usually resolves over a period of weeks.  Delayed motor polyneuropathy starting 2–3 weeks after exposure is a rare complication.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  pyridostigmine or neostigmine toxicity  Guillain–Barré syndrome  botulism  opioid overdose  Lambert–Eaton syndrome  cyanide poisoning  toxic alcohol poisoning  gastroenteritis.

DR. JAMIL  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is centred around clinical features and a history of exposure.  Bloods for erythrocyte and plasma cholinesterase activity should confirm the diagnosis, but treatment should not be delayed while awaiting the result if clinical features are present.  Management  Immediate atropine and oxygen should be given before examination if severe bradycardia, hypoxia or hypotension.  Decontamination and PPE (personal protective equipment) procedures should be followed as per local guidelines.  Management  ABCDE assessment.  Airway management:  give oxygen  suctioning likely to be required for secretions  intubation and ventilation may be required.  Atropine (blocks the action of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors):  administer urgently if increased secretions, rhinorrheoa/bronchorrheoa, hypotension, bronchospasm or bradycardia; otherwise, observe closely for clinical features suggestive of toxicity  2 mg intravenous (IV) atropine, repeated every five minutes as required (doubling the dose every 5–10 minutes may be beneficial in moderate-severe poisoning)  an atropine infusion may be required, but should be carefully titrated to avoid atropine toxicity (agitation, urinary retention, hyperthermia, agitation, ileus and tachycardia).  Pralidoxime chloride should be given as a loading dose to all patients requiring atropine and continued as an infusion for several days.  Consider gastric lavage if presentation is within one hour of ingestion.  Monitor observations closely and perform serial 12-lead ECGs.  Bronchospasm may be treated with nebulised bronchodilators and steroids.  Repeat tidal volume measurement every four hours.  Review strength of neck flexors regularly to assess for neuromuscular junction failure and the development of ‘intermediate syndrome’.  IV fluid resuscitation for hypotension – may require vasopressors or inotropes.  Treat agitation and delirium as per local guidelines.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Treat seizures if prolonged or frequent.  If metabolic acidosis is persistent despite initial treatment, consider sodium bicarbonate.  If cardiac arrest, continue resuscitation for at least one hour (good neurological outcome may still occur).  Prognosis  Complications may arise from aspiration or hypoxic brain injury caused by loss of consciousness and respiratory failure.  The primary cause of death is respiratory failure. Paracetamol Overdose Paracetamol overdose can cause liver damage and even liver failure if not treated promptly.  Overview Key Facts  Most common drug taken in overdose.  Single ingestions > 250 mg/kg or 12 g over a 24-hour period will generally lead to toxicity.  Acetaminophen metabolite (NAPQI) depletes glutathione and forms toxic metabolites in the liver, inducing widespread liver injury.  Usually asymptomatic or mild nausea and vomiting within the first 24 hours. Liver abnormalities start after 24 hours and peak at 72–96 hours after ingestion.  If the patient survives, recovery begins after 96 hours.  Serum acetaminophen levels are key to the diagnosis.  Additional investigations include CBC, LFTs, PT, INR, RFTs, screening for other drugs.  Activated charcoal and Nacetylcysteine are key in the management of toxicity.  Liver transplant may be required in cases of fulminant liver failure.  In case of timely management, prognosis is excellent. Epidemiology  Most common drug taken in overdose.  Accounts for 48% of poisoning admissions to hospital.  Estimated 100–200 deaths per year in the United Kingdom (UK).

DR. JAMIL Aetiology  Maximum recommended daily dose of acetaminophen is 80 mg/kg in children or 4 g in adults.  Single ingestions > 250 mg/kg or 12 g over a 24-hour period will generally lead to toxicity.  Usually occurs due to therapeutic dosage errors or selfharm/suicide attempts.  Risk factors include:  history of self-harm  history of frequent use of pain relief  glutathione deficiency  use of cytochrome P450 inducers, eg rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine. Pathophysiology  Paracetamol undergoes hepatic metabolisation including sulfation and glucuronidation to allow for the excretion of nontoxic metabolites in urine.  Four per cent of the therapeutic dose is metabolised by cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP2E1) to NAPQI (toxic intermediate metabolite).  NAPQI combines with glutathione to produce a non-toxic mercapturate derivative, which is excreted in the urine.  Upon paracetamol overdose, the production of NAPQI outweighs the capacity for glutathione detoxification.  Excess amounts of NAPQI bind to components of cells causing injury to mitochondria and death of hepatocytes which can lead to acute liver failure.  Clinical Presentation Stage I 1st 24 hours  Nausea, vomiting  Diaphoresis, pallor  Lethargy and malaise Stage II 24–72 hours  Evidence of hepatotoxicity  Improvement in clinical symptoms in some patients Stage III 72–96 hours  Peak derangement in liver function tests  Stage I symptoms reappear  Jaundice  Confusion (hepatic encephalopathy)  Hyperammonaemia  Bleeding diathesis Stage IV 4 days to 2 weeks  If the patient survives, recovery begins

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  ischaemic hepatitis  acute hepatitis A  acute hepatitis B  Reye syndrome  other hepatotoxins, eg industrial chemicals, anaesthetic agents.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Serum paracetamol concentration – confirmatory test:  used to stratify risk of liver injury to determine need for treatment with acetylcysteine (see links for treatment nomogram for paracetamol overdose)  paracetamol levels should be taken four hours after ingestion and then repeated again at six hours if the result at four hours is below the treatment threshold.  Full blood count (FBC).  Liver function tests, with levels of AST/ALT above 1000 IU/l.  Prothrombin tests and INR.  Blood glucose.  Urea, creatinine and electrolytes – acute renal failure is seen in 50% of patients.  Venous or arterial blood gas. Investigations to consider  Salicylate level – may be positive in coingestion.  Urinalysis – may be positive for haematuria or proteinuria.  Urine drug screen – may be positive for other drugs like benzodiazepines, opioids, etc.  Management Non-pharmacological  Airway, breathing and circulation (ABC). Pharmacological  Activated charcoal – used if patient presents within one hour of ingestion and has digested more than 150 mg/kg or > 7.5 g acetaminophen, according to the National Poisons Information Service TOXBASE.  N-acetylcysteine is given orally or intravenously if:  serum levels of acetaminophen are above the ‘treatment’ line of the treatment nomogram after four hours of ingestion

DR. JAMIL  serum levels are unavailable but ingestion dose is above 7.5 g  serum levels above 10 μg/ml  any evidence of liver injury.  Intravenous N-acetylcysteine is preferred in patients with:  vomiting  contraindications to oral therapy, such as pancreatitis or bowel ileus  refusal of oral therapy  evidence of hepatic failure.  N-acetylcysteine can cause nausea and vomiting in over 30% of patients; therefore antiemetics are often given along with the antidote:  serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonists (eg ondansetron) is usually preferred  metoclopramide.  Dose of N-acetylcysteine should be repeated if patients vomit within one hour of oral administration.  Surgery  Evaluate for liver transplant in cases of fulminant liver failure. King's College Hospital criteria for liver transplantation in acute liver failure  Acetaminophen-induced Arterial pH < 7.3 OR All 3 of the following:  Grade III/IV encephalopathy  PT > 100 seconds  Cr > 3.4 mg/dl  All other causes PT > 100 seconds OR Any 3 of the following:  Age < 10 or > 40  Non-A, non-B hepatitis, halothane hepatitis, idiosyncratic drug reaction  Duration of jaundice before onset of encephalopathy > 7 days  PT > 50 seconds  Bilirubin > 18 mg/dl

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Excellent prognosis if timely Nacetylcysteine is given.  Hepatic regeneration takes place quickly with LFTs returning to normal in 1–3 weeks for those who survive.  Prognosis thought to be worse in patients with staggered overdose or delayed presentation.  Other  Complications:  acute liver failure  IV acetylcysteine-related anaphylactoid reaction  IV acetylcysteine-related coagulopathy  oral acetylcysteine-related nausea and vomiting. Parkinsonism And Parkinson’s Disease Parkinsonism is a collective term for the clinical syndrome that includes bradykinesia along with at least one additional symptom.  Overview Key Facts  Parkinsonism is a collective term for the clinical syndrome that includes bradykinesia along with at least one additional symptom of:  tremor  rigidity  gait disturbances.  Parkinson’s disease is the most common cause of parkinsonism.  Other causes of parkinsonism include:  drug-induced parkinsonism  cerebrovascular disease  dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)  multiple system atrophy  progressive supranuclear palsy.

DR. JAMIL  Parkinson’s disease is defined as a chronic progressive neurodegenerative disease linked to decreased dopamine production in the substantia nigra.  Reduced dopamine levels lead to a movement disorder with classical parkinsonian features including:  bradykinesia  resting tremor  rigidity  shuffling gait.  Diagnosis is mainly clinical. However, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain and dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) imaging may be helpful in confirming loss of dopaminergic neuronal function and ruling out alternative diagnoses.  Levodopa and dopamine agonists such as ropinirole are potential first-line treatment options.  Parkinson’s plus syndromes are a group of neurodegenerative diseases that consist of cardinal features of Parkinson’s disease (resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity and shuffling gait) along with additional symptoms, which include reduced response to levodopa, dysarthria, autonomic dysfunction and supranuclear gaze palsy.  The syndromes include conditions such as:  multiple system dystrophy  dementia with Lewy bodies  progressive supranuclear palsy  corticobasal degeneration.  Diagnosis is usually clinical. However, MRI brain and Iiodobenzamide SPECT scanning may be of value.  A multi-disciplinary approach is essential for treatment, patients respond poorly to dopamine agonists or l-dopa. Epidemiology  There were approximately 137 000 people living with Parkinson’s disease in the United Kingdom (UK) in 2017, based on a Parkinson’s UK report.  Each year, there are about 17 300 new diagnoses of Parkinson’s disease in people aged 45 years and above.  The prevalence of Parkinson's disease increases with age – the prevalence is 4–5 : 100 000 in those aged 30–39 years, compared with over 1 500 : 100 000 in those aged 80–84 years.  The prevalence is higher in men than in women.  By 2025, due to population growth and an increasingly ageing population, the estimated prevalence and yearly incidence of Parkinson’s disease is expected to increase by around 23%.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI Aetiology  The exact cause of Parkinson’s disease is unknown; however, around 20% of cases have a family history in a first-degree relative.  Early onset Parkinson’s disease is associated with the mutation of the PARK 1 gene, encoding protein Alpha synuclein, sat chromosome 4q, the main component of Lewy bodies. Other genes identified include PARK- Parkin, PARK, PINK 1, PARK DJ1.  Wilson’s disease, Huntington’s disease and spinocerebellar ataxia may all lead to symptoms of parkinsonism.  Medications known to cause parkinsonism include:  antipsychotic drugs  metoclopramide  prochlorperazine  tetrabenazine  sodium valproate  lithium.

DR. JAMIL Pathophysiology Genetic abnormalities:  lead to protein misfolding, resulting in impaired clearance and protein accumulation  this in turn leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and, ultimately, symptoms of Parkinson’s disease. Acquired aetiology:  destruction of dopamine producing neurones in the substantia nigra reduces availability of dopamine, which usually produces an inhibitory effect  this leads to increased excitatory effects, due to excess acetylcholine availability

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  excessive stimulation of neurons of basal ganglia causes increased muscle tone, rigidity and tremors. Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons  loss of melanin containing neurons produce changes, including depigmentation leading to the formation of Lewy bodies.  Clinical Presentation CARDINAL FEATURES MOTOR FEATURES NON-MOTOR FEATURES  bradykinesia (must be present)  mask like facies  depression  ‘cogwheel’ rigidity  reduced blink frequency  fatigue  resting tremor  freezing  sleep disturbances  shuffling gait  dysphasia  cognitive impairment or dementia  postural instability  micrographia  anosmia and other sensory disturbances eg pain  hypophonia  memory and thought processing dysfunction Signs and symptoms more consistent with a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease:  unilateral onset and persistent asymmetry  resting tremor  good response to levodopa  levodopa-induced dyskinesia  long disease course (> 10 years). Signs and symptoms more consistent of other diagnoses:  prominent early autonomic failure (postural hypotension, urinary incontinence, erectile dysfunction) – consider multisystem atrophy (MSA) or DLB  cerebellar signs – consider MSA  prominent pyramidal signs – consider MSA  vascular parkinsonism – consider corticobasal syndrome (CBS)

DR. JAMIL  vertical supranuclear gaze palsy – consider progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP)  early falls (within first year) – consider PSP and normal pressure hydrocephalus  neuroleptic use – consider drug-induced parkinsonism  poor levodopa response – consider MSA, PSP or CBS  early dementia – consider DLB, PSP or CBS.  Differential Diagnosis Differentials for parkinsonian symptoms include:  Parkinson’s disease  MSA  drug-induced parkinsonism  DLB  stroke/transient ischaemic attack (TIA)  PSA  liver failure  trauma  normal pressure hydrocephalus  tumour  infection  Wilson's disease  Huntington’s disease  prion diseases  Alzheimer’s disease.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is predominantly clinical.  If at least 2 of 4 cardinal signs are positive (including bradykinesia), then the diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease should be considered.  Dopamine transporter SPECT imaging may be helpful. It shows reduced and asymmetrical uptake of striatal dopamine biomarkers, particularly in the posterior putamen with sparing of the caudate nucleus.  CT/MRI can be used to rule out alternative diagnoses.  Management Non-pharmacological  If Parkinson's disease is suspected, urgent neurology referral is required.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Look for and either reduce or stop any medications that could potentially cause parkinsonism, wherever possible.  If Parkinson's disease is confirmed:  provide patient, family and/or carers with written information  provide information about local support groups and charity organisations, such as Parkinson’s UK  inform the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA)  give lifestyle modification advice including – diet and exercise and avoidance of alcohol and smoking.  physiotherapy  speech and language therapy may be required in later stages. Pharmacological The first-line medication is levodopa, which is usually given with a dopa decarboxylase inhibitor, such as cobeneldopa or co-careldopa:  usually offered to people in the early stages of Parkinson's disease  typically provides more improvement in motor symptoms and daily functioning  fewer adverse effects, such as excessive sleepiness, hallucinations and impulse control disorders, but may cause more motor complications than other drug classes. Oral dopamine agonists, such as pramipexole or ropinirole, or transdermal dopamine agonists, such as rotigotine:  typically provide less improvement in motor symptoms and daily functioning when compared to levodopa but with fewer motor complications. Adverse effects include more risk of excessive sleepiness, hallucinations and impulse control disorders than other drug classes  Ergot-derived dopamine agonists, such as cabergoline and pergolide, should not be used as first-line treatment due to the risk of cardiac fibrosis with long-term use and need for additional monitoring. Adjuvant medications:  Oral monoamine oxidase-B (MAO-B) inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline or safinamide):  do not cause an interaction after consumption of tyramine-rich foods  typically provide less improvement in motor symptoms and daily functioning, fewer motor complications and fewer adverse effects such as excessive sleepiness,

DR. JAMIL hallucinations and impulse control disorders than other drug classes. Oral catechol-O-methyl transferase (COMT) inhibitors (such as entacapone):  are given as part of the combination preparation of levodopa, carbidopa and entacapone to improve compliance  may be used as an adjunct to levodopa for people who have developed dyskinesia or motor fluctuations despite optimal levodopa therapy  typically provide more improvement in motor symptoms and daily functioning, with more adverse effects such as excessive sleepiness and impulse control disorders, but a lower risk of hallucinations than other drug classes. Oral amantadine:  may be considered if dyskinesia is not adequately managed by modifying existing antiparkinsonian therapy. Subcutaneous apomorphine (dopamine agonist):  may be offered to people with advanced Parkinson's disease on optimal oral treatment, as intermittent subcutaneous bolus injections and/or continuous subcutaneous infusion. Surgical  Surgery involves the insertion of electrodes, usually bilaterally, into deep nuclei within the brain for deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the subthalamic nucleus.  These are connected to a battery-powered generator via leads that are tunnelled beneath the skin.  A generator is usually implanted into the chest wall and it delivers an electric current to the electrodes placed in the targeted areas of the brain.  They may be considered for people with advanced Parkinson's disease with motor complications refractory to optimal medical treatment who are fit, levodoparesponsive and have no co-morbid mental health conditions.  Prognosis  Parkinson's disease is slowly progressive, but the rate of progression is variable.  The mortality rate for elderly people aged 70–89 years with Parkinson's disease is 2–5 times higher than age-matched control subjects without Parkinson’s.  The risk of dementia is 2–6 times higher in people with Parkinson's disease than in those without the disease.

Phenytoin Toxicity Phenytoin is a voltage-gated sodium channel blocker. It has a very narrow therapeutic window, which increases the risk of toxicity.  Overview Key Facts  Phenytoin is a voltage-gated sodium channel blocker. It has a very narrow therapeutic window, which increases the risk of toxicity.  Toxicity may occur as a result of intentional overdose, inadequate monitoring, misinterpretation of phenytoin levels (especially in hypoalbuminaemia when less phenytoin will be bound to albumin) and drug interactions (particularly with cytochrome P450 inhibitors).  Symptoms of phenytoin toxicity are predominantly neurological and include ataxia, nystagmus, impaired coordination, dysarthria, coma, confusion, dyskinesia, seizures and hyperglycaemia.  It is thought that cardiac symptoms (hypotension, bradycardia and asystole) may be caused by the diluent used with intravenous (IV) preparations (propylene glycol).  Phenytoin has also rarely been known to cause DRESS syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens–Johnson syndrome.  Diagnosis is made on the basis of history, examination and serum phenytoin levels.  There is no antidote for phenytoin. Activated charcoal may be of benefit within one hour of ingestion and potentially later than this in large overdoses.  Management is centred around treating individual symptoms, such as cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, agitation, hypotension

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI (may require ICU level care) delirium and electrolyte abnormalities.  Fatal cases are usually when a patient has taken another substance in combination with phenytoin.  10–20% may suffer from major morbidities, such as memory loss and cognitive defects. Epidemiology  Phenytoin is used for the prevention and treatment of seizures and as a second-line drug for trigeminal neuralgia under specialist supervision (unlicensed indication).  Phenytoin has a very narrow therapeutic window, which increases the risk of toxicity.  Older people are at greater risk of toxicity, as phenytoin clearance tends to decrease with age:  phenytoin clearance may be 20% less in patients > 70 years old compared with young adults. Aetiology  Phenytoin toxicity may occur in the following scenarios:  intentional overdose  inadequate monitoring after initiation or dose change  misinterpretation of phenytoin levels:  phenytoin is approximately 90% protein-bound in adults  in patients with hypoalbuminaemia, total phenytoin levels may be misleading as the percentage of unbound phenytoin (which is pharmacologically active) will be higher and may lead to toxicity in the context of seemingly normal total levels.  drug interactions:  phenytoin is metabolised by cytochrome P450, so levels may be increased by drugs or substances that inhibit cytochrome P450. Pathophysiology  Symptoms of phenytoin toxicity are predominantly neurological.  Phenytoin is a voltage-gated sodium channel blocker and it targets neurones with high-frequency activity, prolonging the refractory period and preventing or reducing seizure activity.  It is also a class 1B antiarrhythmic acting on cardiac voltagegated sodium channels:  cardiac effects are rare from oral ingestion and it is thought that they may be a side-effect of propylene glycol, the diluent used for IV administration  rapid infusions of propylene glycol can cause bradycardia, hypotension and asystole.

Photosensitivity Photosensitivity is defined as symptoms, diseases and conditions caused or made worse by sunlight exposure.  Overview Key Facts  Photosensitivity is defined as symptoms, diseases and conditions caused or made worse by sunlight exposure.  Common causes include polymorphic light eruption, juvenile spring eruption or drug-induced photosensitivity.  Patients can present with a sunburn reaction in the sun-exposed area of the body. Erythema and oedema may develop within minutes/hours of light exposure.  Sometimes lesions heal with hyperpigmentation or scarring.

Epidemiology  Photosensitivity occurs in both men and women of all ages and races.  People with Fitzpatrick skin type I are often considered photosensitive.  The highest prevalence of photosensitivity occurs around puberty in women. This may be due to hormonal influence. DR. JAMIL  Drugs causing photosensitivity  Antibiotics/antifungals Tetracyclines ⇢ doxycycline  Fluoroquinolones  Voriconazole  Antipsychotics  Chlorpromazine  Prochlorperazine  Diuretics  Furosemide  Hydrochlorothiazide  Others  Sulfonamides  Amiodarone  Promethazine NSAIDs ⇢ piroxicam, ketoprofen  Metformin  Vemurafenib Pathophysiology  Photosensitivity is caused by an abnormal reaction to a component of the electromagnetic spectrum of sunlight and a chromophore within the skin.  The electromagnetic spectrum has many components, one of them being an invisible ray called ultraviolet radiation (UVR).  UVR has three components:  UVA – longer wavelength rays that cause tanning and suppression of immune reactions in the skin  UVB – short-wavelength rays that cause tan and sunburn  UVC.  Photosensitivity to UVA is the most common photosensitivity.  Properties of UVA are:  more UVA during summer  more UVA during the solar noon, than earlier or later  UVA has lower energy compared with UVB, thus, per photon, UVA causes less damage than UVB to skin cells’ DNA  UVA penetrates through the epidermis into the dermis; damage by UVA is, therefore, deeper within the skin layers compared with UVB.  Porphyria is triggered mainly through exposure to visible light.  Clinical Presentation  Photodermatoses affect sun-exposed areas, eg face, neck, hands, ears. They don’t affect areas that aren’t exposed to the light, eg areas covered by underwear.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Certain areas of the body may only be affected, eg juvenile spring eruption occurs at the top of the ears.  Photodermatoses may only occur after indoor exposure to artificial sources of UVR, eg fluorescent lamps.  Features suggestive of photosensitivity:  summer exacerbation  sharp cut-off between affected skin area and skin covered by clothing/jewellery  sparing of upper eyelid folds  sparing of skin covered by hair  sparing of web spaces between fingers.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  primary photosensitivity, eg polymorphous light eruption  autoimmune photosensitivity, eg lupus erythematosus  photo-exacerbated, eg dermatomyositis  genetic, eg xeroderma pigmentosum  metabolic, eg porphyria cutanea tarda.  Diagnosis/Investigation  History and examination.  Phototests.  Photopatch tests.  Full blood count (FBC).  Anti-nuclear antibodies and other connective tissue antibodies.  Porphyrins in urine, blood and faeces.  LFTs and iron studies in patients suspected of porphyria cutanea tarda.  Management Non-pharmacological  Treatment of the underlying disorder.  Desensitisation:  treating the skin with increasing doses of ultraviolet lights  repeat every spring  it raises the skin’s resistance. Pharmacological  Sun protection:

DR. JAMIL  avoidance of mid-day sun (between 1000 h and 1600 h)  wear protective clothing – long-sleeved shirts and pants, broad brim hats  window films that block ultraviolet radiation for cars and homes  sunscreen can be applied to photosensitive areas; to ensure effectiveness, it needs to be applied frequently (2hourly)  select sunscreen with a high sun protection factor (SPF 50+)  avoiding exposure to artificial UVR sources.  In polymorphic light eruption:  hydroxychloroquine can be given in some cases  a short course of oral steroids may be considered  azathioprine may be considered if the patient is resistant to hydroxychloroquine or oral steroids.  Corticosteroid cream or ointment for the rash.  Vitamin D supplements:  patients with polymorphic light eruption are at increased risk of vitamin D deficiency.  Prognosis  Prognosis depends on the specific disorder.  Patients who are severely light-sensitive may have their quality of life affected. Some people have to work at night and sleep during the day. This leads to an increased risk of depression.  UVA and UVB can cause long-term photodamage. Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI Prescribing Safely (Breastfeeding And Pregnancy) A fetus or breastfed baby may be exposed to drugs due to a lack of maternal understanding and access to ante/postnatal care, additionally, maternal substance abuse can lead to exposure of drugs.  Overview Key Facts  Pregnancy  A fetus or breastfed baby may be exposed to drugs due to a lack of maternal understanding and access to ante/postnatal care, additionally, maternal substance abuse can lead to exposure of drugs.  There is a risk of women of childbearing age taking medications and then becoming pregnant during this period, leaving the growing fetus vulnerable to potentially harmful drug exposure, particularly if the mother has a history of chronic conditions.  There is little drug testing on pregnant and breastfeeding women for ethical reasons but this makes it difficult to advance in terms of effective prescribing for these patients.  In pregnancy, drugs with a molecular weight of < 100 Da can cross the placenta.  Healthcare professionals have a duty to discuss any risks and medication side effects in women of childbearing age who take medications that may be harmful in pregnancy and during lactation.  If a woman of childbearing age is taking a teratogenic drug such as lithium, she must be on an effective long-acting reversible contraception to avoid pregnancy.  Drugs that should be avoided in pregnancy include:  excessive caffeine  excessive alcohol  cocaine  marijuana  topiramate  ACE inhibitors  acebutolol  fluoxetine

DR. JAMIL  sulphonamides  iodine  warfarin  isotretinoin  androgens and diethystilbestrol  lithium  methotrexate  thalidomidpenicillamine  anticonvulsants:  phenytoin  sodium valproate  carbamazepine  trimethadione/paramethadione.  Breastfeeding  Almost all drugs, to some extent, pass into breast milk, but generally, this is less than 1% of a drug.  Clinicians should only prescribe medications while a patient is breastfeeding when absolutely indicated.  Although most drugs are safe to continue taking during lactation, they are often unlicensed for use during this period.  In general, it may be appropriate to prescribe a drug if the maternal risk is greater than the fetal risk.  mothers should be made aware of any negative impacts from not breastfeeding and that stopping breastfeeding abruptly can be difficult and hard to restart.  Before prescribing for a breastfeeding mother these factors should be considered:  mother’s need for the drug  age and maturity of the baby  breast milk volume consumed daily by the baby  any available information on drug safety.  Drugs that are considered safer to prescribe when breastfeeding include those that are or have:  highly protein-bound drugs which are less able to enter the milk  low plasma : milk ratio  shorter half-life as less able to accumulate  drugs known to be safe in pregnancy through experience and/or common use and reports, rather than new drugs  drugs that are available in a children’s formulae are mostly safe for breastfeeding women

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  topical or inhaled drugs, which usually do not reach significant serum levels eg nasal Loratadine for hay fever.  Safe drugs:  poor bioavailability drugs are considered low risk, eg heparin, insulin, gentamicin, third-generation cephalosporins, omeprazole/lansoprazole, inhaled steroids and beta-agonists.  ibuprofen and similar NSAIDs are considered safe  warfarin and heparin are highly protein-bound and thus considered safe  emergency contraception – Levonelle is safe to use when breastfeeding but progesterone may decrease the milk supply momentarily.  Contraindicated drugs while breastfeeding include:  amiodarone  anti-neoplastics  chloramphenicol  ergotamine  iodides  methotrexate  lithium  tetracyclines  cabergoline  pseudoephedrine.  All recreational drugs should be avoided.  cocaine is extremely toxic and after use, breastfeeding should be avoided for 48 hours minimum  methadone that is prescribed and taken correctly is reported as safe.  Some common drugs that can be used while breastfeeding:  paracetamol: often the first-line drug of choice for analgesia, however, caution is recommended in pre-term, low-birth-weight infants  flucloxacillin: found only in trace amounts in breast milk  erythromycin/clarithromycin: only trace amounts found in breast milk, manufacturers advise clarithromycin should be used in breastfeeding women only if the benefits outweigh the risks  fluconazole: only small amounts identified and believed to be too small to be of risk  domperidone and metoclopramide can be prescribed to improve milk supply by increasing the level of prolactin.

Psoriasis An immune-mediated, chronic, multi-system inflammatory disease primarily associated with hyperproliferation of keratinocytes in the epidermis.  Overview Key Facts  An immune-mediated, chronic, multi-system inflammatory disease:  primarily associated with hyperproliferation of keratinocytes in the epidermis  often follows a relapsing/remitting course

JAMIL  plaque psoriasis is the most common form (up to 90% of all psoriasis cases), associated with well-defined, red, disc-like plaques covered by white/silver scales  commonly affected areas include the elbows, knees, back, and scalp.  Approximately 30% of patients have associated joint involvement.  Treatment depends on severity, location of disease, and the impact on the individual. Epidemiology  Psoriasis occurs in 1–2% of the United Kingdom's population.  It affects both genders equally.  It can occur at any age, with peak age ranges of 16–22 and 57– 60 years old.  It is uncommon in childhood. Aetiology  Aetiology is unknown, but multiple genetic factions in combination with environmental factors are thought to be important.  30% of patients with psoriasis have an affected first-degree relative.  If both parents are affected, the risk of a child developing psoriasis is 75%.  There are several psoriasis-susceptibility gene loci (eg PSOR1) and genes involved in interleukin IL-23 signalling, modulation of T-helper Th-2 immune responses (IL-4, IL-13) and activated B-cell (NF-kB) signalling have been identified. Pathophysiology  The understanding of psoriasis has moved from one of a hyperkeratotic disorder of keratinocytes to a dysregulation of the immune system mediated by cytokines.  Th-1, Th-17, and Th-22 cell populations are expanded and stimulated to release inflammatory cytokines, including IL-17, IL-22, and tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α).  Clinical Presentation Chronic Plaque (90% of cases):  well-defined, red, disc-like plaques covered by white/silver scales, which classically affects extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees, and the scalp.
