JAMIL  Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV): psoriasis is more common in patients with HIV; severity may dwindle in later stages.  Endocrine: psoriasis tends to improve during pregnancy and deteriorate in post-partum period.  Drugs: beta-blockers, lithium, antimalarial interferon, and withdrawal of oral steroids may exacerbate psoriasis.  Alcohol  Stress  Smoking: smoking is associated with increased incidence and severity.  Ultraviolet (UV) light: although most patients find UV light beneficial, a small number experience UV light associated flare-ups.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for psoriasis include:  contact dermatitis  seborrhoeic dermatitis  syphilis  lichen planus  lichen simplex  tinea.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is mainly clinical.  Specialist advice should be sought if there is diagnostic uncertainty.  The patient should then be assessed for:  disease severity  impact of physical, social, and psychological wellbeing  psoriatic arthritis  presence of co-morbidities.  Management Non-pharmacological:  Offer support and information tailored to suit individual needs and circumstances so that they can confidently understand the following:  their diagnosis and treatment options  relevant lifestyle risk factors  when and how to use prescribed treatments safely and effectively

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  when and how to seek further general or specialist review  strategies to deal with the impact of psoriasis on physical and social wellbeing.  Refer for specialist advice if there is:  diagnostic uncertainty  severe or extensive psoriasis and/or acute guttate psoriasis  generalised pustular psoriasis or erythroderma (needs same day specialist assessment and treatment)  uncontrolled symptoms despite topical therapy  the patient is a child or young person  a major impact on the patients physical, social or psychological wellbeing. Pharmacological First-line treatment – topical therapy:  Coal tar preparations:  crude coal tar can be useful in thick plaque psoriasis.  Dithranol:  synthetic derivative of anthracene  effective but needs accurate applications as it can burn the surrounding skin and stain clothing.  Vitamin D analogues:  calcipotriol cream/ointment  calcipotriol with betamethasone.  Taraztoene:  a topical retinoid for plaque psoriasis.  Topical steroids:  used alone or in combination or with other topicals for face, genitalia, flexures, hands, feet, and scalp  steroid strength may vary according to severity and body site. Second-line Treatment:  Offer phototherapy or non-biological systemic agents when:  topical therapy alone is unlikely to control disease (eg > 10% body surface area (BSA) or nail disease), and  disease has a significant impact on physical, psychological and/or social wellbeing, or  there is significant functional impairment, or  there are high levels of distress (including severe nail involvement, high-impact site of disease).

DR. JAMIL  Non-biologics may be indicated when phototherapy is ineffective; however, it cannot be used if there is a rapid relapse following phototherapy. Phototherapy:  Ultraviolet B-rays (UVB) narrowband – well established and effective.  Psoralen and ultraviolet A radiation (PUVA) use necessitates the need for protective eyewear and is associated with an increased risk of skin cancers.  Non-biological systemic treatment:  Risk and/or benefits must be weighed up when considering prescribing the following:  methotrexate is a first-line non-biological systemic treatment. It blocks DNA syntheses by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase and is administered once-weekly either orally or by subcutaneous injection. Risks of anaemia/pancytopenia/nausea are reduced with folic acid supplementation. There is a risk of liver fibrosis with long-term use. The serological marker for fibrosis procollagen-3 N-terminal peptide (P3NP) should be measured 3-monthly  ciclosporin is a first-line non-biological systemic treatment where rapid/short-term disease control is required, eg a flare/palmar pustulosis, or when conception is being considered. It inhibits T-lymphocyte transcription of IL-2. Side-effects of ciclosporin include renal toxicity and hypertension  retinoids, for example, acitretin, used alone and/or in combination with UVB/PUVA, if methotrexate or ciclosporin is not appropriate or ineffective. Should be avoided in women with childbearing potential due to teratogenic affects. Mucocutaneous side-effects are common, triglyceride level elevation can occur and should be monitored. Third-line treatment – biologic agents:  Biologics are considered for patients with severe disease. Strict eligibility criteria are in place, indications include:  no response to standard first- and second-line treatments  intolerance to other standard first- or second-line treatments  other treatments contraindicated  severe life-threatening disease  for biological treatments, severity scores such as psoriasis area and severity (PASI) score and dermatology life quality index (DLQI) must be at least ten.  Currently, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) approve biologic target TNF-a or the interleukin pathways:  etanercept: human protein fusion of the TNF receptor that acts as a TNF-a inhibitor. Delivered via subcutaneous injection

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  adalimumab: a human monoclonal antibody that binds to TNF-a. Delivered via subcutaneous injection  infliximab: a chimeric monoclonal antibody that binds to TNF-a. Delivered via infusion  ustekinumab: a human monoclonal antibody that targets IL-12 and IL-23. Delivered subcutaneously.  Other biologics are currently under development.  Prognosis  The condition often has a relapsing/remitting course and is associated with significant functional, psychological, and social morbidity for many patients.  As a systemic condition, inflammatory processes involved are associated with the development of numerous co-morbidities as well as reduced life expectancy.  Associations with psoriasis:  major adverse cardiac events (MACE): studies show that psoriasis sufferers have a 53% increased incidence of MACE (myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiac death). Risk is also increased due to the strong association of the metabolic syndrome (hypertension, obesity, diabetes, dyslipidaemia) with psoriasis  venous thromboembolism: especially with severe psoriasis  arthropathy: psoriatic arthritis occurs in approximately 20% of patients with skin psoriasis. There are several different forms including distal interphalangeal joint disease, arthritis mutilans, sacroiliitis, psoriatic spondylitis  gout: due to deposition of urate crystals  malabsorption: due to associations with Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis  lymphoma: approximately threefold increased incidence with psoriasis  skin malignancy: non-melanoma type.  Other Other relevant information: Skin Disorder Causes of Nail Changes Associated with Skin Disorders  Psoriasis  Onycholysis, nail pitting, hyperkeratosis, pustule, and occasional loss of nail  Fungal  Discoloration, onycholysis, and thickening of the nail

DR. JAMIL  Bacterial  Usually due to staphylococcal infections – pseudomonas infections give nails a green discolouration  Lichen planus  Nail changes occur in 10% of cases, with thinning of nail plate and longitudinal linear depressions – occasionally destruction of the nail (pterygium)  Alopecia areata  Pitting, thickening, and ridging of the nail (sandpaper nail) are seen  Dermatitis  Coarse pits, cross-ridging, and onycholysis may be seen  Causes of the Koebner phenomenon:  psoriasis  lichen planus  vitiligo  viral warts  molluscum contagiosum.  Causes of erythroderma:  psoriasis  eczema  mycosis fungoides  adverse drug reactions  underlying malignancy  pityriasis rubra pilaris. Psychosexual Dysfunction Sexual dysfunction can occur due to a number of organic or psychosexual reason, or a combination of both.  Overview Key Facts  Sexual dysfunction can occur due to a number of organic or psychosexual reason, or a combination of both.  Sexual dysfunction can be primary, ie no history of normal function, or secondary, ie a history of normal function.  Sexual dysfunction can occur at various stages of sexual intercourse including initiation, arousal, penetration, or orgasm.  Psychosexual dysfunction may be defined as persistent impairment in sexual functioning, response, or enjoyment which is not caused by underlying disease.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Common examples of psychosexual disorders in men include premature ejaculation and erectile dysfunction, and in women include anorgasmia and hypoactive sexual desire.  Causes of psychosexual dysfunction can include psychological, environmental, physical, and sexual partner factors; a comprehensive sexual history which explores these areas should be taken to establish causes for sexual dysfunction.  Management includes excluding organic and drug related causes, pharmacological drugs such as sildenafil as well as non-pharmacological methods such as psychosexual therapy which is the mainstay of treatment. Epidemiology  The epidemiology of psychosexual dysfunction is difficult to quantify.  The most common sexual dysfunction disorders are erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation in men and anorgasmia and hypoactive sexual desire in women. Aetiology  Organic causes:  vascular, eg cardiovascular disease and diabetes  neurological, eg multiple sclerosis, stroke, and spinal cord lesions  anatomical, eg Peyronie’s disease  drugs, eg beta blockers, antidepressants, and anticonvulsants.  Psychogenic causes:  psychosexual:  relationship/partner issues  stress  sexual performance anxiety  fear of interruption  physical discomfort  tiredness  recent child birth  psychiatric:  anxiety  depression  psychosis  substance misuse.  Clinical Presentation

DR. JAMIL Sexual dysfunction type Women Men Sexual desire Hypoactive sexual desire (F > M) Sexual aversion Sexual pain  Dyspareunia Orgasm Vaginismus Anorgasmia Premature ejaculation Ejaculatory impotence Sexual arousal  Genital response failure  Erectile dysfunction  Diagnosis/Investigation  Sexual history should include:  number of partners  frequency of sexual intercourse  sexual preferences  contraception  history of physical or sexual abuse.  History suggesting psychogenic causes:  early morning erections  major life events  early collapse of erection  sudden onset of symptoms.  Management Non-pharmacological  Reassurance and advice.  Psychosexual therapy – is often the mainstay of treatment and can be tailored to the specific form of sexual dysfunction experienced.  Couple therapy may be advised.  Lifestyle advice, eg losing weight, stopping smoking, and reducing alcohol intake.  Management of any underlying psychological issue – for example is there co-existing depression – if so, treat as for depression. Pharmacological  Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (eg sildenafil) can be tried in primary care for men with erectile dysfunction, can be very effective, and may only be need to be used short-term.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Other treatments for erectile dysfunction (requires secondary care input and are more beneficial for patients who also have an underlying organic cause):  Intracavernosal injections of prostaglandin E1 (eg alprostadil).  Testosterone replacement.  Vacuum erection devices.  Penile prosthetic implants.  Penile microrevascularisation  Dapoxetine is a short-acting selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitor (SSRI) which is licensed for use in the treatment of premature ejaculation that is causing significant psychological distress.  Prognosis  Overall there is good prognosis for psychosexual dysfunction, especially with psychosexual erectile dysfunction where a combination of drug therapy and psychosexual therapy can be used to cure the condition. Salicylate Overdose Salicylate toxicity is usually caused by aspirin.  Overview Key Facts  Salicylate toxicity is usually caused by aspirin.  As salicylates are metabolised, uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation occurs in the mitochondria, leading to decreased production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which leads to an increase in anaerobic metabolism and build-up of lactic acid, causing metabolic acidosis.  There is also direct stimulation of the medulla which causes the respiratory alkalosis seen early in the clinical course, usually before metabolic acidosis.  When the blood pH becomes more acidic, more salicylate is present in its non-ionised form, which crosses the blood–brain barrier into the central nervous system (CNS) more easily causing neurological symptoms.  Symptoms of mild poisoning include nausea and vomiting, dizziness and tinnitus.  More severe symptoms are seen with higher serum salicylate concentrations, including cardiac arrhythmias, pulmonary or cerebral oedema, neurological signs (coma, seizures, confusion), renal failure and cardiac failure.  Diagnosis is based on an urgent plasma salicylate concentration:

DR. JAMIL  taken at least two hours after overdose in symptomatic patients  taken at least four hours after overdose in asymptomatic patients.  Patients should also have an urgent blood gas to assess acidbase status.  Initial investigations should also include full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&Es), liver function tests (LFTs), blood glucose, a coagulation screen and a toxicology screen (to assess for mixed overdose).  Activated charcoal and gastric lavage may be beneficial based on the time of presentation and amount of salicylate ingested.  Urinary and serum alkalinisation are the mainstay of management.  Manage hypokalaemia, hypotension/dehydration, seizures, hyperpyrexia and pulmonary oedema aggressively.  Haemodialysis should be used in severe poisoning if:  salicylate concentration > 900 mg/l  salicylate concentration > 700 mg/l with metabolic acidosis  coma  consider if salicylate concentration > 700 mg/l.  Most deaths occur in patients with a blood salicylate concentration of > 700 mg/l. Epidemiology  Aspirin is widely available over-the-counter which makes both intentional and accidental overdose more prevalent. Aetiology  Toxicity usually occurs following an overdose of aspirin.  Methyl salicylate (found in ‘wintergreen oil’) is applied topically and is rapidly absorbed through the skin; this can also cause systemic toxicity.  Fatal intoxication results after ingestion of 10–30 g salicylic acid in adults and 3 g in children.  The usual therapeutic range is 10–30 mg/dl and toxicity occurs at levels above 40 mg/dl. Pathophysiology  As salicylates are metabolised, uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation occurs in the mitochondria, leading to decreased production of ATP, which leads to an increase in anaerobic metabolism.  Anaerobic metabolism leads to an increase in lactic acid levels causing metabolic acidosis.  Hyperventilation is caused by direct stimulation of the medulla and is the cause of the respiratory alkalosis seen early in the clinical course, usually before the development of metabolic acidosis.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Hyperventilation tends to worsen when metabolic acidosis develops, in an attempt to blow off carbon dioxide and compensate for the acidosis.  When the blood pH becomes more acidic, more salicylate is present in its non-ionised form, which crosses the blood–brain barrier into the CNS more easily causing neurological symptoms.  Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase enzyme results in decreased synthesis of prostaglandins, prostacyclin and thromboxanes. This causes platelet dysfunction and gastric mucosal injury leading to gastrointestinal bleeding.  Stimulation of the chemoreceptor zone in the medulla causes nausea and vomiting.  Clinical Presentation Severity Features Mild poisoning  Salicylate concentration usually < 300 mg/l  Nausea and vomiting  Tinnitus  Dizziness Moderate poisoning  Salicylate concentration usually 300–700 mg/l  Sweating  Restlessness  Tachypnoea  Bounding pulse Severe poisoning  Salicylate concentration usually > 700 mg/l  Cardiac arrhythmias  Pulmonary oedema  Cerebral oedema  Seizures  Confusion  Hyperpyrexia  Cardiac failure  Coma  Renal failure  Blood gases may show a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap due to:  hyperventilation due to direct stimulation of the respiratory centre (respiratory alkalosis)  accumulation of lactic acid and fatty acid metabolites due to the uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation (metabolic acidosis).  Respiratory alkalosis usually appears first in isolation before metabolic acidosis develops.

DR. JAMIL  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  ethylene glycol toxicity  sepsis  iron toxicity  anxiety disorders  theophylline toxicity  organophosphate poisoning  diabetic ketoacidosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Urgent plasma salicylate concentration:  take at least two hours after overdose in symptomatic patients  take at least four hours after overdose in asymptomatic patients  usually repeated 2-hourly initially.  Patients should also have an urgent blood gas to assess acid– base status.  Initial investigations should also include:  FBC  U&Es; potassium should be monitored closely  LFTs  blood glucose  coagulation  full toxicology screen to assess for mixed overdose.  Management  ABCDE assessment.  Maintain airway:  intubation should be avoided unless respiratory failure, as the loss of hyperventilatory drive can lead to decompensation.  Activated charcoal if the patient presents within one hour having ingested > 125 mg/kg salicylate (airway must be protected):  use of activated charcoal after one hour may be beneficial in large overdoses.  Consider gastric lavage if > 500 mg/kg has been ingested and the patient presents within one hour.  Intravenous (IV) fluids and dextrose.  IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise urine and serum:

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  maintain urinary pH above 7.5 to promote salicylate excretion.  Do not use acetazolamide as it can worsen metabolic acidosis and increase the risk of neurological complications.  Treat hypokalaemia aggressively as bicarbonate therapy can also worsen hypokalaemia.  Haemodialysis should be used in severe poisoning if:  salicylate concentration > 900 mg/l  salicylate concentration > 700 mg/l with metabolic acidosis  coma  consider if salicylate concentration > 700 mg/l.  Further treatment is centred around the patient’s individual presentation (for example treatment for seizures, hyperpyrexia or pulmonary oedema).  Prognosis  Most deaths occur in patients with a blood salicylate concentration of > 700 mg/l.  Fatal poisoning is more likely in patients:  > 70 years old  who develop neurological symptoms (confusion, agitation, coma, seizures)  with severe metabolic acidosis  with pulmonary oedema  with hyperpyrexia. Self-Harm And Suicide Deliberate self-harm is defined as an intentional act of self-injury or poisoning as an expression of emotional distress.  Overview Key Facts  Deliberate self-harm is defined as an intentional act of selfinjury or poisoning as an expression of emotional distress.  It may be caused by:  behaviours, eg self-cutting  overdose (prescription or over-the-counter medications)  poisoning.  Self-harm can be, but is not usually, an attempt at suicide.

DR. JAMIL  It is often used as an attempt to try and maintain control in stressful situations, eg bullying, abuse, etc, or a way to outlet emotional distress.  Self-harm is common, with a lifetime prevalence of 5–6%, especially in younger women.  Risk factors include mental health conditions and lower socioeconomic status.  It may be managed in the short term by preventing absorption of poisons and recurrence of self-cutting.  There is an increased risk of suicide in people who self-harm.  Suicide is defined as a fatal act of self-harm committed with the intention of ending one’s own life.  It can be associated with a long-standing history of suicidal ideation or self-harm.  It is the most common cause of death in men aged 30 and under.  The most common methods of suicide include hanging, strangulation, suffocation and poisoning.  Risk factors include previous attempts of suicide, physical health problems and active mental illness.  Suicidal ideation and threats, or attempts of suicide, should be managed by assessing risk and preventing further attempts using a biopsychosocial management model. Epidemiology  Self-harm is common, with a lifetime prevalence of 5–6%.  It is most common among younger women.  It increases the likelihood that a person will die by suicide by 50–100 times compared with the general population.  There were 5821 suicides in the United Kingdom (UK) in 2017, equating to 10.1 deaths per 100 000 (15.5 male deaths per 100 000 and 4.9 female deaths per 100 000).  Suicide is the most common cause of death in men aged 30 and under.  The highest suicide rate is seen in men aged 45–49 years.  The most common methods are hanging, strangulation, suffocation and poisoning. Aetiology  Associated mental health conditions include:  borderline personality disorder  depression  bipolar disorder  schizophrenia  drug misuse  alcohol abuse

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  eating disorders.  Risk factors include:  domestic violence  lower socioeconomic status  ethnicity – particularly South-Asian women.  Clinical Presentation  Red flags must always be assessed for, and include:  a sense of hopelessness  feeling of entrapment  well-formed plans, eg suicide notes, changes to a will  perception of no social support  distressing psychotic phenomena  significant pain and/or chronic illness.  Management  In most circumstances, patients who have acutely self-poisoned should be referred to the nearest Emergency Department in order to receive appropriate medical treatment as early as possible.  Physical effects of self-harm should be prioritised, such as adequate anaesthesia during suturing.  Following this, patients will require psychiatric assessment focusing on the immediate risk of suicide and requirement for admission, management of ongoing risk, and management of other relevant medical, psychiatric and social issues.  Components of the risk assessment and care plan may include:  actions to prevent further self-harm or suicide attempts  involving mode-deactivation therapy (MDT) to identify risk factors, including support services and form a crisis plan  checking the patient's support network and if the patient is willing to involve them in care  limiting access to possible lethal means to attempt selfharm  maintain regular follow-up.  Specific treatment may include:  addressing co-morbidities  medication, eg antidepressants, mood stabilisers  counselling and information regarding support groups  cognitive behavioural therapy  dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT)  detainment under the Mental Health Act for high-risk individuals.

DR. JAMIL  Prognosis  There is a high risk of self-harm repetition and suicide in patients with long-standing psychosocial problems.  Acts of deliberate self-harm increase the likelihood that a person will die by suicide by 50–100 times compared with the general population.  This is prevented by focusing on protective factors such as:  parental and/or partner support  promotion of healthy lifestyle factors, such as drug and alcohol avoidance  prescribing medications for the patient and relatives at home that are the least dangerous in overdose. Serotonin Syndrome Serotonin syndrome is a cluster of symptoms and signs that occur usually when more than one drug is taken that increases the concentration of serotonin at the synaptic level.  Overview Key Facts  Serotonin syndrome is a cluster of symptoms and signs that occur usually when more than one drug is taken that increases the concentration of serotonin at the synaptic level.  It is an uncommon but potentially fatal complication of selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and selective noradrenaline re-uptake uptake inhibitors (SNRIs) especially when combined with other serotonin-enhancing agents, including:  tricyclic antidepressants  monoamine oxidase inhibitors  St John's wort (hypericum).  Tramadol also has effects on serotonin and noradrenalin and can cause serotonin syndrome, especially when in combination with other medications.  The condition can also be caused by an overdose of SSRIs.  When changing from one potential causative drug to another, a washout period is often required to prevent the syndrome from occurring.  Symptoms usually occur in close proximity to the initiation of one of these drugs, often over a 24-hour period.  Severity can range from person to person, from mild to potentially life-threatening.  Characteristic symptoms include hypomania, agitation, drowsiness, myoclonus, hyperthermia and pronounced

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI autonomic symptoms such as tachycardia and labile blood pressure (the ‘happy drunk’ state).  The diagnosis is made on clinical grounds using the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria.  To fulfil these criteria a patient must have taken a serotonergic agent and meet one of the following conditions:  spontaneous clonus  inducible clonus plus agitation or sweating  ocular clonus plus agitation or sweating  hypertonia plus temperature > 3 8°C plus ocular or inducible clonus.  Serotonin syndrome is often misdiagnosed as neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), but the two can readily be distinguished on the basis of history, examination findings and clinical course:  NMS develops over days to weeks, compared with over 24 hours in serotonin syndrome  serotonin syndrome is characterised by neuromuscular hyper-reactivity (tremor, hyper-reflexia, myoclonus), while NMS involves sluggish neuromuscular responses (rigidity, bradyreflexia)  hyper-reflexia and myoclonus are rare in NMS.  Treatment initially is to stop the causative drug(s) and supportive therapy to prevent complications such as kidney disease caused by rhabdomyolysis.  Cyproheptadine and propranolol have been used as they block serotonin.  Patients may need to be managed in the Intensive Care Unit and treated for hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney disease and disseminated intravascular coagulation.  Severe cases may require a general anaesthetic and muscle paralysis and dantrolene sodium has been used, which reduces calcium efflux from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, although more recent data no longer support its role in managing the condition.  In cases of hyperthermia, supportive measures and standard treatments include muscle relaxants, cooling and intubation. Epidemiology Actual incidence levels are unclear as the condition is thought to be under-diagnosed. Aetiology  Drugs that have been associated with serotonin syndrome include the following - they may have been used in isolation, in combination (most common) or as intentional or unintentional overdose:  SSRIs  serotonin and norepinephrine re-uptake inhibitors  bupropion

DR. JAMIL  tricyclic antidepressants  monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)  analgesics such as tramadol, codeine, fentanyl and oxycodone  lithium  anti-emetics such as ondansetron  anti-migraine medication such as triptans  drugs of misuse - most commonly LSD, ecstasy, cocaine and amphetamines  herbal/over the counter medications - especially St. John's wort  linezolid  ritonavir. Pathophysiology  Serotonin is a neurotransmitter that is produced peripherally by the intestinal chromaffin cells and centrally by nuclei found in the lower pons/upper brain stem.  Serotonin has numerous functions including regulation of:  emotional states  temperature  pain  cardiovascular functions  the central nervous system  muscle tone of vasculature and the gastrointestinal tract.  Serotonin syndrome is caused by increased serotonin activity.  This is caused by the causative drug/drugs increasing serotonin production and/or reducing serotonin metabolism.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms and signs usually occur within hours of taking the causative drug, a dose increase or overdose.  Severity can vary from mild to potentially life-threatening.  Early features include:  tremor  akathisia (restlessness)  diarrhoea.  Followed by:  hypomania  agitation  drowsiness/coma  myoclonus

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  hyperthermia  seizures  pronounced autonomic symptoms such as:  tachycardia  high blood pressure  sweating  mydriasis  hyperactive bowel sounds.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  neuroleptic malignant syndrome (usually comes on over a period of weeks rather than hours)  recreational drug side-effects  tetanus  other forms of poisoning  thyrotoxicosis  infection  delerium.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is predominantly clinical – based on history including drug history and enquiring about over-the-counter and herbal medications; and examination of the patient.  The diagnosis is confirmed using the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria.  To fulfil these criteria a patient must have taken a serotonergic agent and meet one of the following conditions:  spontaneous clonus  inducible clonus plus agitation or sweating  ocular clonus plus agitation or sweating  hypertonia plus temperature > 38 °C plus ocular or inducible clonus.  Patients require monitoring of renal function, with urea and electrolytes measurement, as well as a toxicology screen.  Tests may be required to exclude other differentials, such as a computed tomography (CT) head and infection screen.  Management  The initial step is to stop the causative drug(s), followed by supportive therapy to prevent complications such as kidney disease caused by rhabdomyolysis.

DR. JAMIL  Further management depends on severity; severe symptoms or patients who have taken both a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) and SSRI need hospital admission.  Supportive measurements include:  intravenous (IV) fluids  benzodiazepines to manage agitation.  In patients with relatively recent ingestion of the causative agent/overdose, activated charcoal may be useful.  Cyproheptadine may be of use as the mechanism of action is to block serotonin.  Patients may need to be managed in ICU and treated for hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney disease and disseminated intravascular coagulation.  Severe cases of hyperthermia (temperatures above 40.5 °C) require a general anaesthetic, muscle paralysis and ventilation.  In cases of hyperthermia, supportive measures also include cooling methods to prevent disseminated intravascular coagulation, rhabdomyolysis and organ failure.  Prognosis  Prognosis varies between individuals; in some patients, symptoms will be mild, while in others the condition can be fatal due to complications.  Most complications of serotonin syndrome are due to hyperthermia; these include:  metabolic acidosis  rhabdomyolysis and subsequent acute kidney injury  disseminated intravascular coagulation.  Other complications include seizures, pneumonia (due to aspiration) and respiratory failure.  In patients for whom the condition is fatal (eg patients with severe symptoms in which diagnosis is delayed or who remain untreated), death often occurs within 24 hours of onset of symptoms.  In patients who recover from the condition, there are usually no lasting effects once serotonin levels return to normal (usually within 24 hours in mild cases). Stevens-Johnson Syndrome And Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis are rare but serious skin conditions characterized by a severe reaction that causes the top layer of skin to die and shed, often triggered by

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI medications or infections, leading to widespread blistering, skin peeling, and potential life-threatening complications.  Overview Key Facts  Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are similar conditions with TEN being the more severe form.  They are now both thought to be variants of the same condition.  Both conditions result in skin blistering and mucosal involvement.  They are rare but serious immune-complex mediated hypersensitivity conditions and should be classed as a dermatological emergency.  The conditions are usually caused by an adverse reaction to drugs antibiotics in 40% of cases), but can occasionally be triggered by infection.  There is a flu-like prodrome, followed by a red/purple rash which then blisters/forms bullae, affecting the skin, mucous membranes, eyes and genitalia.  The conditions requires hospital admission; severe cases may require admission to intensive care or a specialist burns unit.  Management aims to identify and remove/treat the underlying cause wherever possible, limit and manage symptoms and prevent complications.  This may include a combination of analgesia, fluids, corticosteroids and antibiotics.  Mortality rates for SJS is around 10% and at least 30% in TEN, however mortality can be up to 90% in TEN depending on severity as assessed by the SCORETEN system.  Mortality is most often due to electrolyte imbalance, sepsis and multiorgan failure.  Both conditions are also associated with long term residual effects of the skin, nails, hair, eyes and mucous membranes. Epidemiology  1-2 cases per million/year.  Incidence is higher in patients with HIV (up to 100 times more common).  Incidence is also higher in females. Aetiology  Triggers are most commonly drugs (80%), or infection (particularly in children). Drugs:  Allopurinol  Cephalosporin

DR. JAMIL  NSAID  Phenytoin  Carbamazepine  Sulfa group antibiotics  Sulfasalazine  Sertraline  Antivirals, eg Nevirapine. Infections:  Herpes simplex  Respiratory infections eg Mycoplasma pneumoniae  Mumps  Epstein-Barr virus  Coxsackie virus  Influenza strains. Risk factors for developing the condition include:  Previous history of SJS.  Family history of SJS.  Genetic predisposition – ie HLA b1502 or HLA B1508 genes increases this risk of developing the condition after taking certain medications (Screening for these genes before initiating treatment with certain drugs associated with the condition may help prevent cases from occurring. Pathophysiology  The condition is caused by a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.  The exact mechanisms are complex and not fully understood however is thought to involve the Fas-Fas ligand pathway of apoptosis and granule-mediated exocytosis resulting in cell death.  Clinical Presentation  Early flu-like symptoms: fever, sore throat, headache, arthralgia, malaise.  Followed by mucocutaneous lesions < 10% of body surface: red, painful macules.  Oral ulcers.  Systemic symptoms include:  mucopurulent productive cough  dysuria  painful red eye, conjunctivitis, blepharitis and photophobia.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Signs include:  skin lesions most commonly found on palms and soles, trunk, hands and extensors (but may appear anywhere)  initially the rash starts as macules, which become papules, vesicles bullae and widespread erythema. Bullae may then rupture and lead to superimposed infection  target lesions are typical  there may be areas of central necrosis  positive Nikolsky sign – pressure to skin causes blistering within minutes to hours  oral/mucosal oedema, blistering, ulceration and necrolysis  balanitis or erosive vaginitis  conjunctivitis and corneal ulceration  mucosal involvement. JAMIL  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses for SJS and TEN are as follows:  pemphigus vulgaris  bullous pemphigoid  erythema multiforme  burns (chemical/thermal)  phototoxic eruption  scalded skin syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is primarily based on history and examination findings and can be confirmed with skin biopsy.  Skin detachment is:  less than 10% of total body surface area (BSA) with widespread macules or targets in SJS  between 10-30% with widespread macules or targets in overlap SJS/TEN

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  greater than 30 BSA with widespread macules or targets in TEN, OR greater than 10% with large epidermal sheets and no purpuric macules.  Electrolytes, blood glucose and bicarbonate should be monitored to assess severity and guide rehydration management.  The SCORTEN system predicts mortality for SJS/TEN using several clinical parameters and should be done within 24 hours of presentation.  One point is scored for each of the following:  age > 40 years  presence of malignancy  heart rate > 120 beats/min  epidermal detachment > 10% of body surface  serum urea > 10 mmol/l  serum glucose > 14 mmol/l  bicarbonate < 20 mmol/l  SCORTEN of 0-1 is associated with around 3% mortality, SCORTEN of 5 or greater is associated with 90% mortality.  Management  Resuscitation and support with ABCDE assessment.  Withdraw any potential triggering agent eg drugs.  Intravenous (IV) fluids.  Patients with > 10% BSA affected require transfer to burn centre/ITU.  Daily ophthalmology review with eye care.  Mouth care.  Emollients and dressings.  Lung care- consider physiotherapy, aspiration, aerosols.  Consider catheterisation.  Manage complications, consider thromboprophylaxis and psychiatric support.  Antibiotics should be added if there are signs of superimposed infection.  Surgical intervention with debridement may be required.  Treatments such as cyclophosphamide, intravenous immunoglobulins and anti-TNF α antibodies may also be of benefit.  Prognosis  Mortality in SJS is 5-12% and in TEN is estimated to be greater than 30% as a result of sepsis, electrolyte imbalances or multiorgan failure.

DR. JAMIL  Mortality correlates with SCORTEN score and is greater than 90% in those with a score of 5 or greater.  Long term sequalae is associated with both conditions but can occur in up to 50% of those patients surviving TEN.  This includes:  permanent skin changes including pigmentation  scarring  temperature sensitivity  nail dystrophy  eye issues including photophobia, visual impairment and Meibomian gland dysfunction  persistent erosions of mucus membranes  vaginal, anal and urethral strictures  hair loss. Syndrome Of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion is the overproduction of antidiuretic hormone or vasopressin causing the body to retain water.  Overview Key Facts  Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is the overproduction of antidiuretic hormone or vasopressin (ADH) causing the body to retain water.  In the absence of hypovolaemia, oedema or diuretics, ADH is inappropriately secreted from the pituitary gland or an ectopic source despite the serum osmolality being low.  This causes a dilutional hyponatraemia.  It occurs secondary to many underlying causes such as malignancy and neurological disorders.  Diagnosis requires:  concentrated urine (sodium (Na+) > 20 mmol/l)  hyperosmolality > 100 mosmol/kg  hyponatraemia (plasma Na+ < 125 mmol/l)  absence of hypovolaemia, oedema, or diuretics.  Management is dependant on underlying cause, degree of hyponatraemia, patient symptoms, and acuteness of onset.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Rapid correction of sodium levels can lead to central pontine myelinolysis.  Commonly misdiagnosed. Epidemiology  Hyponatraemia is the most common electrolyte abnormality faced by doctors in practice, both in the United Kingdom and the United States of America.  There is no sex difference. Aetiology  Many causes (not exhaustive):  malignancy: small-cell lung carcinoma, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, lymphoma  central nervous system (CNS) disorders: meningoencephalitis, abscess, stroke, head injury, subarachnoid haemorrhage  respiratory diseases: tuberculosis, pneumonia, abscess  drugs: opiates, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)  endocrine: hypothyroidism. Pathophysiology  ADH (or vasopressin) is synthesised in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary.  It is released in response to high plasma osmolality and acts on the distal tubule and renal collecting ducts to increase water permeability.  This would result in more water reabsorption and hence the urine becomes more concentrated.  ADH, when inappropriately secreted by the posterior pituitary gland or due to ectopic source such as small-cell lung carcinoma, would result in dilutional hyponatraemia (blood vessels having too much fluid reabsorbed), concentrated urine and low osmolality.  Clinical Presentation  Hyponatraemia can give a confusing clinical picture because a mild sudden drop in the sodium can cause significant symptoms, while severe chronic hyponatraemia can be asymptomatic due to adaptation by the cerebrum.  However, the following signs and symptoms may occur:  mild – anorexia, nausea, malaise, and vomiting  moderate – personality change, muscle cramps and fatigue, confusion, and ataxia  severe – reduced Glasgow coma scale score and seizures.

DR. JAMIL  Differential Diagnosis  Broad differential diagnoses depending on the signs and symptoms (not exhaustive):  alcohol withdrawal  other electrolytes abnormalities  Addison’s disease (especially if serum potassium (K+) is high)  underlying causes (eg lung carcinoma, stroke, and head injury).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood tests:  urea and electrolytes (U&E):  hyponatraemia (plasma Na+ < 125 mmol/l), but first must make sure that the sample is not taken from the site of an infusion to avoid laboratory error  taking blood from a site which has and/or is receiving sodium chloride fluids will cause falsely raised sodium.  serum K+ – if high, consider Addison’s disease  thyroid function test to exclude hypothyroidism  confirming SIADH by paired results of both serum and urine samples:  serum osmolality < 275 mOsm/kg  urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg and Na+ > 30 mmol/l.  Other tests (eg imaging) depends on the likely underlying cause. For example, a brain computed tomography is needed in patients with confusion or altered consciousness.  Management Non-pharmacological Management is dependent on numerous factors, including the underlying cause, the level of hyponatraemia, acuteness of onset and patient symptoms:  Fluid restriction (500-1000 ml/day for adults) with urine output monitoring.  Manage the underlying cause appropriately with endocrinology and multidisciplinary team involvement. Pharmacological  Rapid correction of suspected acute hyponatraemia in the emergency setting should be carried out with caution due to risk of central pontine myelinolysis (CPM).

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Rapid correction is reserved for patient with moderate to severe symptoms of acute onset, the ideal is to raise serum sodium without causing neurological sequaliea.  Hypertonic saline.  Loop diuretics with saline.  Demeclocycline – blocks ADH and induces partial nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.  Vasopressin receptor antagonist (eg tolvaptan).  Prognosis  Prognosis correlates with the underlying cause, severity of hyponatraemia, and rates of correction.  Patients presenting with neurological symptoms or severe hyponatraemia, even if asymptomatic, may progress into developing a lifelong neurological disability.  Rapid correction of Na+, especially those who do not have symptoms, may lead to the development of permanent neurological disability from central pontine myelinolysis. Theophylline Toxicity Theophylline toxicity occurs when the levels of the medication theophylline in the blood become too high, leading to symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, rapid heart rate, seizures and in severe cases, can be life-threatening.  Overview Key Facts  Theophylline has a very narrow therapeutic window.  It is used in the treatment of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).  It acts as a phosphodiesterase inhibitor and adenosine receptor antagonist.  Side effects of theophylline at therapeutic doses may include:  anxiety  arrhythmias  diarrhoea  dizziness  gastrointestinal discomfort/reflux  headache  hyperuricaemia  nausea and vomiting  palpitations

DR. JAMIL  seizure  skin reactions  sleep disorders  tremor  urinary disorders.  In toxicity, the onset of symptoms may be delayed for up to 24 hours if sustained-release preparations have been taken.  Symptoms of toxicity include vomiting, tachycardia, arrhythmias, tachypnoea, headache and convulsions.  Blood tests may show hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia, hypercalcaemia and metabolic acidosis.  Clinical features are the best indicator of diagnosis and treatment should not be delayed while awaiting theophylline concentration.  Treatment includes activated charcoal as soon as possible and then treatment of symptoms (eg cardiac arrhythmias, electrolyte disturbances, convulsions).  Patients may require ventilation or haemodialysis in severe cases.  Chronic toxicity in older patients is particularly dangerous, due to the high risk of significant cardiac arrhythmias. Epidemiology  Toxicity is more likely in patients with underlying liver disease (as theophylline is metabolised by cytochrome P450 enzymes).  Toxicity (especially chronic) is more common in older patients. Aetiology  Theophylline has a very narrow therapeutic window.  Toxicity may occur as a result of:  intentional overdose  inadequate monitoring  if the metabolism of theophylline is altered by:  physiological stress  medications that inhibit the action of cytochrome P450 (which will reduce the metabolism of theophylline)  liver disease  congestive heart failure causing hepatic congestion. Pathophysiology  Theophylline is metabolised in the liver.  The plasma-theophylline concentration is increased in heart failure, hepatic impairment, and in viral infections.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Effects of theophylline toxicity can be explained by the two primary mechanisms of action:  adenosine receptor antagonism:  bronchodilatation  tachycardia and arrhythmias  cerebral vasoconstriction and seizures  phosphodiesterase inhibition at toxic levels (increased adrenergic activity and catecholamine release):  cardiac arrhythmias  metabolic acidosis  hypokalaemia  hyperglycaemia.  In acute theophylline toxicity, catecholamine levels can be 4– 8× higher than normal.  Clinical Presentation  The onset of symptoms may be delayed for up to 24 hours if sustained-release preparations have been taken.  Symptoms of acute toxicity include:  gastrointestinal:  nausea and vomiting, occasionally haematemesis  abdominal pain  pancreatitis.  cardiovascular:  tachycardia  hypotension  sustained ectopics  cardiac arrhythmias  myocardial ischaemia/infarction.  respiratory:  hyperventilation  tachypnoea  acute lung injury.  neurological:  agitation  anxiety  headache  convulsions  coarse tremors.  renal:

DR. JAMIL  rhabdomyolysis can lead to renal failure.  metabolic:  hypokalaemia (worsened by vomiting)  hyperglycaemia  hypercalcaemia  hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia  metabolic acidosis or respiratory alkalosis.  Symptoms of chronic toxicity:  arrhythmias and convulsions more common than in acute toxicity  metabolic acidosis, hyperglycaemia and hypokalaemia are less common than in acute toxicity.  Differential Diagnosis  β2 adrenergic agonist toxicity – seizure and cardiac arrhythmias are rare.  Cocaine and amphetamine toxicity – hypertension and hyperthermia are commonly seen.  Iron toxicity – neurological complications are less likely.  Salicylate toxicity – respiratory alkalosis is commonly seen.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Clinical features are the best indicator of possible theophylline toxicity.  Theophylline concentration is not always rapidly available and treatment should not be delayed while waiting for results.  Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypophosphataemia, hypercalcaemia and hyperglycaemia.  Arterial or venous blood gas may show metabolic acidosis.  Management  Monitor closely; the patient may need ventilation and ICUlevel care.  Activated charcoal as soon as possible:  even late administration of activated charcoal may be of benefit  in severe poisoning, doses of activated charcoal may be repeated.  Serial 12-lead ECGs.  Repeat theophylline levels every 2–4 hours until peak concentration reached.  Correct electrolyte abnormalities and monitor closely with regular urea and electrolytes (U&Es).

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Give 5HT3 antagonists (high-dose ondansetron) and H2 blockers (famotidine) for vomiting.  Treat cardiac arrhythmias – caution with beta-blockers, as patients are likely to have asthma or COPD.  Benzodiazepines are the preferred first-line drugs for the treatment of seizures.  If rhabdomyolysis, give intravenous (IV) fluids and the patient may require sodium bicarbonate or haemodialysis.  Indications for haemodialysis in acute toxicity:  severe toxicity –evident by seizures or life-threatening arrhythmias  theophylline level ≥ 100 μg/ml (555 μmol/l)  refractory to medical therapy  rising theophylline levels.  Prognosis  Theophylline toxicity can be fatal.  Chronic toxicity in older patients is particularly dangerous, due to the high risk of significant cardiac arrhythmias.  Other Pathophysiology  Antagonism of adenosine receptors  Indirect adrenergic activity – inhibits phosphodiesterase at toxic levels Clinical features  Vomiting, abdominal pain  Coarse muscle tremor  ⇡ HR, ⇣ BP  Acute ⇢ level ≥80 μg/ml ⇢ ⇡ risk of seizures and arrhythmias (SVT, VT) Chronic ⇢ relatively asymptomatic ⇢ highrisk for seizures and arrhythmias if age ≤ 6 months or > 65 years and level ≥30 μg/ml Diagnosis  ⇣ K+, ⇡ Ca2+, ⇡ glucose  Metabolic acidosis  Serum theophylline levels ⇢ repeat q2h until peak  ECG Management  IV fluids Vomiting ⇢ 5HT3 antagonists + H2 blocker  Seizures ⇢ benzodiazepines  Activated charcoal + cathartic  Dialysis in high risk

JAMIL Urinary Tract Obstruction Urinary tract obstruction can occur at any point in the urinary tract, from the kidneys to the external urethral meatus.  Overview Key Facts  Urinary tract obstruction can occur at any point in the urinary tract, from the kidneys to the external urethral meatus.  The most common causes of upper urinary tract obstruction include stones, malignancy and pelviureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction.  The most common causes of lower urinary tract obstruction are benign prostate hyperplasia (BPH) and urethral stricture.  Urinary tract obstruction is usually characterised by dilatation of the renal tract (hydronephrosis), although there are other causes of hydronephrosis that are not all associated with obstruction.  Urethral stricture causes bladder outflow obstruction. Injury to the urethral mucosa will heal as a circumferential scar with subsequent fibrosis. This can cause bladder outflow obstruction.  Percutaneous nephrostomy is carried out for acute hydronephrosis with renal sepsis. Aetiology  Causes of urinary tract obstruction include:  renal calculi  malignancy  BPH  congenital: ureteropelvic/ureterovesical narrowing or obstruction  retroperitoneal fibrosis  urinary stricture.  Causes of urethral stricture include:  trauma (eg catheterisation, pelvic fracture)  neoplasm (eg bladder, penile and prostatic cancer)  inflammation (eg urethritis, gonococci). Upper and lower urinary tract causes and sites of obstruction:

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI Pathophysiology  Obstruction of the renal tract usually results in dilatation.  Hydronephrosis is defined as a dilatation of the renal pelvis.  Other causes of renal tract dilatation include vesico-ureteric reflux and congenital megaureter.  Urine leaves the kidney by gravity, aided by the peristaltic action of the pelvis and upper ureter.  If the collecting system is obstructed the pressure in the renal pelvis quickly rises.  A compensatory decrease in muscular tone of the renal pelvis allows a reduction in pressure back towards normal levels and this is followed by a reduction in GFR and impairment of the concentrating ability of the renal tubules.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms depend on the cause, location, and duration of the obstruction.  Obstructive pain is dull in nature and exacerbated by fluid intake;  it is due to distension of the renal pelvis or renal capsule

DR. JAMIL  chronic progressive obstruction is usually painless.  Lower urinary tract symptoms (BPH and bladder outlet obstruction) include storage symptoms and voiding symptoms:  storage symptoms: these include frequency, nocturia, urgency, dysuria and/or pyrexia.  commonly idiopathic but may be due to:  infection  malignancy  reduced functional bladder capacity (inflammation, fibrosis, oedema of the bladder wall)  calculi in the distal ureter (causes trigonal irritation) or the bladder.  voiding symptoms include:  hesitancy and/or straining  poor stream  terminal dribbling.  these symptoms are commonly due to a urethral stricture in young men, and to prostatic hyperplasia or malignancy in older men  us bladder outflow obstruction progresses the detrusor muscle thickens and is less controllable, causing urgency and frequency.  Urinary tract obstruction causes stasis which predisposes to infection.  Symptoms of the underlying cause: malignancy, trauma.  Differential Diagnosis Other causes of hydronephrosis eg:  vesico-ureteric reflux  congenital megaureter  neurogenic bladder.  Diagnosis/Investigation Urological investigations are done according to the cause and presentation and may include:  urinalysis: to exclude urinary tract infection  blood tests: to evaluate renal function  urinary flow rates: these are used for quantifying bladder outflow obstruction. Normal flow rates are > 15 ml/ second  urological imaging:  retrograde urogram: retrograde injection of contrast is used at cystoscopy to visualise ureters  urethrography: useful if traumatic disruption of the urethra is suspected. The meatus only is cannulated and

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI contrast media is introduced. The urethra is visualised by radiography  micturating cystogram: used for demonstrating fistulation, vesicoureteric reflux, urethral strictures and functional bladder studies  ultrasonography: assesses hydronephrosis  CT and MRI:  CT is useful for diagnosis and staging of malignancy  non-contrast CT (CT KUB) is increasingly the standard investigation for urinary calculi and contrast-enhanced CT (CT IVU)  MRI is more sensitive than CT for staging and detection of lymph node metastases in prostate cancer.  Radioisotope imaging of the renal tract: (99mTc)MAG-3 (99mTc-labelled mercaptoacetyltriglycine) is predominantly excreted by tubular secretion with a minimal amount filtered by the kidney and can therefore be used to assess degree of renal obstruction.  Management  Treatment usually aims to relieve the cause of obstruction, treat the cause and manage any complications. Pharmacological  Relief of obstruction – treatment options depend on the cause such as:  benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH): finasteride  prostatic cancer: hormonal therapy  complications of urinary tract obstruction, such as UTIs and kidney failure, if present, are treated promptly. Surgical  Relief of obstruction: treatment options depend on the cause  For example:  BPH: TURP  prostatic cancer: prostatectomy.  renal stones: ESWL  treatment of acute hydronephrosis with renal sepsis:  percutaneous nephrostomy: urine that has accumulated above the obstruction (draining of urine above the obsrtuction with a nephrostomy tube inserted through the back into the kidney)  ureteral stents: insertion of a soft plastic tube that connects the bladder with the kidney.  Urgent relief of obstructions that causes chronic hydronephrosis is usually not required.

DR. JAMIL Management of urethral stricture  Repeated dilation  Urethrotomy with stricture excision and/or stenting  Open reconstruction may be required.  Prognosis  The prognosis depends on the underlying cause of obstruction.  Blockage can usually be relieved, but if delayed, may lead to permanent kidney damage and reduced/loss of function.  Other  Ultrasonography of the genitourinary system.  Ultrasonography is important for visualisation and guided biopsy at many levels of the renal tract.  Renal ultrasonography:  assesses renal size and cortical thickness, renal masses (cystic/solid), calculi and hydronephrosis  also guides nephrostomy insertion and renal biopsy  this carries a small risk of haemorrhage and arteriovenous (AV) fistulation.  Bladder ultrasonography:  residual volume  filling defects (stone, tumour)  bladder wall thickness.  Testis ultrasonography:  masses  blood flow (eg torsion).  Prostate ultrasonography:  transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) is used to guide prostate biopsies or drain prostatic abscesses. Urticaria Urticaria (hives) is condition which involve the onset of erythematous, itchy wheals (raised lesions) and may be accompanied by angio-oedema or anaphylaxis in severe cases.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Urticaria (hives) is condition which involve the onset of erythematous, itchy wheals (raised lesions) and may be accompanied by angio-oedema or anaphylaxis in severe cases.  The condition is common and can be classified as acute or chronic urticaria.  Acute urticaria is common and usually resolves by 48 hours (although urticaria resolving in under 6 weeks is classed as acute).  Chronic urticaria lasts for more than 6 weeks and symptoms may occur daily. Chronic urticaria is divided into:  chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU)  inducible urticaria - this group contains physical, cholinergic, contact, and aquagenic types.  The diagnosis is mostly a clinical one.  Investigations may be required to establish cause, exclude differentials, or diagnosed associated condtions.  If treatment is required, antihistamines are often first line. Corticosteroids can be added for severe symptoms.  If urticaria occurs alongside anaphylaxis, emergency management with adrenaline and ABCDE assessment is required. Epidemiology  There is an 8-10% overall lifetime prevalence rate for all types of urticaria.  Lifetime prevalence of acute urticaria is approximately 20%.  Lifetime prevalence of chronic urticaria is closer to 2%.  Woman are affected more commonly than men with a ratio of 2 : 1.  Although urticaria can affect all ages, incidence levels peak between 20 and 40 years. Aetiology Triggers of urticaria in susceptible individuals include:  Drug allergy, including:  penicillin  salicylates  quinolones  ACE-inhibitors  opiates  cephalosporin

DR. JAMIL  hydralazine.  Food allergy, including:  nuts  shellfish  sesame seeds.  Insect bites.  Latex.  Viruses’ or parasite infections.  Autoimmune.  Variations in temperature (cold and heat urticaria).  Hot/cold water (aquagenic urticaria). Pathophysiology  Mast cells of the dermis release histamine and other vasoactive substances such as bradykinin in response to a trigger that results in increased vascular permeability.  This leads to intradermal oedema and pruritus.  Clinical Presentation  Itchy wheals (swelling of superficial dermis).  May be associated with:  tongue and lip swelling from angio-oedema (swelling of dermis and subcutaneous tissue)  anaphylaxis: bronchospasm, hypotension, oedema affecting larynx and face – potentially fatal if not treated rapidly.  Usually resolves within two days. Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Atopic eczema.  Contact dermatitis.  Erythema multiforme minor.  Pemphigoid.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is often a clinical one.  A full history should be taken to identify trigger and physical examination is required. The history should focus on:  Time of onset.  Frequency and duration of symptoms.  Other associated symptoms – itching, gastrointestinal symptoms.  Size shape and distribution of urticaria.  Suspected triggers and reproducibility.  Drug history.  Family history.  Co-morbidities.  Urticaria activity score to assess severity. Examination:  Size, shape and distribution of rash.  Central selling which may be red or white, surrounded by an area of erythema.  No investigations usually required to diagnoses the condition, however further investigations may be required to help determine underlying cause.  Symptom diaries can help assess severity ad impact on life.

DR. JAMIL  Management  Cases of urticaria associated with suspected anaphylaxis or angio-oedema requires:  adrenaline (anaphylaxis)  resuscitation and support with A to E assessment  removal of any potential triggering agent eg drugs  intravenous (IV) fluids, hydrocortisone and chlorphenamine.  Otherwise:  acute urticaria is usually self-limiting without treatment  advise avoidance of triggers wherever possible  non-sedating oral antihistamines may be tried for patients requiring treatment for up to 6 weeks  corticosteroids can be used (eg prednisolone 40 mg for 7 days) for severe symptoms  referral to dermatologist/immunologist if:  symptoms do not respond or continue to recur  acute severe urticaria is thought to be due to food or latex allergy  or the form of urticaria is difficult to manage in primary care (eg aquagenic urticaria).  Secondary care treatment options include:  leukotriene receptor agonists  cyclosporine  tacrolimus.  Prognosis  Urticaria often resolves spontaneously especially in the case of acute episodes.  Acute urticaria respond well to treatment.  Chronic urticaria may be associated with relapses and remission and may have a more variable prognosis. Warfarin Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist used for anticoagulation as prophylaxis or treatment.

Therapeutics part 2 L ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist used for anticoagulation as prophylaxis or treatment.  Anticoagulants are usually initiated in secondary care, a dedicated clinic in a hospital, or an outreach clinic in primary care.  Warfarin acts by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) as well as the anticoagulant proteins C and S.  Clinical Uses/Dosing  Warfarin is licensed for:  prophylaxis of systemic embolism in people with rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation  prophylaxis after insertion of prosthetic heart valves  prophylaxis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism  transient attacks of cerebral ischaemia (TIA).  Dosing:  initially 5–10 mg taken on day one  subsequent doses dependent on international normalised ratio (INR)  lower induction dose can be given over 3–4 weeks for patients not requiring rapid anticoagulation (eg in atrial fibrillation)  a lower induction dose (5 mg) can be given to: elderly patients, people with low body weight, liver disease, cardiac failure or high bleed risk (maintenance 3–9 mg).  doses should be taken at the same time each day. Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and Pulmonary Embolism (PE):  Duration of treatment will vary for each patient but warfarin should usually be continued for at least:  six weeks in distal DVT  three months in proximal DVT or PE with known temporary risk factors and low risk of recurrence  six months in proximal DVT of unknown cause  long-term treatment in recurrent DVTs/PE. Atrial Fibrillation or Prosthetic Heart Valves:  Warfarin treatment is usually long term.

explanation: B Amitriptyline A prolonged QT interval (measured from the beginning of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave) increases the risk of ventricular dysrhythmias occurring, particularly torsades de pointes, which may then deteriorate to ventricular ﬁbrillation. The normal QT interval is approximately 0.38–0.46 s when corrected for ventricular rate, but may be prolonged due to an underlying genetic abnormality: Romano–Ward syndrome and Jervell–Lange- Nielsen syndrome are examples. Acquired causes include electrolyte abnormalities such as hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia, and drugs. E Sodium valproate The main concerns with respect to sodium valproate use are liver dysfunction, pancreatitis and teratogenicity in women of childbearing potential.
