stem: You review a man who is currently receiving 6-mercaptopurine (6MP) as part of his treatment regimen for inﬂammatory bowel disease. Which of the following drugs may cause a fatal drug interaction when used in conjunction with 6-MP?
explanation:
A Allopurinol 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) is a purine antagonist that interferes with the process of DNA synthesis and the drug is usually used as part of chemotherapy in the treatment of acute leukaemias and as a treatment for inﬂammatory bowel disease. Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, and xanthine oxidase is responsible for the metabolism of 6-MP. Therefore, co-administration of allopurinol and 6-MP may result in a build up to toxic levels of 6-MP. Azathioprine is metabolised to 6-MP and therefore should also be avoided in patients receiving allopurinol therapy. E Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is a moderate inhibitor of CYP 1A2, which can promote accumulation of agents such as theophylline. B Erythromycin

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com The main concern with erythromycin prescription is the fact that it is a potent CYP 450 3A4 inhibitor, which drives accumulation of co-prescribed drugs such as statins which are metabolised via this route. C Theophylline Theophylline undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism, and it is theophylline which is a cause of toxicity when its metabolism is blocked by P450 inhibitors. D Propranolol The main concern with respect to propranolol use is bronchospasm in susceptible patients.

stem: A 27-year-old male is brought to the Emergency Department after he suffered two seizures while he was dancing at a night club. His girlfriend tells you that he was in perfect health up until this incident. On examination, his pulse is 130/min and regular. Blood pressure is 200/110 mmHg, temperature 38 °C. He is anxious and aggressive, and tells you that he doesn’t trust anyone. He is tremulous and you note some myoclonic jerks. Right fundus revealed a sub-hyaloid haemorrhage. Mild meningeal signs are evident. Bibasal crackles are noted on chest auscultation. Investigation Result Normal value WCC 11 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Urea 18 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 280 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine Normal What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Cocaine overdose The hypertension, tachycardia, pyrexia and two seizures ﬁt well with stimulant drug abuse, particularly in the context of admission from a night club where the events occurred. The elevated creatinine may be related to accelerated renovascular disease as a result of the cocaine abuse. Given the signs of cardiac failure, nitrates are preferred in this situation for blood pressure control versus beta blockade, and benzodiazepines can be utilised for the management of anxiety and aggression. E Viral encephalitis 773-555 THERAPE This doesn’t ﬁt with the hypertension at presentation, nor with the rapid deterioration of his neurological status with seizures and confusion. A Hepatic encephalopathy Hepatic encephalopathy presents against a background of chronic alcoholism and is precipitated by an acute event such as infection or an upper GI bleed. B Post-ictal confusion Post-ictal confusion would not be associated with hypertension and pyrexia. D Bacterial meningitis Bacterial meningitis doesn’t ﬁt with the rapid deterioration here, nor with the marked hypertension at presentation.

stem: You are seen by a pharmaceutical representative who asks you to try out a recently launched antihypertensive agent in one of your patients. The second patient who tries the medication returns a few days later with a rash. What frequency of an adverse event is most likely to have been observed during a phase 3 clinical trial? 773-555 THERAPE
explanation: B 1:300 In general, about 10 times as many patients need to be studied in a trial program versus the number needed to see one event from a frequency calculation. Most modern clinical study programmes for drugs with a cardiovascular disease indication study between 5 and 10,000 patients. Hence an event occurring with a frequency of 1 in 300 should be identiﬁed during a phase 3 trial. E 1:50,000 It’s highly unlikely that any events would be seen in either arm of the phase 3 study, (active or control groups), and for this frequency of event post marketing surveillance is essential. A 1:10,000 Events occurring with this type of frequency are only reliably conﬁrmed in post-marketing surveillance via the Medicines and Healthcare Regulatory Agency (MHRA). The yellow card system invites healthcare professionals to report suspected adverse drug reactions, complementary to this system is prescription event monitoring, where doctors identiﬁed from a sample of scripts for a particular medicine are surveyed for any changes in clinical markers in patients given that medicine. C 1:20,000 Events occurring with this frequency may only be identiﬁed signiﬁcantly after launch, particularly if they are related to prolonged drug exposure. D 1:2000 In this frequency a numerical imbalance between arms may be seen in the phase 3 study program, but it’s unlikely a difference could be reliably conﬁrmed between active and placebo.

stem: An 18-year-old student has attended the Emergency Department of a district general hospital, having consumed a bottle of antifreeze for a bet. On arrival, he appears rather unwell, with bloods indicating that he has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, and an 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com elevated osmolar gap. On examination, his BP is 100/60 mmHg, pulse is 95 bpm and regular, and he is drowsy. Arterial blood gasses reveal a severe metabolic acidosis. He can currently be admitted to the highdependency unit, but there are no ITU beds. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for his antifreeze poisoning?
explanation: C Fomepizole Ethylene glycol poisoning is one of the classic causes of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. A few of the causes can be remembered using the mnemonic MUDPILES: methanol, uraemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, paraldehyde, iron, lactate, ethylene glycol and salicylate. Ethylene glycol is metabolised by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase, initially to glycoaldehyde, then forming glycolic acid, glyoxylic acid and ﬁnally oxalic acid. Fomepizole is an inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase but does not lead to intoxication; it is therefore preferred here to ethanol. Useful mnemonic The mnemonic ‘MUDPILES’ (methanol, uraemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, paraldehyde, iron, lactate, ethylene glycol and salicylate) can be used to remember some of the causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis. E Methylene blue Methylene blue is the treatment of choice for methaemoglobinaemia. A Ethanol Ethanol is a competitive antagonist for alcohol dehydrogenase but has the disadvantage here that it increases intoxication. B Methanol Methanol has a signiﬁcant negative toxicity proﬁle, leading to metabolic acidosis and optic neuropathy; hence it is not an appropriate intervention here. D Naloxone Naloxone is a reversal agent for opiates.

stem: An 18-year-old man is brought by his mother for evaluation. He presents with anxiety, irritability and a persistent tremor. She is concerned that he is taking stimulants as he appears to sleep for only 1–2 h per night. These periods of hyperactivity are interspersed with periods of extreme tiredness. His teachers have mentioned a deterioration in his academic performance. On examination, he is unkempt. His blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg and pulse is 110 bpm. He is alert and restless, and appears to be talking to someone who is not in the room. He tells you that his mother is jealous of him and is planning to kill him. His physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Amphetamine abuse These clinical features raise the possibility that the patient is consuming central nervous system (CNS) stimulants which have signiﬁcant hypertensive effects and are analeptics (eg amphetamine or methylphenidate). However, amphetamine is more likely in this patient as the latter drug does not lead to features of psychosis with prolonged use. When amphetamine is consumed chronically in high doses, it could lead to a state that is indistinguishable from paranoid schizophrenia. These drugs are capable of causing vasculitis and intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhages because of signiﬁcant hypertension. Similar vascular complications could also be caused by over-the-counter ‘cold medications’ like ephedrine and phenylpropanolamine. Withdrawal of the drug after sustained use can lead to a period of prolonged sleep, muscle pain, profound fatigue and depression. Treatment includes discontinuation of amphetamine and administering anxiolytics and/or atypical antipsychotics if required. E Opiate abuse Opiate abuse is more likely to present with listlessness and inactivity, rather than the hypertension and hyperactivity seen here. A Depression Depression would not ﬁt with the features of sympathetic activation seen here. B Autism spectrum disorder Autism spectrum disorders are more likely to present with social 773-555 THERAPE withdrawal, and would not be associated with either the sympathetic activation or the features of psychosis present here. D Wilson’s disease Wilson’s disease presents more commonly with asymmetrical cerebellar signs and is not associated with the sympathetic activation and acute psychosis seen here.

stem: A 71-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a large subdural haematoma. He has long- standing confusion due to multi-infarct dementia and takes rivaroxaban. He has extensive bruising and fresh blood around his gums. According to his home help, it appears he has taken a months worth of rivaroxaban over the past 3 days. 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Which of the following is inhibited by rivaroxaban?
explanation: E Factor Xa Rivaroxaban is a factor Xa inhibitor. When patients who are taking rivaroxaban present with serious bleeding, a speciﬁc rivaroxaban reversal agent exists, (andexanet alfa). In the event this is not available then prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) or recombinant factor VII can be given. Activated charcoal to reduce absorption of rivaroxaban can also be considered. An easy way to remember the mode of action of anticoagulants is that Xa inhibitors contain Xa in the name; therefore, they include rivaroXaban and apiXaban, but not dabigatran. D Factor IX Factor IX synthesis is inhibited by warfarin alongside factors II, VII and X. Rivaroxaban is a factor Xa inhibitor. In patients treated with rivaroxaban who have bleeding where andexanet alpha is not available, prothrombin complex concentrate can be given instead. It contains factors II, IX, and X. A Antithrombin (AT) III Heparin binds to AT III, causing a conformational change that results in its activation by increasing the ﬂexibility of its reactive site loop. The activated AT then inactivates thrombin, factor Xa, and other proteases. Rivaroxaban is a factor Xa inhibitor. B Factor VII Factor VII synthesis is inhibited by warfarin. Rivaroxaban has no direct effect on factor VII levels. Where excessive bleeding is noted in the presence of rivaroxaban recombinant factor VII can be used as a reversal agent, but usually only if the speciﬁc reversal agent andexanet alpha is unavailable. C Factor VIII Factor VIII synthesis is not inhibited by rivaroxaban, nor by warfarin. Factor VIII deﬁciency is caused by haemophilia A, and also by acquired haemophilia related to autoimmune disease. It can be treated with recombinant factor VIII replacement.

stem: A 68-year-old man, drowsy and confused, is brought in to hospital during the night by his carer. He accidentally overdosed on his medication from his dosette box approximately 6 h ago. He has a background of Alzheimer’s disease, hypertension, angina and glaucoma. From the dosette box card the patient’s medication include temazepam, atenolol and bendroﬂumethiazide. Pulse 35 bpm, blood pressure 85/45 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, oxygen saturation 98%. There is no pulse response to 2 mg of atropine. Initial investigations: Blood gases on air: Investigation Result Normal value pH 7.41 7.35–7.45 pa(O2) 9.8 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa pa(CO2) 4.9 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 61 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 23 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Glucose 2.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Electrocardiogram Sinus bradycardia 35 bpm He is given intravenous dextrose; which of the following is the appropriate next intervention?
explanation: D Glucagon This man is most likely to have taken an overdose of β-blockers, for which repeated doses of glucagon are known to reverse hypotension and bradycardia; this is thought to be via a β receptor independent effect on cAMP levels and myocardial contractility. It will also help drive correction of his hypoglycaemia. C Activated charcoal 773-555 THERAPE Activated charcoal does not have a role here as all of the atenolol dosed is already likely to have been absorbed. A Flumazenil Flumazenil competitively inhibits the action of benzodiazepines. It is useful in reversal of their effect on the central nervous system, but can increase the risk of seizures. This patient does not have respiratory compromise and is at risk of seizures due to hypoglycaemia; as such ﬂumazenil would not be recommended here. B Haemodialysis Atenolol overdose can be treated with haemodialysis, particularly when excretion of atenolol is reduced, for example where there is pre-existing chronic renal impairment. E Atropine Bradycardia associated with β-blocker overdose responds poorly to atropine, and little incremental response would be expected between 2 and 3 mg total dose.

stem: A 62-year-old man is found confused by his friends holding an empty medication bottle with no label. His friends say he has a background of angina, chronic bronchitis on home oxygen, and osteoarthritis. The patient starts vomiting and has a seizure, which is controlled with diazepam. His temperature is 36.8 oC, pulse 120/min regular, blood pressure 115/86 mmHg. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value ECG Sinus tachycardia Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 2.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 75 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected Calcium (Ca2+) 2.63 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Glucose 9.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Theophylline 290 µmol/l 55–110 µmol/l While in the assessment unit he continues to have further seizures and vomiting episodes with decreased consciousness, so you electively intubate and ventilate him. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: D Charcoal haemoperfusion The patient has overdosed on theophylline medication. This can cause cardiac arrhythmias, vomiting, confusion, seizures, hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia and hypercalcaemia. In this patient, with high theophylline serum levels and persisting seizures, charcoal haemoperfusion is a reasonable option. Blood from the patient is passed through a charcoal resin, and this will remove proteinbound toxins. Seizure activity is difﬁcult to control in this situation and the patient may need transfer to an intensive care unit. Peritoneal dialysis is ineffective. Sodium bicarbonate has a role in the treatment of tricyclic overdose. C Gastric lavage Gastric lavage is rarely instituted for the treatment of overdose. Where patients present early after overdose it may be considered for iron ingestion. A Intravenous (iv) phenytoin iv phenytoin is a potential anti-arrhythmic used in the treatment of ventricular tachycardia for patients with digoxin overdose, particularly where digibind is not immediately available. B Sodium bicarbonate Sodium bicarbonate is used for patients with tricyclic antidepressant overdose where there is QRS prolongation. E Peritoneal dialysis Peritoneal dialysis is less effective for the treatment of theophylline overdose than charcoal haemoperfusion. Haemoperfusion allows potentially more rapid theophylline removal.

stem: You are helping to run a clinical trial of a new oral formulation of a 773-555 THERAPE subcutaneous analgesic agent. It does not undergo signiﬁcant ﬁrstpass hepatic metabolism. Which of the following is the best measure of drug absorption?
explanation:
C Bioavailability Bioavailability is the best measure of drug absorption because it directly relates the amount of drug given to the amount present in plasma. It is calculated by measuring the area under the curve (AUC) for the level of a drug in plasma from administration to when it can no longer be detected after oral dosing, and dividing it by the AUC calculated after intravenous dosing. This gives a value in %. For some peptide drugs administered orally and for bisphosphonates this is less than 5% versus intravenous (IV) dosing. For most small molecules, oral bioavailability varies between around 30-70%. E Volume of distribution Volume of distribution is not a measure of drug absorption; it is a measure of uptake of drug into tissue. Water- soluble drugs tend to have a lower volume of distribution because they largely remain within the plasma. Lipid- soluble drugs have a much greater volume of distribution because they tend to become tissue bound. A C-max The C-max is the peak concentration of an administered drug in the plasma. Although it is a measure of drug absorbed, it has to be related to the oral dose of the drug that was given to measure drug absorption accurately. B Half-life Half-life is the time taken for the concentration of the drug in plasma to fall by 50%. It is not a measure of drug absorption, but it is useful for determining the dosing interval for a given agent. For drugs with a very short half-life, for example, 3-4 hours, twice a day dosing or even three times a day dosing may be required. D T-max T-max is the time taken for a drug to reach maximal concentration in plasma after oral administration. When a drug is given chronically, for example, for hypertension, T-max is less important than for an acute indication, such as analgesia, where time to onset of the drug is all-important.

Increased calcium channel expression in the duodenum
explanation: A Alteration in Parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion PTH secretion is altered by corticosteroid use, which can help drive an increase in bone resorption. Secretion is altered to reduce tonic secretion and increase the amount released as pulses. These changes drive a reduction in bone formation and an increase in bone resorptionthrough stimulating osteoclast activity. Other effects which are important in driving loss of bone muscle density (BMD) with steroid use include antagonism of the effects of vitamin D, decreased synthesis of osteoprotegerin, and increased rank ligand synthesis. E Increased synthesis of osteoprotegerin Corticosteroids decrease the synthesis of osteoprotegrin. Osteoprotegerin inhibits osteoclast differentiation from hematopoietic stem cells of the macrophage lineage. A fall in osteoprotegrin, therefore drives an increase in bone resorption. B Decreased receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B (RANK) ligand synthesis RANK ligand, which stimulates osteoclast activity, is increased by corticosteroids which act directly on pre- osteoclast/stromal cells to increase its synthesis. Denosumab is a RANK ligand inhibitor which is used in the treatment of osteoporosis. It is a monoclonal antibody given as a subcutaneous injection once every 6 months. C Increased calcium channel expression in the duodenum Corticosteroids antagonise the effects of vitamin D in the gut. They decrease calcium absorption at least, in part, by decreasing calcium channel expression in the duodenum, and with respect to the kidneys, they result in increased renal calcium loss. D Increased oestrogen secretion Corticosteroids result in decreased secretion of androgens and oestrogens; this contributes to increased bone loss. This is mediat- 773-555 THERAPE ed by a downregulation of gonadotrophin secretion which is driven by prednisolone use.

stem: You are called to see a 38-year-old man in the Emergency Department. He was brought there by ambulance after his friend administered him a tablet that would apparently make him feel better after a heavy night out and a recent cold. On examination, he looks very unwell. His blood pressure (BP) is 70/40 mmHg with a pulse of 104/min. He is cold and sweaty. He is stridorous and has marked wheeze on auscultation of the chest. There is an urticaria type skin rash in addition. The emergency staff have already started a 500 ml bag of normal saline. How best would you initially manage him?
explanation: E Adrenaline IM Despite initial ﬂuid resuscitation, this patient still has marked hypotension and tachycardia. He is in urgent need of circulatory support. The most likely diagnosis is anaphylaxis related to the unknown medication. Night nurse, a night time cold remedy contains dextromethorphan, to which anaphylactic reactions have been de- 773-555 THERAPE scribed. Treatment of choice in this situation is IM adrenaline (0.5 ml of 1:1000), which can be repeated after 5 minutes. D Chlorpheniramine IV Chlorphenamine will impact on histamine-driven inﬂammation but the impact would be delayed with respect to blood pressure and stridor versus giving adrenaline IM. Guidelines recommend non-sedating oral antihistamines, rather than chlorphenamine, to be given following initial stabilisation, especially in patients with persisting urticaria or angioedema. A Glucagon IV Glucagon is of most potential use in beta-blocker overdose, and the tachycardia here is less suggestive of beta- blockade as the driver for his presentation. B Further normal saline 1l IV stat Although he may respond to further ﬂuid loading, the imminent need is to improve blood pressure and stave off potential respiratory arrest; as such, adrenaline is the most important intervention. C Hydrocortisone IV Corticosteroids are not recommended in the standard treatment of anaphylaxis. They were previously advocated until a change in guidelines in 2021. The evidence regarding their use in refractory anaphylaxis is unclear, and they can be considered.

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department. She has just returned from India where she was prescribed an Ayurvedic medication for her asthma. Over the past few weeks, she has suffered from increasing drowsiness, shortness of breath and extreme lethargy and has not opened her bowels for two days. On examination, her blood pressure is 152/92 mmHg and pulse 84 bpm and regular. She looks pale. Her abdomen is soft, but there is generalised mild tenderness. Her body mass index (BMI) is 28 kg/m2. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 98 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 181 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 85 u/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 97 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 12 µmol/l < 17 µmol/l TSH 2.9 u/l 0.3–4.2 mu/l Zinc protoporphyrin: Elevated You have told her to stop the Ayurvedic medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
A Calcium EDTA The elevation in zinc protoporphyrin, coupled with anaemia and the symptoms of lethargy and constipation seen here, is consistent with lead poisoning. A number of medications prescribed for conditions including shortness of breath and health in pregnancy and to provide ‘vigour’ are recognised to contain lead. C Intravenous IV iron transfusion Although elevated zinc protoporphyrin may be seen in patients with iron deﬁciency anaemia, in this case, given the use of Ayurvedic medication, the underlying cause is more likely to be lead poisoning here.

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com B Carbohydrate loading Carbohydrate loading is considered as a temporalising measure in patients presenting with acute intermittent porphyria, while awaiting haem arginate treatment. Patients are more likely to present with acute abdominal pain, psychiatric disturbance, peripheral neuropathy, hypertension and hyponatraemia, rather than the picture seen here. D Prednisolone Prednisolone is the intervention of choice for autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. There are no signs of haemolytic anaemia such as changes in haptoglobin or elevated unconjugated bilirubin to indicate this as the underlying cause. E Thyroid hormone replacement Hypothyroidism is a cause of anaemia and does lead to constipation, although it would not lead to the elevated zinc protoporphyrin seen here.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Department with a 3-week history of a persistent rash. The rash is dry and scaly and worse over his forearms, but it extends to his back and legs also. He has no known allergies and denies introducing new foods into his diet or new detergents. He takes amlodipine and ramipril daily for hypertension and is receiving treatment for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. On examination, his observations are all within normal range. He removes his T-shirt and reveals a rash. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for this patient’s presentation?
explanation: C Isoniazid This patient has drug-induced lupus, a lupus-like syndrome which usually presents with symptoms of arthralgia, myalgia, fever and skin changes. Skin changes include a symmetrical annular or ringshaped rash, particularly over sun-exposed areas. Causative drugs include procainamide, hydralazine and isoniazid. Treatment of drug-induced lupus mainly involves stopping the causative agent and adopting sun-protective measures to the skin until complete resolution. B Ethambutol Ethambutol is well known for causing optic neuritis, but it is not a cause of drug-induced lupus. A Amlodipine Amlodipine can cause skin reactions. However, this is usually secondary to an allergy to amlodipine and is extremely rare. D Ramipril Ramipril and other angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors cause a skin reaction known as angio-oedema, which is subcutaneous swelling of soft tissues of the face, typically surrounding the eyes and mouth. E Rifampicin Rifampicin is an antituberculosis drug. Side-effects include orange-coloured secretions. Hypersensitivity and skin reactions may occur secondary to rifampicin use, but it is a rare cause of drug-induced lupus.

stem: A 17-year-old girl who is studying for A-Levels now presents with clumsiness and falls. Her mother reports that she frequently drops china and cutlery at home. Her schoolteacher has noticed odd behaviour over the past two months and her work has deteriorated, although previously she has been a straight A grade student. Her brothers and sisters have no health problems. Her father is epileptic. On examination, she has horizontal nystagmus, dysdiadochokinesis, and a broad-based gait. Which of the following represents the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Phenytoin toxicity It seems likely that this girl has suffered stress at school and has begun using her father’s phenytoin tablets. Horizontal nystagmus dysdiadochokinesis and a broad-based gait are all features associated with phenytoin toxicity. D Meningioma A meningioma would be more likely to present with lateralising neurological signs. B Haemochromatosis Haemochromatosis usually presents with abnormal liver function testing but without overt neurological signs, it is also less likely to present early in women because of the menstrual cycle. C Wilson’s disease Although Wilson’s disease may present with neurological dysfunction of this type in the patient’s age group, given the history of parental epilepsy and good health in other siblings, abuse of phenytoin tablets is more likely. E Multiple sclerosis First presentation with MS, only with cerebellar signs would be considered unusual.

stem: A 28-year-old patient is admitted to the Emergency Department 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com after being found to have a generalised tonic– clonic seizure that has terminated. He is on a methadone programme, but his partner says he has not had any methadone for two days. On admission, his BP is 175/110 mmHg and his heart rate is 110 bpm. He is soiled with diarrhoea and appears to have been vomiting. Which of the following is the best treatment for the underlying problem?
options: Recommencement of methadone with specialist advice
explanation: E Recommencement of methadone with specialist advice This patient clearly has opiate withdrawal syndrome, which reaches its peak on the second or third day after opiate abstinence. The syndrome may be characterised by severe agitation or muscular twitching, aches and pains, abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhoea, hypertension, insomnia, anorexia and profuse sweating. The most appropriate intervention is methadone, a long-acting opiate agonist, which, because it is long-acting, is less likely to produce an opiate-related ‘high’. A Chlordiazepoxide Chlordiazepoxide is a long-acting benzodiazepine used in withdrawal from alcohol. It is not indicated in withdrawal from opiates or methadone. B Diazepam as required for seizures The use of benzodiazepines may be required to manage seizures. However, they will not treat underlying opiate withdrawal making it inappropriate here. C Dihydrocodeine as required Dihydrocodeine is short-acting and likely to perpetuate the opiate addiction cycle, which makes it unlikely to help this patient. D IV diamorphine as required Diamorphine is short-acting and likely to perpetuate the opiate addiction cycle in this patient, making it inappropriate here.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a second episode of angio-oedema. He takes treatments for hypertension. Which of the following drugs is most likely to be the cause of his angioedema?
explanation: A Enalapril Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are associated with the development of angioedema. In this case the enalapril should be withdrawn and another blood pressure lowering agent substituted in its place. Episodes of angioedema may occur at any time, even many years after starting the ACE inhibitor. Angioedema may also be inherited; hereditary angioedema is a rare autosomal-dominant condition due to an inherited deﬁciency of 773-555 THERAPE C1 esterase inhibitor. Serum C2 and C4 levels are low. E Atenolol Beta blockers may cause bronchospasm in patients with a history of asthma, and are associated with increased risk of psoriasis. B Amlodipine Patients are approximately ten times less likely to report angioedema in association with calcium channel blockers versus ACE inhibitors. C Furosemide Furosemide is associated with allergic rashes, but is not commonly associated with episodes of angioedema. It is also very uncommonly used as a treatment for hypertension. D Bendroﬂuazide Thiazides are associated with angioedema, but in the ALLHAT study, patients were approximately ﬁve times less likely to report episodes versus ACE inhibitor used to manage hypertension.

stem: A 72-year-old man is referred to the Diabetes Clinic with newonset type II diabetes. He is taking 60 mg of prednisolone per day for a new diagnosis of giant cell arteritis. Which of the following contributes most to hyperglycaemia in this patient?
explanation: D Increased gluconeogenesis Corticosteroids do increase gluconeogenesis, where glucose is produced from other body energy stores such as amino acids. They also drive glycogenolysis and increase insulin resistance. The combination of all these factors drives up glucose levels in people with and without diabetes mellitus already. There is a 10fold increase in the risk of new diabetes for patients taking more than 30 mg of prednisolone versus controls. 773-555 THERAPE E Increased glycogenesis Corticosteroids oppose formation of new glycogen, leading to an overall reduction in hepatic glycogen stores. This contributes to an increase in blood glucose which can push people above the threshold for a diagnosis of diabetes or an increase in existing therapy. There is some evidence that hepatic glucose output can be reduced in patients without diabetes who are taking corticosteroids by co-prescription of metformin. Still, there is no evidence to support this approach in patients with established type II diabetes mellitus. A Decreased glycogenolysis Corticosteroids antagonise a number of actions of insulin which drive the presentation of patients with new- onset type II diabetes. This includes the usual action of insulin to increase glycogen storage. Steroids drive increased glycogenolysis, increasing hepatic glucose output and contributing to an increase in overall blood glucose levels. B Decreased gluconeogenesis Corticosteroids drive increased, rather than decreased, gluconeogenesis, where amino acids are consumed to produce glucose. This is a contributor to an overall increase in blood glucose levels associated with prednisolone use. Protein catabolism may well also contribute to some of the proximal muscle weakness, which is seen in patients taking corticosteroids. C Decreased lipolysis The impact of corticosteroids on lipid metabolism is complex. Although they increase deposition of central fat, leading to the 'pear on sticks' appearance of people who have long term high exposure to corticosteroids, they also impair lipid storage in peripheral fat. This may well contribute to the insulin resistance seen in patients taking corticosteroids.

stem: A 55-year-old patient is under management for chronic back pain. He is accompanied by his wife, who brought him along to the Emergency Department. She is very concerned, as the patient is increasingly confused and lethargic. Past medical history includes depression. On examination, his blood pressure is 125/80 mmHg and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 14; the rest of the physical examination is unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigations Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 124 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 219 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Sodium (Na) 116 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 105 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following medications is likely to be responsible for the hyponatraemia in this man?
explanation: D Citalopram In a patient presenting with altered mental state and confusion, it is essential not only to check the electrolytes, but also to review the medications. This gentleman is diagnosed with depression and is therefore likely to be on an antidepressant. He has hyponatraemia, possibly syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), and initial management would involve stopping the drug and monitoring sodium levels. Although ﬂuid restriction forms part of the management of SIADH, ﬂuid restriction in the presence of continued citalopram is unlikely to be successful in improving the serum sodium level. A Diazepam Diazepam most commonly causes confusion, especially in the elderly, and drowsiness and can lead to dependence. It is not known to cause hyponatraemia. B Lisinopril Lisinopril is less common to cause hyponatraemia but can commonly cause a dry cough and rarely causes angio-oedema (which can be several months or even a year after initiation). C Oxytetracycline Oxytetracycline can cause benign intracranial hypertension but is not known to cause hyponatraemia. It is contraindicated in pregnant or breastfeeding women. E Codeine phosphate Opioids may cause confusion, but less commonly cause hyponatraemia. Therefore, this is not correct.

stem: A 32-year-old arable farmer is brought to A&E one evening having become increasingly confused over the previous 5 h. He had been feeling well at breakfast time before going out to work in the ﬁelds, but staggered into the house in the late afternoon complain- 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com ing of nausea and vomiting, and feeling generally weak. He now has profuse diarrhoea with associated abdominal cramps. On examination, he is diaphoretic and salivating profusely. He is disorientated regarding time, place and person. His pupils are equal and constricted. His temperature is 36.9 oC. His heart rate is 54 bpm, regular, jugular venous pressure (JVP) is not seen and blood pressure (BP) is 102/54 mmHg. Heart sounds are normal. Respiratory examination reveals bilateral expiratory wheeze, but no crepitations. His oxygen saturations are 92% on air. His abdomen is soft and diffusely tender, but there is no guarding or rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds are present. Power is globally reduced in all four limbs (grade 4/5), with slightly depressed reﬂexes, but plantar response is ﬂexor. A few fasciculations are noted in his legs. His coordination and sensation are unimpaired. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Organophosphate poisoning Organophosphate insecticides inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, allowing accumulation of excessive acetylcholine (ACh) at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors, and in the CNS. Signs and symptoms of acute organophosphate poisoning may occur within 1–2 h of exposure, but may also be delayed, especially after skin exposure. Sudden deterioration can occur in a patient with few initial symptoms. Clinical manifestations may be classiﬁed into muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS effects, as follows:  Muscarinic: vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramping, bronchospasm, miosis, bradycardia, excessive salivation and sweating. Severe diaphoresis can lead to dehydration with systemic hypovolaemia, resulting in shock.  Nicotinic: muscle fasciculations, tremor and weakness.  Death is usually caused by respiratory muscle paralysis.  BP and pulse may be decreased due to muscarinic effects, or increased due to nicotinic effects.  CNS poisoning: agitation, seizures, coma. Treatment is with supportive measures, which may include intubation and ventilation. Decontamination of skin and clothes, and reduction of enteral absorption with activated charcoal may be indicated. Intravenous (iv) atropine may reverse the muscarinic 773-555 THERAPE effects but not the nicotinic effects. Pralidoxime is a speciﬁc antidote that acts to regenerate the enzyme activity at all affected sites. E Belladonna poisoning Some symptoms of belladonna poisoning may overlap here, including sweating, tachycardia and blurred vision, although other symptoms such as constipation are not features of the presentation as reported here. A Botulism Botulism begins with CNS symptoms including blurred vision, difﬁculty in speaking and swallowing. Diarrhoea and vomiting may be seen but are not necessarily a prominent feature, and there is a descending ﬂaccid paralysis. B Guillain–Barré syndrome Guillain–Barré presents with gradually progressive ascending weakness, rather than the rapid onset of both CNS and PNS symptoms over a number of hours. D Tetanus Tetanus is associated with a pattern of descending upper motor neurone weakness, rather than the lower motor neurone symptoms seen here, accompanied by signs and symptoms of autonomic nervous system dysfunction.

stem: A 71-year-old man with a long history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents to the Emergency Department with profuse vomiting, syncope and tachycardia. Apparently, he attended the general practitioner (GP) a few days earlier and was prescribed oral antibiotics for a lower respiratory tract infection. Medications include high-dose Seretide®, theophylline tablets and carbocisteine. Examination reveals a pyrexia of 37.8°C, a blood pressure of 105/62 mmHg and a pulse of 105 bpm and regular. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 11.0 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 200 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l CRP 85 mg/l (181 at presentation to GP) 0–10 mg/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate 15 mmol/l 22–30 mmol/l Creatinine 118 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 11.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: E Theophylline toxicity The picture of vomiting, coupled with hypokalaemia, mild acidosis and hyperglycaemia, is consistent with theophylline toxicity. Both ciproﬂoxacin and clarithromycin are known to inhibit the metabolism of theophylline. Ciproﬂoxacin inhibits theophylline metabolism via CYP1A2 inhibition and clarithromycin via CYP3A4 inhibition and inhibition of theophylline uptake into hepatocytes. Either option is a possible choice of oral antibiotic to treat a COPD exacerbation. Treatment is with multidose activated charcoal or with dialysis in severe cases. B Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) There is only a very modest increase in blood glucose, which is not consistent with DKA. The presentation with syncope is also not classically seen in DKA. A Carbocysteine toxicity Carbocisteine is a mucolytic with predominantly local action. Excessive doses of carbocisteine can lead to gastrointestinal discomfort but would not present with tachycardia and syncope. C Salmeterol toxicity Salmeterol toxicity would cause a patient to have tachycardia, but it is not known to cause profuse vomiting and is therefore unlikely in this case. D Septic shock The normal WCC and improvement in the patient’s CRP make sepsis unlikely.

stem: You are called to see a 59-year-old man on the coronary care unit who has suffered an upper GI haemorrhage of 250 ml of fresh blood. He is recovering on the cardiology ward following PCI and stenting for inferior myocardial infarction some 3 days earlier. He is still under treatment with fondaparinux, clopidogrel and aspirin. On examination his BP is 100/70 mmHg, and there is a postural drop of 15 mmHg on moving from lying to sitting. Heart sounds are normal and his chest is clear. He has epigastric pain on palpation and admits to taking over-the-counter indigestion medications for many months before admission. PR examination reveals melaena. Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 79 g/l 135 - 175 g/l 773-555 THERAPE WCC 11.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 189 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 112 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urea 14.2 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l You start IV ﬂuids and arrange a blood transfusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: D Stop fondaparinux This patient has developed a signiﬁcant upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage on the background of a recent angioplasty. The patient is on three medications, each of which will increase the risk of bleeding. Both clopidogrel and aspirin are important to reduce the risk of stent thrombosis and should be continued if possible. As a result, fondaparinux is the most appropriate medication to be stopped initially. A Stop aspirin This patient has had recent angioplasty. Dual anti-platelet therapy (DAPT) is required to reduce the risk of acute stent thrombosis. The risk of stent thrombosis is highest in the acute period and, if possible, DAPT should not be stopped in this patient. B Stop clopidogrel Clopidogrel or another anti-platelet agent in combination with aspirin is the standard of care for patients following the implantation of a cardiac stent. If stopped in the acute setting, the risk of stent thrombosis will increase. C Stop aspirin and clopidogrel As above, both these agents are required to reduce the risk of stent thrombosis. They should not be stopped unless the bleeding remains uncontrolled following further management and cessation of fondaparinux has not improved the situation. E Stop aspirin, clopidogrel and fondaparinux Stopping all three of these agents would signiﬁcantly risk stent thrombosis in this patient. Fondaparinux is the least important of these three in the post-myocardial infarction period, and should be stopped while both aspirin and clopidogrel are continued initially.

stem: A 46-year-old homeless man is brought to the Emergency Department after he was found unconscious on a park bench by a bystander. He is rousable but unable to give a coherent history. On examination, he has a temperature of 35.5 °C. His heart rate is 55 bpm and regular, with a blood pressure of 101/60 mmHg. On auscultation, his chest is clear, with saturations of 96% on room air. He is drowsy and unable to hold a full conversation, with noticeably slurred speech. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 12 (E3 V4 M5). His pupils are 3 mm and reactive to light. He smells strongly of alcohol. Arterial blood gas: Investigation Result Normal value pH 7.21 7.35–7.45 p(CO2) 5.1 kPa 4.9–6.1 kPa p(O2) 9.8 kPa 10–13.1 kPa Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Chloride (Cl−) 110 mmol/l 95–105 mmol/l Haemoglobin (Hb) 119 g/l 115–155 g/l Bicarbonate (HCO3−) 13 mmol/l 22–28 mmol/l Base excess −8.2 mmol/l −2 to 2 mmol/l Lactate 3.6 mmol/l 0.5–1.6 mmol/l Glucose 5.1 mmol/l 4–6.9 mmol/l 773-555 THERAPE What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
explanation: A Fomepizole This patient has raised anion gap metabolic acidosis [calculated by (Na+ + K+) – (HCO3− + Cl−)]. Causes of raised anion gap metabolic acidosis include methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning, uraemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, paracetamol overdose, lactic acidosis and salicylate overdose. Given the clinical history of a reduced GCS score and strong suspicions of alcohol or alcohol-like ingestion, the most likely diagnosis here is methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning. The treatment for the two is the same with the antidote fomepizole. Fomepizole is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase and prevents the production of toxic metabolites. C Intravenous (IV) bicarbonate Intravenous bicarbonate therapy can be considered in some severe cases of metabolic acidosis. However, it is not indicated in the treatment of methanol poisoning. B Haemoﬁltration Indications for haemoﬁltration include barbiturates, lithium, alcohol, salicylates and theophylline overdose. Other indications include refractory hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, uraemia and ﬂuid overload. While haemoﬁltration can be used for methanol poisoning, alternative treatments such as fomepizole can be trialled initially. D IV ﬂuids This patient very likely has methanol poisoning. IV ﬂuid resuscitation is an appropriate treatment to initiate in patients with signs of toxicity. However, IV ﬂuid resuscitation alone will not reverse the effects of methanol poisoning. E Naloxone Naloxone is used in the treatment of opioid overdose. While an opioid overdose can cause a reduction in a patient’s GCS score, it does not typically cause raised anion gap metabolic acidosis. This ﬁnding should prompt the consideration of alternative diagnoses.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents for review. She has recently returned from a holiday to Spain and complains of a rash mainly on her face and upper chest, but also present, to a lesser extent, on non- sun exposed areas of the body. She complains of joint pains affecting multiple small joints of the upper and lower limbs. You conﬁrm the presence of the rash on examination, and joint pains when you ask her to move her ﬁngers, wrists and elbows. Medication includes captopril for hypertension, and sulfasalazine for arthritis. Blood testing reveals positive antinuclear antibodies, positive rheumatoid factor, normal C3/C4 levels and negative anti- dsDNA antibodies. Which of the following diagnoses ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
C Drug-induced lupus Sulfasalazine is a known drug-culprit of drug-induced lupus; this lady has a photosensitive rash with normal complement and negative anti-dsDNA antibodies. Features of drug-induced lupus include an average age of onset at 50–70 years, and equal male and female sex ratio. Anti-histone antibodies are positive in more pa-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com tients with drug-induced lupus than systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and C3/C4 levels are normal, whereas complement levels may be decreased in SLE and anti-dsDNA levels are usually normal in drug- induced SLE. The commonest drugs associated with drug-induced lupus are hydralazine, procainamide, minocycline and quinidine, although captopril, sulfasalazine and a number of other drugs may be causative agents. Treatment involves removal of the offending agent; low-dose corticosteroids may speed recovery in patients who are slow to improve. E Drug-induced photosensitivity Photosensitivity alone doesn't ﬁt with this patient's symptoms of joint pain. The rash and joint pains here are more consistent with a diagnosis of drug-induced lupus. A Mixed connective tissue disease In order to make a diagnosis of mixed connective tissue disease, one needs a positive anti-RNP antibody. B Flare of rheumatoid arthritis Photosensitive rashes are not a feature of rheumatoid arthritis. D Systemic lupus erythematosis This lady has normal complement and negative anti-dsDNA antibodies and is on a medication that can cause drug-induced SLE, making the latter the likely diagnosis.

stem: A 48-year-old woman was admitted to hospital for investigation of a 2-month history of polyuria and polydipsia. She had bipolar affective disorder, which was well-controlled on lithium, and no other medical problems. She smoked 5–10 cigarettes per day and did not drink alcohol. There was no relevant family history. Physical examination was unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Sodium (Na+) 148 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 92 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.30 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Glucose (fasting) 5.0 mmol/l < 7.0 mmol/l Plasma osmolality 340 mosmol/kg 278–305 mosmol/kg Urine osmolality 280 mosmol/kg 350–1000 mosmol/kg The patient proceeded to a water deprivation test, the results of which are below: Investigation Urine osmolality After 8 hours of ﬂuid deprivation 200 mOsmol/kg After desmopressin administration 240 mOsmol/kg What is the diagnosis?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion
explanation: C Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus DI is due to either reduced vasopressin (ADH) secretion from the posterior pituitary gland (cranial DI) or renal resistance to its action (nephrogenic DI). It must be distinguished from psychogenic polydipsia, which is excessive ﬂuid intake usually secondary to psychiatric disturbance. In DI, there should be high plasma and low urine osmolality. The diagnosis is conﬁrmed by the water deprivation test. The patient is ﬂuid-restricted for 8 h, and the blood/urine osmolality and weight are measured hourly. In cranial DI, the urine osmolality should rise to > 660 mOsmol/kg after desmopressin, whereas there will be little to no response in nephrogenic DI. The causes of nephrogenic DI include drugs (eg lithium), hypokalaemia and hypercalcaemia, or it can be inherited. Management mainly involves treating or removing the cause, although bendroﬂumethiazide can be used. Cranial DI will respond to intranasal desmopressin. D Psychogenic polydipsia Psychogenic polydipsia is excessive ﬂuid intake, usually secondary to psychiatric disturbance. There would be an increase in urine osmolality after water deprivation. A Conn syndrome Conn syndrome is a cause of hypertension, but with no abnormality in urine osmolality. B Cranial diabetes insipidus (DI) In cranial DI, the urine osmolality should rise to > 660 mOsmol/kg after desmopressin. Cranial DI will respond to intranasal desmopressin. E Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion is associated with low sodium in plasma.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department, having taken a large paracetamol overdose after an argument with her partner some three days earlier. She looks very unwell and has vomited twice during the ambulance journey. On examination, her blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg, her pulse is 95 bpm and she is confused. There is marked bruising affecting her arms and legs, and she has a liver ﬂap. Her respiratory rate is 32 breaths/minute, and abdominal examination reveals severe tenderness in the right upper quadrant. There is no sign of active bleeding. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 81 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 13.3 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 115 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 302 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* Bicarbonate 14 mmol/l 22–30 mmol/L 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com ALT 5400 U/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 580 U/l 30–130 IU/l Bilrubin 104 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l pH 7.1 7.35–7.45 PT 105 s 10.6–14.9 s APTT 40 s 22–41 s Which of the following is the most important management step?
explanation: E Referral for liver transplantation This patient ﬁts the criteria for referral to a Specialist Transplant Unit: List for transplantation if:  arterial pH < 7.3 or arterial lactate > 3.0 mmol/l after adequate ﬂuid resuscitation,  OR if all three of the following occur in a 24-hour period: o creatinine level > 300 μmol/l o PT >100 s (international normalised ratio > 6.5) o grade III/IV encephalopathy. D IV vitamin K Like FFP, vitamin K may be of value in correcting any underlying clotting disorder, although the chances of recovery for hepatic synthetic function are very low. A N-acetylcysteine for 48 hours With this degree of metabolic derangement, the chance of recovery is very small. Hence, this patient should be transferred before further deterioration takes place. N-acetylcysteine does have some impact on outcomes when given late in paracetamol-related liver failure, although it should be given in addition to referral to the Transplant Unit. B Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) Although correction of the marked clotting abnormality seen here is valuable in reducing the risk of acute haemorrhage, it will not impact on this patient’s outcome from liver failure.

stem: A 57-year-old man, who is taking long-term amiodarone therapy, 773-555 THERAPE comes to the clinic complaining of heat intolerance, anxiety, regular resting palpitations and diarrhoea. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 145/82 mmHg, his resting pulse is elevated at 90/min. He appears to have a multinodular goitre. Investigations reveal the following; Investigation Result Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 120 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 178 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 142 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l TSH < 0.05 U/l < 0.5–4.5 U/l Free T3 8.5 pmol/l 5–10 pmol/l Free T4 32 pmol/l 10–22 pmol/l Thyroid autoantibodies Positive Ultrasound Multinodular goitre You discontinue his amiodarone. Which of the following other treatments is the most appropriate treatment to control his thyrotoxicosis?
explanation:
C Carbimazole The picture seen here is very suggestive of amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 1, related to iodine excess and associated with more pronounced symptoms of thyroid disease, formation of a goitre and positive thyroid autoantibodies. Whilst changing the amiodarone to another appropriate anti-arrhythmic is a crucial ﬁrst step in therapy, the long half-life of amiodarone means that symptoms do not immediately improve and carbimazole is only usually effective at high dose. D Potassium perchlorate Perchlorate is designed to gain acute control of thyrotoxicosis in patients with life-threatening symptoms before progressing to surgery. A Radioiodine This patient is likely to be iodine overloaded because of amiodarone dosing, and hence radioiodine is highly unlikely to be successful in managing the thyrotoxicosis. B Corticosteroids Corticosteroids are of value in controlling amiodarone-related thy-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com roiditis, which is less likely to be the cause of thyroid disease here. E Thyroidectomy Thyroidectomy is usually undertaken once thyroid function has been stabilised, because of the risks of progressing to surgery in patients with ongoing cardiovascular morbidity.

stem: A 25-year-old man presented to an inner-city general practitioner (GP) in a very agitated state. The GP suspected that he may have schizophrenia and has prescribed chlorpromazine and arranged an outpatients’ clinic review. He presents to the Emergency Department with a temperature of 38.8 °C, muscle rigidity, tachycardia and hypertension (blood pressure (BP) of 155/100 mmHg). Blood testing reveals a raised creatine kinase (CK) of 345 U/l and a raised ALT of 115 U/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this man?
explanation: C Bromocriptine Neuroleptic malignant syndrome occurs in 0.2% of patients taking dopamine D2-receptor antagonist drugs, particularly the more potent ones such as haloperidol or chlorpromazine. Symptoms include hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, autonomic instability and ﬂuctuating level of consciousness. Abnormal investigations include raised CK, raised white blood cell count and abnormal liver biochemistry. In patients presenting with the syndrome the neuroleptic should be discontinued and bromocriptine is the treatment of choice. Dantrolene was also considered previously as a treatment for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and also as a treatment of malignant hyperthermia, but analyses suggest its use as monotherapy is associated with poorer prognosis than use of anticholinergics or dopamine agonists like bromocriptine. E Fluoxetine Like paroxetine, ﬂuoxetine is an SSRI; it is therefore likely to worsen the risk of seizures, and may itself increase the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome occurring. A Diazepam Although diazepam may have a role in reducing anxiety, it does not treat the underlying cause of his acute presentation. 773-555 THERAPE B Methadone Methadone is used in the treatment of opiate addiction, and does not have a role in the treatment of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. D Paroxetine Paroxetine is an SSRI used in the treatment of depression and may lower the seizure threshold, as such it is not recommended here. It may actually increase the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome occurring.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for a review of his Crohn’s disease management. He was diagnosed at the age of 15 years and has had several ﬂares of his disease, three of which required hospital admission. He was reluctant to start immunosuppressive medication to control his disease but has since changed his mind. The options are discussed with him and he decides to trial monotherapy with azathioprine. His past medical history includes hypertension and gout, for which he takes amlodipine, ramipril and allopurinol. What additional measures should be taken before the initiation of this patient’s treatment?
explanation:
E Suspending allopurinol This patient is about to commence treatment with azathioprine. Azathioprine is a prodrug of mercaptopurine that is metabolised by the enzyme thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT). Adverse effects of azathioprine include anaemia and myelosuppression. Allopurinol is also capable of similar effects and the two drugs when combined can cause signiﬁcant haematological toxicity. Therefore, allopurinol should be suspended in this patient, and an alternative option considered. A Bone proﬁle The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend monitoring full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests during azathioprine treatment. However, commencing azathioprine therapy does not require monitoring a patient’s bone proﬁle. B Chest X-ray Unlike other immunosuppressive therapies such as methotrex-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com ate, azathioprine does not cause lung ﬁbrosis and a pretreatment chest X-ray is not required. C Commencing omeprazole Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that is often co-prescribed with additional medications to aid gastric protection. However, it is not indicated to be prescribed for this patient. D Liver ultrasound The NICE guidelines recommend frequent liver function tests during azathioprine treatment, with particular focus on alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase and bilirubin levels. However, a liver ultrasound is not required before azathioprine therapy.

stem: A 35-year-old farm worker has been brought to the Emergency Department having attempted to kill himself by ingesting several mouthfuls of paraquat 2 h previously. He is alert, and his main complaint is pain in his mouth and a retrosternal burning. His heart rate is 95 beats/min and his blood pressure is 135/70 mmHg. He has a respiratory rate of 18/min, with oxygen saturations reading 97% via a digital probe. What is the most important step in his management?
options: Application of high-ﬂow oxygen via a tight-ﬁtting face mask
Conﬁrm signiﬁcant paraquat absorption via a urine test
explanation: B Conﬁrm signiﬁcant paraquat absorption via a urine test Paraquat is a bipyridium herbicide used as a weedkiller, and if ingested can be incredibly toxic, affecting almost every organ system. The qualitative urine test for paraquat is performed by adding 1 ml of urine to a solution of sodium dithionate and sodium hydroxide. If the solution turns blue, paraquat is present; a lighter green indicates diquat or low paraquat concentrations. Local gastrointestinal irritation occurs initially, followed by hepatocellular dysfunction, kidney disease and chemical pneumonitis/acute respiratory distress syndrome. Perhaps the most wellknown consequence of its ingestion is pulmonary ﬁbrosis. This is thought to occur due to oxygen free radical damage, with initial destruction of type I and II alveolar cells and club cells, for which 773-555 THERAPE paraquat has a predilection, with an energy- dependent uptake via the polyamine pathway. Superoxide radicals are formed in the lungs in the presence of oxygen, which exacerbates lung damage, and therefore its application should be restricted unless absolutely necessary. E Administer atropine Atropine is the other step, apart from use of pralidoxime, in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning. A Application of high-ﬂow oxygen via a tight-ﬁtting face mask Application of high-ﬂow oxygen has no impact on prognosis with respect to pulmonary ﬁbrosis. C Measure plasma paraquat concentration If the urine test is positive then a plasma paraquat concentration is the next step. This will give an idea of prognosis and whether haemodialysis/haemoperfusion is warranted, although in practice a very small number of patients are likely to beneﬁt. D Administer pralidoxime Pralidoxime is an initial step in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning and doesn’t have a role in the treatment of paraquat overdose.

stem: A 32-year-old garage manager, who has recently split from his wife, is admitted via ambulance. He was found virtually unarousable with a rapid respiratory rate by colleagues a few hours after he told them to go to a local parts supplier and leave him alone at the garage. There is no particular past medical history of note, and a recent routine blood screening test by an insurance company was normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 141 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 10.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 x 109/l Platelets (PLT) 230 × 109/l 150–400 x 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Chloride (Cl-) 104 mmol/l 98-106 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 230 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 13.0 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Ethylene glycol poisoning The most likely diagnosis is ethylene glycol poisoning; given that this man is a garage manager, it would be expected that he has easy access to the material. Ethylene glycol poisoning results in a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, accompanied by hyperventila-

773-555 THERAPE tion then Kussmaul respiration, decreased consciousness level and eventually coma, kidney disease and death. Management involves either sedation and infusion of ethanol, which is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase, or the use of fomepizole. Kidney disease with this degree of creatinine elevation is likely to require haemodialysis. E Lactic acidosis Lactic acidosis is seen in metformin toxicity and where there is signiﬁcant tissue hypoxia - for example, after a period of profound hypotension. A Diabetic ketoacidosis Although this does result in raised anion gap metabolic acidosis, access to ethylene glycol and the motive for overdose make this the greater concern. B Aspirin poisoning At this point, compensated metabolic acidosis with hyperventilation would be expected in aspirin poisoning. D Ethanol poisoning Ethanol poisoning is much less likely to result in kidney disease and acidosis than ethylene glycol overdose.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department complaining of nausea. She has taken an overdose of paracetamol about four hours earlier. She denies having taken any other tablets or alcohol. The overdose was impulsive and she regrets it. On examination, she is alert and orientated. Her heart rate is 70 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are normal and her chest is clear. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no organomegaly and with normal bowel sounds. Neurological examination is unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 132 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Platelets (PLT) 216 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Creatinine (Cr) 108 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 14 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Urea 5.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l ALT 32 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 63 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Albumin 39 g/l 35–55 g/l INR 1.1 < 1.1 4-hour paracetamol level 160 mg/l Image of new treatment nomogram for paracetamol overdose: 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com What is the most appropriate next step in your management?
options: Discharge patient home and arrange outpatient psychiatric follow up
Admit the patient for observation, repeat blood tests and paracetamol level in 4 hours
explanation: D Start N-acetylcysteine The 4-hour paracetamol level is above the level required for starting treatment with N-acetylcysteine. The best way to determine the appropriate level at which treatment should be initiated is to use the nomogram available online via the National Poisons Information Service. B Admit the patient for observation, repeat blood tests and paracetamol level in 4 hours Delaying treatment by a further four hours potentially misses the important time period when intervention may prevent, or at least signiﬁcantly reduce, liver damage. A Discharge patient home and arrange outpatient psychiatric follow up This patient’s paracetamol level places her above the treatment line and, therefore, at signiﬁcant risk of hepatotoxicity. Because of this, treatment is indicated. C Carry out gastric lavage Gastric lavage has only a very limited role in the treatment of overdoses (eg in the ﬁrst few minutes after an overdose of agents such as tricyclic antidepressants). Here, the blood paracetamol level is 773-555 THERAPE already over the treatment line and the focus of management should be on reducing it to prevent hepatotoxicity. E Arrange psychiatric review Given the patient currently regrets the overdose, the risk of further suicide attempts while receiving N- acetylcysteine in a hospital seems to be lower than the risk of hepatoxicity. Although an inpatient psychiatric review is required, it is not the ‘next step’.

stem: 34-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department after being found by his estranged wife having drunk a quantity of paraquat and ingested an unknown quantity of codeine phosphate tablets. It is thought that he took the overdose some 3 h previously. On examination in the department, his blood pressure (BP) is 112/74 mmHg, pulse is 74/min and regular and he is drowsy due to having taken the codeine phosphate tablets. Which one of the following is an important step in the management of paraquat overdose?
explanation:
A Activated charcoal Activated charcoal, dosed at 50 g for an adult, should be given via nasogastric tube. Maximum efﬁcacy is thought to be within the ﬁrst 2 hours but there may beneﬁt up to 12 hours from ingestion. As with any poisoning, the national poison service should be consulted. Plasma levels of paraquat > 0.1 mg/l at 24 hours are associated with a poor prognosis; ingestion of > 10 g is associated with a mortality of 100%. Death has been associated with as little as 3 g of ingested paraquat. The cause of death is usually progressive pulmonary ﬁbrosis, which begins during the second week after ingestion. Often the oliguric kidney disease seen with paraquat, which develops within 12 hours of ingestion, is beginning to resolve at this stage. Fuller’s earth is an alternative with similar efﬁcacy to activated charcoal but is far less widely available. E N-Aacetylcysteine IV Although N-acetylcysteine has a role as an anti-oxidant across a range of diseases, evidence does not support its use in the treatment of paraquat overdose. B Dexamethasone IV

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Modest beneﬁts only were seen for dexamethasone IV in a retrospective case series analysis. It may be more useful when combined with haemoperfusion. C Praliodoxime chloride IV Praliodoxime chloride is used as an adjunct to atropine in patients who are symptomatic following organophosphate poisoning. Its role is primarily as a cholinesterase reactivator. It has no use in paraquat poisoning. D Haemodialysis Intermittent hemodialysis or hemoﬁltration should be nearly as effective in enhancing elimination at comparable blood ﬂow rates because paraquat has low protein binding. Concomitant hemodialysis and hemoperfusion may even be superior. Thus, in patients who present soon after ingestion, it is reasonable to use these therapies if hemoperfusion or charcoal is unavailable.

stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance. She has been found by her mother, lying on the ﬂoor having taken an unidentiﬁed overdose and a quantity of alcohol. Her mother is known to be hypertensive, for which she takes medication. On examination, she is obtunded and hypotensive with a BP of 75/50 mmHg; her heart rate is 38 bpm. Finger prick glucose is 3.2 mmol/l. She has been given atropine 3 mg by the ambulance crew with little effect. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management in this case after having assessed her airway?
explanation:
A IV Glucagon Given the history and ﬁndings on examination, the most likely diagnosis is overdose of her mother’s beta (β)- blockers. She presents with decreased conscious level, profound hypotension and

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com bradycardia, features typical of β-blocker overdose. Bronchospasm rarely occurs in overdose of β-blockers, except where there is a history of asthma. Immediate management is to give IV glucagon (50– 150 μg/kg) followed by a glucagon infusion to treat hypotension, and atropine if needed to treat bradycardia. Because of the large quantities of glucagon required to achieve therapeutic effect, a number of commentaries recommend moving rapidly to transcutaneous pacing. Patients should be monitored for occurrence of hypoglycaemia. If the patient is seen within the ﬁrst 4 h of overdose, gastric lavage may be of value. E Insertion of pacing wire Pacing is the optimal solution in the event that large volumes of glucagon are not available. B IV Adrenalin This runs the risk of driving signiﬁcant rhythm disturbance versus glucagon as the alternative. C IV Noradrenalin Like adrenaline, this is best avoided because of the risk of precipitating VT. D Salbutamol nebuliser Although this may cause a small increase in heart rate it is unlikely to be effective versus IV glucagon.

stem: A 78-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with confusion which has occurred following three days of vomiting and diarrhoea. She has a past medical history of mild chronic kidney disease, with a baseline creatinine level of 149 µmol/l and atrial ﬁbrillation, which is rate-controlled with digoxin. On examination, her BP is 95/50 mmHg and her heart rate is 110 bpm. She is alert to painful stimuli only. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 132 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 216 × 109/l 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Potassium (K+) 5.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 11.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 211 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Her ECG is shown below: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention in this case?
options: Give phenytoin 250 mg IV over ﬁve minutes
Wait for IV Digibind® to become available
explanation: D Give phenytoin 250 mg IV over ﬁve minutes The ECG demonstrates monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT). Phenytoin prolongs the effective refractory period and depresses spontaneous depolarisation in ventricular tissue. It can therefore be used to terminate VT in affected patients with digoxin overdose. A Arrange for DC cardioversion This patient is maintaining a systolic BP of 95 mmHg, with a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg, and DC cardioversion in the context of digoxin overdose is usually unsuccessful. Attempts at chemical cardioversion are therefore preferred in the ﬁrst instance. B Dialysis Dialysis is not effective as a treatment for digoxin toxicity, owing to the large volume of distribution of the drug. C Give insulin and dextrose IV Although correction of hyperkalaemia may be required, it is VT that requires immediate intervention, which this would not address. E Wait for IV Digibind® to become available Digibind® consists of digoxin-binding antibody fragments, and the dose used depends on the digoxin level and the patient’s weight. Prognostic indicators of severe digoxin toxicity include digoxin 773-555 THERAPE levels of over 15 ng/ml and serum potassium levels of over 5 mmol/l. Susceptibility to toxicity is further increased by kidney disease, hypothyroidism or hypomagnesaemia. If Digibind® is available, then it should be given concurrently with phenytoin. Waiting risks this patient suffering a cardiac arrest.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with chronic asthma presents to her General Practitioner with a history of nausea and vomiting for the past two days. She had argued with her mother over something trivial while watching her regular television show just before the onset of her symptoms. She had vomited several times after supper that night and had gone to bed early. From the next day onwards, she has been feeling unwell with a headache and abdominal pain. On examination, she is drowsy but oriented, and a coarse tremor is evident. Pupils are normal and reactive. Her chest is clear. She has normal heart sounds and there is epigastric discomfort on palpation of her abdomen. Observations reveal a heart rate of 130 bpm, respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute and blood pressure of 100/66 mmHg. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 120 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 10 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 250 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 2.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 2.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 60 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Calcium 2.9 mmol/l 2.12–2.65 mmol/l Phosphate 0.65 mmol/l 0.74–1.4 mmol/l Magnesium 0.70 mmol/l 0.75–1.05 mmol/l An ECG reveals sinus tachycardia with a rate of 134 bpm. What is the next step in management for this patient?
explanation:
B Intravenous (IV) K+ replacement This patient presented with evidence of theophylline toxicity, possibly an overdose prompted by her argument with her mother. Features of theophylline toxicity include nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, sinus tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension, tremor, headache, agitation, confusion and hallucinations. Metabolic features include hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypercalcaemia. Severe toxicity can cause convulsions and cardiac ar-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com rhythmias. Activated charcoal can be given, even late after ingestion, to reduce absorption. Serum theophylline level can be measured to gauge the severity of toxicity (mild/moderate > 20 mg/l; chronic > 40 mg/l; severe > 60 mg/l). However, this patient has presented with severe hypokalaemia and tachycardia. Due to the risk of cardiac arrhythmia, it is essential to replace her potassium as the ﬁrst step in management. A Activated charcoal every four hours Activated charcoal (50 g for adults) should be given to this patient to reduce the absorption of theophylline. However, the regime in this option is the treatment of choice for severe toxicity, and therefore, this is not the correct option as we do not know her theophylline level. Further, treatment of her hypokalaemia should be initiated ﬁrst, which is relatively straightforward to do. Activated charcoal may need to be given via a nasogastric tube for this patient due to her drowsiness and therefore is relatively more complicated to initiate. C IV magnesium replacement Although this patient has a low magnesium level and magnesium should be replaced, the next step in management is to replace this patient’s K+ due to the risk of cardiac arrhythmia. Magnesium replacement should be initiated following this to prevent rebound hypokalaemia. D IV propranolol Intravenous propranolol can be used in cases of sinus tachycardia and supraventricular tachycardia due to theophylline toxicity. However, this is not always required if adequate cardiac output is maintained. Furthermore, beta-blockers should be avoided in this patient due to her history of chronic asthma and the risk of precipitating an exacerbation of her airway’s disease. E Measurement of serum theophylline level This patient’s serum theophylline level should be measured to determine the severity of toxicity. However, the next best step is to initiate K+ replacement due to her risk of arrhythmia and this should be started regardless of her theophylline level.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is admitted after a collapse at a nightclub. Her friends tell you that she does not drink alcohol. She was out celebrating her birthday with friends. Apparently, she was looking for water to drink and seemed a little confused just before she collapsed. On examination, she is pyrexial (40 °C) and unconscious. She has bilateral dilated pupils. Her BP is 165/92 mmHg and her pulse is 110/min. 773-555 THERAPE Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 149 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 72 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 6.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 190 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Creatinine kinase (CK) 1210 U/l 24–170 U/l Urine Blood ++, no red cells on microscopy Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Cocaine toxicity While cocaine and MDMA toxicities both can be associated with hypertension, tachycardia and rhabdomyolysis, MDMA access as a drug of abuse is less than for Cocaine. Cocaine may produce toxicity in virtually any organ; few complaints (particularly focal complaints) can be dismissed. Chest pain, shortness of breath, headache, focal neurologic symptoms, and extremity symptoms are particularly worrisome.
