Succinylcholine relatively contraindicated in rapid sequence intubation; consider rocuronium (1 mg/kg IV) or other non-depolarizing agent as alternative. For symptomatic hypertension and psychomotor agitation, benzodiazepine is used. In cocaine associated myocardial ischemia, Aspirin (325 mg), Nitroglycerin infusion and benzodiazepine (for agitation and hypertension) be used. Beta blockers including labetalol is contraindicated in acute cocaine toxicity. Powder cocaine is the most commonly used stimulant in the UK. The prevalence of use in the last year reported in England and Wales in 2018 to 2019 (2.9%) was the highest since 2008 to 2009. Lifetime use among 15 year olds in England increased from 2% in 2013 to 4.2% in 2018, and was 5.4% in Scotland in the same year. D 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine toxicity Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) toxicity can be associated with hypertension, tachycardia and rhabdomyolysis, but access to it as a drug of abuse is less than for cocaine.MDMA toxicity is associated with picture of extreme hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, renal impairment, low platelets and decreased consciousness level with dilated pupils is typical of the condition. Initial basic life support with assessment of ABC is crucial, with benzodiazepines the main agents used for sedation and for control of seizures. Hypertension is managed aggressively with agents

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com such as phentolamine and sodium nitroprusside. Where there is signiﬁcant rhabdomyolysis as in this case, urinary alkalinisation may reduce progression to acute kidney disease. A Neuroleptic malignant syndrome This is most often seen in patients prescribed conventional dopamine antagonist anti-psychotic medication, and this is very rarely seen as a drug of abuse. B Malignant hyperthermia Malignant hyperthermia is seen in response to anaesthetic agents, particularly in patients with inherited neuromuscular disorders. C Serotonin syndrome Serotonin syndrome is associated with SSRIs, prescribed for depression, which are not associated with an immediate neuropsychological impact, and therefore not used as drugs of abuse.

stem: A 62-year-old man returns to the Emergency Ward with confusion some two weeks after discharge post- anterior myocardial infarction. He made a relatively good recovery and was started on a range of medications, including an antidepressant, as he said he was feeling really very depressed after his myocardial infarction. He did have depression which required medication a few years earlier, and felt that his old symptoms were returning. His wife tells you that he has become increasingly vague over the past three to four days. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 125/75 mmHg, his pulse is 78/min and regular. He is euvolaemic. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 127 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following agents is most likely to be responsible for his low sodium?
explanation: D Citalopram He has been started on citalopram for his depression, and like other CNS-active agents, citalopram may cause syndrome of in- 773-555 THERAPE appropriate ADH. Presentation with SIADH is unpredictable and may occur some time after starting therapy. Other CNS drug causes include carbamazepine, tricyclic antidepressants, thioridazine and nicotine. Management in this case would involve discontinuation of the citalopram and offering psychotherapy as an alternative, bearing in mind that other SSRIs and tricyclics may also cause SIADH. If citalopram is continued then ﬂuid restriction is unlikely to be effective. Evidence on the relative increase in risk of SIADH for a range of antidepressants comes from a Danish registry study. Conﬁdence intervals for risk increase are: citalopram 7.8 (CI 7.42-8.20); clomipramine 4.93 (CI 2.72- 8.94); duloxetine 2.05 (CI 1.44-292); venlafaxine 2.90 (CI 2.43-3.46); mirtazapine 2.95 (CI 2.71-3.21); and mianserin 0.90 (CI 0.71-1.14). C Spironolactone Spironolactone is used at low dose in the treatment of heart failure, and is therefore less likely to cause hyponatraemia. A Ramipril Ramipril is not associated with SIADH; the main concern with respect to ACE inhibitor use is hyperkalaemia. B Atenolol Atenolol is not associated with hyponatraemia. E Furosemide Furosemide promotes both salt and water excretion, and it is therefore rarely associated with hyponatraemia in a patient who appears euvolaemic. Hyponatraemia is seen more commonly in patients taking loop diuretics combined with a thiazide, or where there is marked ﬂuid overload.

stem: A 54-year-old woman who has taken multiple courses of steroids over the past few years for rheumatoid arthritis and brittle asthma, comes to the clinic for review. She is concerned that she may have osteoporosis and wants to know if she will require bone protection therapy. Which of the following is the best investigation to determine the need for bone protection?
options: Calcium, vitamin D, and alkaline phosphatase measurement
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of the hip and spine
explanation: B Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of the hip and spine DXA scanning is the best way to assess osteoporosis in patients treated with corticosteroids. A T-score ≤ - 2.5 is indicative of a diagnosis of osteoporosis and should prompt treatment with a bisphosphonate as the ﬁrst-line intervention. Low vitamin D should also be ruled out. A T-score threshold value of – 1.5 SD is usually the cut- off for patients under glucocorticoid treatment in Europe. Where the T-score is between - 1 and - 2.5 further assessment of fracture risk using a tool such as the fracture risk assessment tool (FRAX) should be considered. D Micromagnetic resonance imaging (micro-MRI) Like micro-CT, micro-MRI is useful for evaluating bone microarchitecture, although there is no evidence as to how this links to prognosis/fracture risk. It is currently used as a research tool to evaluate the effect of interventions on bone structure. A Calcium, vitamin D, and alkaline phosphatase measurement Calcium, vitamin D, and alkaline phosphatase are normal in patients with corticosteroid related osteoporosis. Low-normal calcium and raised alkaline phosphatase is suggestive of an alternative diagnosis, osteomalacia, due to low levels of vitamin D. Elevated calcium and alkaline phosphatase at the upper end of the normal range raises the possibility of primary hyperparathyroidism. C High-resolution micro-computed tomography (microCT) High-resolution micro-CT provides information on bone microarchitecture in patients who have been treated with corticosteroids, although no links to fracture outcomes are provided. For this reason, DXA is the preferred investigation. E Plain lumbar spine X-ray Plain lumbar spine X-ray may be useful in those patients with a T score between - 1.0 and - 2.5 where there is not already a reason for intervention. It may identify previous osteoporotic lumbar spine fractures which are a strong predictor of future fragility fractures occurring.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset shortness of breath and tongue swelling. On examination, his BP is 100/70 mmHg and his heart rate is 100 bpm and regular. He is sweating and erythematous, and has stridor. He has a past medical history of hypertension and asthma. He takes amlodipine 5 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily and occasional salbutamol inhalers. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Give the patient an EpiPen® for use in case of a further attack
Screen the whole family for C1 esterase deﬁciency
explanation: B Stop ramipril This patient has angio-oedema, which may have been precipitated by him taking an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. This can occur at any time of therapy, not just on introduction. Given the severity of this condition, the precipitating drug should be stopped – therefore, ramipril should be discontinued. Angiotensin II receptor blockers are another possible cause. Angio-oedema can occur with other classes of antihypertensives, such as calcium channel blockers, but is reported much less frequently. The frequency of angio-oedema with thiazide diuretics and alphablockers are intermediate. The ACE inhibitor should be substituted with another antihypertensive. E Screen the whole family for C1 esterase deﬁciency C1 esterase deﬁciency is a cause of hereditary angio-oedema. 773-555 THERAPE Symptoms tend to start at around puberty, although this is variable, and other family members will be affected. It can present with varying symptoms, depending on the degree of C1 esterase deﬁciency and the genetic mutation that causes it. This is an unlikely cause in this patient where there is a clear precipitant of angiooedema. A Stop amlodipine Amlodipine is a calcium channel antagonist, and although angiooedema has been reported in association with these drugs, it is much less common than with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. C Give oral cetirizine Cetirizine is an antihistamine used in allergic reactions. Although it can be used for angio-oedema, the severity of this presentation would make it of secondary use. A priority would be steroid treatment. D Give the patient an EpiPen® for use in case of a further attack This patient has angio-oedema from a speciﬁc precipitant which can easily be removed without any need for further exposure. Stopping ramipril should prevent any further episodes. If an episode were to recur within three months of stopping the ACE inhibitor, then the patient should be referred to an Immunologist. An EpiPen® is not indicated for angio-oedema.

stem: A 25-year-old hairdresser is brought in via ambulance to the Emergency Department, and you have been asked to attend. She has ingested an unknown quantity of her father’s dothiepin tablets in the previous few hours. She has a Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) of 9 with dilated pupils, has a heart rate of 95 beats/min and a blood pressure of 110/65 mmHg. Her ﬁnger-prick blood glucose is 5.6 mmol/l. You are given a copy of her ECG, which shows broadening of the QRS complexes. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
options: iv Calcium chloride 10 ml of 10% solution
explanation: C iv Sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol QRS widening is a bad prognostic sign in patients who have taken a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose. Once QRS is greater than 100 ms, the risk of seizures and ventricular arrhythmias rises signiﬁcantly and IV sodium bicarbonate is the intervention of choice. It works by reducing TCA binding to the myocardium. A Intravenous (iv) Glucagon 5 mg 773-555 THERAPE High-dose glucagon, where available, is an intervention for beta blocker overdose, because it exerts a beta blocker-independent effect on increasing both heart rate and contractility. B iv Naloxone 800 mcg Naloxone is a reversal agent for opiate overdose, and is a potential option for patients in peri-respiratory arrest who have suffered an iatrogenic opiate overdose or who are recreational users of heroin. D iv Flumazenil 200 mcg Flumazenil is a reversal agent for benzodiazepine overdose. Use in patients who are habituated to benzodiazepines is, however, not recommended because rapid reversal may drive an increased risk of seizures. E iv Calcium chloride 10 ml of 10% solution Calcium chloride is given for cardioprotection where there is signiﬁcant hyperkalaemia.

stem: A 28-year-old car mechanic, who specialised in battery repair, is admitted with history of episodic abdominal pain for the past six months. This time, he had a severe episode and was admitted to a surgical unit for evaluation. He has a history of anorexia, constipation and intermittent nausea and vomiting from the inception of his illness. He has also found it increasing difﬁcult to use his gadgets, due to weakness of hands, for the past three weeks.
explanation: D Serum lead This scenario is typical of chronic lead poisoning in adults. A combination of gastrointestinal symptoms with pure motor polyneuropathy and predominantly bilateral wrist drop should raise the suspicion of this toxicity. There is usually a microcytic anaemia, proximal renal tubular acidosis and amino acid leak. Moderate poisoning occurs at blood lead concentrations of 450–750 μgm/l. Basophilic stippling may be seen. Because lead inhibits the conversion of delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydrase and ferrochelatase, delta-aminolevulinic acid cannot be converted to porphobilinogen, and iron is not incorporated into protoporphyrin. Hence, erythrocyte protoporphyrin is elevated to levels >35 mcg/dl, a ﬁnding that is also common in iron deﬁciency anaemia. The most important aspect of management is to remove the patient from the source of lead poisoning. Chelation therapy with oral DMSA (2–3 dimercaptosuccinic acid) or IV EDTA (sodium calcium edetate) should be discussed with a poison centre. B Serum magnesium Symptoms of magnesium toxicity are similar to those of calcium toxicity with nausea, vomiting, depression and lethargy, rather than the picture of renal tubular acidosis and microcytic anaemia seen here. A Serum cadmium Cadmium toxicity is seen less frequently than inadvertent lead exposure, although the pictures seen with respect to renal impairment and proximal renal tubular acidosis are similar. C Serum copper Copper toxicity is rare, and is usually seen in association with cooking of acid foods in copper cooking utensils or with exposure to copper in water. Symptoms of very long-term copper exposure include hepatic dysfunction. E 24 h urinary copper excretion This is most useful in screening for patients with Wilson’s disease.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with symptoms of weakness. She describes intermittent double vision and difﬁculty chewing and swallowing food. The patient has a background of angina, rheumatoid arthritis, atrial ﬁbrillation and hypertension. On examination, she has a general paucity of facial expression and she appears to be frowning her forehead intermittently. There is symmetrical upper limb weakness, while lower limb power is normal. She has normal sensation and reﬂexes are normal. She has ptosis that appears to ﬂuctuate. Eye movements appear to be normal. What is the most likely medication in this patient that could cause these symptoms?
explanation:
B Penicillamine This patient has symptoms suggestive of myasthenia gravis (MG). Symptoms include weakness of facial muscles, ptosis (which can cause compensatory use of the frontalis muscle), extraocular muscle weakness, poor swallow and speech. Respiratory muscle involvement is a serious complication. The weakness worsens with exercise and reﬂexes are normal. Penicillamine can cause MG, and patients can have raised acetylcholine receptor antibodies. It is used for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis and as a chelator for copper in Wilson’s disease. Side-effects of penicillamine also include proteinuria and a lupus-like syndrome. Stopping penicillamine should reverse the myasthenic symptoms in the majority of cases. E Amiodarone Amiodarone is associated with pulmonary ﬁbrosis and skin photosensitivity.

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com A Nitrates Nitrates can result in headaches and syncope rather than MG. C Methotrexate Methotrexate results in hepatic and pulmonary ﬁbrosis; liver function test and pulmonary function test monitoring during therapy is advised. D Hydralazine Hydralazine is most strongly associated with drug-induced lupus (seen in up to 20% of patients who take the medication).

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents two days after a paracetamol overdose. She complains of persistent vomiting. On examination, she looks unwell, is markedly tender in the epigastrium, and she has a pulse of 100/min, regular, and a blood pressure (BP) of 115/60 mmHg. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 109 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 100 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l INR 2.7 < 1.1 Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 235 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l pH 7.2 7.35–7.45 pO2 8.5 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa pCO2 3.9 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 14 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Glucose Urine output 3.9 mmol/l 35 ml in the past 4 hours 3.5–5.5 mmol/l She is admitted to the high-dependency unit. Which of the following other interventions is likely to have the biggest positive effect on her prognosis?
explanation:
B Haemodialysis Of most concern is the tailing-off of this woman’s urine output, metabolic acidosis and elevated potassium. This is suggestive of acute tubular necrosis. Kidney disease associated with paracetamol overdose is recoverable, and even this woman has a reasonable chance of attaining normal renal function after the acute event, as such, haemodialysis is the most appropriate next step. A Haemoﬁltration Haemoﬁltration is much less effective than haemodialysis in this situation, and her blood pressure would support haemodialysis, making this the preferred option. C Sodium bicarbonate IV This may promote ﬂuid retention and not have a major impact on

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com urine output or creatinine. D N-acetylcysteine IV N-acetylcysteine, even when used late, may reduce liver damage and hence it should be used even now, although the relative impact on outcome is less than that for haemodialysis. E Activated charcoal via NG At this stage all of the paracetamol will have been absorbed from the GI tract, meaning there is little role for activated charcoal here.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with progressive muscle weakness and aching in her thighs and shoulders over the last two months. She reports no recent trauma or changes in activity level. Her medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and type II diabetes mellitus. Her current medications include lisinopril, metformin and atorvastatin, which she started six months ago for hyperlipidaemia. On physical examination, she has symmetrical proximal muscle weakness but no joint swelling, skin changes or focal neurological deﬁcits. Laboratory tests are shown below. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 137 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Creatine kinase (CK) 1080 U/l 30–200 U/l Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 60 U/l 10–35 U/l ALT 45 U/l 10–40 U/l ESR 12 mm/hour < 20 mm/hour What is the most appropriate initial management step for this patient?
options: Start corticosteroid therapy for suspected polymyositis
Add vitamin D and calcium supplements 773-555 THERAPE
Start a muscle relaxant for pain relief
explanation: C Discontinue atorvastatin Statins can cause myopathy, which presents as muscle weakness, with elevated CK levels. Discontinuing the statin is the appropriate initial management to determine whether symptoms will improve, which would, in turn, conﬁrm statin-induced myopathy as the likely cause. B Add vitamin D and calcium supplements Vitamin D deﬁciency can cause muscle pain and weakness. However, this patient's symptoms and elevated CK levels are more suggestive of statin-associated myopathy, making discontinuation of the statin as the most appropriate ﬁrst step. A Start corticosteroid therapy for suspected polymyositis Polymyositis can present with muscle weakness and elevated CK levels, but this patient's history of recent statin use and the absence of other systemic ﬁndings make drug-induced myopathy more likely. Corticosteroid therapy is not indicated as an initial step without conﬁrmation of an inﬂammatory myopathy. D Initiate methotrexate therapy Methotrexate is used in inﬂammatory and autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis but is not indicated for statinassociated myopathy. Discontinuing the suspected drug (atorvastatin) should be attempted ﬁrst. E Start a muscle relaxant for pain relief Muscle relaxants are not typically used in the management of statinassociated myopathy. Addressing the underlying cause by discontinuing the statin is the most appropriate approach.

stem: A 37-year-old man known to be in the early stages of Huntington’s disease is admitted to the Emergency Department by ambulance. His wife found him unconscious on the ﬂoor with an empty bottle of codeine phosphate at his side. He had left a suicide note and on further questioning his wife admits that her husband has been depressed for a few weeks. On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 7, with a respiratory rate of 10/min and BP of 100/60 mmHg. Investigations: 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Investigation Result Normal Values pH 7.25 7.35 - 7.45 pO2 6.8 kPa > 10.5 kPa pCO2 7.5 kPa 4.7 - 6.0 kPa Which of the following represents the most appropriate management in this case?
options: Ask his wife to decide whether he is to be treated
Make a decision that he has a terminal illness and should not be treated
Ask your senior to rule on whether resuscitation is appropriate
Contact the hospital solicitor to rule with respect to resuscitation
explanation: E Treat with IV naloxone Depression is common in the early stages of Huntington's and responds very well to treatment. His wife has given a reliable history that he was depressed at the time of the overdose and, as such, he was not able to make a rational decision to end his life. As such, given the fact that you must act in his best interests, naloxone is the only appropriate next step. D Contact the hospital solicitor to rule with respect to resuscitation This risks an unacceptable delay, and the view of the solicitor is highly unlikely to be at variance from the need to treat in this patient’s best interests. A Ask his wife to decide whether he is to be treated Although it is desirable to reach agreement with the patient’s wife, the ﬁnal decision to treat rests with you as his doctor. Given the history of depression, you should consider that the overdose was not taken against a background of rational decision making. B Make a decision that he has a terminal illness and should not be treated Given the history of depression, you cannot conclude that he made a rational decision to take an overdose of codeine. C Ask your senior to rule on whether resuscitation is appropriate This patient has severe respiratory depression, and is at risk of aspiration and type 2 respiratory failure. As such, it’s inappropriate to wait for advice from your senior and you should instigate therapy.

stem: A 52-year-old man with a history of COPD presents with jaundice. He has a history of hypertension for which he receives ramipril and amlodipine, and hypercholesterolaemia which is treated with a statin. He takes theophylline tablets for his COPD. He consulted his general practitioner (GP) two weeks earlier and was prescribed an antibiotic for two weeks for a lower respiratory tract infection. On examination, he is jaundiced and has signs of scratch marks over his upper body. He tells you he has been passing dark urine. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 204 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 204 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Alkaline phosphatase 320 IU/l 30–130 IU/l ALT 95 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Which of the following antibiotics is most likely to have been responsible?
explanation: C Co-amoxiclav Co-amoxiclav is strongly associated with obstructive jaundice, particularly when used for a period of 2 weeks or longer. It was the subject of a drug safety update from the MHRA speciﬁcally to discourage prolonged prescribing. It is also a recommended initial intervention for the treatment of respiratory infection. A Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is rarely used in conjunction with theophylline because as a CYP450 inhibitor it can lead to a marked increase in theophylline levels. Hence GPs are educated not to use it in this 773-555 THERAPE situation. It is associated with obstructive jaundice, but more rarely than co-amoxiclav. B Cephalexin Cephalexin is rarely associated with transient hepatitis and cholestatic jaundice. Elevation in transaminases is much more commonly seen. D Erythromycin Like ciproﬂoxacin, erythromycin is a P450 inhibitor, which means it is less likely to be used here given the prescription of theophylline. It is more likely to be associated with elevated transaminases rather than obstructive jaundice. E Penicillin V Penicillin V is usually reserved for treatment of S. pyogenes pharyngeal infection, rather than respiratory tract infection, and amoxicillin/co-amoxiclav are favoured under BTS guidelines.

stem: A 64-year-old man, who is taking long-term amiodarone therapy for recurrent episodes of ventricular tachycardia, presents to the clinic with symptoms of weight loss and heat intolerance. His daily medication is ramipril 10 mg, aspirin 75 mg and amiodarone 200 mg. On examination, he is tachycardic with a pulse of 95/min, and his BP is 105/70 mmHg. He has evidence of mild left ventricular failure. There is no evidence of goitre. Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 115 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 245 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 135 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l TSH < 0.5 mu/l 0.4 - 5.0 mu/l Thyroid autoantibody - Thyroid isotope uptake scan Low uptake Thyroid Doppler ultrasound Decreased blood ﬂow Which of the following represents the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) type 2 773-555 THERAPE Amiodarone thyrotoxicity tends to result in two distinct patterns of disease associated with thyrotoxicosis. Type 2 is a destructive thyroiditis, and this explains the ﬁndings here with low thyroid uptake and decreased thyroid blood ﬂow on Doppler ultrasound. AIT type 2 does not respond well to standard therapy for thyrotoxicosis. It may burn itself out after a course of corticosteroids; hence, as the amiodarone cannot be easily discontinued, a course of corticosteroids is most appropriate and is the therapy of choice. B Multinodular goitre The lack of evidence of goitre effectively counts against a diagnosis of multinodular goitre here. A Graves’ disease Graves’ disease is associated with positive thyroid autoantibodies and increased thyroid uptake. C Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) type 1 Type 1 is related to the excess iodine provided by amiodarone leading to excess production of thyroid hormone, often in the presence of latent thyroid disease related to another cause. E Thyroid carcinoma A speciﬁc thyroid mass would be elucidated on both the ultrasound scan and isotope investigation, and neither has raised a concern here.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with a 6-week history of enlarged breast tissue. He is ﬁnding this distressing as his clothing does not ﬁt as well as it used to. There is no history of breast pain or nipple discharge. His past medical history includes depression, chronic back pain, benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension. On examination, he appears well. All observations are within normal limits. There is a visible enlargement of breast tissue bilaterally. On palpation, there are no breast lumps or tenderness. His GP suspects his medication may be contributing to his symptoms. Which of the following medications is most likely to be responsible for this patient’s presentation?
explanation:
B Finasteride This patient has gynaecomastia, an increase in the production of breast tissue secondary to an imbalance between oestrogen and androgen production. It should not be confused with galactorrhoea, which is an increase in breast milk production, usually as a result of the loss of inhibition of prolactin release. Oestrogen stimulates breast tissue production and conditions that involve an increase in oestrogen release or a reduction in testosterone production can cause gynaecomastia. These include androgen resistance, Klinefelter syndrome, obesity, adrenal tumours, testicular tumours and liver disease or cirrhosis. The condition can also arise from drug use with common drugs, including oestrogens, or drugs that inhibit the production or action of testosterone such as ketocona-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com zole, metronidazole, spironolactone and ﬁnasteride. Finasteride is a 5-reductase inhibitor that leads to inhibition of conversion of testosterone into the more potent androgen dihydrotestosterone. E Tramadol Tramadol is an opioid medication. Opioids and other illicit substances have been shown to increase prolactin levels and play a contributing role in developing galactorrhoea. However, opioids do not directly increase breast tissue alone and cause gynaecomastia. A Citalopram Citalopram is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used in the treatment of depression. Citalopram does not cause gynaecomastia. Rather, it increases prolactin levels which can lead to galactorrhoea. C Indapamide Thiazide diuretics have a number of side effects, including electrolyte disturbances. However, they do not cause gynaecomastia. D Tamsulosin Tamsulosin is an alpha-adrenergic antagonist. It reduces prostatic tone and causes relaxation of the arterioles to lower blood pressure. Side-effects include postural hypotension, arrhythmias and chest pain.

stem: A 72-year-old man, who has suffered from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) for some years, is admitted to the Emergency Department having suffered a grand mal seizure. According to his wife, he has also been vomiting for a couple of days. Apparently, the general practitioner (GP) had started him on an antibiotic for a respiratory tract infection. Additional medication includes a high-dose salmeterol ﬂuticasone inhaler for his COPD and oral theophylline. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 121 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 211 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 140 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l You suspect theophylline toxicity related to a drug interaction. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: D Ciproﬂoxacin Drugs known to reduce clearance of theophylline include allopurinol, cimetidine, ciproﬂoxacin, corticosteroids, diltiazem, erythromycin, furosemide, isoprenaline, oral contraceptives, thiabendazole and verapamil. Ciproﬂoxacin is an inhibitor of CYP 1A2 and this, coupled with some effect on 3A4 metabolism, may drive theophylline accumulation. Note that recent recommendations suggest that ciproﬂoxacin use should be avoided if alternative effective antibiotic choices are available; due to the risk of rare but signiﬁcant long-lasting or permanent debilitating side effects. A Amoxicillin Penicillins do not impact on theophylline metabolism. B Co-amoxiclav Clavulanic acid, like penicillins, does not impact on theophylline metabolism. C Rifampicin Rifampicin is a P450 enzyme inducer, which is likely to reduce theophylline levels. E Trimethoprim Case reports of hyponatraemia exist when trimethoprim and theophylline are co-administered, but theophylline toxicity itself isn’t reported.

stem: You review a 58-year-old man with severe hypertension who has presented to the Emergency Department with intractable headache, diplopia, nausea and vomiting. 773-555 THERAPE On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 195/115 mmHg and he has papilloedema, diplopia, nausea and vomiting. You begin an infusion of labetalol but he is still hypertensive. You consider trying a sodium nitroprusside infusion. Which of the following ﬁts best with use of sodium nitroprusside?
options: It can be used when there is suspected coarctation of the aorta
It leads to relaxation of gut smooth muscle as well as vascular smooth muscle
It should not be used where there is B12 deﬁciency
Blood pressure begins to fall after 5–10 min of infusion
explanation: E Cyanide accumulation occurs in overdose Sodium nitroprusside is a potent short-acting vasodilator, which acts via the nitric oxide pathway to increase cGMP within smooth muscle cells. Side effects include nausea, sweating, headache and twitching, and overdose may be associated with accumulation of cyanide. A It can be used when there is suspected coarctation of the aorta It should not be used in coarctation of the aorta because the marked reduction in preload could precipitate dangerous hypotension. B It leads to relaxation of gut smooth muscle as well as vascular smooth muscle Although nitroprusside does lead to relaxation of vascular smooth muscle, it doesn’t impact on GI smooth muscle – for example, in the duodenum. C It should not be used where there is B12 deﬁciency Although historical papers recommended avoiding nitroprusside in B12 deﬁciency, there is no evidence that it signiﬁcantly impacts on B12 levels when used at therapeutic dose. D Blood pressure begins to fall after 5–10 min of infusion Sodium nitroprusside has a rapid hypotensive effect that begins to appear within 30–60 s of commencing the infusion.

stem: A 50-year-old builder has been referred as an emergency, having been rescued from his burning ﬂat. He has evidence of smoke inhalation, with soot around his nostrils and on the roof of his mouth. He has a carboxyhaemoglobin level of 4%, and since arri- 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com val in the department has had a decreased level of consciousness. He has no evidence of a head injury, and 800 μg of naloxone have not caused any increase in his conscious level. You consider the diagnosis of hydrogen cyanide poisoning. His blood pressure is 85/40 mmHg, with a pulse of 95/min and regular. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Dicobalt edetate 300 mg IV over 1 min
Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min
explanation: B Dicobalt edetate 300 mg IV over 1 min Cyanide can be produced in house ﬁres, when materials such as polyurethane and rubber combust. Cyanide binds with high afﬁnity to cytochrome a3 of the mitochondrial electron transport chain and thereby prevents the utilisation of oxygen at a cellular level. With low levels, the body is able to naturally detoxify cyanide compounds via the enzyme rhodanese (a sulphur transferase), which relies on the presence of sulphur- containing substrate. Dicobalt edetate, sodium thiosulphate and sodium nitrite are all recognised treatments for cyanide poisoning. E Pralidoxime 30 mg/kg IV over 5–10 min Pralidoxime is used in conjunction with atropine to reduce the parasympathetic effects of organophosphate poisoning. A N-acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg intravenous (IV) over 15 min N-Acetylcysteine and methionine are glutathione donors used in the treatment of paracetamol poisoning. C Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min Methylene blue is used as a treatment for methaemoglobinaemia, with ascorbic acid a second-line therapy for methaemoglobinaemia. D Flumazenil 200 μg IV over 15 s Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist licensed for the treatment of iatrogenic overdose.

stem: An 88-year-old man with a background of osteoarthritis is admitted to the Elderly Care Ward following a fall at home. During his admission, he has a further witnessed fall and sustained a 4-cm laceration to his forehead. His observations are taken following the 773-555 THERAPE fall and are all within normal limits. Other than his laceration, the remainder of his examination is unremarkable, with no other identiﬁable injuries. His wound is cleaned and 1% lidocaine is injected around the margins of the laceration. A few minutes later, the man complains of numbness around his lips and pins and needles in his tongue. He starts to feel dizzy and becomes progressively more agitated and restless until it is impossible to continue with suturing. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
D Lipid emulsion This patient is suffering from local anaesthetic toxicity. Symptoms of local anaesthetic toxicity can be remembered by: SAMS (Slurred speech, Altered mental status, Muscle twitching, Seizures). Typically, perioral paraesthesiae and numbness can be seen initially, with decreased consciousness and respiratory arrest occurring at much later stages of toxicity. Treatment of local anaesthetic toxicity is 20% lipid emulsion given as an initial bolus followed by an infusion. E Urgent computed tomography (CT) head This patient has had a fall and sustained a head injury. A deterioration in mental status and increased agitation should always raise suspicion of an intracranial bleed. Therefore, it is likely that a CT head would be appropriate for this patient. However, the immediate life-threatening concern is the onset of symptoms very soon after lidocaine administration. Furthermore, perioral paraesthesiae and numbness are more indicative of local anaesthetic toxicity. If left untreated, local anaesthetic toxicity can be fatal and should be treated ﬁrst. A Haemodialysis Haemodialysis can be utilised for the removal of barbiturates, lithium, alcohol, salicylates and theophylline. However, it is not a treatment for lidocaine toxicity. B Intramuscular adrenaline This patient is having symptoms of local anaesthetic toxicity. Perioral tingling can be an initial symptom of an allergic reaction and anaphylaxis should always be considered. However, the absence of airway compromise and the presence of agitation are more suggestive of local anaesthetic toxicity. C Intravenous sodium bicarbonate

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Intravenous sodium bicarbonate does not play a role in local anaesthetic toxicity.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with a known history of manic-depressive psychosis is admitted unconscious after having been found ﬁtting in the street. Her husband is contacted and reports that they had a serious argument some 7 h ago. On examination to the Emergency Department, she is hypertonic and has a GCS of 8. Her blood pressure is 95/55 mmHg and pulse is 105/min. Lithium level is measured at 3.2 mmol/l. She is intubated and ventilated. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.7 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 134 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 87 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Lithium 3.2 mmol/l 0.4–1.2 mmol/l Which of the following initial interventions would be most appropriate in this case?
options: IV Normal saline should be started
NSAIDs may be useful in reducing lithium levels
explanation: B IV Normal saline should be started Where lithium levels are >3 mmol/l, normal saline should be instigated, particularly here given the hypotension and tachycardia. C Activated charcoal should be given Activated charcoal is not effective after lithium overdose, although gastric lavage can be considered in some patients, European guidelines recommend within the ﬁrst 1-2 h, although anecdotal reports suggest beneﬁt up to 6-8 h. A IV 5% dextrose should be started In this situation normal saline is preferred as IV ﬂuid replacement to 5% dextrose. D NSAIDs may be useful in reducing lithium levels NSAIDs actually lead to an increase in lithium levels. E Gastric lavage should be commenced Given the time period elapsed, gastric lavage is not likely to be useful in this scenario. 773-555 THERAPE

stem: A 36-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department having taken a combined overdose of amitriptyline, diazepam and codeine phosphate. She is known to the department with multiple previous admissions due to alcohol intoxication, and left a suicide note after a recent split from her partner. On examination, her BP is 100/60 mmHg, with pulse 95/min and regular. GCS is 7. ECG reveals a QRS of 90 ms. Arterial blood gas reveals a pH of 7.29. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?
explanation: C Intubation and ventilation With a GCS of 7, which may fall further as the overdose continues to take effect, there is signiﬁcant risk of airway compromise. Reversal agents may actually increase agitation or raise the risk of seizures, and should therefore be avoided here. E IV normal saline Although ﬂuid resuscitation is important, airway protection is the most important next step. A IV sodium bicarbonate IV sodium bicarbonate is indicated for QRS prolongation (>100 ms) and for signiﬁcant acidosis. B IV ﬂumazenil In patients who are habitual users of benzodiazepines, particularly in conjunction with tricyclic antidepressants, reversal should be avoided because it can signiﬁcantly increase the risk of seizures. D IV naloxone Naloxone is short-acting, and therefore boluses have a limited impact on improving consciousness. It can be given as an infusion, but given the mixed nature of the overdose here, intubation and ventilation is the better option.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after being discovered by a male friend. On examination, she has a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 8, blood pressure (BP) 90/55 mmHg and a supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) with a rate of 160 bpm. There are a number of bottles of amitriptyline 75 mg tablets found empty in the house. Investigation Result Normal value pH 7.15 7.35–7.45 pa(CO2) 6.2 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa pa(O2) 6.1 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa She is intubated and ventilated and admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). Which of the following other measures is most appropriate in the management of this tricyclic overdose?
explanation:
B Sodium bicarbonate IV Death may follow as little as 1000 mg of tricyclic antidepressant overdose. QRS prolongation to >100 ms is an early sign of signiﬁcant toxicity, while QRS prolongation >120 ms is associated with the risk of ventricular arrhythmias. Guidelines suggest that sodium bicarbonate is the most appropriate ﬁrst-line intervention. E Flumazenil IV Flumazenil is used for reversal of benzodiazepine overdose, and in the situation of tricyclic antidepressant toxicity may actually increase the risk of seizures. A Verapamil IV Verapamil is associated with PR prolongation and is therefore not recommended for management of SVT in this situation. C Propranolol IV Propranolol is associated with QRS widening, which can actually increase the risk of arrhythmia in tricyclic anti- depressant overdose. D Flecainide IV

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Flecainide produces dose-related increases in the PR, QRS and QT intervals, again actually increasing the risk of rhythm disturbance in tricyclic anti-depressant overdose.

stem: A 21-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department by ambulance. She was found by her parents having taken an overdose of her father’s amlodipine tablets following a breakup with her partner. On admission to the department, her blood pressure is 75/50 mmHg, and her pulse is 92 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. She has had intravenous (IV) normal saline started by the paramedics. Which of the following is the next most appropriate intervention?
explanation: A IV calcium chloride Calcium is the optimal initial intervention for calcium channel blocker overdose. It is given as an initial bolus of 10% calcium chloride 20 ml IV, which can be repeated up to 3 times. A calcium infusion can also be considered to keep calcium above 2.0 mmol/l. Atropine, often used to treat hypotension and bradycardia, is ineffective in calcium channel blocker overdose. High-dose insulin and dextrose therapy has been shown to drive an improvement in blood pressure, although it takes some time to take effect. Activated charcoal should be given for oral decontamination. E IV sodium bicarbonate IV sodium bicarbonate is indicated to correct acidosis in patients with tricyclic anti-depressant overdose, where improving acid-base balance can signiﬁcantly reduce the risk of ventricular arrhythmias. It does not have a role in the treatment of calcium channel antagonist overdose. B IV ﬂumazenil Flumazenil has no role in the treatment of calcium channel antagonist overdose. It is a benzodiazepine antagonist which can be used for reversal of acute benzodiazepine overdose. It should not be used for the treatment of benzodiazepine overdose in chronic users, or in alcoholics, because it may precipitate seizures. C IV glucagon Glucagon at high-dose is an antidote for beta-blocker overdose. It has to be given at high-dose to affect pulse and blood pressure, 773-555 THERAPE meaning that isoprenaline infusion and pacing is often considered a better alternative. Glucose monitoring for hypoglycaemia in beta-blockers an essential component of management. D IV naloxone Naloxone is used as an antidote for opiate overdose. It has no role in the treatment of calcium channel antagonist overdose. In opiate overdose, it may need to be given on repeated occasions, or given as an infusion, because the half-life of naloxone is much shorter than the half-life of opiate analgesics. For this reason, many patients admitted with opiate overdose are managed with airway support rather than naloxone.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with a range of chronic illnesses is admitted to the Emergency Department having suffered an overdose of paracetamol tablets. Which of the following agents, when used chronically, leads to increased risks from paracetamol overdose? 773-555 THERAPE
explanation: A Phenytoin It is not acetaminophen but it’s metabolite NAPQI which is hepatotoxic. CYP2E1 enzyme inducers causes more rapid metabolism of acetaminophen and formation of NAPQI. Hence, enzyme inducers including phenytoin, alcohol, carbamazepine and phenobarbital may all increase the risks from paracetamol overdose. Blood is taken at least 4 h after overdose and the paracetamol level is plotted on a graph indicating the need for intervention. This was previously reﬂected in a high- and low-risk treatment line, although now all patients who present are considered high risk. E Ramipril Ramipril is almost completely metabolised to ramiprilat, which is excreted in the urine. It is neither a CYP450 enzyme inducer nor inhibitor. B Clarithromycin Clarithromycin is a CYP3A4 inhibitor, and it is enzyme inducers that increase the risks from paracetamol overdose. C Glimepiride Glimepiride is partially metabolised by CYP2C9, although it is not an enzyme inducer; as such, it has no impact on risks from paracetamol overdose. D Atenolol Between 85 and 100% of the absorbed atenolol dose is excreted unchanged in the urine; it does not undergo signiﬁcant hepatic transformation, and therefore does not impact on risks associated with paracetamol overdose.

stem: A 44-year-old Asian woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a new rash. She reports ﬁrst noticing the rash four weeks ago affecting her arms, legs and back. Her past medical history includes pulmonary tuberculosis, for which she recently completed a 6-month course of rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide and pyridoxine. She takes no other medications and has no allergies. On examination, her observations are stable. There are multiple annular, scaly lesions over her face, arms, legs and back. The rash is more prominent over her face and forearms and there is some 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com blistering at the margins of the lesions. She has no palpable lymphadenopathy and the remainder of her examination is unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 118 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 9.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 6.1 × 109/l 2.5–7.5 × 109/l Lymphocytes 2.3 × 109/l 0.8–5.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 300 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.3 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 85 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l EGFR 65 ml/min/1.73 m2 60+ ml/min/1.73 m2 CRP 9 mg/l < 10 mg/l What is the most appropriate investigation to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation: B Antihistone antibodies This patient has drug-induced lupus, a lupus-like syndrome with symptoms of arthralgia, myalgia, fever and skin changes. Skin changes include a symmetrical annular or ring-shaped rash, particularly over sun-exposed areas. Causative drugs include procainamide, hydralazine and isoniazid. The diagnosis is made from the clinical history, examination and blood tests, including ESR and autoantibody testing. Antihistone antibodies are positive in 75– 95% of cases of drug-induced lupus. C Anti-Jo antibodies Anti-Jo antibodies are speciﬁc for myositis and are not seen in druginduced lupus. A Anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) antibodies Positive anti-dsDNA antibodies, along with the clinical history, are highly suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus. However, a positive anti-dsDNA result is rarely seen in drug-induced lupus and is not the investigation of choice. D Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are positive in vasculitis and are not positive in drug-induced lupus. E Antinuclear antibodies Antinuclear antibodies are commonly seen in multiple autoimmune conditions and are not speciﬁc for drug- induced lupus, making it a 773-555 THERAPE less reliable investigation.

stem: A 55-year-old man with well-controlled ulcerative colitis (on azathioprine 100 mg), hypertension (on lisinopril) and diabetes (on metformin), presents to his general practitioner (GP) with exquisite pain affecting the right big toe. He has had several attacks this year, which usually subside with regular diclofenac for a week. His GP starts him on colchicine and when the attack has settled, adds in allopurinol. He returns to the GP two months later to pick up his repeat prescriptions. Before his GP issues the prescription, he reviews this gentleman’s blood tests (below) and is alarmed. He phones the gastroenterology registrar on call, as he suspects azathioprine toxicity. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 58 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 1.8 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 88 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Neutrophils 0.5 × 10 9/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Lymphocytes 0.4 × 10 9/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l ESR 20 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour CRP 8.0 mg/l < 10 mg/l What is the underlying cause of azathioprine toxicity?
explanation: B Allopurinol This patient is pancytopenic following an interaction between allopurinol and azathioprine. The combination of xanthine oxidase inhibition (allopurinol) and azathioprine potentiates the formation of mercaptopurine metabolites, which leads to signiﬁcant and lifethreatening bone marrow suppression due to elevated 6- mercaptopurine, the major metabolite of azathioprine. Allopurinol should never be co-prescribed with azathioprine. 773-555 THERAPE D Diclofenac Although the more likely drug culprit is allopurinol, diclofenac may lead to renal impairment and decreased clearance of azathioprine. A Gout Gout per se does not cause azathioprine toxicity. C Colchicine Very rarely colchicine may cause myelosuppression. E Metformin Metformin does not interact with azathioprine.

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department some 45 minutes after taking 70 × 75 mg aspirin tablets. She is known to the department with a personality disorder and has taken multiple previous overdoses. On examination, her blood pressure is 135/80 mmHg and pulse 90 bpm and regular. Her weight is 45 kg. Her respiratory rate is 23 breaths/minute, and she looks distressed. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 134 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate 28 mmol/l 22–30 mmol/l Creatinine 102 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
A Activated charcoal This patient presents within the ﬁrst hour of an aspirin overdose and, as such, activated charcoal to limit absorption is the most appropriate next step. It is clear, given the amount of tablets this patient has taken and her body weight, that this is a signiﬁcant overdose. D N-acetylcysteine

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com N-acetylcysteine is the antidote of choice for paracetamol overdose where it acts as an –SH group donor, preventing toxicity from Nacetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), the toxic metabolite of paracetamol. It has no role in the treatment of aspirin overdose. B Forced alkaline diuresis Urinary alkalinisation is a key intervention in the management of salicylate overdose, although alkaline diuresis can drive signiﬁcant ﬂuid shifts and may be detrimental with respect to outcomes in salicylate overdose. C Intravenous (IV) normal saline with potassium Although ﬂuid rehydration is important in the management of aspirin overdose, the crucial next step is activated charcoal to have as great an impact as possible in reducing aspirin absorption. E Haemodialysis Indications for haemodialysis are listed below:  profoundly altered mental status  pulmonary or cerebral oedema  renal insufﬁciency  ﬂuid overload  a plasma salicylate concentration of > 7.2 mmol/l in acute ingestion OR > 4.3 mmol/l in chronic ingestion  clinical deterioration despite aggressive and appropriate supportive care.

stem: A 49 year old woman who has bipolar disease with psychotic episodes, and suffered a road trafﬁc accident some 3 years ago, comes to the clinic complaining of polyuria and polydipsia. She has taken lithium for the past 8 years but takes no other regular medication. On examination her BP is 122/82 mmHg; pulse is 78/min and regular. Her BMI is 31. Investigations; Hb 131 g/l WCC 5.4 x109/l PLT 189 x109/l Na+ 143 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l Creatinine 112 micromol/l Glucose 6.6 mmol/l (fasting) Water deprivation test: Plasma osmolality 350 mosmol/kg post dehydration, urine osmolality 240 mosmol/kg post dehydration Urine osmolality fails to increase after DDAVP 773-555 THERAPE Which of the following is the most likely cause of her polyuria and polydipsia?
explanation: D Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus The answer is Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (DI) - The symptoms and results of the water deprivation test are consistent with nephrogenic DI. Urine remains dilute following a period of dehydration and fails to concentrate although plasma osmolality is elevated, even after the administration of DDAVP. The likely cause is chronic lithium prescription. E Primary polydipsia Primary polydipsia is incorrect because the urine osmolality fails to rise during a period of dehydration. A Cranial diabetes insipidus Cranial diabetes insipidus, is incorrect because the urine osmolality fails to increase after administration of DDAVP. B Diabetes mellitus Diabetes mellitus, is incorrect because of the water deprivation test results and because it is unlikely that the glucose levels have risen high enough to promote osmotic diuresis. C Impaired glucose tolerance Impaired glucose tolerance, is incorrect because of the water deprivation test results, and because in IGT it is impossible for the glucose results to have risen high enough to promote osmotic diuresis.

stem: An unknown middle-aged man has been brought into the Emergency Department, having been found collapsed in the street. He has a suicide note in his pocket, along with a quantity of various loose tablets. One of the nursing staff recognises that some of the tablets are temazepam and others may be amitriptyline. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 9. Pupils are dilated, blood pressure (BP) is 122/82, pulse is 72 and regular and a ﬁnger-prick glucose is 5.6 mmol/l. His O2 sats measured by probe are 90%. ECG reveals a QRS of 90 ms. What would the next optimal treatment be? blockers 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com
explanation: D Airway protection We are unaware of the time lapse since this patient took his overdose, and the relative contribution of benzodiazepines versus amitriptyline to his conscious level. As such, the most appropriate next intervention is protection of his airway, particularly as the GCS is signiﬁcantly reduced at 9 and benzodiazepine reversal agents are contraindicated here. A Intravenous (iv) sodium bicarbonate Sodium bicarbonate is indicated in tricyclic antidepressant overdose when the QRS is greater than 100 ms, to reduce the risk of seizures and ventricular arrhythmia. B iv ﬂumazenil Flumazenil is indicated only for acute overdose of benzodiazepines where there is no history of either chronic use of the class of medication or concomitant use of tricyclic antidepressants because of the risk of inducing seizures. C iv naloxone iv naloxone is a reversal agent for opiates, not for benzodiazepines. E iv glucagon iv glucagon used at high dose is a reversal agent in those patients who have taken an overdose of beta

stem: A 38-year-old woman with a diagnosis of stage IIIa breast cancer affecting the left breast, comes to the Oncology Clinic for review. Her tumour has undergone receptor analysis for targeting of chemotherapy. 773-555 THERAPE For the patient to beneﬁt from trastuzumab, which receptor should be positive on tumour histology?
explanation: B Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) The HER2 receptor a growth receptor expressed on some breast cancers. It is the target of trastuzumab which is a HER2 antagonist. Blocking of HER2 has been shown to improve life expectancy in patients with HER2 positive tumours signiﬁcantly. HER2 is also involved in the pathogenesis of cardiomyopathy, and antagonism of the HER2 receptor can precipitate the development of dilative cardiomyopathy in some patients. This necessitates detailed cardiac monitoring before and during trastuzumab treatment. D Programmed cell death protein 1 (PD1) The PD1 receptor lies on the surface of cells, and its role is to promote self-tolerance, down-regulating the T cell-mediated immune response and preventing autoimmune destruction of key tissues. Unfortunately, it is also expressed by a number of cancer cell lines, including breast cancer cells, protecting them from autoimmune attack. PD1 inhibitors are a potential option to promote autoimmune attack on cancer cells. A Prostaglandin D2 (DP2) DP2 is the prostaglandin D2 receptor. Pathophysiology of the DP2 receptor is thought to underly the development of some cases of asthma, hives, and allergic rhinitis, and DP2 antagonists have been trialled as potential treatments for male pattern baldness. C Oestrogen The oestrogen receptor is the target of tamoxifen, a selective oestrogen receptor modulator (SERM). Tamoxifen has been shown to reduce the risk of breast cancer recurrence and improve mortality. Adverse effects of therapy include menopausal symptoms and increased risk of venous thromboembolism. E Progesterone Progesterone receptors are the target of progesterone receptor modulators or PRMs. They are used in combination with SERMs for the treatment of breast cancer; examples include mifepristone and onapristone. An aromatase inhibitor is also used in combination with the SERM and PRM.

stem: 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com
explanation: A Cyanide toxicity Improperly stored nitroprusside for infusion, or nitroprusside which has been exposed to sunlight on the ward, is subject to degradation which may result in the formation of sodium cyanide. Cyanide poisoning is associated with hypertension and bradycardia, followed later by hypotension and coma. Abdominal pain and shortness of breath are other prominent features. The characteristic ﬁnding on examination is a marked elevation in lactate. Sodium thiosulphate, dicobalt edetate or sodium nitrite are possible treatments for cyanide poisoning. C Subarachnoid haemorrhage Signiﬁcant subarachnoid haemorrhage is more likely to be associated with either a further rise in blood pressure or at least stabilisation at the higher level. Again it would not be associated with abdominal pain. B Hypertensive encephalopathy Given that there has been a slight fall in blood pressure, hypertensive encephalopathy is less likely and it isn’t associated with abdominal pain. D Encephalitis Against a background of marked hypertension and no clinical signs of infection, encephalitis is extremely unlikely to be the cause of 773-555 THERAPE the deterioration seen here. E Methaemoglobinaemia Methaemoglobinaemia is associated with tissue hypoxia; however, other signs such as cyanosis would be expected given the symptom picture seen here.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review of her rheumatoid arthritis. She is currently taking weekly methotrexate but still has evidence of active tenosynovitis affecting her wrists and the small joints of her ﬁngers. She has recently got married and wants to start a family, but agrees that her joint disease needs to be stabilised before she gets pregnant. Routine bloods are unremarkable. Which of the following treatment strategies is likely to be most appropriate in pregnancy?
explanation:
D Switch Methotrexate for Azathioprine Of the two switching options, azathioprine is the most appropriate choice. While there are no randomised controlled trials of secondline immunomodulators in pregnancy, the evidence base suggests that azathioprine carries the least risk with respect to a successful outcome. Meta-analyses do, however, suggest it is less effective than methotrexate at controlling symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis. For this reason, additional corticosteroid therapy may also be required. E Switch Methotrexate for Cyclophosphamide Cyclophosphamide carries an increased risk for teratogenicity, when compared to azathioprine, and is therefore less favourable in this case. A Add Inﬂiximab Inﬂiximab can be used in rheumatoid arthritis, and in the ﬁrst trimester of pregnancy, it is relatively safe, though it must be discontinued before the second and third trimesters. However, methotrexate use is not advised in pregnancy because of a high risk for neural tube defects. Therefore, switching is essential before she tries to get pregnant. The addition of inﬂiximab to this will not solve the underlying issue. B Add Prednisolone

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Prednisolone can be used in low to medium doses in pregnancy, as it crosses the placenta at low concentrations and is therefore relatively safe to use during pregnancy, especially during ﬂares. However, use of prednisolone in conjunction with methotrexate use is not advised in pregnancy because of a risk for neural tube defects. Therefore, switching is essential before the patient tries to get pregnant. This effectively rules out adding prednisolone. C Add Rituximab It is advised that rituximab is best avoided in pregnancy, though some studies suggest no speciﬁc pattern of embryotoxicity or teratogenicity exists. Importantly, in this case, it is the use of rituximab in conjunction with methotrexate, because of a risk for neural tube defects from methotrexate. Therefore, switching is essential before the patient tries to get pregnant.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of tiredness, lethargy, headaches and tremor. She received a renal transplant one year earlier and takes a ciclosporin-based immunosuppression regime. One week prior to her visit to the GP she had been started on a prolonged course of ﬂuconazole by a doctor in an attempt to clear up a long-standing fungal infection. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 92 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 2.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelet (PLT) 79 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 230 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l You suspect a probable drug interaction. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her problems?
options: CYP450 induction leading to increased ciclosporin metabolism
CYP450 inhibition leading to decreased ciclosporin metabolism
explanation: D CYP450 inhibition leading to decreased ciclosporin metabolism Fluconazole is a CYP-P450 enzyme inhibitor, leading to an elevation of 50% or more in levels of ciclosporin, which is speciﬁcally metabolised by CYP-3A4. If ﬂuconazole treatment is required, 773-555 THERAPE then a temporary reduction in ciclosporin dose is usually advised, the peak in levels occurring from around day 4 of ﬂuconazole treatment onwards. Symptoms of ciclosporin toxicity include tremor and headache, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain. Raised creatinine, anaemia and thrombocytopenia are also seen. In this situation, ciclosporin levels are a crucial part of the workup in diagnosing the underlying cause of any elevation in creatinine. C CYP450 induction leading to increased ciclosporin metabolism Fluconazole is an enzyme inhibitor, not an inducer of the P450 system. A Decreased ﬂuconazole excretion Approximately 80% of ﬂuconazole is excreted unchanged in the urine; it isn’t directly nephrotoxic and this isn’t therefore the cause of the clinical picture seen here. B Decreased ciclosporin excretion Only 6% of the oral dose of ciclosporin is excreted unchanged in the urine. It is extensively metabolised by the P450 system in the liver, meaning that the cause of ciclosporin toxicity is decreased biotransformation rather than decreased excretion. E Increased formation of 6-mercaptopurine 6-mercaptopurine is a metabolite of azathioprine responsible for azathioprine toxicity when it accumulates to excess; it isn’t connected with ciclosporin metabolism.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the clinic with increased thirst and excessive urination for the past three weeks. He drinks up to 5 litres of water per day and wakes up several times at night to urinate. His medical history includes bipolar disorder, for which he has been on lithium therapy for the past year. He denies any recent changes in medication, fever or a history of diabetes mellitus. Physical examination is unremarkable, and vital signs are within normal limits. Initial laboratory investigations are shown below. Investigation Result Normal value Serum sodium 146 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Serum osmolality 305 mOsm/kg 275–295 mOsm/kg Urine osmolality 150 mOsm/kg 500–800 mOsm/kg Serum creatinine 85 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l What is the most appropriate initial management step for this patient?
options: Increase daily water intake to prevent dehydration
Discontinue lithium and consider alternative therapy
explanation: C Discontinue lithium and consider alternative therapy Lithium is a well-known cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Stopping lithium can improve or resolve symptoms, and alternative medications should be considered for the patient's bipolar disorder. Managing lithium-induced diabetes insipidus often involves removing the drug as the ﬁrst step. E Restrict ﬂuid intake Fluid restriction is generally not recommended in diabetes insipidus due to the risk of dehydration, but is used in treatment of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone. Instead, patients should be encouraged to drink to thirst, and the primary intervention should target the underlying cause. A Increase daily water intake to prevent dehydration While adequate hydration is important to manage the polyuria associated with diabetes insipidus, simply increasing water intake does not address the underlying cause of drug-induced diabetes insipidus. Furthermore, excessive intake may worsen electrolyte imbalances if the underlying issue persists. B Start hydrochlorothiazide Hydrochlorothiazide is sometimes used as a treatment for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus because it can paradoxically reduce urine output. However, it is not the initial treatment when drug-induced diabetes insipidus is suspected, as stopping the causative agent (in this case, lithium) is preferred. D Start desmopressin Desmopressin is a synthetic analogue of vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) used to treat central diabetes insipidus but is not effective in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus caused by lithium where the kidneys are resistant to antidiuretic hormone.

stem: A 34-year-old taxi driver is admitted to your ward having taken a mixed overdose. His partner is en route to the hospital with the empty packets and bottles. Your house ofﬁcer questions whether the use of multiple-dose activated charcoal could be used. For which of the following overdoses is multiple-dose activated charcoal most useful?
explanation:
D Carbamazepine Delayed gastric emptying is recognised in carbamazepine overdose, and multiple-dose activated charcoal is therefore a useful option. Repeated administration prevents delayed absorption of carbamazepine and is associated with improved outcomes. Other agents where multiple doses of activated charcoal can be given include dapsone, phenobarbitone, digoxin, theophylline and quinine.

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com E Lithium carbonate Activated charcoal has no impact on absorption of charged particles such as lithium and is therefore not the correct answer here. Where there is signiﬁcant lithium overdose, haemodialysis is considered. A Cyanide Cyanide is found in insecticides, photographic solutions, and jewellery cleaner. Activated charcoal does not readily bind to cyanide and as such has no role in toxic states. B Ferrous sulphate Ferrous sulphate does not have signiﬁcant binding to activated charcoal. Removal of tablets via gastric lavage or whole-bowel irrigation are important potential options for treatment. C Ethylene glycol Activated charcoal is not of value in the treatment of methanol or ethylene glycol administration. The most important step here is inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase, either with ethanol itself or fomepizole.

stem: A 69-year-old woman had been referred from Medical Admissions to the Cardiology Ward after two episodes of syncope and palpitations. She was admitted 3 days ago for cardioversion of her lone atrial ﬁbrillation (AF). This had been successfully converted to sinus rhythm, and she was started on disopyramide 250 mg twice daily and discharged. 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com She has been readmitted today with palpitations; a standard 12lead ECG is shown below. Following this, she was placed on telemetry, and an episode of palpitations was captured on the monitor. This is shown below. Her urea and electrolyte levels and full blood counts are within normal range. What would be the most appropriate step in the longterm management of this patient?
explanation: B Stop the disopyramide This woman had torsades de pointes, often translated as a ‘twisting of the points’, which refers to the beat-to- beat changes in the QRS axis. Although torsades de pointes can occur in many settings (such as heart block), it is usually seen in patients with one of the congenital long QT syndromes or in association with drug therapy. The drugs commonly involved are: disopyramide, procainamide, quinidine, sotalol and terfenadine. Other drugs where the risk is associated with the dose are: amiodarone, arsenic trioxide, cisapride, calcium channel blockers, clarithromycin, erythromycin, pentamidine, anti-emetic agents, antipsychotic agents and methadone. The arrhythmia in this patient was provoked by disopyramide, and it is possible that she could have the subclinical form of a long QT syndrome (subclinical forms are often revealed by QT-prolonging drugs). This is why, in her case, the prolonged QT would not have been picked up on testing at the time of her cardioversion. 773-555 THERAPE A Add in amiodarone This risks further prolongation of the QT interval, leading to an increased risk of sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT). C Add in digoxin Digoxin has no effect on reducing the risk for torsades de pointes and has a limited role in the management of AF in patients where other options are not appropriate. D Increase the disopyramide to tds Disopyramide has precipitated the episode of torsades de pointes; therefore, increasing it will further increase the risk for sustained VT. E Add in low-dose atenolol Low-dose atenolol prolongs the action potential, although it doesn’t increase the risk of torsades, it isn’t an effective treatment for the condition.

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a 3-month history of an intermittent itchy rash. She has noticed that the rash can appear at any time of the day without an identiﬁable trigger. Her face, torso, upper and lower extremities have been affected, with the rash lasting up to three hours each time. The rash improves following cetirizine use. She has a past medical history of hypertension, chronic pain and recurrent urinary tract infections. She has no known drug allergies. On examination, her observations are recorded, which are all within normal range. Her chest is clear and her heart sounds are normal. She has a soft abdomen and no palpable organomegaly. She has multiple wheals over her lower shins and back, with erythematous margins. Which of the following medications is likely to contribute to this patient’s symptoms?
explanation:
B Aspirin The prolonged history of symptoms is suggestive of chronic urticaria. Chronic urticaria has a number of causes, including autoimmune diseases, lymphoma and drug reactions. Common causative drugs include aspirin and non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com medications such as ibuprofen and opiates. These drugs should be avoided. E Trimethoprim Trimethoprim can cause skin reactions as a result of an allergic reaction or photosensitivity or a more severe cutaneous reaction, including Stevens–Johnsons syndrome. However, it does not cause chronic urticaria. A Amitriptyline Amitriptyline does not cause chronic urticaria. Instead, it is a treatment for refractory chronic urticaria. C Bendroﬂumethiazide Thiazide diuretics are a common cause of photosensitivity, a dermatological reaction secondary to ultraviolet radiation that causes exaggerated burns or dermatitis in sun-exposed areas of skin. Thiazides do not cause chronic urticaria. D Propranolol Propranolol does not cause chronic urticaria. However, it can exacerbate other existing dermatological conditions, including psoriasis and should be avoided in these patients.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with fever, agitation and restlessness. He was found by his wife muttering inaudible sounds to himself in the bathroom. There is no history of headache and he was well yesterday evening. His past medical history includes depression and chronic pain, for which he has just been started on tramadol. On examination, he appears ﬂushed with a temperature is 38.2 °C. He is tachycardic, with a BP of 109/66 mmHg and tachypnoeic with oxygen saturations of 98% on air. During his examination, he complains of palpitations. An ECG is taken: What is the most immediate treatment to initiate?
explanation: D Magnesium sulfate 2 g This ECG demonstrates torsades de pointe, a polymorphic broad complex ventricular tachycardia that is often triggered from QTc interval prolongation. A prolonged QTc interval can be congenital or acquired. There are many drugs that increase the QTc interval, including antidepressants and neuroleptics. This patient has depression and is likely to be taking a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) such as citalopram. In addition to this, he has recently been prescribed tramadol as a new pain medication. Tramadol increases the risk of serotonin syndrome when taken alongside SSRIs. In fact, the presenting complaint of this patient is in keeping with serotonin syndrome with autonomic instability and an altered mental status. Provided the patient is haemodynamically stable, the treatment of torsades de pointe is intravenous magnesium sulfate. E Synchronised electrical cardioversion Synchronised electrical cardioversion would be appropriate if this patient were haemodynamically unstable. Although this patient is tachycardic, his blood pressure is relatively stable and intravenous magnesium sulfate would be more appropriate. A Adrenaline 1 mg 1 : 10 000 Adrenaline 1 mg 1 : 10 000 is incorrect. Adrenaline given at this dose is given in a cardiac arrest situation. As the patient is not in cardiac arrest, it is not appropriate. B Amiodarone 300 mg Amiodarone is given for monomorphic broad complex tachycardias such as ventricular tachycardia. This ECG, in fact, demonstrates a polymorphic broad complex ventricular tachycardia leading to a diagnosis of torsades de pointe that is treated with magnesium sulfate. C Diazepam Diazepam is the initial treatment of serotonin syndrome. However, this patient has since developed ventricular tachycardia and treatment for this now takes priority. Therefore, the most appropriate treatment to be given now would be magnesium sulfate.

stem: An 18-year-old male is admitted with a history of being confused since a couple of hours before. His mother confessed 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com that her son was trying to lose weight and had joined a local gym. He was consuming a powder which she recalled as being called ‘Cherry Meth’. This is mixed with water and he had told her that it tasted like seaweed. On examination he was agitated, but drowsy. His pulse was 45/min and blood pressure was 90/70 mmHg. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. However, he gradually lapsed into coma during the period of observation and had Cheyne–Stokes breathing. Respiration became progressively depressed and he was intubated and ventilated. Supportive treatment was started. Surprisingly, he regained consciousness spontaneously and pulled out the endotracheal tube within 3 h. Investigation Result Normal value Glucose 10.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Sodium (Na+) 150 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 6.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l pH 7.3 7.35–7.45 Bicarbonate 23 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Base excess 2 mmol/l -2 to +2.0 mmol/l Urea 6.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 120 mmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 34 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Ammonia 25 μmol/l 11–32 µmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Gamma-hydroxybutyrate overdose Gamma-hydroxybutric acid (GHB) is sold illegally for bodybuilding, weight loss and as a replacement for L- tryptophan. It is in a powder form and dissolved in water. Its taste is similar to that of seaweed. It is popularly known as Liquid X, Cherry Meth, Easy Lay, Scoop or GBH. Dependent on the dose, patients develop gastrointestinal effects, euphoria, drowsiness, Cheyne–Stokes respiration, coma, decreased cardiac output and severe respiratory depression. Fatalities have been reported, usually in malicious overdose when taken with other substances. Patients recover quickly, often within 1–2 h, and they may have rapid reversal of coma and may remove the endotracheal tube themselves. Metabolic acidosis, hyperglycaemia, hyperkalaemia and hypernatraemia can occur. Supportive care includes activated charcoal for up to 1 h after ingestion, so it is a little outside the time window here. For a couple of hours, monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate and oxygenation should be done. Naloxone has shown beneﬁt in animals. Diazepam is the drug of choice 773-555 THERAPE for treating convulsions. B Metabolic encephalopathy Metabolic encephalopathy is a differential, but the history of Cherry Meth consumption drives us more towards drug-induced metabolic disorder as the most likely answer. A Urea cycle disorder Urea cycle disorders are inborn errors of nitrogen metabolism that lead to accumulation of ammonia. D LSD overdose LSD overdose is associated with hallucinations and agitation, rather than the obtunded picture seen here.
