E Dextropropoxyphene overdose Codeine overdose may present with decreased consciousness, but of course it isn’t marketed as a weight loss agent.

stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted via ambulance. You attend as part of the crash team when initial observations reveal that he has a pulse rate of 35 bpm and blood pressure of 82/40 mmHg. He has a history of cardiac failure. His glucose is 3.6 mmol/l. On initial survey, members of the casualty staff have discovered a note explaining that he has taken an overdose after the recent death of his wife. One of the nurses calls the GP and it transpires he is on a range of cardiovascular medications. You give him 1 mg of atropine IV. Which of the following interventions would be the next most appropriate step in his management?
explanation: A IV glucagon administration Key initial measures for this patient include establishment of IV 773-555 THERAPE access, ECG and blood pressure recording. Apart from that, IV glucagon administration exerts an inotropic effect independent of β- receptor activation by raising myocardial cAMP levels: 5-10mg over 1-2 minutes, followed by IV infusion of 50- 150micrograms/kg/hr, titrated according to the response. If hypoglycaemia develops in response to possible β- blocker overdose, then 25 ml of 50% dextrose followed by dextrose infusion is recommended in addition to IV glucagon. E IV salbutamol administration IV salbutamol is of most use where there is bronchospasm associated with β-blocker overdose. B IV dopamine administration Dopamine is most commonly used as an inotrope to preserve renal perfusion rather than to increase heart rate in β-blocker overdose. C IV adrenaline administration IV adrenaline is not recommended because of the risk of precipitating a ventricular arrhythmia. D Cardiac pacing This is the option in the event that enough glucagon to deliver repeated high doses is not available.

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for a symptom review. She has a past medical history of ulcerative colitis and has had a number of ﬂares that have required hospital admission and high-dose corticosteroid therapy. She has been on maintenance therapy with oral mesalazine for the last 18 months but has seen little improvement in her symptoms and even had a mild ﬂare two months ago. The decision is made to trial an alternative medication and initiate azathioprine. There is no other past medical history of note and she has no allergies. What is the recommended monitoring required with regular azathioprine use?
options: Full blood count and coagulation proﬁle
Full blood count and liver function tests
Full blood count and peripheral blood ﬁlms
Full blood count and thyroid function tests
Full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests
explanation:
E Full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend that patients taking azathioprine should

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com have monitoring of their full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests. This is important as azathioprine is an immunosuppressant that can cause myelosuppression. Azathioprine can sometimes affect renal and hepatic function and doses should be reduced in hepatic or renal impairment. Therefore, monitoring full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests is correct. A Full blood count and coagulation proﬁle A full blood count is needed when starting azathioprine to detect bone marrow suppression. There is a risk of increased bleeding. However, this is secondary to thrombocytopenia, rather than impaired clotting function. Therefore, regular coagulation proﬁle monitoring is not needed. B Full blood count and liver function tests The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend that patients taking azathioprine should have their full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests monitored. This is important as azathioprine is an immunosuppressant that can cause myelosuppression and can sometimes affect renal and hepatic function. C Full blood count and peripheral blood ﬁlms Azathioprine is an immunosuppressant. Therefore, adverse effects include bone marrow suppression. For this reason, NICE recommends monitoring full blood count to assess for myelosuppression. However, a peripheral blood ﬁlm is not needed to monitor the effects of azathioprine. Furthermore, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests are needed. D Full blood count and thyroid function tests A full blood count is needed when starting azathioprine to detect the onset of anaemia or myelosuppression. Renal and hepatic monitoring is also essential and is recommended by current NICE guidelines. However, azathioprine does not impair thyroid function and does not require regular monitoring.

stem: You attend a lecture where you view data on a new beta-receptor agonist for the treatment of asthma. According to your understanding of agonism and antagonism, which of the following agents is best described as a noncompetitive antagonist drug?
explanation: E Phenoxybenzamine Phenoxybenzamine is a non-competitive α-adrenoreceptor antagonist, which cannot be displaced by endogenous α-receptor ligands. It is the most potent α-blocker available and is used in presurgical treatment of hypertension associated with phaeochromocytoma. D Salbutamol Salbutamol is an example of an exogenous β2-adrenoreceptor agonist. It is relatively short acting, which accounts for its use as a relieving agent in the treatment of asthma. A Salmeterol Salmeterol is an example of a partial beta agonist. It has a longer half-life than salbutamol and is therefore a component of preventer therapy in the treatment of asthma. When used to excess however it may blunt the effectiveness of salbutamol in the management of asthma exacerbations. B Noradrenaline Noradrenaline is a potent endogenous adrenoreceptor agonist, which accounts for its use as an inotropic agent. C Prazosin Prazosin is a competitive α-receptor antagonist and is commonly used as add-on therapy in the treatment of hypertension. It isn’t used as a ﬁrst line agent for phaeochromocytoma because of difﬁculties in obtaining full agonism.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Deprtment with a 3-day history of fever, abdominal pain and dysuria. Her past medical history includes migraine, for which she takes sumatriptan as required and mild childhood asthma for which she has a salbutamol inhaler which she has not needed to use for years. She is looking forward to going on holiday to Tanzania in a week’s time and has just started primaquine for malarial prophylaxis. She is a non-smoker and drinks alcohol socially. She works for an advertising company. Clinical examination is unremarkable, except for some suprapubic tenderness but no loin pain. Her urinalysis is positive for white blood cells and nitrites, and a pregnancy test is negative. She is discharged on trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection and given codeine for abdominal pain. She returns to the Emergency Department two days later with headache, nausea, dizziness and mild dyspnoea. On examination, she is slightly agitated and appears cyanosed. Her temperature 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com is 36.2 °C. Her heart rate is 100 bpm, regular and BP is 106/66 mmHg. Heart sounds are normal. Her respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute, but her chest sounds clear, with no crepitations or wheeze. Oxygen saturations are 85%. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, with normal bowel sounds. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Her ABG reveals a PO2 of 12.6 kPa. Her primaquine and trimethoprim are stopped. Her CXR is shown below: What would be the next most appropriate step?
explanation: A Give IV methylene blue The patient has methaemoglobinaemia, which may be due to trimethoprim and/or primaquine. Other causative agents include sulphonamides, lidocaine, dapsone, phenacetin, chloroquine, amyl nitrate, metoclopramide and aniline dyes. Methaemoglobin inducers act by oxidising ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric (Fe3+) haemoglobin. This abnormal haemoglobin is incapable of carrying oxygen, inducing a functional anaemia. In addition, the shape of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve is altered, aggravating cellular hypoxia. Severity of symptoms usually correlates with measured methaemoglobin levels, and they are caused by decreased oxygen content and cellular hypoxia. They include 773-555 THERAPE headache, dizziness and nausea, progressing to dyspnoea, confusion, seizures and coma. Even at low levels, skin discolouration (‘chocolate cyanosis’), especially of the nails, lips and ears, is striking. Diagnosis is suggested by a normal PO2 in the presence of cyanosis and low O2 saturations. The blood also appears chocolate brown when compared with normal blood. Methaemoglobin levels can be measured by the co-oximeter type of arterial blood gas analyser. There are no particular ﬁndings on the chest x-ray and they are usually normal, as here. Usually mild methaemoglobinaemia (<15–20%) resolves spontaneously and requires no intervention. Methylene blue is indicated in the symptomatic patient with methaemoglobin levels >20% or when even minimal compromise of oxygen-carrying capacity is potentially harmful (pre-existing anaemia, cardiac failure, ischaemic heart disease). Methylene blue is given at 1–2 mg/kg over several minutes. The causative agent should also be discontinued. B Give IV hydrocortisone The picture here is more consistent with hypoxia related to methaemoglobinaemia rather than acute asthma; IV hydrocortisone is therefore not of value here. C Stop sumatriptan Although this patient has headache, it is as a result of hypoxia rather than migraine, hence sumatriptan is not of value. D CT head Given the lack of focal neurology and normal blood pressure, an intracerebral lesion accounting for the headache is very unlikely. E Commence IV piperacillin with tazobactam (Tazocin) The absence of ﬁndings on auscultation of the chest and the normal chest x-ray point away from an infection as the cause of her symptoms.

stem: You attend a ﬁre at a large chemical factory as the ﬁrst response doctor. The factory manufactures various types of polyurethane foams. A 45-year-old man is removed from the main part of the 773-555 THERAPE factory complaining of chest tightness and dizziness. You examine him and there are signs of pulmonary oedema. A tight-ﬁtting facemask and high-ﬂow oxygen are applied. He quickly deteriorates and suffers a respiratory arrest. He is intubated and ventilated. Given the likely cause for his deterioration, which of the following actions would be the most appropriate next step?
options: Start a glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) IV infusion
explanation: B Give dicobalt edetate 300 mg IV This man is involved in a ﬁre at a polyurethane foams factory. Presentation with this clinical scenario may ﬁt with cyanide poisoning, either through inhalation or through substantial skin contamination. Dizziness and confusion may be rapidly followed by chest tightness, pulmonary oedema, paralysis and eventual cardiovascular collapse. Treatment of choice is dicobalt edetate 300 mg IV bolus, which may be repeated three times depending on response. E Start a glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) IV infusion Circulatory collapse as a result of cyanide poisoning is imminent; GTN is only really effective in the acute situation in managing hypertensive heart failure. A Give furosemide 80 mg IV bolus The signs of pulmonary oedema may be related to ARDS or due to circulatory failure as a result of cyanide poisoning, and furosemide will not be effective. C Give sodium nitroprusside IV bolus Sodium nitrite or sodium thiosulfate, not sodium nitroprusside, can be utilised as a second-line intervention for cyanide poisoning. D Give adrenalin IV Adrenalin is ineffective in the presence of a metabolic poison such as cyanide. It is the time to delivery of dicobalt edetate that is most closely related to patient survival.

stem: A 17-year-old girl is admitted to the Emergency Department by paramedic ambulance after being found collapsed at home. Apparently, she has had a recent row with her boyfriend, and she is thought to have taken an overdose. Her mother has insulin- 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com dependent diabetes and breast cancer with metastases, taking a number of different medications for pain relief. On examination, her respiratory rate is 8/min and saturations are 95% on air. Her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg and her pulse is 85 bpm and regular. She is deeply unconscious with small, poorly reactive pupils. The paramedics have already obtained IV access and checked her glucose, which is recorded as 4.0 mmol/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: E Naloxone IV Naloxone is the most appropriate next step. The small, poorly reactive pupils and signiﬁcantly reduced respiratory rate clinically reﬂect opiate toxicity. It is likely that she has had access to her mother’s medication. Naloxone can be given intravenously, subcutaneously and intramuscularly. It is likely an infusion may be required following an initial bolus due to its short half-life. 50% dextrose would be a reasonable option if insulin overdose was suspected but clinically not indicated at present. Despite naloxone, intubation and ventilation should be considered as a next step. A 50% dextrose intravenously (IV) While the glucose is on the low side of normal, it would be unlikely to be the cause of this patient’s depression in consciousness. B Flumazenil IV Flumazenil is used in suspected benzodiazepine overdose and although it should be considered the clinical scenario indicates opiate toxicity and therefore is not the most appropriate next step. C Glucagon intramuscularly (IM) Glucagon is not clinically indicated as the patient’s glucose is 4.0 mmol/l. Glucagon is often reserved for patients if access cannot be obtained and glucose levels are below 4.0 mmol/l. D Intubation and ventilation The patient’s airway is still patent at present; therefore, this is not clinically indicated. Intubation is something to consider in patients that do not respond to naloxone and the airway is compromised.

stem: A 21-year-old man is brought to hospital by ambulance. The vehicle was called by his girlfriend who found him semiconscious and hyperventilating, surrounded by a number of empty packets of 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com aspirins. Apparently, there had been a row that morning some 5 h earlier. On examination, his blood pressure is 112/72 mmHg, pulse is 85 bpm and regular. He is hyperventilating with a respiratory rate of 27/min, with saturations of 96% on air. The abdomen is generally tender, particularly in the epigastrium. Investigations (arterial blood gas), reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 10.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 15 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 132 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l pH 7.42 7.35–7.45 Salicylate 500 mg/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation: B Intravenous (IV) bicarbonate The elimination of salicylate may be increased by alkalinisation of the urine. There is a 10-fold to 20-fold increase in renal salicylate clearance associated with an increase in urine pH from 5 to 8 and renal excretion of salicylate depends much more on urine pH than ﬂow rate. A urine pH of 7.5 or higher is indicated and careful monitoring of the urine pH is necessary. The pH of blood should not exceed pH 7.55 however. The most common recommendation is to continue treatment until the plasma salicylate concentration decreases to the therapeutic range but cessation of the patient's symptoms are also a crucial factor in the decision to discontinue alkalinisation. Although it is prudent to administer supplemental potassium to hypokalaemic patients, it is inappropriate to delay the administration of sodium bicarbonate solution until normokalaemia is achieved. E IV magnesium Although magnesium replacement may be required, correction of potassium and initiation of bicarbonate therapy are the initial most important steps. A Haemodialysis Haemodialysis should be considered primarily for patients with: 773-555 THERAPE  Plasma concentrations greater than 700 mg/l (5.1 mmol/l)  Acute kidney injury  Congestive cardiac failure  Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema  Coma  Convulsions  CNS effects not resolved by correction of acidosis  Persistently high salicylate concentrations unresponsive to urinary alkalinisation Severe metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.2). C IV potassium Hypokalemia, if present, must be treated aggressively. Hypokalemia promotes the absorption of potassium in the distal tubule; this absorption occurs via a K+/H+ exchange pump. The secretion of protons involved in this pump interferes with efforts at urinary alkalinisation, which are a mainstay of therapy. Hypokalemia, if present, must be treated aggressively. Although it is prudent to administer supplemental potassium to hypokalaemic patients, it is inappropriate to delay the administration of sodium bicarbonate solution until normokalaemia is achieved. Potassium supplement and sodium bicarbonate can be started simultaneously. D IV normal saline with furosemide Forced alkaline diuresis is not recommended in the management of aspirin overdose.

stem: A 72-year-old man is known to have ischaemic heart disease and atrial ﬁbrillation. He takes a number of medications, including rivaroxaban for anticoagulation. He is admitted unconscious to the Emergency Department having taken a mixed overdose. Which of the following is the optimal way to assess if he is at risk of bleeding due to rivaroxaban?
explanation:
D Factor Xa activity level The bioavailability of Rivaroxaban reduces as the dose consumed increases, due to poor solubility. At 10 mg the bioavailability is

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com 80% but 66% at 20 mg. Absorption takes between 2-4 hours with a half-life between 5-13 hours, which increases with advanced age. Although measuring the presence of rivaroxaban is also possible, levels of rivaroxaban correlate poorly with anticoagulant activity and the varying pharmacokinetics in different patients, as outlined, meaning that it is less useful to access bleeding risk. Measuring Factor Xa activity level is therefore the most useful way to quantifying bleeding risk. Where not present, prothrombin time can be used as a less useful alternative. However, due to variation in laboratory sensitivities to rivaroxaban, possibly caused by interactions between Factor Xa inhibitors and phospholipids in thromboplastin reagents, the PT result can be abnormal despite intact haemostatic function. E INR INR is speciﬁc for monitoring anticoagulation due to vitamin K antagonists. Due to variation in laboratory sensitivities to rivaroxaban, possibly caused by interactions between Factor Xa inhibitors and phospholipids in thromboplastin reagents, the PT result can be abnormal despite intact haemostatic function. As INR is calculated directly from PT it is therefore less reliable than Factor Xa activity levels. A APTT Although APTT is prolonged by rivaroxaban, the relationship between the two is non-linear and there is signiﬁcant variability between laboratories performing the assay and reagents. For this reason, it is less useful than Factor Xa levels or PT for assessing the presence of rivaroxaban and the risk of haemorrhage. B Factor VII levels Rivaroxaban is an inhibitor of factor Xa; it does not have a signiﬁcant effect on factor VII levels. However, recombinant factor VII can be given to patients with signiﬁcant bleeding related to rivaroxaban if the direct reversal agent is unavailable. C Platelet count Platelet count is poorly reﬂective of bleeding risk with factor Xa inhibitors. It is also not useful for the assessment of bleeding risk in patients prescribed PY12 inhibitors such as clopidogrel. Platelet transfusion is usually considered when there is active bleeding, and the platelet count falls below 20 × 109/l.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department a few days after discharge following placement of three stents after nonST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). He has been discharged on aspirin and clopidogrel and is extremely worried because of indigestion, which has increased over the past two days. On the morning of presentation, he has vomited 100–150 ml of fresh and altered blood. Other medications of note include ramipril, atorvastatin and bisoprolol. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 130/70 mmHg, with a postural drop of 20 mmHg, and a pulse of 80 bpm and regular. There is epigastric tenderness on palpation of the abdomen. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 105 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 181 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 105 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l 773-555 THERAPE Upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy: Oesophagitis and duodenitis with areas of haemorrhage Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: A Add Lansoprazole 30mg In this situation, trials have conﬁrmed that dual antiplatelet therapy is associated with superior outcomes with respect to ischaemic cardiovascular events at least out to the end of the ﬁrst year. It is particularly important during the ﬁrst 30–60 days postintervention to minimise the risk of in-stent thrombosis. As such, it is most preferable to continue the antiplatelet therapy and to add a proton pump inhibitor at high dose. E Withdraw Aspirin and Clopidogrel This carries the highest risk for in-stent thrombosis and should be avoided unless the patient is suffering from life-threatening haemorrhage. B Change Clopidogrel to Dipyridamole This puts the patient at an increased risk for a major adverse cardiac event and therefore should be avoided. C Withdraw Aspirin This carries an increased risk for in-stent thrombosis and should be avoided unless the patient is suffering from life-threatening haemorrhage. D Withdraw Clopidogrel This carries an increased risk of in-stent thrombosis and should be avoided unless the patient is suffering from life-threatening haemorrhage.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents to the clinic. He has a 2-year history of rheumatoid arthritis, has been attending the hospital clinic for 6 months and is taking weekly methotrexate with folic acid coverage and diclofenac. For the past few days he has had a sore throat. On examination he is thin and looks anaemic; there are joint changes consistent with severe active rheumatoid arthritis. There is clear evidence of severe pharyngitis. 773-555 THERAPE Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 102 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 0.5 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 45 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Which of the following diagnoses ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation: D Methotrexate- related marrow suppression Methotrexate even when used weekly may be associated with neutropenia. Few researchers have attempted to estimate the incidence of neutropenia, although one paper from the Journal of Postgraduate Medicine puts it at around 1 in 58 patient-years of therapy. Methotrexate should be discontinued at least temporarily, with folinic acid started as rescue; granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (GCSF) has been investigated as a therapy to allow more rapid recovery of white cell count. His dose should of course be reviewed, and the possibility of diclofenac as a cause of reduced methotrexate excretion investigated. E Diclofenac- related marrow suppression Diclofenac reduces methotrexate excretion, leading to increased risk of methotrexate toxicity, but doesn’t itself cause bone marrow suppression. A Chronic myeloid leukaemia Chronic myeloid leukaemia is associated with a more chronic disease course, and hepatosplenomegaly. B Acute myeloid leukaemia Acute myeloid leukaemia is unlikely in this scenario, given we’re already told about exposure to methotrexate, and other symptoms such as night sweats, anorexia, weight loss and easy bruising are absent. C Felty’s syndrome Felty syndrome is associated with splenomegaly, which is absent here.

stem: A 75-year-old woman is admitted with confusion and general deterioration. She was found in her ﬂat in a state of self-neglect. 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com In hospital, she is diagnosed with a left lower lobe pneumonia and commenced on antibiotics. Her medical background includes angina, atrial ﬁbrillation, osteoarthritis, asthma and diabetes. Her medication is: glyceryl trinitrate spray, digoxin, warfarin, codeine phosphate, salbutamol inhaler, becotide inhaler and metformin. She is commenced on amoxicillin in hospital. While an inpatient, she improves and the house physician on the ward notices a lesion on her scalp. It is a small, irregular, erythematous papule surrounded by pale, brittle hair. A dermatologist reviews the lesion and takes some hair samples for further examination. After a microscopic examination, the dermatologist returns to the ward and prescribes a shampoo for the patient and an oral antifungal agent that works by inhibiting the mitotic spindle of the fungus. What would be the most likely effect of the anti-fungal agent on this patient’s blood tests?
explanation: B Decreased INR The drug commenced in this patient is griseofulvin. This oral antifungal is thought to work by inhibiting the mitotic spindle of the fungus and is used for the treatment of dermatophytes. It is a liver enzyme inducer, resulting in increased metabolism of anticoagulants, and hence a decrease in the INR. The azoles work by inhibiting the conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol, which is a step required in the synthesis of fungal cell membrane. They tend to be liver enzyme inhibitors. E Increased serum creatinine Amphotericin B, not griseofulvin, which is used for serious systemic fungal infections, may lead to renal impairment. A Increased INR Azole antifungals and a range of antibacterials, including macrolides and quinolones, are recognised to increase the INR. C Pancytopenia Mammalian cell membranes are composed of cholesterol rather than ergosterol, Griseofulvin therefore has no effect on cell maturation/production, and hence doesn’t lead to pancytopenia. D Hypoglycaemia Metformin reduces hepatic glucose output. Its metabolism isn’t 773-555 THERAPE signiﬁcantly affected by griseofulvin, and even if levels of metformin were increased this wouldn’t lead to hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after consuming a large number of 500 mg soluble aspirin tablets. She is thought to have taken 30 of them around 50 minutes earlier. She is distressed and hyperventilating on admission, complaining of severe tinnitus. Her BP is 135/70 mmHg, pulse is 95/min and regular and her respiratory rate is 36/min. Weight is 75 kg. Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 132 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 188 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 112 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 28 mmol/l 22 - 29 mmol/l Glucose 8.1 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l pH 7.54 7.35 - 7.45 Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation:
A Activated charcoal Guidelines recommend administering activated charcoal as soon as possible after presentation with aspirin overdose, and repeating it, particularly where the aspirin level is steadily rising. This would be considered a signiﬁcant overdose (30 × 500 mg = 15 g aspirin, 15,000/75 = 200 mg/kg) with a mild-moderate risk of toxicity. E IV diazepam Diazepam is not recommended for the management of hyperventilation in this situation, because a compensated metabolic acidosis develops as the second stage of aspirin overdose. B Gastric lavage Gastric lavage is now no longer recommended for aspirin overdose, unless the patient presents during the ﬁrst hour after overdose and has consumed more than 500mg/kg of aspirin C IV ﬂuids

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Although IV ﬂuids are an essential part of the management of aspirin overdose, giving activated charcoal as early as possible impacts signiﬁcantly on peak aspirin levels. D IV glucose Although hypoglycaemia does occur later in aspirin overdose, given that the glucose is 8.1 there is no need to currently intervene.

stem: A 47-year-old man is reviewed by his General Practitioner, complaining of low libido. He describes that his partner is frustrated with his apathy towards sex. He denies having a problem with making or maintaining an erection. He has a past medical history of mild asthma and epilepsy. He also has a history of male pattern baldness, for which he purchased a cream and a PO daily medication from an online pharmacy. What is the most likely cause of this patient's low libido?
explanation:
C Finasteride Finasteride is a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor. This prevents the metabolism of testosterone into dihydrotestosterone. While it may be useful for male pattern baldness, it commonly results in low libido due to the effects of low testosterone levels. The exact frequency is unknown, with some trials reporting up to 90% of patients experiencing some degree of reduced libido. D Levetiracetam Levetiracetam is an anti-seizure medication used for generalised or focal-onset seizures. It can result in mood disorders but has

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com been only linked to low libido in case reports. A Montelukast Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist. It is not widely known to result in low libido but can cause other adverse effects, such as GI symptoms. B Beclomethasone While PO steroids can result in low libido, this is quite rare with inhaled steroids. Inhaled steroids most commonly result in oral candidiasis. E Zinc Zinc supplementation is proposed to improve symptoms of male pattern baldness, although no clinical trial data support this. There are limited robust data regarding the adverse effect proﬁle, but it is not known to reduce libido.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is brought in unconscious by ambulance. On admission to casualty, she has a Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) of 6. Her airway appears to be compromised. Her sister follows by car, and suggests the woman has taken a large overdose of temazepam tablets. She is known to use these on a regular basis and also takes amitriptyline. Urea and electrolytes are unremarkable, but arterial blood gasses are suggestive of respiratory depression with both raised CO2 and decreased O2 levels. What is the most appropriate management step?
options: Anaesthetic review with consideration for intubation and ventilation
explanation: B Anaesthetic review with consideration for intubation and ventilation In patients who are habituated to benzodiazepines and who also suffer overdose of tricyclic antidepressants, there is a markedly increased risk of seizure activity if ﬂumazenil is used to reverse the benzodiazepine component. As such, with a GCS of < 8, intubation and ventilation is recommended. E Continuous ﬂumazenil infusion Although this will reverse benzodiazepine overdose, it substantially increases the risk of seizures. A Observation on a high-dependency unit Given the GCS is < 8, airway protection is essential, therefore intubation and ventilation is preferred. C Repeat dose intravenous (iv) ﬂumazenil This may cause only short-term improvement in conscious level, and also increase seizure risk. D Repeat dose iv naloxone Naloxone is used for reversal of opiate overdose.

stem: A 73-year-old woman is admitted to the Medical Admissions Unit with fast atrial ﬁbrillation and cardiac failure. She has ischaemic heart disease and long-standing atrial ﬁbrillation for which she takes a range of medications. You understand that over the past few months she has been suffering increasing indigestion and has 773-555 THERAPE been purchasing over the counter sodium alginate. On examination, her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, her pulse is 129 beats per minute (bpm) (atrial ﬁbrillation), and there are bibasal crackles on auscultation of the chest. Her digoxin level is 0.3 ng/ml (therapeutic range is 0.6 - 1.2 ng/ml). Which of the following is the most likely cause of her low digoxin level?
options: Decreased absorption due to sodium alginate
explanation:
A Decreased absorption due to sodium alginate Over the counter antacids such as sodium alginate are well known to interfere with the absorption of digoxin. In this case, a signiﬁcant amount of digoxin is now not absorbed because of the alginate, and the patient’s digoxin level has fallen below the therapeutic range. Given this patient’s age, an upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy is advised, and the alginate should be switched to an alternative agent such as a proton pump inhibitor (PPI). PPIs may, however, require the patient to reduce her dose of digoxin over time. E Poor compliance with therapy We are given no reason to suspect this patient has poor compliance with therapy. It is much more likely that her recent use of sodium alginate has interfered with digoxin absorption, leading to her presentation with fast atrial ﬁbrillation. B Increased excretion due to furosemide Loop diuretics do not promote increased excretion of digoxin. They may promote hypokalaemia which is recognised to increase the risk of digoxin toxicity. They can also precipitate prerenal failure, which can lead to accumulation of digoxin and symptoms of toxicity. C Incorrect dispensing by the pharmacy Incorrect dispensing is thankfully very rare. In the case of digoxin, a few cases are described: these are not usually related to underdosing of digoxin, but confusion between mg and μg dosing. This can, unfortunately, drive signiﬁcant toxicity. D Increased metabolism due to amlodipine Digoxin is excreted in urine as an intact drug. Amlodipine is metabolised by the cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) system. There is no interaction between calcium antagonists and digoxin which drives increased metabolism. Diltiazem when co-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com prescribed with digoxin may increase plasma levels of the drug.

stem: A 30-year-old man who emigrated from Pakistan two years ago presents to the Tuberculosis (TB) Clinic. He was started on treatment for pulmonary TB ﬁve months ago and attends routine monitoring. He has been adherent to his medication regime (rifampicin, isoniazid and pyridoxine) and has gained 8 kg in weight and his sputum smear is negative. However, he has noticed a rash over his face for the past week, which seems to get worse when he goes out in the sun. On examination, there is redness and swelling over both cheeks, with sparing of the nasolabial folds. A drug reaction is suspected and a decision is made to alter his medication. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue anti-TB treatment and give topical steroids
Stop isoniazid, continue rifampicin and pyridoxine
Stop pyridoxine, continue isoniazid and rifampicin and give antihistamines
Switch to ethambutol and streptomycin and refer to Dermatology Clinic
Stop all treatment and monitor the rash
explanation: E Stop all treatment and monitor the rash This patient has drug-induced lupus (DIL), indicated by the photosensitive malar rash described. Both isoniazid and rifampicin have been associated with DIL, and therefore, the most important ﬁrst step in this patient’s management is to stop his medications. Diagnosis can be conﬁrmed by measurement of antinuclear antibodies; DIL is associated with antihistone antibodies. An alternative antituberculosis (TB) regimen should be considered if his infection was severe and he was still highly infectious with positive sputum smears. Given that he is well, with a negative sputum smear, treatment can be stopped and response to withdrawal of treatment can be monitored. Further management will require an interprofessional team approach, including the TB team, Pharmacists and Rheumatologists. A Continue anti-TB treatment and give topical steroids Skin reactions to anti-tuberculosis (TB) medications are common. In mild skin reactions, continuing anti-TB treatment and giving symptomatic treatment with antihistamines would be appropriate. However, due to the nature of this rash, it is likely that this patient has drug-induced lupus (DIL). Appropriate management of DIL is to stop the offending agent. Treatment with non-steroidal antiinﬂammatory drugs or oral steroids may be considered, but not with topical steroids. B Stop isoniazid, continue rifampicin and pyridoxine 773-555 THERAPE This patient has DIL, as indicated by the photosensitive malar rash described. Although isoniazid is a known cause of DIL, cases of DIL have also been reported with rifampicin and therefore, continuing treatment with one of these agents is not appropriate here. C Stop pyridoxine, continue isoniazid and rifampicin and give antihistamines Pyridoxine is vitamin B6 which is given with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy. This is unlikely to be the offending agent causing this patient’s skin rash, and it would be inappropriate to continue isoniazid without pyridoxine due to the risk of neuropathy. D Switch to ethambutol and streptomycin and refer to Dermatology Clinic The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines recommend this option in cases of cutaneous reactions to anti-TB treatment in patients who have severe or highly infectious TB. However, given that this man seems to be making a good recovery and his sputum smear is negative, his infection is not severe and he is no longer classiﬁed as highly infectious.

stem: You are called to the resuscitation room by an anxious Emergency Department Senior House Ofﬁcer. A middle- aged male farmer has been brought in by ambulance, and there is little history to be gained from the paramedics, but he appears extremely unwell. He appears agitated, is sweating profusely, hypersalivating, and producing frothy white sputum. His wet trousers smell strongly of urine. You examine his pupils in darkness and ﬁnd the appearances below. What is he most likely to have been poisoned with?
explanation:
C Organophosphate insecticide The symptoms and signs including myosis, demonstrated are classical of the toxidrome seen in poisoning with a cholinomimetic agent. Organophosphate insecticides act as cholinesterase inhibi-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com tors, thereby increasing the amount of acetylcholine at various receptors by inhibiting its breakdown. The effects seen are due to the acetylcholine acting at postganglionic parasympathetic nerve endings, on nicotinic receptors and on the central nervous system. Therapeutic strategies include the use of atropine, oximes (pralidoxime and obidoxime) and benzodiazepines. E Dosulepin Dosulepin presents with the typical features of tricyclic antidepressant overdose, including decreased consciousness, seizures, progressive metabolic acidosis, long QT and consequent ventricular arrhythmias. A Morphine Morphine is associated with respiratory depression, decreased consciousness and pinpoint pupils. B Paraquat Poisoning with paraquat may be associated with no symptoms initially, but it later presents with persistent vomiting, acidosis and kidney disease. D Venlafaxine Venlafaxine overdose is associated with tachycardia, seizures, vomiting and hypertension.

stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to the Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) Clinic with sensorineural deafness. You are examining her medication history. This includes use of aciclovir, amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, oral furosemide and intravenous (iv) erythromycin for a serious lower respiratory tract infection a few months ago, where she was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) for a period of time. Which of these agents would fall under suspicion as a possible contributory cause?
explanation: D iv erythromycin Like iv gentamycin and iv vancomycin, iv erythromycin is recognised as a rare cause of sensorineural hearing loss. This is likely to be related to overly rapid administration, with loss of hearing linked to the cmax of the drug. It has now largely been replaced by oral clarithromycin; absorption of macrolides is such that iv administration is rarely warranted in the conscious patient. E Oral furosemide Although iv furosemide is recognised as a cause of sensorineural deafness, particularly in the ITU setting; oral furosemide is not thought to lead to signiﬁcant hearing loss. A iv aciclovir Aciclovir is recognised to cause dizziness and headache, although it does not lead to hearing loss. B iv ciproﬂoxacin The main concern with respect to quinolone use is increased risk of tendon rupture and P450 interaction potential. C iv co-amoxiclav Co-amoxiclav is recognised to increase the risk of obstructive jaundice, particularly when used for a period of more than 2 weeks.

stem: A 30-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Ward following a mixed overdose. He was found unconscious in his ﬂat and was surrounded by empty pill packets. Other than a recent lower respiratory tract infection, for which he was prescribed antibiotics from his General Practitioner two days ago, he has been well with no new issues. His past medical history includes anxiety, chronic back pain and gastritis, for which he takes paracetamol, codeine, clonazepam and omeprazole. Over the next 24 hours, he makes a good recovery on the ward. However, later that evening, he reports feeling faint and complains of intermittent palpitations. He is sweating profusely and clutching his chest before becoming unresponsive. His ECG shows: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, QTc interval > 500 ms. What is the most likely cause for this presentation? 773-555 THERAPE
explanation: A Clarithromycin This patient’s ECG demonstrates torsades de pointe, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia triggered by a prolonged QTc interval. Clarithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that commonly increases the QTc interval. The emergency management for this patient is intravenous magnesium sulfate. E Paracetamol Paracetamol toxicity can cause hepatic failure due to the accumulation of toxic metabolites. However, it does not cause QTc interval prolongation. B Clonazepam Clonazepam is a benzodiazepine. Similarly to opioids, an overdose of benzodiazepines causes central nervous system and respiratory depression. It does not explain the prolonged QTc interval. C Codeine Codeine is a weak opioid used in the management of pain. Overdose of opioids commonly induces constipation, drowsiness and respiratory and central nervous system depression in more severe cases. It does not cause QTc interval prolongation. D Omeprazole Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor. Features of toxicity include headache, dizziness and gastrointestinal upset. In rare circumstances, omeprazole can lower serum magnesium levels that, in turn, can predispose patients to a prolonged QTc interval. However, this is more likely with prolonged use.

stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea. He has recently suffered from a respiratory tract infection, for which he was given a 1-week course of clarithromycin. He has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, for which he takes ﬂuticasone 250 two puffs twice daily, theophylline tablets and an ipratropium inhaler as required. While in the department, he suffers a run of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), with a heart rate of 149 bpm, and his BP falls to 90/60 mmHg. A bolus of ﬂuid brings his systolic BP back up to 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com 110 mmHg. Investigation Result Normal value Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 145 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Magnesium (Mg2+) 0.87 mmol/l 0.65–1.05 mmol/l Potassium replacement is commenced, and a venous blood gas result later shows the K+ level to be 3.6 mmol/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: B IV verapamil This patient has theophylline toxicity, most likely as a result of his course of clarithromycin. Macrolide and quinolone antibiotics are known to increase plasma theophylline levels because of CYP450 inhibition. Although beta blockers can be used in stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, in this situation, there may be some reversibility, making verapamil a better option for controlling this patient’s SVT than sotalol or propranolol. C IV propranolol Although propranolol will reduce the risk of further episodes of SVT, it may result in clinically signiﬁcant bronchoconstriction in a patient with unstable airway disease. A Switch antibiotics to ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is recognised to increase theophylline levels, and it is therefore not of value to switching antibiotics here. Quinolone treatment is also no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to a small but signiﬁcant risk of debilitating adverse effects. D IV sotalol Sotalol will reduce the risk of future episodes of SVT but may cause bronchoconstriction. It is, therefore, not an appropriate next step. E Haemodialysis Haemodialysis is effective at clearing theophylline. Many patients, however, require supportive care for complications such as hypokalaemia and arrhythmia only. Haemodialysis is usually performed in patients who have seizures, shock that is unresponsive to ﬂuid therapy, and life-threatening arrhythmias. Here, verapamil is the most appropriate option, given the stability following a ﬂuid bolus. 773-555 THERAPE

stem: A 76-year-old woman with known vascular dementia is sent in to the Accident and Emergency (A&E) Department by nursing home staff with a 2-day history of fever, reduced mobility and drowsiness. Four days earlier, she had been seen by the on-call general practitioner (GP), as she had been agitated and hallucinating. He had started her on haloperidol for this. In A&E, her temperature is 39.4 °C. She is drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 12/15 (E3 V4 M5). She has a sinus tachycardia 116 bpm. Blood pressure is 112/56 mmHg and heart sounds are normal. Her chest is clear and her abdomen is soft and non-tender, with normal bowel sounds. Neurological examination reveals generalised hypertonia, but normal power and reﬂexes. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Haemoglobin (Hb) 124 g/l 115–155 g/l MCV 82.4 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Platelets (PLT) 224 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 9.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 167 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 14 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 35 U/l 5–30 IU/l Alkaline phosphate (ALP) 124 U/l 30–130 IU/l Albumin 38 g/l 35–55 g/l ECG Sinus tachycardia Chest X-ray (CXR) Normal cardiac silhouette, no focal consolidation What test would you request to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation:
B Creatine phosphokinase This patient has neuroleptic malignant syndrome precipitated by the administration of haloperidol. Clinical features of neuroleptic malignant syndrome include:  Hypertension, tachycardia and pyrexia  Muscular rigidity (sometimes with dysphagia and dysarthria)  Extrapyramidal signs, tremor  Catatonia–muteness

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com  Increased serum creatine phosphokinase/aspartate aminotransferase (AST)  Urinary myoglobin. A Blood cultures Although this patient has a signiﬁcant pyrexia, the normal white count and recent commencement of haloperidol steers us away from sepsis as the likely diagnosis. C Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) Although there are extrapyramidal signs and tremor, they are more likely to be related to haloperidol rather than to an acute neurological event. D Urine culture Although urine dipstick is expected to be positive for blood (due to urinary myoglobin) culture is uninformative. E Renal ultrasound scan Although urine dipstick is positive for blood in this situation it is not due to an anatomical cause that can be identiﬁed on USS.

stem: A 24-year-old homeless man, well known to the Accident and Emergency Department, is admitted by ambulance after having a convulsive seizure in the street. On examination, he is post-ictal and cannot be woken up. His BP is 95/60 mmHg, pulse is 90 and regular. You arrange a toxicology screen that demonstrates ethylene glycol levels of 8.2 mmol/l. He also has a metabolic acidosis with a pH of 7.15 and bicarbonate levels of 10 mmol/l. A bag of N saline to run over 1 h is commenced. Which of the following is the most important next intervention for him?
explanation: B IV 8.4% sodium bicarbonate Ethylene glycol toxicity is caused by its metabolites. The compound is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase; as such, competitive inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase via ethanol infusion or using 4-methylpyrazole (fomepizole) represents the most appropriate treatment. 4-Methylpyrazole may be preferable where it is availa- 773-555 THERAPE ble, as it does not cause intoxication. Where pH is <7.2, correction with IV sodium bicarbonate is recommended. E IV N-acetylcysteine N-acetylcysteine etylecysteine is used in the treatment of paracetamol overdose, and in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy. A Methanol infusion Methanol is metabolised to formic acid, which in itself is toxic, leading to metabolic acidosis and optic atrophy. C IV furosemide In this case aggressive ﬂuid replacement, rather than diuresis, is the intervention of choice. D IV disulﬁram Disulﬁram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, and is used as an adjunct to behavioural therapy in the treatment of chronic alcoholism.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with cyanosis, headache and confusion. You understand he has been recently started on primaquine as malaria prophylaxis prior to a trip to Africa on holiday. On examination, he has a respiratory rate of 16/min and is relatively comfortable breathing air. There is clear cyanosis; in particular, his tongue is blue. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 130 g/l 135–175 g/l MCV 86 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ WCC 4.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 195 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Sat 94% MetHb 10% Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
explanation: D Methylene blue Primaquine and its metabolites can act as oxidising agents, increasing the risk of methaemoglobinaemia where iron in haemoglobin is in the Fe3+ state, meaning that the haemoglobin holds strongly onto oxygen. This leads to tissue hypoxia. Methylene blue IV is the ﬁrstline therapy for methaemoglobinaemia. It must be administered with care, however, as at doses >7 mg/kg it becomes an oxidant itself. Other drug-induced causes of methaemoglobinaemia in- 773-555 THERAPE clude nitrites, aniline dyes, nitroprussides, local anaesthetics and dapsone. C N-acetylcysteine N-acetylcysteine is more conventionally used as an antidote to paracetamol toxicity, although case series suggest it may be of value in resistant methaemoglobinaemia. A Ascorbic acid Ascorbic acid is used as a second-line therapy, usually when methaemoglobin levels approach 30% or greater. B Exchange transfusion Exchange transfusion can be considered when patients fail to respond to 1st- and 2nd-line interventions for methaemoglobinaemia and still suffer signiﬁcant tissue hypoxia. E Chlorpheniramine Chlorpheniramine is an antihistamine and is not of value in treating methaemoglobinaemia.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is seen in clinic, complaining of low mood and anhedonia. Her only past medical history is of atrial ﬁbrillation, for which she takes digoxin and warfarin. Her rate is well controlled at 68 bpm. She feels she has become more withdrawn and would like to consider an antidepressant treatment. Which is the most appropriate treatment which would minimises any additional risk of bleeding or loss of warfarin efﬁcacy?
explanation: C Mirtazapine Mirtazapine is a presynaptic alpha2-adrenoreceptor antagonist, its mode of action is to increase central noradrenergic and serotonergic neurotransmission. NICE guidelines recommends that SSRI's should be avoided in patients who use warfarin; instead, the use of mirtazapine should be considered in patients with depression who also take heparin, aspirin or warfarin. When Mirtazipine is taken with warfarin, the INR may increase slightly; therefore the patient should be monitored closely until the INR has stabilised. E Paroxetine Paroxetine, like ﬂuoxetine, is an SSRI, which is recognised to interfere with platelet function. A Fluoxetine SSRIs enhance the anticoagulant effect of warfarin by interfering with platelet function and should therefore be avoided here. B Venlafaxine Like SSRIs, SNRIs also inhibit platelet function, this is thought to be because of a decrease in intraplatelet 5-HT. D St John’s Wort St John’s Wort is derived from the herb Hypericum perforatum, and can reduce the anticoagulant effect of warfarin because of P450 enzyme induction.

stem: A 64-year-old woman, known hypertensive on amlodipine, was diagnosed with breast cancer six months ago. She received six cycles of chemotherapy, last one four weeks ago, with a view to have 773-555 THERAPE radical mastectomy and axillary clearance. She presents to the Oncology Clinic with shortness of breath. Her blood pressure is 105/80 mmHg, pulse is 90 bpm and regular. She has bilateral crackles to the mid zones on auscultation of her chest. Her ECG shows non- speciﬁc ST changes in the anterior leads. Her chest X-ray is shown below. What is the most likely cause of this woman’s presentation?
explanation:
B Dilated cardiomyopathy The chest x-ray shows blunted costophrenic angles, ‘Kerley B lines’ and upper lobe blood diversion in keeping with pulmonary oedema. Anthracycline cytotoxic agents such as doxorubicin are frequently used as antitumour agents to treat acute leukaemia, lymphomas and a variety of solid tumours. There is an association between overall dose given (cumulative effect) and dilated cardiomyopathy. Therefore, it is recommended that patients undergoing such treatments should have a baseline assessment of their heart with either an echocardiogram or a radionuclide ejection fraction measurement. According to the Summary of Product Characteristics, contraindications to doxorubicin include severe arrhythmia, heart failure, previous cardiac infarct and acute inﬂammatory heart disease. The negative effects on cardiac function may be synergistic when agents such as Herceptin, an HER-2 antagonist, are coprescribed.

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com A Acute coronary syndrome Her ECG shows non-speciﬁc ST segment changes and does not support a diagnosis of myocardial infarction. C Neutropaenic sepsis Neutropenia usually presents at 10–14 days post chemotherapy, and would not necessarily precipitate an episode of cardiac failure. D Metastatic disease Although metastatic disease may result in lymphangitis carcinomatosa, presenting with crackles on auscultation of the chest, the clinical picture here, is more consistent with cardiac failure. E Acute kidney disease The hypotension and tachycardia coupled with heart failure is more consistent with underlying cardiac rather than renal pathology.

stem: A 65-year-old man with a long history of alcohol abuse was brought to the Emergency Department by his son. He had been diagnosed with liver cirrhosis several years in the past, but had not had any contact with medical services since then. Neighbours had called the son after the patient had not been seen out for 48 hours. He had been consuming even more alcohol than usual since the death of his wife three months ago. His only other past medical history was osteoarthritis, for which he took codeine and paracetamol as required. On examination, he had a Glasgow Coma Scale of 9 and was deeply jaundiced. He was pyrexial, tachycardic and hypotensive. There were stigmata of chronic liver disease and asterixis was present. He had a large, tense distended tender abdomen with scanty bowel sounds. Rectal examination was normal. Cardiorespiratory examination was unremarkable. He was poorly co-operative with the neurological examination; however, his pupils were equal and reactive and he had increased tone and reﬂexes throughout all four limbs. Investigation results are below: Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 128 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 14.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 100 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l MCV 108 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ Sodium (Na+) 130 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.6 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.6 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 170 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Glucose 3.4 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Bilirubin 110 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l ALT 520 u/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 320 u/l 30 - 150 u/l 773-555 THERAPE Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) 600 u/l < 50 u/l PT 22 s 11 - 14 s Chest X-ray No focal abnormality Urinalysis Protein + Which investigation will most likely reveal the cause of his encephalopathy?
explanation:
C Paracetamol levels Possible causes of this patient’s deterioration of heath and hepatitis include: drug over-dosage, Infection (e.g. spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), subdural hematoma and alcohol binge. In this patient, possibility of hepatotoxic drug over-dosage or exposure must ﬁrst be excluded, in view of recent family bereavement. Thus, paracetamol levels should be checked initially to exclude paracetamolinduced acute liver Injury. Management of such patient includes; identifying and removing the cause by activated charcoal in those presented less than 4 hours after oral dosage of paracetamol. Nacetylcysteine can be started if patient presents less than 10-12 hours since overdose with no vomiting and high plasma levels of paracetamol. A Urgent oesophagogastroduodenoscopy There is no evidence of acute GI bleeding at this stage of the disease. Upper GI endoscopy may be indicated at a later stage to visualize any variceal bleeding, according to clinical signs and symptoms. B Electroencephalogram (EEG) Acute liver injury and hepatic encephalopathy can lead to increased intracranial pressure (ICP) with cerebral oedema, which is the leading cause of death. EEG is useful in monitoring of hepatic encephalopathy and predicts outcomes of acute liver disease. EEG can be requested in accordance with the clinical picture of the patient. It will not however reveal the underlying cause. . D Serum alpha-fetoprotein levels Serum alpha-fetoprotein level is used to evaluate prognosis in patients with paracetamol-induced fulminant hepatic failure, thus a wrong option to select. Increased levels of alpha-fetoprotein predicts favourable outcomes in paracetamol induced hepatic failure cases. E Serum ammonia levels

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Serum ammonia levels are typically elevated in acute liver injury and also correlate with the development of encephalopathy. They do not however reveal an underlying cause. The possibility of paracetamol overdose must be excluded before testing for other causes and complications of acute liver disease.

stem: A 42-year-old former nurse is reviewed in the Hypertension Clinic. She has a history of latex fruit syndrome, with two episodes of anaphylaxis over the past year, and she carries an adrenaline autoinjector with her at all times for this reason. Her general practitioner is asking about appropriate medications to treat her blood pressure. She has no other past medical history of note. In the clinic, her blood pressure is 165/90 mmHg, and pulse 82 bpm and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 22 kg/m2. Which of the following antihypertensive agents is known to potentiate the severity of anaphylactic reactions?
explanation: E Ramipril Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are thought to have the most risk for worsening the severity of episodes of anaphylaxis in those at risk. A number of mechanisms are postulated as to why this occurs, including preventing a compensatory rise in angiotensin II at the time of anaphylaxis and through reduced breakdown of bradykinin. A Amlodipine This would be the most appropriate initial intervention for the management of this patient’s blood pressure. B Atenolol There is no association between beta blockers and potentiation of anaphylaxis. They should be avoided in patients who are asthmatic due to the risk of triggering an asthma attack. C Bendroﬂumethiazide This would be an appropriate second-line intervention in the management of this patient’s blood pressure. It is not associated with potentiation of anaphylaxis. D Losartan Potentiation of anaphylaxis is not seen with angiotensin receptor blockers, although, of course, they may still drive episodes of an- 773-555 THERAPE gio-oedema in their own right.

stem: You see a 43-year-old man with rigors. He suddenly became unwell 12 h ago and had four episodes of diarrhoea. According to his home help, she found him lying on the ﬂoor when she arrived. He was discharged from hospital 2 weeks ago after treatment for osteomyelitis. His medications included paracetamol, tramadol, ﬂuoxetine and linezolid. On examination, he was confused and agitated, with a temperature of 40.7 °C. His pulse was 142 bpm and regular and his respirations were 32 breaths per min. Cranial nerve examination revealed rapid sustained eye movements. Peripheral nerve examination demonstrated generally increased tone, rapid contraction and relaxation of his ankle and hyper-reﬂexia. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Potassium (K+) 6.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 181 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 12.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatine kinase 959 IU/l 23–175 IU/l CRP 243 mg/l < 10 mg/l WCC 24.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Haemoglobin (Hb) 124 g/l 135–175 g/l Platelets (PLT) 93 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Prothrombin test (PT) 21 s 10.6–14.9 s What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Serotonin syndrome Serotonin syndrome is associated with increased serotonergic activity, and the diagnosis is made on clinical grounds using the Hunter criteria. To fulﬁl these criteria a patient must have taken a serotonergic agent and meet one of the following conditions:  Spontaneous clonus  Inducible clonus plus agitation or sweating  Ocular clonus plus agitation or sweating  Tremor plus hyperreﬂexia  Hypertonia plus temperature >38 plus ocular or inducible clonus Serotonin syndrome is often misdiagnosed as neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), but the two can readily be distinguished on the basis of history, examination ﬁndings and clinical course. NMS develops over days to weeks, whereas serotonin syndrome develops over 24 h. Serotonin syndrome is characterised by neuromuscular hyper-reactivity (tremor, hyper-reﬂexia, myoclonus), while NMS involves sluggish neuromuscular responses (rigidity, bradyreﬂexia). Hyper-reﬂexia and myoclonus are rare in NMS. This patient takes a combination of high-risk medications: linezolid (monoamine oxidase inhibitor) and ﬂuoxetine (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor). Importantly, tramadol has effects on serotonin and noradrenalin and can cause serotonin syndrome, especially when in combination with other medications. Treatment involves stopping the offending medications. Cyproheptadine and propranolol have been used as they block serotonin. The patient may need to be managed in ITU and treated for hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney disease and disseminated intravascular coagulation. In cases of hyperthermia, supportive measures and standard treatments include muscle relaxants, cooling and intubation. 773-555 THERAPE C Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome HUS is deﬁned by the triad of micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. It can be primary (complement gene mutations, antibodies to complement factor H) or secondary (infection, drug toxicity or autoimmune). HUS usually presents with bloody diarrhoea, oliguria, abdominal pain and acute kidney injury. A Neuroleptic malignant syndrome NMS is a life-threatening condition associated with the use of neuroleptic agents. Features include mental status change, rigidity, fever or dysautonomia occurring in the setting of neuroleptic use or dopamine withdrawal. It typically develops over days to weeks. B Meningitis Although this patient has a fever and raised inﬂammatory markers, the presenting symptoms do not suggest meningitis, especially in the absence of any meningism. E Lethal catatonia Catatonia is a behavioural syndrome characterised by the inability to move normally, often occurring in the context of an underlying psychiatric disorder. Malignant catatonia is a subtype and consists of fever, autonomic instability, delirium and rigidity. The signs and symptoms overlap with NMS, and are indistinguishable in 20% of cases. NMS is considered a drug-induced form of malignant catatonia.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is rushed into the Emergency Department after taking an overdose of her grandfather’s warfarin. She admits to experiencing low mood for the past four months and has been having suicidal ideation. She says she took between 12 and 15 tablets eight hours ago. There is no history of epistaxis, haematuria or bruising in the last eight hours. Her past medical history includes depression and mild asthma, for which she takes Clenil Modulite® two puffs twice a day and salbutamol as required. On examination, she appears upset. Her observations are within normal range. There are no signs of bruising or petechiae over her body. On auscultation, her chest is clear and heart sounds are normal. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no guarding or palpable masses. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 124 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 212 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.1 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 73 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l EGFR 67 ml/min/1.73 m2 60+ ml/min/1.73 m2 INR 1.5 0.9–1.2 APTT 39 s 30–40 s Fibrinogen 2.1 g/l 2–4 g/l D-dimer 205 ng/ml < 400 ng/ml Urinalysis: negative What is the next step in the immediate management of this patient?
explanation:
C Oral vitamin K The patient has taken an intentional overdose of warfarin. The ﬁrst thing to consider is the presence of signiﬁcant bleeding, as this inﬂuences the overall management plan. As this patient has not shown signs of bleeding after ingesting warfarin, the next consideration needed is the INR. In those who have ingested an excess of warfarin and are not bleeding, an INR > 1.4 warrants treatment with oral vitamin K (the reversal agent to warfarin). B Intravenous (IV) vitamin K Intravenous vitamin K would be recommended in the initial setting if this patient showed signs of active bleeding. However, in the absence of bleeding, this patient would need to be observed for

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com a minimum of 48 hours post-ingestion to regularly check full blood count and clotting times. A Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) Like PCC or IV vitamin K, FFP can be used to reverse the action of warfarin in those with active bleeding. It would not be used in this patient, as she is relatively stable with no signs of bleeding. D Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) PCC would be used if this patient showed signs of signiﬁcant bleeding. IV vitamin K would likely be given, along with PCC. However, as this patient is not actively bleeding, this treatment is not indicated. E Tranexamic acid Tranexamic acid can be used in cases of signiﬁcant bleeding (eg epistaxis or heavy menstrual bleeding). However, it does not have a role in warfarin reversal and would not be the treatment of choice in this setting.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the Pharmacology Clinic for review. She has been referred by her general practitioner for management of hypertension, as she is planning on trying for her ﬁrst child over the next few months and the family doctor is unsure of how to manage her. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 155/95 mmHg and a pulse of 75 bpm and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m2. Renal function testing and an ultrasound of the renal tract are unremarkable. She is thought to have essential hypertension. Which of the following is the optimal therapy for treating her blood pressure?
explanation:
B Labetalol The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines on the management of hypertension in pregnancy recommend labetalol as the ﬁrst-line agent. The recommended alternative in patients who are unable to take beta blockers is nifedipine and methyldopa. E Ramipril Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are potentially teratogenic and are not recommended in patients who are considering pregnancy. A Candesartan Angiotensin II receptor blockers are potentially teratogenic and are not recommended in patients who are considering pregnancy. C Methyldopa This can be considered if both labetalol and nifedipine are not suitable for the management of hypertension in pregnancy as per NICE. D Nifedipine Extensive data exist on the use of dihydropyridine calcium antagonists in pregnancy. As such, nifedipine considered for women in whom labetalol is not suitable as per NICE.

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com

stem: A 52-year-old man is seen in Cardiology Clinic as follow-up after a recent admission with paroxysmal atrial ﬁbrillation and a myocardial infarction. Since discharge, he has noticed a rash develop over his face and neck when he is out in the garden. On examination, his pulse is 65 bpm and regular. His blood pressure is 123/82 mmHg. There is an erythematous rash on sunexposed skin. What is the most likely causative agent?
explanation: C Amiodarone Amiodarone therapy is associated with a 30–50% incidence of photosensitivity. Symptoms develop within two hours of sun exposure, followed by erythema. A minority of affected patients develop a slate-grey pigmentation on light-exposed areas. Photosensitivity may persist for up to four months after the drug is withdrawn. Cutaneous pigmentation slowly fades after amiodarone is stopped but may persist for months to years. In affected patients, skin cells and the cells of other organs have been found to contain myelin-like lysosomal structures and membrane-bound granules. This generalised derangement of lysosomal storage may also be the basis for other adverse effects of amiodarone such as interstitial alveolitis, acute hepatitis and disturbed thyroid function. E Ramipril Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors have been known to causes photosensitivity, but less commonly than amiodarone. They are also associated with episodes of angioedema. A Simvastatin This may be associated with a hypersensitivity rash, alopecia, myositis, hepatitis, pancreatitis and peripheral neuropathy. B Metoprolol Beta blockers are known to exacerbate psoriasis and may cause dry eyes. D Warfarin Warfarin, like statins, may cause alopecia; it is also associated with easy bruising and areas of skin necrosis. 773-555 THERAPE

stem: A 69-year-old male is reviewed in the Neurology Clinic. He has Parkinson’s disease and takes madopar 100/25 QDS, and ropinirole M/R 8 mg daily. He has problematic ‘off’ periods which can vary from day to day. Higher doses of madopar previously led to confusion. Neurological examination reveals cogwheel rigidity, an asymmetrical resting tremor and bradykinesia, worse on the right. Review of which aspect of the patient’s symptoms and lifestyle may lead to improved motor control?
explanation:
B Diet Levodopa is absorbed in the duodenum and its transport across the blood-brain barrier is facilitated by a large neutral amino acid transporter protein. Dietary protein can therefore compete with levodopa transport in both the gastrointestinal system and across the blood-brain barrier, reducing its effect. Some patients ﬁnd it beneﬁcial to have medications on an “empty stomach” i.e 60 minutes before or after a meal. E Orthostatic hypotension Orthostatic hypotension is common in advanced Parkinson’s disease and can be challenging to treat. Nonpharmacological methods include increasing salt and water intake and using compression stockings and abdominal binders. Thereafter ﬂudrocortisone or midodrine can be trialled. Improvement in orthostatic hypotension however, does not result in improvement in motor symptoms. In some severe cases, levodopa may actually need to be reduced thereby risking worsening motor control. A Bladder function Although Parkinson’s disease can result in frequency, urgency and nocturia and the symptoms should be managed appropriately, improving these symptoms will not lead to better control of motor symptoms. C Smoking Interesting smoking has been shown to have an inverse relationship with the development of Parkinson’s disease (i.e smokers have a slightly lower risk). Starting to smoke, or stopping, has no alteration on motor control, however. D Caffeine

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Like smoking, caffeine intake has been associated with lower risk of Parkinson’s disease but not an improvement in motor control has not been demonstrated.

stem: A 24-year-old woman who is eight weeks pregnant suffers two generalised tonic-clonic seizures on awakening. There is a family history of epilepsy. She has no other past medical history of note and following brain imaging and electroencephalogram (EEG), a diagnosis of idiopathic epilepsy is made. You are considering treatment with an anti-epileptic drug. Which of the following would prove the most appropriate option for her?
explanation: C Lamotrigine According to 2016 data across 69 pregnancies, the rate of congenital malformation used at low dose is approximately 2%. This puts it amongst the safest options for treatment of epilepsy in pregnancy. E Sodium valproate/levetiracetam combination Combination therapy may have as a baseline the same risk as sodium valproate, or a potentially cumulative increased risk of malformations across the two compounds. A Topiramate Across 17 reported pregnancies in 2016, rates of congenital malformation are estimated at between 4 and 7%. B Sodium valproate MHRA advice (due to the risk of impaired fertility in men and teratogenicity in women) suggests that no patient under the age of 55 should be commenced on valproate, unless two consultants agree that there is no suitable alternative treatment. Valproate results in an 11% risk of birth defects and a 30-40% risk of neuro- developmental disabilities. 773-555 THERAPE D Levetiracetam Although low rates of congenital malformation are seen for levetiracetam, exposure as reported for 2016 across only 11 pregnancies, this drives lamotrigine as the correct answer due to insufﬁcient evidence for levetiracetam.

stem: An 18-year-old man is admitted to Accident and Emergency after collapsing in a night club. He is drowsy but oriented and able to answer questions. This was his ﬁrst week at university and he had decided to go out to a night club with his friends. He was given some ‘tablets’ in the night club to make him more relaxed and he was advised to drink a lot of ﬂuids. All he remembers was that he went onto the dance ﬂoor and everything blacked out. When he came round, he was lying on the ﬂoor with people standing all around him and then he was brought to the hospital. On examination, his temperature was 37.1 °C, blood pressure was 140/85 mmHg and his pulse was 104 bpm and regular. Apart from being slightly drowsy, his neurological examination was essentially normal. Investigation Result Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 120 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 200 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 123 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 67 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urea 1.8 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l MCV 90 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ What is the most appropriate step in the immediate management of this patient?
explanation:
A Restrict ﬂuid intake Ecstasy is the common usage name for 3,4methylenedioxymethamphetamine, which is a psychoactive drug. It is a class A drug and is illegal in the UK. It is commonly used at dance parties and changes the mood through its effects on dopaminergic and serotoninergic pathways. It has a short duration of action of about 4–6 h and is usually ingested in a dose of 75– 150 mg orally. Its effects are said to relax the users and make them more friendly to other people. Its side effects are unpredictable and include:

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com nausea, sweating, hypertension, tachycardia, disseminated intravascular coagulation and liver failure. Deaths have been reported from heat stroke and water intoxication. In this case, given the serum sodium, it is water intoxication which is the likely problem and ﬂuid restriction is the intervention of choice. B Give dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV Dantrolene was formerly used as a treatment for malignant hyperthermia, although now anti-cholinergics are the usual preferred intervention of choice. C IV hypertonic saline Hypertonic saline is not required, given this patient’s normal current neurological status. Only in the event that there was signiﬁcant CNS depression with seizures would hypertonic saline, given in the ITU environment, be considered. D Metoprolol 5–10 mg IV Metoprolol is only required in the event of signiﬁcant hypertension or SVT related to ecstasy use. It isn’t therefore required here. E Diazepam 0.1–0.3 mg/kg PO This is the appropriate intervention where there is signiﬁcant agitation or seizures associated with ecstasy use.

stem: A 32-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis and bipolar disorder is brought to the Emergency Department complaining of bilateral deafness, tinnitus and blurred vision. These symptoms had started 3 h ago. He is vomiting repeatedly on arrival in the Emergency Department and is restless, sweating and dehydrated. Respiratory rate is 34/min. His blood pressure is 102/70 mmHg and pulse is 86 and regular. His GCS is 13. Investigation Result Normal Values WCC 12 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Haemoglobin (Hb) 120 g/l 135 - 175 g/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 2.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Arterial blood gases initially reveal: Investigation Result Normal Values pH 7.64 7.35 - 7.45 paCO2 2.8 kPa 4.7 - 6.0 kPa Bicarbonate 22 mmol/l 22 - 29 mmol/l Chloride (Cl-) 90 mmol/l 98 - 106 mmol/l and some 3 h later: Investigation Result Normal Values pH 7.3 7.35 - 7.45 paCO2 2.8 kPa 4.7 - 6.0 kPa 773-555 THERAPE Bicarbonate 10 mmol/l 22 - 29 mmol/l What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
D Salicylate poisoning This patient presented with bilateral deafness, tinnitus, visual blurring, repeated vomiting and initially had respiratory alkalosis followed by severe metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap. These features are typical of salicylate poisoning. Increased anion gap metabolic acidosis occurs is several conditions which include (1) diabetic ketoacidosis; (2) methanol overdose; (3) ethylene glycol poisoning; (4) lactic acidosis; (5) salicylate poisoning. It is calculated by the formula: anion gap = plasma ([sodium] + [potassium]) – ([chloride] + [bicarbonate]) Normal values in health range between 8 and 14 mmol/l; in this patient the anion gap is 25 mmol/l.
