Fluid resuscitation and urinary alkalinisation are mainstays of management for salicylate poisoning; in severe cases, where plasma concentration is >700 mg/l, haemodialysis may be considered. Indications for haemodialysis include:  kidney disease  congestive cardiac failure  non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema  coma, convulsions, CNS effects not resolved by correction of acidosis  persistently high salicylate concentrations unresponsive to urinary alkalinisation  severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2). C Naproxen poisoning Naproxen poisoning is associated with headache, nausea, vomiting and epigastric pain, but is less likely to be associated with tinnitus compared to aspirin overdose A Ethylene glycol poisoning

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Ethylene glycol poisoning is associated with a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis, but tinnitus and deafness are not features of ethylene glycol poisoning. B Metformin poisoning Metformin is associated with raised anion gap metabolic acidosis, but again is not associated with tinnitus. E Sulfasalazine poisoning Sulfasalazine is associated with very low levels of acute toxicity in overdose.

stem: A 22-year-old medical student is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance. She was found collapsed in her bedroom the morning after a university freshers’ ball. On examination, she is drowsy and confused. Her temperature is 39.2 °C, blood pressure (BP) 145/80 mmHg. On further questioning, her friends admitted that she avoids alcohol but does take Ecstasy. Investigation Result Normal value Sodium (Na+) 148 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 210 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 19.1 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Alanine transaminase (ALT) 42 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Bilirubin 48 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l PT 12.1 s 10.6–14.9 s Urine Blood+++ on dipstick, microscopy no red cells Which of the features noted is most associated with a poor outcome?
explanation: A Creatinine 210 µmol/l This woman is suffering from Ecstasy toxicity. Poor prognostic indicators in Ecstasy overdose include hyperpyrexia (>42 oC), rhabdomyolysis (as evidenced here by myoglobinuria), kidney disease and liver failure. In this case, the creatinine of 210 µmol/l already implies insipient kidney disease related to rhabdomyolysis. Most deaths from Ecstasy are due to hyperthermia and complications of hypertension and DIC, such as cerebral infarction or 773-555 THERAPE haemorrhage. Management of the hyperpyrexia is with rapid convection cooling, in an attempt to reduce core temperature to below 38.3 °C. Agitation is managed with the use of benzodiazepines, IV rehydration is used to manage rhabdomyolysis, and IV agents such as nitroprusside, which can be easily titrated, are optimal in the management of hypertension. C ALT 42U/l This ALT value is in the normal range and wouldn’t be considered as inﬂuencing prognosis. B Temperature 39.2 oC Although pyrexia is associated with increased risk of rhabdomyolysis, worsening kidney disease and neurological sequelae, aggressive rehydration and cooling measures can minimise the potential impact on outcome. D Potassium 5.6 mmol/l Potassium is likely to fall with aggressive rehydration, and the value quoted here is only just above the upper limit of normal. E BP 145/80 mmHg A BP towards the upper end of the normal range implies continued renal perfusion and is therefore associated with improved outcomes.

stem: A 29-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by a university friend who lives with him. He was found confused a few hours earlier by his friend who thought he was drunk, but despite watching over him, he appeared to be getting worse. His friend is aware he has bipolar disorder and takes a range of medications, and along with several other university peers, had been experiencing frequent vomiting over the last 48 hours. Examination reveals a BP of 95/60 mmHg; his heart rate is 105 bpm and regular, and his temperature is 37.7 °C. Skin turgor is increased. He is drowsy and disoriented to time and place. He appears to be uncoordinated and has a coarse tremor. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 9.1 g/dl 11.5–16.0 g/dl WCC 7.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 173 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 177 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ECG Flattened T waves, sinus rhythm What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Lithium toxicity Acute lithium toxicity secondary to hypovolaemia, following the recent GI symptoms, is the most likely diagnosis. The low K+ level, from frequent vomiting, reduced skin turgor, raised Cr level and low BP are all indicators of hypovolaemia. ECG changes in lithium toxicity include a prolonged QTc and ﬂattened T waves. Lithium levels should be measured, with levels higher than 4 mmol/l requiring dialysis. C Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome typically presents subacutely with muscular rigidity, hyperthermia, confusion, agitation and even catatonia. Autonomic instability can be challenging to manage. These features are not seen here, making it an unlikely diagnosis. A Sodium valproate toxicity Sodium valproate toxicity results in reduced consciousness, ranging from lethargy to coma, respiratory depression, GI side-effects, miosis, agitations and myoclonus. Similarly to carbamazepine, it is metabolised in the liver, following which it is renally excreted as the glucuronide conjugate. As such, acute renal failure does not predispose to carbamazepine toxicity. D Lamotrigine toxicity Lamotrigine is much safer compared to other mood-stabilising or anti-seizure medications. In cases of lamotrigine overdose, the majority of patients are asymptomatic, although symptoms can include drowsiness, lethargy, nausea and ataxia. It is metabolised by glucuronic acid conjugation in the liver and acute renal failure is therefore unlikely to result in toxicity. E Carbamazepine toxicity Carbamazepine toxicity results in reduced consciousness, seizures, ataxia and anticholinergic symptoms (tachycardia, feeling hot, dry skin). It is metabolised in the liver to its active metabolite and is then renally excreted. As such, acute renal failure does not predispose to carbamazepine toxicity.

stem: You make a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in a 30-year-old woman. She has one 4-year-old son and informs you that she is interested in having another child. Her arthritis is very active, and she needs to have treatment started. 773-555 THERAPE According to current guidelines, which one of the following agents would be the most appropriate choice?
explanation:
C Sulphasalazine None of the medications used in the treatment of arthritis is absolutely safe during pregnancy. Careful consideration of the risk– beneﬁt ratio is needed, on an individual basis. Drugs that are deﬁnitely contra- indicated in pregnancy include NSAIDs (ﬁrst trimester, due to risk of abortion) and methotrexate (teratogenicity). At present the recommended therapies are sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine, or azathioprine if the beneﬁt– risk ratio is in favour of this. Sulfasalazine can be safely used prior to and during all stages of pregnancy. It is compatible with breastfeeding, though should be advised with caution because of the rare possibility that the mother is a slow acylator. E Inﬂiximab No increase in pregnancy or birth complications has been shown with inﬂiximab, etanercept or adalimumab. While data on newer biological treatments (including anti-tumour necrosis factor A inhibitors) is reassuring, as research is still limited, this would not be the best choice here. Current recommendations are that patients already on anti-TNF drugs may continue use until the end of pregnancy week 16 but should be avoided later in pregnancy as these drugs do cross the through the placenta. A Methotrexate Methotrexate (MTX) is teratogenic and patients should not conceive while on MTX. Pregnancies should be planned, allowing MTX to be stopped and a wash-out period of 3–6 months before safe conception. Patients should take high-dose 5 mg daily folic acid prenatally and during pregnancy. B Leﬂunomide Leﬂunomide is teratogenic and has a very long wash out period (up to 2 years). If a patient wishes to conceive, an accelerated washout may be achieved with activated charcoal or cholestyramine, and the leﬂunomide level can be measured post wash out to ensure it is below a safe limit to allow conception. D Azathioprine Azathioprine can be safely used in pregnancy but less is known about its safety in pregnancy versus sulphasalazine and therefore sulphasalazine is preferred. Women with severe rheumatic disease that is otherwise hard to control may use azathioprine during preg-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com nancy. No apparent congenital malformations are known with doses up to 2 mg/kg/day. However in case series, the maternal use of azathioprine in pregnancy was associated with small-forgestational-age infants, premature rupture of membranes, and intrauterine growth retardation.

stem: A 42-year-old homeless man is admitted to the Emergency Department having been found collapsed outside a nightclub. He is hypoxic, confused and extremely unwell. His blood pressure (BP) is 100/70 mmHg, with pulse 97/min and regular. Respiratory rate is 32/min. Pulse oximetry reveals oxygen saturations of 84%. In his pocket is an empty ﬂask of amyl nitrite. Which of the following represents the best treatment to reverse his tissue hypoxia?
explanation:
A Methylene blue This patient has methaemoglobinaemia as a result of ingestion of amyl nitrite. Amyl nitrite promotes the formation of methaemoglobin, which avidly conserves oxygen and leads to decreased tissue oxygen saturations. Treatments of choice include methylene blue and vitamin C. These act by reducing methaemoglobin to haemoglobin.

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com D Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) Because O2 is avidly bound to methaemoglobin, NIPPV does not improve tissue hypoxia. B Hyperbaric oxygen In other circumstances, for example carbon monoxide overdose, hyperbaric oxygen may improve tissue delivery of O2 but where there is methaemoglobinaemia, it has little impact. C Intubation and ventilation Methaemoglobinaemia means that even under conditions of artiﬁcial ventilation, oxygen delivery cannot be improved. E GTN infusion Infusion of further nitrate has no positive impact in the treatment of methaemoglobinaemia. It may reduce blood pressure further and have a negative impact on outcomes.

stem: A 49-year-old woman is admitted with nausea and vomiting. She had also noticed the development of a skin rash on her left arm and mouth sores. While on the ward she had an episode of haematemesis. She has a background of rheumatoid arthritis and has recently been commenced on methotrexate. On further questioning, she tells you that she has been taking the methotrexate daily. Which of the following treatments is likely to be most effective in treating her symptoms?
explanation: C Calcium folinate The most likely diagnosis here is severe bone marrow suppression due to the methotrexate. Methotrexate is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor, which converts dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate. Calcium folinate (Leucovorin™), a derivative of tetrahydrofolate, bypasses the folate step blocked by methotrexate and can be used in the management of an overdose. E Prednisolone Corticosteroids are only of value in treating a rash related to acute drug reaction, and the distribution of the rash here, coupled with other symptoms, counts against this being an acute drug reaction. 773-555 THERAPE A Vitamin K Vitamin K is an option for reversal of warfarin therapy, as warfarin blocks the production of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors. B Folic acid Folic acid is ineffective as a treatment for methotrexate-related bone marrow suppression, because production of tetrahydrofolate is prevented. D Vitamin B12 In this case vitamin B12 is ineffective in promoting bone marrow recovery because the ability to produce tetrahydrofolate is still impaired.

stem: A 59-year-old man, who has spent a long period of time on the ITU after MRSA septicaemia, a myocardial infarction and subsequent left ventricular failure, attends the clinic for follow-up. He complains of dizziness and tinnitus; he says the dizziness is worse if he goes out at night or he turns his head quickly. On examination, you can reproduce his dizziness on rapid movements of the head. The remainder of the clinical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
A Vancomycin toxicity Vancomycin may be used as part of the treatment regime for MRSA. Given that this man has spent a considerable amount of time on the intensive therapy unit, it is likely that he has been treated with vancomycin. Several reports of toxicity exist, which is manifest primarily as tinnitus, but other vestibular symptoms may be reported, including dizziness. Adequate testing of vancomycin levels, aiming to maintain them within the target range, is crucial to avoid toxicity E Vestibular neuronitis Given the history of exposure to vancomycin, this is much more likely to be the underlying cause of symptoms than viral neuronitis. B Furosemide toxicity Furosemide toxicity is more commonly associated with hearing

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com loss as the primary symptom and is very rarely seen as a result of awareness of the need for slow IV administration. C Vestibular stroke A vestibular stroke without other neurological signs would be highly unlikely. D Aspirin toxicity Aspirin toxicity is associated with acute tinnitus in the ﬁrst few hours after overdose, not with chronic vestibular dysfunction of the type seen here.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is brought to Emergency Department after being found unresponsive on her bed. She takes paroxetine for depression, and her mother has previously been treated for depression with evidence of delusions. On examination, she is drowsy; her temperature is 40.3 °C and her heart rate is 140 bpm and regular. She has dilated pupils, a coarse tremor, hypertonia, hyperreﬂexia and sustained clonus. Which of the following medications is most likely to be responsible?
explanation: C Risperidone Serotonin syndrome, given hyperthermia, dilated pupils, muscular rigidity and hyperreﬂexia, is the likely diagnosis. Risperidone is the most likely medication from the options available to have been the culprit for the patient’s symptoms. It is a well-recognised cause, particularly in combination with paroxetine, of serotonin syndrome. E Aspirin Mild to moderate salicylate toxicity can lead to nausea, vomiting, tinnitus, headache, confusion, fever and hyperventilation. Severe toxicity presents with delirium, hallucinations, seizures and even respiratory arrest. A Citalopram The patient has serotonin syndrome, as evidenced by hyperthermia, dilated pupils, muscular rigidity and hyperreﬂexia. Citalopram is relatively safe when taken in overdose – hence its common use as a ﬁrst-line agent in the pharmacological treatment of depression. Note also that the patient is taking paroxetine and, therefore, 773-555 THERAPE will not be co-prescribed citalopram. B Thyroxine Thyroxine does not cause serotonin syndrome. In overdose, thyroxine typically causes tachycardia, agitation, sweating, diarrhoea and hypertension. It takes about 48 hours for symptoms to develop, as thyroxine must ﬁrst be converted peripherally to tri-iodothyronine, its active form. D Bisoprolol Beta-blocker toxicity can produce bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmias, hypothermia and hypoglycaemia, as well as seizures. Depending on the severity, the clinical presentation may range from asymptomatic hypotension to shock.

stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to the Oncology Clinic for review. She has advanced melanoma with multiple metastases. She is to be treated with ipilimumab. Which of the following is the mode of action of ipilimumab?
options: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) inhibitor
explanation: B Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA4) inhibitor Ipilimumab is a CTLA-4 immune checkpoint inhibitor that blocks T-cell inhibitory signals induced by the CTLA-4 pathway, increasing the number of reactive T-effector cells which mobilise to mount a direct T-cell immune attack against tumour cells. It is licensed for a range of advanced cancers, including for malignant melanoma and renal cell carcinoma. Autoimmune disease such as thyroid disease and type I diabetes are seen as adverse events in association with CTLA-4 inhibition. 773-555 THERAPE E Programmed cell death protein 1 (PD1) inhibitor PD1 inhibitors are immune checkpoint inhibitors. They are used to enhance T cell immune attack on cancer cells and improve their recognition by the immune system. By inhibiting the PD1 receptor, they also increase the risk of T cell-mediated autoimmune diseases, including thyroiditis and type I diabetes. A B-Raf inhibitor Vemurafenib is a B-Raf inhibitor. It works only in patients with melanoma who carry the V600E BRAF mutation, present in around 60% of melanomas. In patients who do not carry the mutation, there may be stimulation of tumour growth. Inhibiting BRaf leads to programmed cell death. Use of vemurafenib is associated with improved progression-free survival in melanoma. C Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) inhibitor Trastuzumab is a HER2 inhibitor. It is used in the treatment of advanced breast cancer where cells express the HER2 receptor, and in some other cancers which are HER2 receptor expressing including a subset of gastric cancers. The HER2 receptor is a member of the epidermal growth factor receptor family, and agonism of HER2 drives tumour growth. Antagonism of the receptor also increases the risk of cardiomyopathy occurring. D Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MEK) inhibitor MEK inhibitors inhibit the mitogen-activated protein kinase enzymes MEK1 and/or MEK2 and are licensed for the treatment of advanced melanoma. The MEK pathway is known to drive cell replication. Cobimetinib is an example of a MEK inhibitor which is licensed for the treatment of advanced melanoma.

stem: A 42-year-old man is referred to a Dermatology Clinic with a rash which has developed over his arms over the past two weeks. His past history includes hypertension, for which he takes lisinopril and bendroﬂumethiazide. He is also known to suffer from manic depression with signiﬁcant psychotic episodes, and had been taking chlorpromazine for six years. He was reviewed by his psychiatrist six months ago, who started him on lithium. He has recently been complaining of some indigestion, and so his general practitioner (GP) started lansoprazole two months ago. You observe the rash and it appears quite characteristic, as below. 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Which agent is most likely to have precipitated his rash?
explanation: D Lithium The scaly plaque over an extensor surface is characteristic of psoriasis, which can be precipitated by lithium. Drugs which are known to trigger or exacerbate psoriasis include lithium, antimalarials, nonsteroidal anti- inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and βblockers. Lisinopril is also rarely associated with this adverse effect. Precipitation of the rash may take up to a year to develop after initiation of the medication. Treatment involves withdrawal of the causative agent, and the use of emollients, topical compresses or topical steroids. It may be necessary to use etretinate, methotrexate or phototherapy. Of course, lithium prescription with ACE inhibition is not recommended due to the problem of a signiﬁcant increase in serum lithium levels. E Lisinopril Lisinopril is less likely to be associated with psoriasis than lithium, and the two are contraindicated in co- prescription. A Chlorpromazine Chlorpromazine is associated with dermatitis and urticaria, rather than with psoriasis. B Bendroﬂumethiazide Bendroﬂumethiazide is associated with exfoliative dermatitis and photosensitivity, rather than with psoriasis. C Lanzoprazole Lanzoprazole is associated with an urticarial rash, rather than with psoriasis. 773-555 THERAPE

stem: A 21-year-old woman with a history of well-controlled asthma on salmeterol/ﬂuticasone combination inhaler goes out to an Indonesian restaurant with friends. While eating her main course she suddenly develops a wheeze, feels very light-headed and looks ﬂushed in the face. A taxi is called, which brings her to the Emergency Room. On examination she looks unwell with a BP of 95/55 mmHg, a pulse of 100/min and severe wheeze on auscultation of the chest. She has signiﬁcant facial ﬂushing and a hives-like rash over her neck. Which of the following therapies is most appropriate for her?
explanation:
E IM adrenaline This woman has presented with severe anaphylaxis, possibly due to something contained in her meal. Immediate therapy centres IM adrenaline to assist blood pressure and relieve bronchoconstriction. Common causes of anaphylaxis, particularly where a trip out for an oriental meal is involved, include allergies to shellﬁsh proteins. Many referral centres have a batch of antigens that can be tested against, either via patch or RAST testing. Of course, she may require long-term anti-histamines or even an adrenaline auto-injector pen, but some attempt at least should be made to identify the precipitating antigen ﬁrst. Desensitisation therapy may be particularly effective where bee or wasp stings precipitate the anaphylactic attack. D SC adrenalin SC adrenalin leads to local vasoconstriction, which can drive unpredictable absorption and potentially reduced systemic effects. As such, this is not advised. A IV adrenaline IV adrenalin has a greater propensity to lead to arrhythmia, and as such would not necessarily be the ﬁrst choice ahead of the IM option. B IV hydrocortisone Corticosteroids are not recommended in the treatment of anaphylaxis. They were previously advocated until a change in guidelines in 2021. The evidence regarding their use in refractory anaphylaxis is unclear, and they can be considered. C IV magnesium

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Although IV magnesium has a role in the treatment of acute asthma, it doesn’t have a positive effect on blood pressure compared with IM adrenalin.

stem: A 32-year-old man with a history of HIV diagnosed some two years ago is admitted to the Emergency Department, with abdominal pain and a small increase in his serum creatinine. He has apparently recently had an alteration made to his antiretroviral medication. Abdominal examination reveals signiﬁcant left loin pain consistent with renal colic. Which of the following medications is recognised to cause the clinical picture seen here?
explanation: D Nelﬁnavir Although nephrolithiasis is rare with modern protease inhibitors, it is still reported in some patients taking nelﬁnavir. In contrast to indinavir, which is approximately 20% excreted into the urine, excretion of nelﬁnavir into urine is less than 3%. E Stavudine Stavudine is associated with proximal renal tubular dysfunction rather than the nephrolithiasis picture seen here. A Abacavir Abacavir is associated with acute interstitial nephritis, associated with eosinophilia, blood and proteinuria. B Efavirenz Efavirenz is not thought to be associated with signiﬁcant adverse renal effects; it is commonly associated with hypertriglyceridaemia. C Nevirapine Nevirapine is most commonly associated with rash and hepatitis, but not with adverse renal effects.

stem: A 45-year-old man with hypertension and dyslipidaemia is diagnosed with early type 2 diabetes and commenced on glitazone therapy. He has suffered from psoriasis for many years, which has been resistant to treatment and his dermatologist elects to com- 773-555 THERAPE mence ciclosporin therapy. He is warned about the potential for drug interactions with ciclosporin and told to carry a card, but you warn him about a few of the common interactions he should be concerned about. Which of the following drugs or foods should he be most concerned about with respect to increasing his ciclosporin levels?
explanation: B Verapamil Verapamil, cyclosporine. affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Verapamil and cyclosporine may inhibit CYP3A4 metabolism. Coadministration of verapamil and cyclosporine may increase plasma concentrations of either drug. As such, if possible an alternative agent should be substituted. D Cranberry juice Cranberry juice is an inhibitor of CYP 2C9, leading to an increase in exposure to warfarin. A Orange juice Grapefruit, not orange juice, is an inhibitor of CYP3A4 and can therefore drive an increase in ciclosporin levels. Examples of other agents that increase ciclosporin levels include antifungals, diltiazem, nicardipine, metoclopramide, oral contraceptives, danazol, methylprednisolone (high dose), allopurinol, amiodarone, ursodeoxycholic acid and protease inhibitors. C Amoxicillin Macrolides are inhibitors of CYP3A4 and lead to an increase in ciclosporin levels, but penicillins do not. E Rifampicin Rifampicin is a potent CYP450 inducer, leading to a decrease in ciclosporin levels. Other agents known to decrease ciclosporin levels include barbiturates, carbamazepine and phenytoin, octreotide, orlistat and Hypericum perforatum (St John’s wort).

stem: A 27-year-old woman, who is 16 weeks pregnant, is referred by her GP with hypertension. The midwife noted her booking visit BP to be 135/82 mmHg, and it is now 155/92 mmHg. She has no previous signiﬁcant medical history, but is overweight with a BMI 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com of 28. Investigation Result Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 114 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 201 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 92 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l You elect to start treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for her?
explanation: C Labetalol Labetolol is the ﬁrst choice for managing hypertension in pregnancy according to NICE guidelines. Unlike other beta blockers such as atenolol, it isn’t associated with intra-uterine growth retardation. A Valsartan Valsartan is contraindicated due to the risk of renal agenesis and subsequent fetal death. This is true for the ACE inhibitor and ARB classes. B Bendroﬂumethiazide Diuretics interfere with natural volume expansion associated with pregnancy and are associated with increased risk of renal tract abnormalities. D Nifedipine There is evidence to support the use of dihydropyridines in pregnancy, although they are the second or third choice option for patients who are unable to take beta blockers or methyldopa. E Nitroprusside This is a consideration for acute management of hypertension and is delivered intravenously.

stem: You are asked to urgently review a 27-year-old zookeeper. He has been bitten by a coral snake and has become acutely unwell. He is hypotensive with a blood pressure of 85/60 mmHg, pulse is 95 bpm and regular. He is losing consciousness with obvious muscle weakness and difﬁculty swallowing his saliva. Which of the following statements is most correct regard- 773-555 THERAPE ing acute treatment for this snake bite?
options: The affected part should be immobilised above the level of the heart
A tourniquet should be immediately applied
Any clothing should not be disturbed
Use of ice on a snake bite is discouraged
Patients should be given a warm drink
explanation: D Use of ice on a snake bite is discouraged Ice is discouraged in the management of snake bites because it has been associated with increased necrosis of the skin and soft tissue around the bite. A The affected part should be immobilised above the level of the heart The affected area should be immobilised below the level of the heart, to minimise venous return. B A tourniquet should be immediately applied As tourniquets may exacerbate tissue necrosis, their use should only be considered by an experienced physician. C Any clothing should not be disturbed Any constricting clothing should be removed. E Patients should be given a warm drink The victim should be kept warm, but caffeine-containing drinks and alcohol should be avoided. Coral snake venom results in neurological symptoms such as ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria, intense salivation and later loss of deep tendon reﬂexes and respiratory depression. In the USA there are around 9–15 snake bite fatalities per year, mostly in children and the elderly and where treatment has been delayed.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive numbness and tingling in his feet, which has gradually spread to his hands. He also describes a burning sensation and mild weakness in his lower limbs. His medical history is signiﬁcant for hypertension, type II diabetes and tuberculosis (treated 18 months ago). His medications include metformin, lisinopril and isoniazid. On examination, he has reduced sensation to light touch and vibration in a stocking-and-glove distribution. Reﬂexes are mildly diminished in his lower limbs. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 140 g/l 135–175 g/l HbA1c 6.5% < 7.0% Serum vitamin B6 Low 5–50 nmol/l 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Serum vitamin B12 Normal 130–700 pmol/l What is the most likely cause of this patient’s neuropathy?
explanation: D Isoniazid-induced neuropathy Drug-induced neuropathy is a common complication of certain medications, including isoniazid. Isoniazid, which is used for tuberculosis treatment, can lead to peripheral neuropathy due to vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) depletion. Supplementation with vitamin B6 is often recommended during isoniazid therapy to prevent this side-effect, and a low serum vitamin B6 level here supports this diagnosis. E Metformin-induced vitamin B12 deﬁciency Long-term metformin use can lead to vitamin B12 deﬁciency, which, in turn, may cause neuropathy. However, this patient’s vitamin B12 level is within the normal range, making this an unlikely cause of his symptoms. A Alcohol-induced neuropathy Chronic alcohol use can cause neuropathy due to direct neurotoxic effects and associated nutritional deﬁciencies. However, there is no indication of alcohol use in this patient’s history, and the presence of isoniazid therapy with low vitamin B6 levels points to a drug-induced cause. B Idiopathic polyneuropathy Idiopathic polyneuropathy is a diagnosis of exclusion and is considered only when all other causes have been ruled out. Given this patient’s medication history, isoniazid-induced neuropathy is a more likely diagnosis. C Diabetic neuropathy Diabetic neuropathy is a common cause of peripheral neuropathy in patients with diabetes, particularly if there is poor glycaemic control. However, this patient has well-controlled diabetes (HbA1c within target), and his history of isoniazid use with low vitamin B6 level is more consistent with drug-induced neuropathy.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with a long history of anxiety and depression is brought into the Emergency Department at 0900 h by her husband following a suspected overdose. He had found her 773-555 THERAPE slumped in a chair downstairs with two empty medication bottles on the ﬂoor. He had last seen her at 2300 h the previous night when they had gone to bed. On examination, she was drowsy but rousable with a GCS of 12/15. Her heart rate was 130 bpm and her BP was 90/60 mmHg. Her skin was hot and dry and she had dilated pupils. . She had convulsion and hyperthermia with extensor plantar responses. Arterial blood (on air): Investigation Result Normal value pH 7.185 7.35–7.45 p(O2) 7.2 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa p(CO2) 3.2 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa Investigation Result Normal Value ECG Sinus tachycardia, widened QRS complex Bicarbonate 15 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l An IVI is commenced; which of the following is an appropriate next step?
options: Immediate intubation and transfer to the intensive therapy unit (ITU)
explanation:
C IV sodium bicarbonate This patient has the signs of tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) poisoning. Other features include dry mouth, urinary retention, skin blistering, hyperthermia, ataxia, nystagmus and hyperreﬂexia. Seizures occur in 10% of cases. Deep coma and respiratory depression may ensue. Cardiac arrhythmias can occur due to a quinidine-like type Ia effect on myocardium. After clearing the airway and maintaining adequate ventilation, the most important initial steps are to correct acidosis with sodium bicarbonate and relieve hypoxia. These measures can help to prevent arrhythmias without the need for anti-arrhythmic drugs. A IV naloxone Naloxone is used to reverse the effects of opiate toxicity and does not have a role here. B Immediate intubation and transfer to the intensive therapy unit (ITU) Although this patient requires early ITU involvement and monitor-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com ing in a high-dependency area, immediate intubation is not indicated (no profound hypoxia or hypercapnia). In total, tricyclic coma may last 24–48 h. Delirium and hallucinations may persist for 2–3 days and often require sedation with diazepam. D IV ﬂumazenil This is used to reverse benzodiazepine toxicity and in this situation may increase the risk of seizures; as such it should be avoided. E IV amiodarone Intravenous amiodarone prolongs the action potential and actually increases the risk of VT occurring in this situation.

stem: A 56-year-old man is brought to Accident and Emergency (A&E) one evening by the police, having been arrested for breach of the peace. He had been found wandering along the street shouting at passers-by, and had then proceeded to vomit over a parked car. Since his arrest, he has become increasingly confused and agitated, complaining of headache and nausea, and vomiting profusely. He was not known to have any past medical history, but was wellknown to the police as having no ﬁxed abode, and would be frequently picked up by the police when drunk. The police decided to bring the patient to A&E as his agitation and vomiting have been worsening. On arrival in A&E, he is disorientated and confused. On examination, he is unkempt, and his breath smells of ketones. He is afebrile. His heart rate is 90 bpm, regular, and blood pressure is 116/70 mmHg. Heart sounds are normal. His respiratory rate is 28/min, but his chest is clear. Oxygen saturations are 96% on air. Abdominal examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness but no guarding or rebound. He is uncooperative with neurological examination, and apart from complaints of blurred vision, and dilated, sluggish pupils, no focal signs are elicited. His investigations are as follows: 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 126 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.7 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 268 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 7.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 116 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Chloride (Cl–) 106 mmol/l 98-106 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3–) 11 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Glucose 4.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Lactate 3.6 mmol/l 0.5–2.2 mmol/l ECG Normal sinus rhythm PaO2 13.6 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa PaCO2 4.4 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa pH 7.24 7.35–7.45 Urinalysis No crystals seen He is started on sodium bicarbonate IV in an attempt to correct his acidosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?
explanation:
C IV ethanol This patient has methanol toxicity. Methanol is sometimes used as a substitute for ethanol by alcoholics, as it similarly causes inebriation. The metabolites of methanol produce metabolic acidosis, blindness, and death after a characteristic latent period of 6–30 hours. Methanol is slowly metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde, and subsequently by aldehyde dehydrogenase to formic acid. Systemic acidosis is caused by both formate and lactate. Both ethanol and methanol compete for the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase and block metabolism of methanol to its toxic metabolites. In the ﬁrst few hours after ingestion, methanol-intoxicated patients present with inebriation and gastritis. Acidosis is not usually present because metabolism to toxic products has not occurred yet. There may be a noticeable elevation in the osmolar gap. After a latent period of up to 30 hours, severe anion gap metabolic acidosis, visual disturbances, blindness, seizures, coma and death may occur. Fundoscopic examination may reveal disc hyperaemia, venous engorgement or papilloedema. Diagnosis is based on history, symptoms, large anion gap, serum methanol and serum formate levels. Treatment includes correction

773-555 THERAPE of the acidosis with IV bicarbonate, and administration of IV ethanol or fomepizole which saturate the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase and prevent metabolism of methanol. Haemodialysis may be necessary to rapidly remove methanol and formate. A IV thiamine IV thiamine is essential in the treatment of Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome, and should therefore be considered here, but it will not correct the acidosis or prevent methanol-related optic nerve damage. B IV tazocin There are no signs of sepsis to indicate a need for broadspectrum antibiotics. D IV naloxone IV naloxone is the ﬁrst-line intervention for the treatment of opiate overdose. E IV dexamethasone IV corticosteroids would be considered where there is evidence of cerebral oedema or adrenal crisis. It does not prevent the optic neuropathy associated with methanol intoxication.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who has a 3-week-old child presents to the Emergency Department for review. She has mastitis affecting the left breast, and you are considering potential antibiotic options for her. Which of the following would be considered safe to give to the woman as she wants to continue breastfeeding?
explanation:
A Cefalexin Cephalosporins, penicillins, and macrolides are considered the safest options to give to women who wish to continue breastfeeding if an antibiotic is required. They may have a negative impact on infant bowel ﬂora or promote sensitisation, but if an antibiotic is required for the mother, these risks would be considered acceptable. If a woman wishes to continue breastfeeding but not to expose her

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com child to breast milk containing antibiotics anyway, she should be advised to express the milk and then throw it away, rather than to cease feeding completely. E Oxytetracycline Oxytetracycline is a tetracycline like doxycycline. There use is not recommended in breastfeeding because they may impact on growth of bones and/or teeth. B Ciproﬂoxacin Quinolones are not recommended for use in adults because of the risk of neurological adverse effects and musculoskeletal adverse events, including joint pains, inﬂammation, and possible tendon rupture. They are contraindicated for use in pregnancy and breastfeeding because the musculoskeletal adverse effects were predominantly described in juvenile animals during toxicology testing. C Doxycycline Tetracyclines are not recommended for use in pregnancy or in breastfeeding. In pregnancy they’re known to cause permanent tooth staining, and in breastfeeding it is thought they may also impair tooth and bone plate growth in the infant receiving the milk. D Metronidazole Metronidazole is not recommended in breastfeeding. Metronidazole is present in breast milk at very high levels, driving a weightadjusted dose of 36% of that given to the mother. This is higher than the guideline amount for avoidance of antibiotic use in breastfeeding, which is 10%. If anaerobic cover is required, then coamoxiclav is the preferred option.

stem: A 22-year-old Chinese man is started on phenytoin for epilepsy. He subsequently presents with a severe blistering skin rash and oral and genital ulceration. On examination he is pyrexial (38.2 °C); his BP is 105/72 mmHg, with pulse is 85/min and regular. There are extensive target lesions and a number of de-roofed, blistered lesions. Which of the following is his most likely HLA type?
explanation:
B HLA B1502 HLA types related to drug reactions have appeared in a number of

773-555 THERAPE examinations over recent years, because they have featured in EMA and FDA alerts. HLA B1502 is associated with StevensJohnson syndrome in patients of Chinese origin taking phenytoin. E HLA DQ2 DQ2 HLA type is associated with the development of dermatitis herpetiformis. A HLA A3101 A3101 is associated with Stevens-Johnson syndrome in European or Japanese patients treated with carbamazepine. C HLA B5701 HLA B5701 is associated with abacavir hypersensitivity, which resulted in the development of HLA screening before the medication was initiated for HIV. D HLA B5801 HLA B5801 is associated with allopurinol hypersensitivity.

stem: A 51-year-old man is reviewed on the Endocrinology Ward. He was admitted ﬁve weeks ago with a complicated diabetic foot infection. He has received a prolonged course of antibiotics, as well as changes to his diabetic regimen and adjustments to his antihypertensives. During his rehabilitation over the last week, he has been experiencing an ache behind his left lower leg and is unable to complete his physiotherapy sessions. 773-555 THERAPE There is tenderness and swelling just above the posterior calcaneus of the left foot. There is a debrided wound on the plantar surface of the left foot. Which medication is the most likely cause of restricted mobility?
explanation: C Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is a ﬂuoroquinolone. The entire class of ﬂuoroquinolones may result in tendinopathy (as here) or tendon rupture. While ciproﬂoxacin has a slightly lower frequency than levoﬂoxacin, it is well known to result in problematic musculoskeletal sideeffects. E Bendroﬂumethiazide Bendroﬂumethiazide is a thiazide diuretic used in resistant hypertension. Adverse effects include hypokalaemia (due to renal potassium loss), hypercalcaemia, hyponatraemia and gout. While diuretics can induce muscle cramps, these would be likely to be more widespread and they are not linked to tendinopathy, which is the issue here. A Doxazosin Doxazosin is an alpha-1 adrenoceptor antagonist. Adverse effects include headaches, peripheral oedema, postural hypotension and muscle cramping, but not tendonitis or tendinopathy. B Flucloxacillin Flucloxacillin may be used for treatment of a diabetic foot infection. Common adverse effects include GI symptoms and thrombocytopenia. It does not result in musculoskeletal side-effects. D Canagliﬂozin Canagliﬂozin is a sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor. Common side-effects include an increased risk of infection, particularly UTIs, although there is no increased risk of musculoskeletal symptoms.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has been admitted via the Emergency Department with an overdose of dothiepin. She is drowsy and confused with dilated pupils and hyperreﬂexia. Her blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg with a pulse of 95 bpm. Whilst you examine her, you notice that the cardiac monitor shows intermittent runs of ventricular tachycardia and torsades. This coincides with more severe episodes of hypotension. Result of arterial blood gas are: Investigation Result Normal value pH 7.30 7.35–7.45 pa(O2) 13.2 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa pa(CO2) 4.8 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa Base excess –4 -2 to +2.0 mmol/l The Emergency Department consultant has already begun a magnesium infusion. Which of the following is the next most appropriate management step?
explanation: B IV sodium bicarbonate Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) like dothiepin and amitriptyline 773-555 THERAPE are mainly used for the treatment of depression. In overdose they can cause anticholinergic effects resulting in mydriasis, confusion, dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention. They can have a profound effect on cardiac conduction with resultant QT prolongation and torsades de pointes. Sodium bicarbonate is the mainstay of therapy, with many guidelines also recommending magnesium sulphate particularly when torsades, rather than QRS prolongation alone, is noted on the ECG. E Metoprolol Prolongation of the action potential will increase the risk of VT occurring in this patient. A Charcoal haemoperfusion Haemodialysis and haemoperfusion are not effective in removing TCAs. C Amiodarone infusion This leads to prolongation of the action potential; hence it actually increases the risk of arrhythmia here. D Ammonium chloride Alkalinisation of urine is not indicated in TCA overdose.

stem: A 32-year-old patient is admitted to hospital with increasing short- 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com ness of breath, cough, wheeze and chest tightness. He has a background of testicular cancer and mild asthma.
explanation: A Bleomycin Bleomycin is an antimitotic agent used for the treatment of testicular tumours. It is associated with pulmonary ﬁbrosis, which ﬁts with the presentation and chest X-ray (which demonstrates diffuse basal changes). A typical regimen for testicular cancer includes bleomycin, etoposide and a platinum-based agent. D Cyclophosphamide Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent used for Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and a wide spectrum of tumours. Side-effects include alopecia, nausea, vomiting, bone marrow suppression and haemorrhagic cystitis. B Busulfan Busulfan is an alkylating agent not usually used in the treatment of testicular tumours. It is more commonly used in the treatment of chronic myeloid leukaemia and can lead to pulmonary ﬁbrosis. C Methotrexate Methotrexate is a folate antagonist and is used often in combination to treat a variety of tumours. Side effects are mainly myelosuppression, hepatic ﬁbrosis and lung ﬁbrosis. Methotrexate is usually part of the chemotherapy regimen in patients with human chorionic gonadotrophin (HCG)-producing tumours, which are a 773-555 THERAPE subset of testicular carcinomas. E Daunorubicin Daunorubicin, like doxorubicin, is an antimitotic agent used for acute leukaemias and lymphomas. The class causes alopecia and cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a history of severe bipolar disorder treated with lithium is in the midst of an extended period of psychotic depression. She tells you that she has thought about suicide and had begun 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com drafting a suicide note, but threw it away the preceding week, and that she was considering a number of methods and had researched them on the Internet. She does not want to be admitted and tells you she will try to be compliant with drug therapy. Which of the following regimes for her would carry the least risk in overdose?
explanation: D Sodium valproate Sodium valproate overdose is rarely fatal, with a case fatality rate of only around 0.2% in a US case series. CNS depression is seen with hypotension and lactic acidosis in severe overdose. Repeat-dose activated charcoal may be given and haemodialysis may be considered in patients with very high valproate levels. MHRA advice (due to the risk of impaired fertility in men and teratogenicity in women) suggests that no patient under the age of 55 should be commenced on valproate, unless two consultants agree that there is no suitable alternative treatment. E Amitriptyline A number of deaths occur each year due to tricyclic anti-depressant overdose, particularly when taken with alcohol. Metabolic acidosis, QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias are common sequelae. A Lithium and ﬂuoxetine Although lithium and ﬂuoxetine given in combination may be very effective in treating refractory depression, lithium carries signiﬁcant risk in overdose and should therefore be avoided here. B Lithium and sodium valproate Taken together in overdose, lithium and sodium valproate carry signiﬁcant risk, particularly with respect to synergistic effects on CNS depression. C Lithium Even when used as monotherapy, lithium carries signiﬁcant risk of CNS toxicity and renal impairment in acute overdose. Haemodialysis is considered when levels of lithium breach 4 mmol/l and there is evidence of renal impairment, or when levels breach 5 mmol/l, even in the absence of kidney disease.

stem: 773-555 THERAPE You review a woman in the general practitioner (GP) surgery who is 24 weeks pregnant. She has a history of epilepsy, but presents today with a urinary tract infection. Having suffered a respiratory tract infection only one month earlier, she asks you about which antibiotics are considered most safe for use in pregnancy. Which of the following agents is safest for use in pregnancy?
explanation: D Amoxicillin Penicillin based antibiotics are generally considered safest for treating infections in pregnancy; however, because of prevalent resistance to amoxicillin in common pathogens causing urinary tract infection, sensitivity testing is considered before using this as a treatment option. At week 24 in pregnancy trimethoprim would generally be considered a safe alternative. E Ciproﬂoxacin Quinolone antibiotics are associated with tendon rupture in juvenile models of drug toxicity, and should therefore be avoided here. Also, current advice is that quinolone use should be avoided in all individuals if there is an alternative antibiotic that is suitable, due to potential long term or permanent side effects such as tendonitis. A Oxytetracycline Tetracycline based antibiotics are not considered safe because of irreversible staining and deterioration of dentition. B Gentamicin Gentamicin is not considered an option because of the risk of vestibular nerve toxicity. C Chloramphenicol Chloramphenicol is associated with “grey baby” syndrome, and should therefore be avoided.

stem: A 34-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia was brought to the Emergency Department after being found confused with a fever at home by his key worker. He was found in bed and his key worker suspected that he had probably been there and not moved for the preceding three days. His only pre- 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com scribed medication was ﬂuphenazine. The patient’s observations were as follows: blood pressure 90/50 mmHg, pulse 130 bpm, temperature 38 °C, saturations 97% on air, respiratory rate 22/min. On examination, he was mildly confused and sweating profusely. He had no neck stiffness and did not appear to have any photophobia. Neurological examination showed a marked increase in tone in all four limbs, and the patient found it difﬁcult to move any of his limbs. Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations did not reveal any further abnormalities. Which one of the following interventions is the most suitable in this patient’s case?
explanation: B IV ﬂuid replacement The diagnosis in this case is neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a life-threatening adverse drug reaction seen in patients taking antipsychotic drugs. The condition is characterised by rigidity, fever, autonomic dysfunction and delirium. A high creatinine kinase and white cell count are often seen in affected patients. Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury are recognised complications. Supportive treatment is key, with aggressive cooling and maintenance of hydration with IV ﬂuids being particularly important in the management of this condition. Bromocriptine and dantrolene may be used, but there is a scarcity of good evidence to support this. It is presumed that an increase in the dose of the patient’s ﬂuphenazine has precipitated the development of neuroleptic malignant syndrome in this case. D Carbamazepine This is not useful in the management of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Carbamazepine is an anti-epileptic drug used in the management of partial and generalised seizures and neuropathic pain. A Prednisolone This is not used in the management of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. The steroid dexamethasone is useful in the management of meningoencephalitis, but the ﬁndings in this case are not in keeping with this diagnosis. C Atenolol This is not useful in the management of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Autonomic dysfunction can result in labile blood pressure and treatment with atenolol may exacerbate this and result in dan- 773-555 THERAPE gerous hypotension. E Urinary alkalinisation This is not useful in the management of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Urinary alkalinisation may be useful in patients presenting with salicylate or phenobarbital overdoses as it can increase excretion of these drugs. It has been suggested that this may be a useful intervention in the management of rhabdomyolysis (which may complicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome), but there is limited evidence to support this.

stem: A 25-year-old man is admitted from the Accident and Emergency Department with increasing confusion over the past few weeks. He works as a demolition expert. He had recently attended his general practitioner (GP) with increasing headaches, hypersomnolence and abdominal pains. Examination reveals pale conjunctivae and blue lines on his gums. No focal neurology, and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 9.8 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 156 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Mean cell volume (MCV) 79 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Lead level 61 μg/dl < 10 μg/dl What is the best initial treatment?
explanation:
A Dimercaptosuccinic acid Lead poisoning occurs mainly in children and presents mainly in those adults with an occupational exposure risk. The heavy metal affects many enzymes including those involved in the production of haem. The symptoms are varied and patients can have abdominal pains, headaches, confusion, peripheral motor neuropathy and lethargy. Examination may reveal lead lines on the gums or signs consistent with anaemia. A plasma lead level conﬁrms the diagnosis and chelation therapy can be achieved by dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) or calcium disodium edetate. After treatment a cause must be found to prevent re-exposure when discharged. D N-acetylcysteine

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com N-acetylcysteine is used in the treatment of paracetamol overdose, and may have a role for some patients in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. B Desferrioxamine Desferrioxamine is a chelating agent primarily used in the treatment of iron toxicity. C Haemodialysis In this context, with chronic lead poisoning, chelation therapy with DMSA or calcium disodium edetate is the most appropriate intervention. E Plasma exchange Plasma exchange is of most utility in the management of antibody mediated conditions.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for a review of his Crohn’s disease management. He was diagnosed at the age of 15 years and has had seven ﬂares of his disease, three of which have required hospital admission. He was reluctant to start immunosuppressive medication to control his disease but has since changed his mind. The options are discussed with him and he decides to trial monotherapy with azathioprine. He has no other past medical history of note and no allergies. What is the next most appropriate investigation to consider before initiating treatment?
explanation: D Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity This patient is about to commence treatment with azathioprine. Azathioprine is a prodrug of mercaptopurine that is metabolised by the enzyme TPMT. Adverse effects of azathioprine include anaemia and myelosuppression. Therefore, it is important to measure TPMT levels in patients before starting azathioprine, as low levels or absence of the enzyme increase the circulating concentration of azathioprine metabolites and increase the risk of myelosuppression. The same applies before starting mercaptopurine therapy. A Bone proﬁle The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend monitoring full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests during azathioprine treatment. 773-555 THERAPE However, commencing azathioprine therapy does not require monitoring a patient’s bone proﬁle. B Chest X-ray Unlike other immunosuppressive therapies like methotrexate, azathioprine does not cause lung ﬁbrosis and a pretreatment chest X-ray is not required. C Liver ultrasound NICE guidelines recommend frequent liver function tests during azathioprine treatment, with particular focus on alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase and bilirubin. However, a liver ultrasound is not required before azathioprine therapy. E Thyroid function tests NICE guidelines recommend monitoring full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests during azathioprine treatment. Commencing azathioprine therapy does not require checking thyroid function tests.

stem: A 21-year-old woman, who is eight weeks pregnant, presents for review with very difﬁcult to control nausea and vomiting. She is very worried as she feels unable to eat and is concerned that she is losing weight. She has tried home remedies such as ginger and has been resting as much as possible. She is tolerating oral ﬂuids but very little solid foods. You are considering starting the medication. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 115 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following would be the most appropriate medication for her?
explanation:
B Promethazine NICE suggests that antihistamines such as cyclizine or promethazine are the recommended ﬁrst line options for the medical management of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. This is due to high

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com levels of effectiveness, lack of extra-pyramidal side effects and good overall tolerability proﬁle in this class of drugs. D Ondansetron Ondansetron is thought to be safe for the treatment of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, although exposure data are limited. Of the options available, promethazine is the most appropriate ﬁrst line treatment. A Domperidone The dopamine antagonist domperidone can be used in the treatment of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, however antihistamines are preferred as there is no risk of extra-pyramidal side effects with antihistamine use. C Metoclopramide Metoclopramide is not used as a ﬁrst line agent in the management of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy due to the increased risk of extrapyramidal side effects. These side effects are particularly common in the younger population. E Chlorpromazine Chlorpromazine is not recommended in pregnancy induced nausea and vomiting as there is a lack of consistent evidence available for its effectiveness. High doses may be required to treat symptoms however doses greater than 50mg a day can cause peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with a 1-day history of increased confusion and restlessness. She has become progressively more unwell throughout the day and has started vomiting within the last two hours. Her past medical history includes type I diabetes and depression. On examination, she has a temperature of 38.5 °C. She is tachycardic with a heart rate of 133 bpm and her blood pressure is 170/110 mmHg. Her face is red and ﬂushed. Her examination is difﬁcult due to increased agitation, but there is an obvious tremor and hyperreﬂexia of her upper and lower limbs. What is the most appropriate step in the management of this patient?
explanation: B Diazepam 773-555 THERAPE This patient is exhibiting symptoms of serotonin syndrome – altered mental status (in up to 40%), hyperthermia, autonomic instability (in up to 50%) and neuromuscular hyperactivity (in up to 50%). This woman has a history of depression and is likely to be taking a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) which is probably the underlying cause. While most cases resolve within 24 hours, if treatment is required, the initial treatment of choice is benzodiazepine administration to treat agitation. D Intubation and ventilation Increasing temperature in serotonin syndrome has a signiﬁcant impact on mortality. Failure to control agitation and hyperthermia with initial measures or concerns regarding airway patency are requirements for a rapid sequence induction and intubation and ventilation of patients. As alternative treatments have not been tried at this stage, it is not the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient. A Cyproheptadine Cyproheptadine is used in severe cases of serotonin syndrome that do not respond to initial benzodiazepine administration. C Haemodialysis Haemodialysis does not directly treat serotonin syndrome. Instead, it is a supportive measure to treat complications of serotonin syndrome such as acute renal failure or to help remove excessive concentrations of myoglobin in rhabdomyolysis. E Procyclidine Procyclidine is the treatment of choice for an oculogyric crisis, a dystonic reaction where the eyes deviate upwards. Associated symptoms include wide mouth opening and tongue protrusion. An oculogyric crisis results from excessive neuroleptic use such as olanzapine and haloperidol.

stem: A 39-year-old woman with a history of manic–depressive disorder visits her general practitioner (GP) for review. She is currently treated with lithium therapy. The GP has been monitoring her blood pressure for the last few months; it is 155/105 mmHg in the clinic and he is keen to commence pharmacotherapy. Which of the following antihypertensives carries least risk when co-prescribed with lithium?
explanation: C Amlodipine Diuretics, ARBs and ACE inhibitors lead to an increase in lithium concentration. Although the calcium channel antagonist class that includes amlodipine may lead to a syndrome of ataxia, confusion and sleepiness, this is uncommon, meaning that the balance of risk–beneﬁt is positive in favour of amlodipine versus the other options given here. E Valsartan Like ACE inhibitors, ARBs increase the risk of retention of lithium, signiﬁcantly raising the risk of lithium toxicity in patients where they are co-prescribed. A Bendroﬂumethiazide Thiazide diuretics lead to paradoxical salt and water retention and are a recognised cause of lithium intoxication. B Acetazolamide Acetazolamide, like other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, can drive increased lithium excretion, actually leading to increased symptoms of bipolar disorder. D Enalapril ACE inhibitors are recognised to decrease GFR on initiation, although over time they retard progression of renal disease. This is associated with a 7-fold increase in admission for lithium toxicity where they are co-prescribed.

stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department following an overdose of 20 quinine sulphate 300 mg tablets following the death of her husband one week earlier. She has hypertension and ischaemic heart disease and takes a range of medications. Her blood pressure is 95/70 mmHg, and her pulse is 95 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. She is drowsy and confused. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 118 g/l 115–160 g/l WCC 6.1 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l Platelets (PLT) 223 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 3.1 mmol/ 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO ) 14 mmol/l 23–30 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 145 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ECG Short runs of torsades de pointes ventricular tachycardia (VT) on the monitor 773-555 THERAPE Which of the following is the most important next intervention?
options: 1 litre 0.9% sodium chloride with 40 mmol potassium chloride (KCl)
explanation:
C Magnesium sulphate Magnesium sulphate is proven to reduce the risk of torsades and is the most important next step in this patient’s treatment. 10 mmol of magnesium sulphate should be administered over 15 minutes. Following magnesium sulphate and correction of acidosis, hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia, the patient should be reassessed. If there are still episodes of torsades and the heart rate is less than 100 bpm, overdrive pacing or an isoprenaline infusion should be considered. A Activated charcoal Although activated charcoal may aid decontamination in quinine poisoning, in this case, the patient is drowsy and confused, and may well require a nasogastric (NG) tube to deliver the charcoal. Given there are short runs of torsades de pointes, this is the more urgent priority, where magnesium should be administered as the next treatment intervention. If possible, 50 g or more of charcoal should be given via the NG. B Calcium chloride This patient is likely to be hypocalcaemic and require calcium replacement, although there is better evidence at this stage for giving magnesium sulphate to prevent further episodes of torsades. Correction of acidosis, hypokalaemia, and hypocalcaemia should follow as soon as possible after magnesium sulphate. D 1 litre 0.9% sodium chloride with 40 mmol potassium chloride (KCl) Rapid correction of hypokalaemia is desirable in this situation and given the size of this patient’s overdose; she should be managed on the intensive care unit (ITU). This has the advantage that higher rates of potassium infusion can be given, and ﬂuid balance centrally monitored. She will require potassium replacement, but this can be instituted as soon as possible after magnesium is commenced. E Sodium bicarbonate Patients with quinine overdose have both QRS and QT prolongation. Correction of acidosis will reduce QRS prolongation signiﬁcantly and reduce the further risk of VT. In the event that acidosis is not fully corrected with sodium bicarbonate, then intubation and ventilation with hyperventilation to correct pH should

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com be considered.

stem: A 53-year-old civil servant has been referred to the medical team having suffered sudden onset of lip swelling. She is known to have hypertension, and her general practitioner has recently made a medication change for this. On examination, she has swelling of her lips and tongue, but fortunately no evidence of airways compromise. What is the most likely pharmacological culprit?
explanation: C Ramipril Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, like most drugs, have many side effects/adverse drug reactions. One wellrecognised adverse effect is angioedema, with swelling of the lips and tongue, and this reaction may occur with variable delay after commencing the drug. It is thought to be related to inhibition of bradykinin metabolism and increased levels of substance P. Epidemiological data suggest an incidence of up to 0.7% in patients taking ACE inhibitors, and that the risk is 10 times higher in African Americans. E Amlodipine Although case reports exist which support a role for amlodipine in causing angioedema, rates were low at 0.03% of patients prescribed amlodipine as part of the ALLHAT study. A Metoprolol Although metoprolol may be associated with the development of angioedema, the incidence with hypertensives other than ACE inhibitors is approximately 10-fold lower. B Chlorthalidone Angioedema occurred in 0,05% of elderly patients prescribed chlorthalidone in the ALLHAT study versus 0.41% of patients allocated to lisinopril. D Doxazosin Data from ALLHAT also support low rates of angioedema in patients prescribed alpha blockers, running at 0.06%. 773-555 THERAPE

stem: A 26-year-old patient is admitted drowsy and confused. History from her friends reveals a past history of depression and previous suicide attempts. She was found with an empty bottle of phenobarbital, which she apparently obtained on the internet. Examination reveals slurred speech, ataxia and nystagmus. What therapy will best aid elimination of phenobarbital?
explanation:
A Sodium bicarbonate The barbiturates have largely been replaced by the benzodiazepines, but they are still used for induction anaesthesia and for patients with epilepsy resistant to conventional therapies. Barbiturate overdose causes drowsiness, respiratory depression, impaired coordination and coma. They are inducers of hepatic en-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com zymes. As a drug they are acidic, and elimination through the kidneys is aided by forced alkaline diuresis with sodium bicarbonate. Other treatments include charcoal and haemodialysis. Forced alkaline diuresis is not routinely recommended. E Mannitol Mannitol has a role in the treatment of cerebral oedema related to ciguatera poisoning (which can occur in relation to consumption of reef ﬁsh). B Ammonium chloride Forced acid diuresis with ammonium chloride can be helpful in amphetamine poisoning. It is not useful here. C Succinylated gelatine Succinylated gelatine is used as a volume expander for patients with acute blood loss, and doesn’t therefore have a key role here. D Dicobalt edetate Dicobalt edetate has a role in the treatment of cyanide poisoning. It forms stable complexes with cyanide and therefore can signiﬁcantly impact on symptoms of poisoning.

stem: A 62-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department. A neighbour has found him on the ﬂoor, and it appears that he has been there for some time, having taken an overdose of aspirin tablets. He has a past history of chronic kidney disease stage 3 and an inferior myocardial infarction some 15 years earlier. On examination, his blood pressure is 115/60 mmHg and his pulse is 95 bpm and regular. His respiratory rate is 33 breaths/minute. There are bilateral crackles on auscultation of the chest, consistent with cardiac failure. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 129 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 11.0 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 192 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 6.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate 13 mmol/l 22–30 mmol/L Creatinine 197 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l pH 7.22 7.35–7.45 Creatine kinase (CK) 6540 U/l 23–175 IU/l Salicylate 7.9 mmol/l 1.1–2.2 mmol/l Urine blood +++ on dipstick He is given intravenous (IV) calcium gluconate. Which of the following is the deﬁnitive way to manage his hyperkalaemia?
explanation: A Haemodialysis This patient has a number of circumstances that will preclude nondialysis management of his aspirin overdose. He is above the threshold for recommending haemodialysis for aspirin overdose, has life-threatening hyperkalaemia, acute renal failure on top of chronic renal failure with rhabdomyolysis and evidence of ﬂuid overload. As such, the best way to manage him is to plan for haemodialysis. C IV normal saline IV normal saline will have a relatively minor impact on lowering the potassium level here and will worsen ﬂuid overload, in turn worsening gas exchange and having a potential negative impact on acidosis. B Intravenous (IV) insulin and dextrose IV insulin and dextrose are a short-term ﬁx for managing the potassium level. At best, the combination will buy a period of a few hours for deﬁnitive intervention, which here is haemodialysis. D IV sodium bicarbonate Sodium bicarbonate is useful early in aspirin overdose to enhance aspirin excretion. In this case, it is unlikely to have a signiﬁcant impact, given signiﬁcant evidence of ﬂuid overload is already present. Dialysis is the only effective option here. E Oral calcium risonium Oral resonium takes some time to reduce the serum potassium level, by limiting potassium absorption from the gut. In this case, its onset of action is too slow to be of value and it will not impact on acidosis or ﬂuid overload.

stem: A 25-year-old woman was brought to the Emergency Department with a history of episodic abnormal posturing of her torso and neck for the past few hours. She had a long history of behavioural problems and was known to have had brawls with her neighbours. Her mother had recently taken her to the psychiatrist and she has been initiated on antipsychotic medication. On examination, she was afebrile. Her neck was in forced extension, there was arching of her back and her arms were internally rotated. There was extension of the elbows and wrists. What is the correct description of her clinical picture?
explanation: C Opisthotonus This is the typical picture of an acute generalised dystonic reaction to neuroleptic drugs (e.g. phenothiazines, butyrophenones, metoclopramide and even atypical antipsychotic agents such as olanzapine). The description given here (retrocollis, arching of the back, internal rotation of the arms and extension of the elbows) suggests an extreme dystonic reaction in the form of opisthotonus. Opisthotonus also occurs in other neurological situations, including (classically) tetanus or hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury. It is also seen in strychnine poisoning. E Decorticate posturing Decorticate posturing is characterised by arm ﬂexion and inward turning, extended lower limbs. A Decerebrate rigidity Decerebrate rigidity results from a midbrain lesion and is manifest by an exaggerated extensor posture of all four limbs. B Anterocollis Anterocollis is forward ﬂexion of the head and neck, rather than the extensor posture seen here. D Chorea Chorea is abnormal involuntary movement characterised by brief, abrupt, irregular, unpredictable, non- stereotyped movements.

stem: A 17-year-old girl with a long history of epilepsy is admitted to the Emergency Department after taking a carbamazepine overdose following a row with her boyfriend. She took almost a full 773-555 THERAPE month’s worth of her tablets roughly two hours earlier. On presentation to the Emergency Department, she is drowsy and vomiting. Additionally, she is complaining of slurred speech and blurred vision. On examination, her BP is 90/50 mmHg, heart rate is 61 bpm and there is obvious nystagmus, dystonia and athetosis. She suffered a generalised tonic-clonic seizure during the ambulance journey. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 130 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 4.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 295 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 7.9 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l 12 lead ECG QRS 78 ms Her ECG is shown below. Activated charcoal is commenced and IV normal saline. Which of the following would be the most appropriate management step in the event of further seizures?
explanation:
D Lorazepam IV In this situation, with a signiﬁcant carbamazepine overdose, further seizures are possible and lorazepam IV is the intervention of choice. If this does not achieve control, or there is a deteriorating conscious level, intubation and ventilation is the most appropriate next step. The ECG here shows normal sinus rhythm with a QRS of 78ms meaning that sodium bicarbonate is not required currently. B Intubate and ventilate

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Intubation and ventilation is appropriate in the event that lorazepam fails to achieve seizure control. A Sodium bicarbonate IV Sodium bicarbonate is indicated in the treatment of tricyclic antidepressant and carbamazepine overdose, where there is seizure activity, acidosis and evidence of QRS >120 ms. The ECG here shows normal sinus rhythm with a QRS of 78ms. C Phenytoin IV Phenytoin is more difﬁcult to titrate than lorazepam, and given that seizure activity is likely to increase for a short period only, lorazepam is a more appropriate intervention. E Sodium valproate IV It would be more logical to consider loading with levetiracetam if a switch in epileptic medication is being considered. Given an increase in seizure activity is expected to be short term, lorazepam is the more appropriate option.

stem: An 82-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department as his wife has become concerned about his behaviour. She reports that this evening, she found him packing a suitcase because he thought he was on a cruise and it was time to go home. Two days ago, he was started on some antibiotics for a urinary tract infection (UTI) by his General Practitioner. His past medical history includes benign prostatic hyperplasia, osteoarthritis, hypertension and gout. On examination, he is disorientated, with lower abdominal discomfort. Which one of this patient’s current medications is most likely to be contributing to his presentation?
explanation:
D Oxybutynin Oxybutynin is associated with a high risk of confusion in older patients due to anticholinergic effects. It is often prescribed, in addition to alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) or 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (eg ﬁnasteride), for patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia to reduce symptoms of urinary urgency and frequency. Long-term use of anticholinergic agents is associated with an increased risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older patients. This patient’s symptoms of urinary retention and disorientation could be precipitated by, or confused with, a urinary tract infection (UTI). Drug reviews in older patients can prevent the risk of adverse effects. E Nitrofurantoin Nitrofurantoin may have been given for this patient’s UTI however, it is not associated with anticholinergic effects. It may cause confusion, although this is rare. A Atenolol Atenolol may contribute to the risk of confusion, dizziness and falls in older people but the risk of anticholinergic effects is lower than that of oxybutynin. B Codeine

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Codeine can increase the risk of urinary retention, constipation and confusion in older patients. However, there is less risk of this than with the use of oxybutynin and he is likely to be taking this as required for his osteoarthritis rather than daily. C Colchicine Colchicine can contribute to the risk of confusion in older patients; however, it is not usually a long-term medication and there is nothing to suggest this man is having a ﬂare of his gout at present.

stem: A 27-year-old professional bodybuilder is referred to the Hepatology Clinic with abnormal liver function tests. He tells you he takes a number of food supplements, but he denies using any medications. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 138/85 mmHg and a pulse of 65 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. He has extensive muscle development and normal pubic and axillary hair. His testes appear to be signiﬁcantly reduced in volume. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 191 g/l 135 -175 g/l WCC 7.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 305 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Which of the following is most likely to be reduced?
explanation: C Luteinising hormone (LH) Patients who abuse androgens often do not tell the whole truth about the use of exogenous testosterone. The clinical scenario here with a reduction in testicular volume with maintenance of androgenisation is consistent with androgen abuse. The elevated haemoglobin also ﬁts with this underlying diagnosis. LH is under negative feedback by testosterone, leading to a reduction in LH in individuals who abuse exogenous testosterone. A Haematocrit The suspicion here is of androgen abuse, which is more common among the bodybuilding community and is associated with diminished testicular volume over the longer term. Abnormal liver function occurs with the use of oral 17-alpha-alkylated androgens, which may have formed part of his steroid regimen at some stage. 773-555 THERAPE Both haemoglobin and haematocrit are increased in patients who abuse androgens. B Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol Lipid abnormalities are common in patients who abuse androgens. A reduction in high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol is seen, with a rise in LDL cholesterol, resulting in a more atherogenic lipid proﬁle.
