This is predictive of an increase in cardiovascular risk for patients who abuse androgens. D Protein S Androgen administration leads to activation of the haemostatic system. In particular, this leads to an increase in levels of prothrombin fragment 1, antithrombin III and protein S. There is a concomitant reduction in levels of tissue plasminogen activator (TPA) and its inhibitor. The impact of these changes versus the risk of thrombosis is unclear. E Testosterone The picture with androgenisation in the presence of reduced testicular volume suggests exogenous testosterone administration with consequent turning off of LH secretion because of the negative feedback loop. Initial investigations by anti-doping agencies include measurement of the testosterone/epitestosterone ratio, where a signiﬁcant elevation in the ratio, (usually > 6 : 1) would be expected.

stem: A 24-year-old school teacher has been admitted to the Emergency Medical Unit with diarrhoea and vomiting. Apparently, she became ill some two days earlier after eating a take-away burger and was unable to keep any food or water down at all. She was given an antiemetic intravenously by the paramedic crew, and is now having involuntary spasms of her head and neck, with upward rolling movements of her eyes. On examination, she looks distressed. Her blood pressure is 145/82 mmHg and her pulse is 84 bpm. She looks to have a left-sided torticollis and her jaw is held in spasm. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to resolve her symptoms?
explanation:
C Trihexyphenidyl hydrochloride

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com This patient is suffering an oculogyric crisis, which is an acute dystonic reaction secondary to dopaminergic blockade at the basal ganglia. In this case, the offending pharmaceutical agent is probably metoclopramide. These types of dystonic reaction are mainly seen in young women, and can be treated by withdrawal of the drug and administration of procyclidine hydrochroride or trihexyphenidyl hydrochloride (formerly known as benzhexol). These are antimuscarinic drugs, often used in the treatment of parkinsonism. Because of the risk of acute dystonia, metoclopramide and prochlorperazine are not recommended for use in young women, with other agents such as cyclizine or domperidone being the preferred options. E Olanzapine This is a ﬁrst-line atypical antipsychotic agent used in the treatment of schizophrenia. A Metoclopramide This is a dopamine antagonist antiemetic and is most likely to be the cause of this patient’s presentation with an oculogyric crisis. B Domperidone Reports of oculogyric crisis do exist for domperidone, although they are far less frequent than for metoclopramide. It is not a treatment for oculogyric crisis. D Clozapine Clozapine is used for resistant psychosis and is an atypical antipsychotic agent.

stem: A 50-year-old Asian man had recently been diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and was started on quadruple anti-TB therapy. He seemed withdrawn, however, and had insomnia. He had attempted suicide on several occasions in the presence of friends by trying to stab himself, though had been rescued every time. He had been referred urgently to the psychiatrist. However, he was brought to the Emergency Department in a comatose state with ongoing generalised convulsions and vomiting. On examination, temperature was 38 °C, pulse 120/min and blood pressure 90/50 mmHg. Investigation Result Normal value Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Chloride 95 mmol/l 98-106 mmol/l Bicarbonate 20 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l pH 7.2 7.35–7.45 Urea 18 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 440 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Given the overall clinical picture, what is the most likely cause of his acute symptoms and signs?
explanation: C Overdose of isoniazid This patient has taken an overdose of isoniazid, possibly in combination with rifampicin. He has presented with refractory convulsions and metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap and coma. This is calculated as ([Na+] + [K+]) – ([Cl–] + [HCO3 –]). Its normal value is 10–14 mmol/l, but in this patient it is 28.3 mmol/l. The kidney disease is probably due to rhabdomyolysis. Isoniazid is recognised as inhibiting conversion of pyridoxine to both its active form, and to lactate dehydrogenase, which is thought to contribute to a presentation with metabolic acidosis. D Overdose of ethambutol Ethambutol overdose is associated with headache, confusion, pyrexia and GI upset. A Tuberculous meningitis Tuberculous meningitis is associated with a subacute course, and the rapid deterioration in association with presentation to the psychiatrist is more suggestive of overdose. B Fungal meningitis Fungal meningitis is more likely to be seen in patients with signiﬁcant immunosuppression, and we are given no history of immunosuppressive disease here. E Overdose of pyrizinamide Pyrazinamide overdose is associated with abnormal liver function testing and hyperuricaemia.

stem: A 53-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis is admitted to the Emergency Department with confusion and decreased consciousness. According to his wife, he has become progressively more confused over the past few days and is now unmanageable at home. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13, his blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg, and his pulse is 85 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. His temperature is 38 oC. He has abdominal distension with ascites, and his abdomen is generally tender. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 98 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 13.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 95 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 131 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 135 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 92 mg/l < 10 mg/l ALT 195 U/l < 50 U/l Albumin 22 g/l 35–45 g/l You plan to prescribe rifaximin. How does rifaximin work to reduce symptoms of encephalopathy?
explanation:
D Decreases ammonia production Rifaximin is an oral antibiotic which has virtually no systemic absorption. It is used in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy because it reduces colonies of ammonia-forming bacteria. Elevated ammonia is a signiﬁcant contributor to confusion associated with encephalopathic disease.

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com B Antagonises aldosterone Aldosterone antagonists are used in the management of ascites related to cirrhosis and portal hypertension, with spironolactone the mainstay of therapy. Dose up-titration may be limited by hypotension and a negative impact on serum creatinine. A Antagonises antidiuretic hormone (ADH) Hyponatraemia is common in patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension and occurs because of excessive production of ADH. Fluid restriction is the initial mainstay of management, with loop diuretics also deployed in some patients. Selective ADH antagonists such as tolvaptan may be useful in managing some patients. C Antagonises alpha-adrenergic receptors Alpha-adrenergic antagonists are not used in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. They are used in the management of resistant hypertension and in the treatment of symptoms of benign prostatic hypertrophy. Beta blockade, usually in the form of carvedilol, is used in the treatment of portal hypertension. E Decreases purine production Purine production drives acute episodes of gout. Xanthine oxidase inhibitors such as allopurinol reduce purine production and are used as prophylactic agents in the treatment of hyperuricaemia. They do not have a role in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department. She has begun vomiting and feels that she cannot keep any food down at all. She admits to taking an overdose of 48 × 500 mg paracetamol tablets some three days earlier because of concerns about her A-level exams. There is no past medical history of note. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 100/60 mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. She is markedly tender in the right upper quadrant of her abdomen. Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 122 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 11.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelet (PLT) 203 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 18 mmol/l 22 - 29 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 141 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l INR 4.2 < 1.1 Alanine transaminase (ALT) 3430 u/l 7 - 55 u/l Which of the above is the most important indication for 773-555 THERAPE referral to a specialist unit?
explanation: D INR 4.2 Elevated INR is a strong indicator of impaired hepatic synthetic function, and INR >2.0 at or before 48 h or >3.5 at or before 72 h (peak elevation occurs around 72-96 h), is an indication for referral to a specialist liver unit. INR >6.5 is an indication for referral for liver transplant. C Creatinine 141 μmol/l/l Creatinine >200 is considered a criterion for specialist referral, with creatinine >300 one of the criteria for referral for liver transplant. A ALT 3430 U/l Although ALT elevation is indicative of hepatocellular necrosis, it is impaired hepatic synthetic function that is most predictive of poor outcome in paracetamol overdose. B Bicarbonate 18 mmol/l Bicarbonate isn’t called out as an indicator for specialist referral, although arterial pH <7.3 or lactate >3.0 mmol/l after adequate ﬂuid resuscitation are reasons to refer. E K+ 5.3 mmol/l This is towards the upper end of the normal range, but is likely to correct with adequate ﬂuid resuscitation.

stem: A 78-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit following a ﬁre at his property. He has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), dementia, hypertension and type II diabetes. He smokes 20 cigarettes per day. He has evidence of smoke inhalation, with minimal oedema in the oropharynx and no evidence of airway obstruction. He reports to you that he has a headache and mild nausea. On examination, he has a respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute, with oxygen saturations of 92% on room air, a heart rate of 100 bpm, a temperature of 37.2 °C and blood pressure of 110/55 mmHg. His chest has bilaterally reduced air entry, and a chest Xray reveals hyperexpanded lungs, with no evidence of consolidation. A routine electrocardiogram shows ST depression in the 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com anterior leads. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: A Arterial blood gas This patient has carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning due to smoke inhalation and therefore needs an arterial blood gas to measure his carboxyhaemoglobin level. Symptoms of CO poisoning are nonspeciﬁc and include headache, nausea and vomiting, vertigo and altered consciousness. Patients with CO poisoning should be checked for cardiovascular symptoms, including angina or cardiac ischaemia. Neuropsychiatric symptoms may present in later stages of the illness. Heart rate oximetry does not accurately measure oxygen levels, as it cannot determine the difference between oxyhaemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin. Therefore, in suspected CO poisoning, an urgent arterial blood gas is needed to measure the CO concentration. High-ﬂow oxygen is the treatment of choice in CO poisoning, with ﬂow rates of up to 60 litres per minute required. D Start IV antibiotics This patient has CO poisoning and there is no evidence from his observations, examination ﬁndings or primary investigations that he has an infection. Therefore, IV antibiotics are not the next best step in his management. It would be appropriate to complete blood tests and a urine culture for this patient to ensure that an initial infection has not put him at greater risk of setting ﬁre to his house by causing delirium (on his background of dementia). However, given the evidence of smoke inhalation, his breathlessness, headache and evidence of cardiac ischaemia on the electrocardiogram, an arterial blood gas to check his carboxyhaemoglobin levels is the next most appropriate step. B Intravenous (IV) ﬂuids Intravenous (IV) ﬂuids may be required for this patient to maintain adequate ﬂuid status, especially as there is evidence of burns due to smoke inhalation in the oropharynx and therefore, oral ﬂuid intake is likely to be reduced. However, this is not the most important step for this patient. C Send troponin T levels This patient is suffering from CO poisoning as a result of smoke inhalation. This can result in cardiac ischaemia and therefore, sending blood for troponin T levels is an important part of managing this patient and the complications of this condition. However, 773-555 THERAPE troponin levels will not reveal the underlying diagnosis and therefore, this is not the next best step. E Start salbutamol nebulisers Although this patient has a background history of COPD, with low peripheral oxygen saturations, on examination, he has no evidence of COPD exacerbation. He needs an arterial blood gas to check his carboxyhaemoglobin level. This will also reveal whether he has evidence of chronic carbon dioxide retention, which will help guide target oxygen saturations.

stem: A 61-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with concerns regarding an increased size in his breast tissue for the last four weeks. He denies breast pain or discharge and has remained well. There is no history of constitutional symptoms. He has a background of ischaemic heart disease, atrial ﬁbrillation and heart failure. On examination, he is afebrile. He has a heart rate of 78 bpm and an irregularly irregular pulse, with a blood pressure of 123/76 mmHg. On auscultation, his chest is clear, with oxygen saturations of 94% on room air. There is a mild ejection systolic murmur which radiates to the carotids. His abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no organomegaly or stigmata of liver disease. He has bilateral breast enlargement, with no palpable lumps or surrounding skin changes. Which of the following medications is most likely to be responsible for this patient’s presentation?
explanation: C Digoxin This patient has gynaecomastia, an increase in the production of breast tissue secondary to an imbalance between oestrogen and androgen production. It should not be confused with galactorrhoea which is an increase in breast milk production. Oestrogen stimulates breast tissue production and conditions that involve an increase in oestrogen release or a reduction in testosterone production can cause gynaecomastia. These include androgen resistance, Klinefelter syndrome, obesity, adrenal tumours, testicular tumours and liver disease or cirrhosis. The condition can also arise from drug use with common drugs, 773-555 THERAPE including oestrogens, or drugs that inhibit the production or action of testosterone such as ketoconazole, metronidazole, spironolactone and ﬁnasteride. Digoxin causes gynaecomastia by exhibiting an oestrogen-like effect and this can be exacerbated in coexisting liver disease. E Metoclopramide Metoclopramide is a cause of galactorrhoea, an increase in breast milk production. Breast milk production is stimulated by the hormone prolactin secreted from the anterior pituitary gland. The production of prolactin is under inhibitory control by dopamine. As a dopamine receptor antagonist, metoclopramide reduces the activity of dopamine receptors and indirectly raises prolactin levels. A Aspirin Side-effects of aspirin include bronchospasm and urticaria. However, aspirin does not cause gynaecomastia. B Atenolol Atenolol is a beta-blocker that has a number of side effects, including bradycardia, bronchospasm, cool peripheries and nightmares. However, it does not cause gynaecomastia. D Furosemide Furosemide is a loop diuretic. A common side-effect of loop diuretics is electrolyte abnormalities. Gynaecomastia is not seen.

stem: A 52-year-old man with hypertension is admitted following an overdose of one month’s supply of amlodipine 5 mg tablets. On arrival in the Emergency Department, his blood pressure is 70/50 mmHg, while his pulse is 100 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Why does amlodipine overdose cause hypotension and tachycardia?
explanation:
A L-type calcium channel blockade L-type calcium channels are found in skeletal muscle, smooth muscle, osteoblasts, and ventricular myocytes. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine are speciﬁc for vascular smooth muscle; hence on overdose, they lead to marked hypotension and tachycardia. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as diltiazem and verapamil are cardio- speciﬁc, such that in overdose they lead to both hypotension and bradycardia. Intravenous (IV) calcium is a key component of the treatment of calcium channel blocker overdose. D R-type calcium channel blockade R-type calcium channels are found in cerebellar granule cells. Their function is poorly understood, and they have a high threshold of activation versus other calcium channel subtypes.

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com B N-type calcium channel blockade N-type calcium channels are found throughout the brain and the peripheral nervous system. Blockade of N- type calcium channels is thought to be a promising target for the treatment of chronic neuropathic pain. C P-type calcium channel blockade P-type calcium channels are found in Purkinje cells in the cerebellum. Speciﬁc P-type calcium channel blockers are not currently available as therapeutics, although non-selective calcium channel blockers including agents used for hypertension have off-target effects on the P-type channel. E T-type calcium channel blockade T-type calcium channels are voltage-activated calcium channels that become deactivated during cell membrane hyperpolarisation but then open to depolarisation. They are found on neurones and the surface of cardiac pacemaker cells. They are a potential target for diabetic neuropathy and the treatment of Parkinson’s disease.

stem: A 74-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after being found lying on the ﬂoor by his home help. It appears he had left a suicide note and taken an overdose of unknown medication. According to his last hospital discharge, he is taking a range of medications, including atorvastatin, ramipril, bisoprolol, clopidogrel and quinine sulphate. His blood pressure is 95/70 mmHg, and his pulse is 100 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. . 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 128 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 10.3 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 241 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 12 mmol/l 23 - 30 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 155 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l ECG QRS 130 ms QT 490 ms Which of the following is the patient most likely to have taken?
explanation: D Quinine sulphate This patient has hypokalaemia, metabolic acidosis, QRS and QT prolongation. This ﬁts with a signiﬁcant overdose of quinine sulphate. Reversal of acidosis with intravenous (IV) sodium bicarbonate and if required, intubation and hyperventilation is key to correct ECG abnormalities and reducing the risk of ventricular tachycardia. Hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia should also be corrected. A large overdose of quinine runs the risk of permanent sight loss. Decontamination should be attempted with activated charcoal to reduce the risk of long-standing visual disturbance. C Clopidogrel Overdose of clopidogrel may lead to prolonged bleeding time and signiﬁcant haemorrhage. No speciﬁc antidote to clopidogrel exists. In patients with severe haemorrhage and clopidogrel overdose, platelet transfusion may be an option to control bleeding. A Atorvastatin Statin overdose is rare, and no speciﬁc antidote is available. Atorvastatin is highly protein-bound, and for this reason, dialysis does not remove it. Where overdoses of statins have been described, rhabdomyolysis and subsequent renal impairment can follow. Maintaining ﬂuid replacement and urine output is key to avoiding acute kidney injury in this situation. B Bisoprolol Beta-blocker overdose leads to bradycardia, hypotension, and hyperglycemia, rather than the presentation here with metabolic 773-555 THERAPE acidosis, QRS and QT prolongation. Options to reverse the effects of beta-blocker overdose include glucagon and high dose insulin, glucose, and potassium infusion. Conventional IV ﬂuid replacement and pacing may also be required. E Ramipril Symptoms of ramipril overdose may include excessive peripheral vasodilatation (with marked hypotension, shock), bradycardia, electrolyte disturbances, and acute kidney injury. Primary detoxiﬁcation with oral activated charcoal should be considered as ramiprilat, the active metabolite of ramipril, is poorly removed by haemodialysis.

stem: A 40-year-old, previously ﬁt and well farmer is admitted to hospital with shortness of breath. Associated with the shortness of breath are nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. The patient has widespread expiratory polyphonic wheeze and there are observable muscle fasciculations. According to his wife he has been out for most of the past two days crop spraying his ﬁelds. On examination, there is bilateral pupillary constriction, his blood pressure (BP) is 95/50 mmHg with a pulse of 38 bpm. Which of the following medications is likely to be most beneﬁcial?
explanation: C Atropine This patient presents with organophosphate poisoning, probably due to unintentional exposure as a result of his crop-spraying activity. Organophosphates are strong cholinesterase inhibitors. Symptoms are mainly those of muscarinic and nicotinic overstimulation. Before arrival into hospital the patient should be decontaminated. Atropine is used as a muscarinic receptor antagonist; as well as treating bradycardia, it also relieves bronchospasm and diminishes excess respiratory secretions. Pralidoxime is a cholinesterase activator and can reverse organophosphate-driven inhibition of cholinesterase. It should be given as soon as possible in addition to atropine. Time to admission of pralidoxime and atropine is closely linked to chances of survival. (Normally 600 – 1000 mg of pralidoxime and 2 mg of atropine are given IM at scene if possible). E Isoﬂurophate Isoﬂurophate is an organophosphate itself, and therefore has no role in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning. A Physostigmine Physostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor which will worsen symptoms of organophosphate poisoning, not improve them. B Phenoxybenzamine Phenoxybenzamine is an α-receptor blocker and is for treatment of hypertension caused by phaeochromocytomas. D Rocuronium Rocuronium is a competitive neuromuscular blocker and can be used to facilitate intubation. 773-555 THERAPE

stem: A 17-year old girl is referred with a 2-week history of poor coordination. She has become generally clumsier, with increasing difﬁculty using her cutlery, and her handwriting has also deteriorated. Her mother had noted that her speech was more slurred. She had no signiﬁcant past medical history of note, and had achieved her developmental milestones normally. She had just ﬁnished her GCSEs in which she achieved good grades, and had just started at a sixth form college to study for her A-levels. Her only family history of note was that her father had partial epilepsy, which was well controlled. She denied smoking, alcohol or recreational drug use. Her appetite was good and her weight was stable, although she does admit to anxiety about her upcoming exams. On examination, she appears well. Her pulse is 72/min, regular and jugular venous pressure is not raised. Blood pressure is 116/68 mmHg. Heart sounds are normal and her chest is clear. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Neurological examination reveals bilateral nystagmus on lateral gaze, mild tremor affecting her hands, scanning dysarthria, bilateral dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesis, and an ataxic gait. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 144 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 324 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 68 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 3.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Bilirubin 22 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 110 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 108 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Albumin 44 g/l 35–55 g/l Glucose 6.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Ferritin 290 µg/l 10–120 µg/l Caeruloplasmin 0.36 g/l 0.2–0.6 g/l Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain and spinal cord Normal What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Phenytoin toxicity Phenytoin toxicity can cause mental slowing, unsteadiness and a

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com cerebellar-like syndrome. Nystagmus occurs even with mild toxicity. Phenytoin can result in abnormal liver function values. The indication here is that the patient may have taken her fathers Phenytoin as an act of self-harm. B Haemochromatosis This disorder does not present with an ataxic syndrome. Clinical symptoms associated with haemochromatosis and consequent iron overload are not normally seen in women until they enter the post-menopausal period. A Wilson’s disease Wilson’s disease is associated with tremor, parkinsonism and dystonia. The ataxic signs seen here are not typical. Caeruloplasmin within the normal range makes Wilson’s less likely as the underlying diagnosis. It should be noted that in some cases of acute hepatitis related to Wilson’s, caeruloplasmin may be within the normal range, and 24 h urinary copper excretion is the best test. D Spinocerebellar syndrome The normal MRI of the brain and spinal cord make spinocerebellar ataxia less likely, as atrophy is often present. In addition there are no myelopathic signs in conjunction with the cerebellar signs to make one suspicious of this. E Demyelinating disorder Signs conﬁned to the cerebellum would be very unusual in the context of a demyelinating disorder, in MS, optic neuritis is also a usual presenting feature.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her daughter found her unresponsive. The daughter, who lives next door, frequently visits her mother. Today, her mother did not respond to the doorbell, and when she opened the door, she found her mother sprawled on the couch. She also found the gas stove switched on, but there was no ﬂame. She then quickly called the ambulance. On examination, the patient is drowsy, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 12/15, a blood pressure (BP) of 154/90 mmHg, a pulse of 98 bpm and a respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min. Oxygen saturation is 99%. The following results are obtained: Investigation Result Normal Value pH 7.27 7.35–7.45 pa(O2) 9.8 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa pa(CO2) 2.8 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa Bicarbonate (HCO3-) Carboxyhaemo20 mmol/l 45% 24–30 mmol/l 773-555 THERAPE globin (COHb) What would be the most appropriate ﬁrst step in her immediate management?
options: Apply a tight-ﬁtting non-rebreather mask and give 100% oxygen
The patient should be intubated and ventilated
Treat the metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate infusion
Put the patient on a cardiac monitor
explanation:
A Apply a tight-ﬁtting non-rebreather mask and give 100% oxygen The correct answer is Apply a tight-ﬁtting non-rebreather mask and give 100% oxygen (Option A). This is a classic history of carbon monoxide poisoning. COHb levels have prognostic implications, which are summarised here:  < 30% cause only headache and dizziness  40–60% produces syncope, tachypnoea, tachycardia and ﬁts  60% cause an increasing risk of cardiorespiratory failure and death. Given the situation, a tight-ﬁtting non-rebreather mask should be applied and 100% oxygen administered. D Put the patient on a cardiac monitor Put the patient on a cardiac monitor (Option D) is incorrect. Given the patient’s COHb levels, cardiorespiratory failure is not an immediate threat. Instead, treatment with high-ﬂow oxygen should take priority. B The patient should be intubated and ventilated The patient should be intubated and ventilated (Option B) is incorrect. Intubation and ventilation should be reserved for patients that are comatose. In this case, the patient is drowsy, but not comatose, and is able to maintain a patent airway. C Treat the metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate infusion Treat the metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate infusion (Option C) is incorrect. In cases of carbon monoxide poisoning, treatment with sodium bicarbonate is controversial, as acidosis may increase tissue oxygen availability. Instead, the administration of oxygen therapy is usually enough to correct the acidosis. E Hyperbaric oxygen

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Hyperbaric oxygen (Option E) is incorrect. Hyperbaric oxygen will shorten the washout of COHb, but access and transfer times to a hyperbaric chamber can make this not practical. Of course, it should be considered here after ﬁtting the nonrebreather.

stem: A 71-year-old man is being treated for a wound infection postabdominal surgery. He has a past medical history of hypertension and mild chronic kidney disease. The current dose is 50 mg three times daily (TDS). Investigation Result Normal value Pre-dose gentamicin (trough) 2.8 mg/l < 2 mg/l Post-dose gentamicin (peak) 7 mg/l 5–10 mg/l Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action with respect to this patient’s gentamicin dosing?
explanation: D Make the dose 100 mg OD The key points here are that there is scope to increase the dose of gentamicin because the maximum peak level has not been reached and TDS dosing has resulted in trough levels which are too high. As such, the best option is potentially to dose at about two-thirds of the daily dose so far, and reduce the dosing frequency. E Make the dose 25 mg TDS Although this will reduce the trough levels of gentamicin to within target, it will most likely mean that optimal peak levels will not be achieved. A Stop the gentamicin Stopping the gentamicin risks a recrudescence of bacterial sepsis, and there is clear scope to manipulate the dosing regimen to achieve better trough levels. B Make the dose 50 mg BD This would risk a fall in peak levels of gentamicin to below those for optimal drug exposure, making it inappropriate with this patient. C Make the dose 75 mg BD 773-555 THERAPE Twice-daily dosing is unlikely to reduce the trough levels of gentamicin to within the target, so it would not be suitable here.

stem: You are called to the Emergency Department to assist in the management of a 30-year-old man who has been brought in by a friend. On examination, he is agitated and confused, with dilated pupils, is rather tremulous, sweating and grinding his teeth. He has a regular heart rate of 120 beats/min and a temperature of 38.5°C. His deep tendon reﬂexes are exaggerated. There is little previous history, although the friend believes that he has suffered from depression for a number of years and recently had his medications changed by his general practitioner. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Serotonin syndrome Serotonin syndrome is a cluster of symptoms and signs that occur usually when more than one drug is taken that increases the concentration of serotonin at the synaptic level, although it has been reported following overdose of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) alone. It may occur when SSRIs are taken in combination with monoamine oxidase inhibitors or tricyclic antidepressants. If changing from one drug to another, a washout period is often required to prevent the syndrome from occurring. Treatment initially is to stop the causative drug(s), and prevent complications such as kidney disease caused by rhabdomyolysis. The diagnosis of serotonin syndrome is made solely on clinical grounds using the Hunter Criteria; a detailed history and thorough physical and neurologic examination are essential. To fulﬁl the Hunter Criteria, a patient must have taken a serotonergic agent and meet ONE of the following conditions – • Spontaneous clonus • Inducible clonus PLUS agitation or diaphoresis • Ocular clonus PLUS agitation or diaphoresis • Tremor PLUS hyperreﬂexia • Hypertonia PLUS temperature above 38°C PLUS ocular clonus or inducible clonus Severe cases may require a general anaesthetic and muscle paralysis, and dantrolene sodium has been used, which reduces calcium

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com efﬂux from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, although more recent data no longer support its role in managing the condition. E Carcinoid syndrome Carcinoid syndrome presents with gradually progressive diarrhoea, weight loss and episodes of ﬂushing, usually in patients signiﬁcantly older than 30 years of age. A Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is characterised by fever, muscle rigidity (lead pipe), altered mental status and autonomic dysfunction. The patient described here does not appear to have any generalised muscular stiffness, and so serotonin syndrome is much more likely than neuroleptic malignant syndrome. C Malignant hyperthermia Malignant hyperthermia is seen in response to inhalational anaesthetics, and is genetic in origin. D Thyrotoxic crisis There are no symptoms of thyrotoxicosis which predate this acute presentation, and the recent change of medication is a better pointer to serotonin syndrome.

stem: A 35-year-old woman attends the Gastroenterology Clinic. She has a history of alcohol abuse and has recently discovered she is pregnant. The patient is concerned about fetal alcohol syndrome that she has read about in the newspapers and is asking about the detrimental effects her alcohol consumption would have on her baby. What advice would you give her?
options: thickened upper lip is a characteristic feature of the syndrome
Drinking up to 10 units of alcohol per week is potentially healthy for her pregnancy
Even drinking 1–2 units of alcohol per week confers increased risk
The IQ is usually lower in children affected by the syndrome
Vitamin supplementation in pregnancy prevents cognitive deﬁcits associated with fetal alcohol syndrome
explanation:
D The IQ is usually lower in children affected by the syndrome Fetal alcohol syndrome is associated with: (1) mental retardation

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com and/or behavioural abnormalities, (2) growth retardation, and (3) mid-facial abnormalities. The fetus relies on maternal hepatic detoxiﬁcation of alcohol. Heavy drinking, including binge consumption of alcohol, is thought to be associated with particular risk. Alcohol appears to cross freely between mother and fetus, yet the fetal liver has only 10% of the capacity of the adult liver to detoxify alcohol. Unfortunately it appears that deﬁcits remain throughout adulthood, with individuals who experience fetal alcohol syndrome much more likely to suffer from behavioural difﬁculties, alcoholism and to be involved in criminal activity. Of note however is that IQ may be normal or even elevated in some cases. E Vitamin supplementation in pregnancy prevents cognitive deﬁcits associated with fetal alcohol syndrome Unfortunately vitamin supplementation does not prevent development of the condition. A A thickened upper lip is a characteristic feature of the syndrome Thinning of the upper lip is characteristic of the condition. B Drinking up to 10 units of alcohol per week is potentially healthy for her pregnancy Drinking 1–2 units of alcohol up to 1–2 times per week is not thought to confer increased risk. C Even drinking 1–2 units of alcohol per week confers increased risk Modest alcohol consumption of 1–2 units of alcohol 1–2 times per week is not associated with increased risk of fetal alcohol syndrome.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) comes to the clinic for review. She is currently taking methotrexate and has quiescent disease, but wants to begin trying for a family. Examination reveals no evidence of active joint disease, and her ESR is 13 mm/1st h. Liver function testing reveals transaminases within the normal range. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage her RA?
options: Continue methotrexate at the same dose
explanation: D Switch methotrexate to azathioprine Approximately 50–70% of women with RA improve during pregnancy. This usually starts in the ﬁrst trimester and lasts through the duration of pregnancy, but patients will often ﬂare in the postpartum period. Glucocorticoids are safe to use during pregnancy, but NSAIDs should be avoided in early pregnancy and the third trimester due to premature closure of the ductus arteriosus. Azathioprine, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine are relatively safe to use during pregnancy. E Switch methotrexate to inﬂiximab Evidence suggests a relatively benign safety proﬁle for inﬂiximab in pregnancy, although discontinuation after 16 weeks is recommended as the drug is able to cross the placenta into the fetus. . A Continue methotrexate at the same dose Methotrexate is an abortifacient that can also induce congenital anomalies if taken during pregnancy. It is therefore contraindicated in pregnant women. Contraceptive use is advised in women taking methotrexate, as well as discontinuation of therapy in both women and men at least three months prior to conception. Oligospermia and chromatid breaks have been described in men on methotrexate. B Halve the dose of methotrexate This strategy would not abolish the risks to the foetus and would leave the patient with suboptimal rheumatoid arthritis (RA) control. C Stop methotrexate Stopping methotrexate without a replacement agent is not advised as will likely result in ﬂare of RA.

stem: A 54-year-old veterinarian attends the Emergency Department, having been bitten by a snake while out walking his dog. He is sure that it was an adder, and asks whether he requires the antidote. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 125/60 mmHg, his pulse is 85 bpm and regular and he feels anxious. You can see the marks from the adder bite with some surrounding erythema on his left lower leg. Which of the following is an indication for administration of antivenom?
options: History of ischaemic heart disease 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com
Visible puncture mark at the bite site
explanation: E Severe limb swelling The adder (Vipera berus) is the UK’s indigenous venomous snake, although others, more poisonous, are kept in captivity. There is an available antivenom, but it must be remembered that there is a 1% chance of having an anaphylactic reaction to this, and so adrenaline should be available during its administration. Indications for its use include signs of systemic envenomation such as persistent hypotension, ECG abnormalities, vomiting, haemostatic abnormalities, white cell count above 20 × 109/l, and severe localised swelling extending proximally up a limb within 2–4 hours of the bite occurring. A Previous anaphylaxis to antivenom Previous anaphylaxis to antivenom is of course a contraindication to future use. B History of ischaemic heart disease ECG changes in response to a viper bite are an indication for antivenom, but a history of ischaemic heart disease per se is not. C Visible puncture mark at the bite site Although this indicates that a bite has occurred, it does not necessarily relate to the amount of venom injected, nor is it indicative of the symptoms. D History of asthma Most patients suffer a vascular type reaction to an adder bite, including problems with haemostasis and localised limb swelling. A history of asthma is not an indication or contra-indication to antivenom administration.

stem: A 23-year-old computer engineer presents to his GP with symptoms suggestive of a mixed anxiety–depression disorder. His GP prescribes ﬂuoxetine 20 mg daily and alprazolam 0.25 mg per day. The following day, the patient presents to the Emergency Department accompanied by his mother. She explains that he has become unduly euphoric and hyperactive. On examination, he appeared confused and had frequent sudden, brief jerking in various parts of his body. On further questioning about his drug history, he admitted to self-medication with St John's wort as well as his prescribed medication. He brings a urine specimen to the Emergency Department which is positive for blood. 773-555 THERAPE Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Serotonin syndrome This patient has serotonin syndrome, an uncommon but potentially fatal complication of selective serotonin re- uptake inhibitors (SSRIs) especially when combined with other serotoninenhancing agents, including tricyclic antidepressants, monoamine oxidase inhibitors and the herbal treatment St John's wort (hypericum). It develops over hours with characteristic hypomania, drowsiness, myoclonus, hyperthermia and pronounced autonomic symptoms (the ‘happy drunk’ state). It may resemble the neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Hyper-reﬂexia, not hyporeﬂexia, is typical. Conjunctival haemorrhage is not a typical feature. Support with IV ﬂuid rehydration, and treatment of symptoms of anxiety with benzodiazepines are the therapies of choice. E Bipolar disorder Bipolar disorder is associated with ﬂuctuations between depression and hypomania/mania; the presentation here with intermittent seizures is inconsistent with bipolar disorder. B Myoclonic epilepsy Myoclonic epilepsy presents for the ﬁrst time in teenagers, and in the presence of potential precipitating factors such as use of SSRI and St John’s wort, serotonin syndrome should be excluded ﬁrst. C Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome occurs in patients exposed to dopamine antagonists, rather than SSRIs. D Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures The discrete episodes of brief limb jerking coupled with confusion are more consistent with actual, rather than non-epileptic, seizures.

stem: An 18-year-old man, the son of a farmer, is admitted with a history of progressive weight loss, anorexia, nausea and constipation for the past four months. He had recently been taking a keen interest in helping his father to eradicate mice from their grain storage silos. He also had episodes of headaches and was at times losing his way around his home for a few minutes, though subsequently would 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com recover completely. He had also been aware of numbness in his toes for the past two months. On examination, he had thickened palms and some transverse lines were evident on his nails. He was alert and cooperative. Mild weakness and wasting was evident in the small muscles of his feet. Tendon reﬂexes were absent and plantar responses were ﬂexor. Diminished sensation to pinprick was seen in the distal feet and ﬁngertips. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Arsenic poisoning This patient has been involved in distributing rodent pesticides over a period of at least 4 months. He has developed weight loss, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyperkeratosis of the palms and some transverse lines on the nails. probably suggestive of Mees’ lines. He also has features of a sensorimotor polyneuropathy. All of these symptoms ﬁt very well with chronic arsenic poisoning. There is increased risk of cancers in such patients. Arsenic can be detected in the hair and nails for months following exposure. Dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA, succimer) and penicillamine have been used successfully in the treatment of arsenic poisoning. The family should of course be warned about the safe handling of poisons. E Lead poisoning Lead poisoning is associated with a microcytic anaemia, renal tubular acidosis and a motor neuropathy. A Acute intermittent porphyria AIP is associated with acute episodes of hypertension and hyponatraemia, accompanied by psychiatric symptoms. As such, it doesn’t ﬁt with the picture seen here. B Coproporphyria Coproporphyria, like AIP, is an acute porphyria associated with acute episodes of abdominal pain and psychological disturbance. It is, however, also associated with a skin rash, unlike AIP. C Erythropoietic protoporphyria EP presents with a photosensitive skin rash and hepatic dysfunction. 773-555 THERAPE

stem: You are working as the duty physician at an athletics meeting and are collecting samples to look for drugs of abuse. Which of the following initial tests is most useful to look for testosterone abuse?
explanation:
E Urinary testosterone/epitestosterone ratio The urinary testosterone/epitestosterone ratio is the best initial test for abuse of testosterone. A ratio greater than 6 : 1 is seen as conﬁrmatory for doping with testosterone, because as well as increasing measured levels in urine, doping with testosterone also reduces levels of epitestosterone. Where the ratio lies between 4 : 1 and 6 : 1, other measures such as carbon 13/carbon 12 ratio may be needed to conﬁrm the diagnosis. Exogenous testosterone preparations made from plant sterols have a lower ratio of carbon 13 to carbon 12, which can be detected by sampling. A Luteinising hormone (LH) levels Although LH levels are suppressed by exogenous testosterone abuse, there are other reasons why they may be low, including pituitary dysfunction. Testosterone abuse will lead to both elevated urinary testosterone, and it will suppress levels of epitestosterone, making this ratio in urine a much better way to test for abuse. B Prolactin levels Prolactin levels are increased in patients who abuse exogenous androgens, although there are a number of other reasons for prolactin increase, these include physiological and psychological stress, use of some medications, and pituitary prolactinoma. As such, they are too non-speciﬁc a screening test for testosterone abuse.

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com C Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) levels SHBG levels are reduced in patients who abuse exogenous androgens. A number of other causes exist for low SHBG, including type II diabetes, hypothyroidism, and Cushing syndrome. This makes it too non-speciﬁc a test for androgen abuse. D Urinary human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) Urinary hCG is a useful measure in patients who abuse hCG itself. A cut off to signify abuse is proposed to be 5 IU/l. hCG is also elevated in patients with testicular cancer - this means that occasionally a false positive for abuse may be seen in a patient with an underlying cancer.

stem: A 50-year-old man who is a known alcoholic is reviewed on the Medical Ward 2 days after admission with a variceal haemorrhage. He has been diagnosed with cirrhosis and portal hypertension some 2 years earlier but defaulted from follow up. His blood pressure is 125/80 mmHg, and his pulse is 75 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. His abdomen is soft, but he is tender in the epigastrium. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 94 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 75 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 139 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 32 mg/l < 10 mg/l ALT 103 U/l < 50 U/l Albumin 31 g/l 35–45 g/l Which of the following is the most appropriate way to treat this patient’s long-term risk from portal hypertension?
explanation: A Carvedilol Although propranolol was originally used for the treatment of portal hypertension in advanced cirrhosis, trials have shown that carvedilol achieves a higher rate of haemodynamic response versus propranolol. The overall response versus propranolol in a trial of 110 patients showed a numerically better response rate in favour of carvedilol, (49 vs 31%). However, in patients with more advanced disease, the rate of response was 58% vs 0% in favour of 773-555 THERAPE carvedilol. A daily dose of 12.5 mg of carvedilol is usually used for prophylaxis against varices. B Doxazosin Doxazosin is an alpha-blocker used in the treatment of resistant hypertension. It is not a ﬁrst-line agent for blood pressure lowering and is not used for the treatment of portal hypertension, where beta-blockers such as carvedilol are preferred. C Octreotide Octreotide is an alternative to terlipressin in the acute treatment of variceal haemorrhage. Octreotide lowers portal blood pressure, reducing bleeding from primary haemorrhage, and reduces the risk of a secondary variceal haemorrhage occurring. Deﬁnitive treatment with variceal banding can be instituted once haemorrhage is controlled. D Spironolactone Spironolactone is used primarily to reduce oedema and ascites associated with cirrhosis and portal hypertension. It does have antiﬁbrotic effects and some effect in reducing intrahepatic vasoconstriction, which make it a default option on top of carvedilol but not in terms of portal hypertension management only as the question asked. E Terlipressin Terlipressin is recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines as soon as possible after admission for the acute treatment of variceal haemorrhage. The drug results in an acute reduction in portal blood pressure. It should not be used in patients with coronary artery disease. According to NICE guidance, it can be continued either until haemostasis is achieved, or for a maximum period of 5 days.

stem: An 18-year-old student attends the Emergency Department having ingested a couple of handfuls of tablets after an argument with her boyfriend, 2.5 h previously. She fully regrets her actions and does not want to die. She is unsure as to which tablets she has taken, but believes that they may have been painkillers. On examination, she has a Glasgow Coma Score of 15, blood pressure (BP) is 122/80 mmHg, pulse is 78 and regular and, apart from being rather tearful, is asymptomatic. Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: B Paracetamol levels at 4 h Paracetamol intoxication generally has no signs or symptoms in the initial time period post-overdose. Treatment depends on taking blood for paracetamol concentration, and relating this result to the nomogram in order to decide whether N-acetyl cysteine should be initiated. This probably offers full protection if administered within 15 h. C Salicylate levels at 4 h The absence of symptoms of salicylism, including hyperventilation and tinnitus, means that signiﬁcant aspirin overdose is highly unlikely here. A Liver function tests Liver function tests do not predict outcome in paracetamol overdose versus other investigations such as PT and renal function. They are of less value here. D International normalised ratio INR is most predictive of outcomes in paracetamol overdose from the 24 h stage. Therefore, early after overdose it isn’t of value with respect to outcomes prediction. E Arterial blood gas Given there are no symptoms and the patient is cardiovascularly stable, there is little utility in testing arterial blood gas at this stage.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is admitted with a paracetamol overdose. She has a background history of depression and is on a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). Her friends and family are concerned she may have taken other medications beside paracetamol, as she had stockpiled at least three months’ supply of her citalopram. Which of the following ﬁndings might you ﬁnd if the patient had overdosed on an SSRI?
explanation: A Hyperreﬂexia Overdose of SSRIs can cause the serotonin syndrome, although toxicity is rarely seen unless a massive overdose of SSRI is tak- 773-555 THERAPE en. Examples of symptoms of toxicity include restlessness, hallucinations and sweating. Signs include hyperthermia, hyperreﬂexia, myoclonus, ataxia, mydriasis and tachycardia. Management of SSRI overdose is supportive, with benzodiazepines the drug of choice to reduce agitation, intervention may also be required for blood pressure control. E Apraxia Apraxia is not commonly seen in association with SSRI overdose, but is seen in offspring of mothers treated with SSRIs. B Upgoing plantars Upgoing plantars are seen in the serotonin syndrome and in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, although they are less likely to be present than hyperreﬂexia. C Miosis Mydriasis, not miosis, is seen in patients with the serotonin syndrome/where there is an SSRI overdose. D Bradykinesia Bradykinesia is a feature of the neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

stem: A 45-year-old woman who is a known asthmatic attends the Emergency Department following an episode of chest tightness and shortness of breath while at home. Her shortness of breath subsided after a period of six hours. There is no history of fever or coryza and she has been ﬁt and well recently. She has recently been started on new medications and wonders if one of these is the cause. Her past medical history includes depression, glaucoma and trochanteric bursitis and she has no known allergies. Her observations are taken, which are all within normal range and her examination is unremarkable. Clinical investigations, including blood tests and imaging, are all normal. Which of the following medications is safe to continue?
explanation: B Citalopram Chest tightness, wheeze, shortness of breath and a dry cough are all symptoms of bronchospasm. Bronchospasm occurs due to constriction of bronchioles, hence increasing resistance to airﬂow. Common causes of bronchospasm are NSAIDs, aspirin, betablockers and cholinergic medications. Citalopram is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor used in the treatment of depression. It does not cause bronchospasm. E Timolol Timolol is a beta-blocker that can cause constriction of the bronchioles, which leads to symptoms of bronchospasm, as seen in this patient. Due to their effects on the respiratory system, beta-blockers are often contraindicated in patients with underlying respiratory illnesses such as asthma. A Aspirin This patient is experiencing symptoms of bronchospasm. Aspirin is a known cause of bronchospasm and should be avoided in these patients. C Naproxen This patient is experiencing symptoms of bronchospasm. Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drug (NSAID). These drugs are a known cause of bronchospasm and should therefore be avoided. D Pilocarpine Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist used to lower intraocular pressure in the treatment of glaucoma. Side-effects are those of increased parasympathetic drive and include diarrhoea, hypersalivation and vomiting. Increased cholinergic transmission can cause bronchospasm, which is why targeted treatment for airway disease such as asthma includes antimuscarinic agents such as ipratropium.

stem: A 32-year-old nursing student has been admitted to the Emergency Medical Unit having taken an impulsive overdose of paracetamol 5 h previously. You have taken paracetamol levels, which indeed are above the treatment line, and have commenced N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) at the appropriate dose. A few minutes after the infusion begins, the patient complains of facial ﬂushing and generalised pruritus. She has 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com no orofacial swelling, and there is no evidence of airways compromise. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Stop the infusion and switch to oral methionine
explanation: C Stop the infusion temporarily It is not uncommon for individuals prescribed N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) to suffer a mild anaphylactoid reaction. This may occur in 5% of cases, and can usually be treated by temporarily halting the infusion and giving an antihistamine if required. In most cases, the NAC can be recommenced at a slower infusion rate (usually 50 mg/kg over 4 h). A Subcutaneous (sc) 1 mg adrenaline Adrenaline is not required in this case as the anaphylactoid reaction is not severe. In any case, sc delivery drives unpredictable absorption. im delivery is usually warranted where adrenalin is required. B Intramuscular (im) 5 mg adrenaline Adrenalin im is warranted for patients with airway compromise. In this case, the symptoms will resolve rapidly once the NAC is temporarily discontinued. D Intravenous (iv) 200 mg hydrocortisone In this case, the symptoms will resolve rapidly once the NAC is temporarily discontinued. Hydrocortisone is only warranted for patients with evidence of signiﬁcant anaphylaxis. E Stop the infusion and switch to oral methionine Patients often vomit after paracetamol overdose, particularly when they have also taken alcohol. This makes it difﬁcult to achieve sufﬁcient oral administration of methionine to be effective.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is undergoing cycles of chemotherapy with a paclitaxel- and trastuzumab-based regime. As per guidance, she is monitored after every cycle of chemotherapy for changes in her ejection fraction. After the second cycle, she develops increased shortness of breath and reduced exercise tolerance. Ejection fraction has reduced from 54% at baseline to 40%. Her blood pressure is 105/82 mmHg. There are bi-basal crackles on auscultation of the 773-555 THERAPE chest, although there is no ankle swelling. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: E Temporarily discontinue trastuzumab Guidance from the prescribing information on trastuzumab is clear: that it should be discontinued when there is a 10% or worse deterioration in ejection fraction. The statement from the drug information leaﬂet is reproduced below: ‘If LVEF drops 10 ejection fraction (EF) points from baseline AND to below 50%, treatment should be suspended and a repeat LVEF assessment performed within approximately three weeks. If LVEF has not improved, or declined further, discontinuation of Herceptin™ should be strongly considered, unless the beneﬁts for the individual patient are deemed to outweigh the risks. All such patients should be referred for assessment by a cardiologist and followed up’. The her2 receptor is thought to play a key role in protection against the development of cardiomyopathy. As such, antagonising her2 with trastuzumab signiﬁcantly increases the risk of development of cardiomyopathy (see weblink below). A Start bisoprolol Although bisoprolol does improve outcomes in heart failure, there is limited scope to institute beta blockade given her blood pressure, and it’s more important to discontinue the causative agent. B Start furosemide Limited ﬂuid retention means that ofﬂoading with diuretics will only have a minor impact at best on her symptoms. C Start ramipril Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are the intervention of choice in this scenario in the event that ejection fraction does not improve given the cessation of trastuzumab. D Start valsartan ARBs such as valsartan would be considered in the event that ACE inhibition is not tolerated – for example, due to chronic cough.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has been given a course of iron supplements 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com to correct iron deﬁciency anaemia, which has occurred after the birth of her second baby. She is known to be suffering from postnatal depression and presents to the Emergency Department having taken 28 iron sulphate tablets some 5 h previously. She is complaining of abdominal pain and vomiting and asks for assistance. On examination, she looks unwell, but is maintaining her airway; she has a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg and pulse 95/min regular. While in the department she becomes drowsier and suffers profuse diarrhoea. Which one of the following would be an appropriate initial intervention in this case?
explanation: A IV desferrioxamine Ingestion of large amounts of iron may lead to acute circulatory collapse accompanied by hypotension, as in this case. IV desferrioxamine at the rate of 15 mg/kg/h is an initial treatment of choice, and starting it as early as possible is important. If hypotension/circulatory collapse is not present, then it may be given IM at the rate of 2 g every 6–12 h. E Exchange transfusion Severe iron intoxication can be treated with exchange transfusion, although this is reserved for patients who fail to respond to other interventions ﬁrst. B Oral- activated charcoal Activated charcoal is a poor absorber of iron, and gastric lavage with instillation of desferrioxamine via the NG is the preferred approach. C Oral penicillamine Oral penicillamine is primarily used as a copper chelator in the treatment of Wilson’s disease. D Haemodialysis This is used as an option for patients who fail to respond to ﬂuid resuscitation and IV desferrioxamine alone.

stem: A 26-year-old man is prescribed thalidomide for erythema nodosum that has been resistant to other therapeutic interventions. He has recently acquired a new female partner and asks about contraceptive advice. Which of the following represents the correct advice with respect to contraception?
options: No precautions are needed as thalidomide only represents a risk if it is taken by the female partner
He should use barrier contraception and his partner should use effective contraception
Only the female need use contraception
The male should refrain from starting a family for 3 years after using thalidomide
Thalidomide is only teratogenic in the last trimester of pregnancy
explanation: B He should use barrier contraception and his partner should use effective contraception Thalidomide can be transferred in semen and, as such, males should be advised to use barrier contraception until at least 1 week after cessation of therapy. Two modes of contraception (male and female) are recommended to minimise the risk of the female becoming pregnant. E Thalidomide is only teratogenic in the last trimester of pregnancy The original thalidomide malformations were identiﬁed following use for ﬁrst trimester morning sickness. A No precautions are needed as thalidomide only represents a risk if it is taken by the female partner As thalidomide can be transmitted in semen, adequate contraception for the male and female is essential. C Only the female need use contraception Due to the (albeit low) failure rate of female contraception, protection for the male and female is recommended. D The male should refrain from starting a family for 3 years after using thalidomide Only a 1-week thalidomide-free period is needed.

stem: A 46-year-old man, who you have seen begging outside the station, is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance. He is unconscious and hyperventilating. The nurses tell you that he is frequently admitted intoxicated, has a history of cataracts potentially related to previous methanol ingestion and has suffered epileptic seizures, which have precipitated several hospital admissions. On examination is blood pressure (BP) is 100/70 mmHg, with a pulse is 100/min regular. Unusually, there is no smell of alcohol. He has crackles on auscultation of both lung ﬁelds consistent with cardiac failure. When you try and wake him, he just groans and tries to turn over. You notice that he has nystagmus. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 110 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 11.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 190 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 195 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Chloride (Cl-) 92 mmol/l 98-106 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 12 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l pH 7.1 7.35–7.45 Glucose 9 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Ethylene glycol intoxication Ethylene glycol intoxication presents with decreased consciousness level, severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis and renal, respiratory and cardiac failure. Multi-organ failure is thought to occur at least in part due to widespread deposition of calcium oxalate crystals around 12 h after the initial insult. Inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase by either ethanol or fomepizole, if availa-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com ble, is the mainstay of therapy. High-dose thiamine and pyridoxine should also be used as this reduces the formation of oxalate from glyoxylic acid. Because of the potential formation of calcium oxalate, calcium levels should also be assessed. Unfortunately, with delayed presentation, ingestion of relatively small amounts of ethylene glycol is fatal. C Metformin overdose Because we aren’t given a clear history of a previous diagnosis of diabetes mellitus, metformin overdose is unlikely as the driver for his presentation. A Diabetic ketoacidosis Given there is only a modest increase in glucose, this is inconsistent with a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis. B Phenytoin overdose Although there is nystagmus, this is more likely to be related to chronic alcoholism and optic atrophy from methanol overdose. D Ethanol intoxication The clue here is the lack of a smell of alcohol, which doesn’t ﬁt with alcohol intoxication.

stem: A patient is admitted for treatment of multi-drug resistant tubercu- 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com losis. The patient is currently taking rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide. He is commenced on streptomycin. What is the main concern with respect to streptomycin use?
explanation: A Vestibular damage Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside bactericidal antibiotic. It is used in the treatment of tularaemia and resistant mycobacterial infections. The most common neurological side-effect is vestibular damage causing persistent vertigo and vomiting. For this reason, ethambutol is usually added to tuberculosis regimes in preference to streptomycin. E Peripheral motor neuropathy Isoniazid results in peripheral neuropathy, the risk of which is partially ameliorated by pyridoxine supplementation. B Hepatic dysfunction Aminoglycosides including streptomycin impact most on renal function and are a cause of neuropathy. They would not be expected to lead to signiﬁcant hepatic dysfunction. C Optic neuropathy Ethambutol is the agent associated with optic neuropathy. D Autonomic neuropathy Isoniazid is recognised to result in peripheral, rather than autonomic neuropathy.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her daughter found her unresponsive. The daughter, who lives next door, frequently visits her mother. Today her mother did not respond to the doorbell and when she opened the door she found her mother sprawled on the couch. She also found the gas heater switched on but there was no ﬂame. She then quickly called the ambulance. On examination, the patient is drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12/15, blood pressure of 154/90, pulse of 98/min and a respiratory rate of 28/min. The patient has already been started on high ﬂow oxygen via a non- rebreather mask. What single initial investigation would be most helpful in determining the prognosis for this patient? 773-555 THERAPE
options: Full blood count (FBC), U and E, creatine phosphokinase (CPK) and cardiac enzymes
explanation: B Carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) COHb levels have prognostic implications in carbon monoxide poisoning, the diagnosis here:  <30% causes only headaches and dizziness,  40–60% produces syncope, tachypnoea, tachycardia and ﬁts,  >60% causes increasing risk of cardiorespiratory failure and death. Apply a tight-ﬁtting non-rebreather mask and give 100% oxygen. If the patient is comatose, she should be intubated and ventilated with 100% oxygen. Hyperbaric oxygen will shorten the wash-out of COHb. D Full blood count (FBC), U and E, creatine phosphokinase (CPK) and cardiac enzymes Whilst these investigations may be helpful, they are unlikely to lead to a diagnosis for this patient. A Toxicology screen A toxicology screen would be useful in a drowsy patient, to look for barbiturates or benzodiazepines as a cause of sedation, but it is very unlikely in a 72-year-old woman who collapsed at home. Had empty blister packets been found, benzodiazepine overdose could be considered. C 12-lead electrocardiogram Patients who have collapsed should have an ECG, and in general it is useful in establishing an ECG baseline. This patient is unlikely to have a diagnosis revealed by an ECG as there is no evidence of chest pain, suggesting a large ischaemic event, abnormal heart rate suggesting arrhythmia, or cardiopulmonary compromise. E Oxygen saturation with pulse oximeter Pulse oximetry cannot distinguish between haemoglobin bound to oxygen and that bound to carbon monoxide. Therefore it would give a falsely reassuring oxygenation reading.

stem: You are called to see a 26-year-old man on the ward. He was ad- 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com mitted for the treatment of cellulitis, and has a background of depression. He has become unwell with confusion, abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea the morning after admission. The nurses have also noticed that when he opened his bowels the stool was dark black. His pulse was 100 bpm, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 24/min. Initial investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 140 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 13.5 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 250 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l (INR) 1.1 0–1.1 Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 11 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Glucose 7 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Creatinine 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erect chest and abdominal X-rays Multiple rounded radio-opacities in the small intestine Iron level 90 μmol/l (12–30 μmol/l) What is the next appropriate management step?
explanation: E Parenteral desferrioxamine This is a case of iron overdose. Initial stages are of abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea with gastrointestinal blood loss. There can also be a lucid period where the person appears well and then becomes progressively drowsier. X-rays can reveal the tablets in the bowel. Serum iron indicates the severity of the overdose, with severe toxicity at >90 μmol/l. Parenteral desferrioxamine to chelate iron is the intervention of choice. C Cautious venesection Venesection is indicated in the treatment of haemochromatosis, but has no role in the treatment of iron overdose. A Oral activated charcoal Charcoal does not bind iron sulphate tablets and therefore has no value. As the pills in this case are in the small intestine it is recommended to cleanse the bowel with a polyethylene glycol electrolyte solution (Klean-Prep). Gastroscopy does not reach far enough to retrieve the tablets. B Oral desferrioxamine Oral absorption of desferrioxamine is too little and unpredictable to 773-555 THERAPE reliably treat iron overdose, as such IV delivery is preferred. D Haemodialysis Haemodialysis is indicated in patients where iron chelation therapy is inadequate and kidney disease and acidosis develop.

stem: A 61-year-old man is admitted having taken an overdose of unspeciﬁed medication. He is known to have type 2 diabetes, controlled with tablets, hypertension and a previous myocardial infarction. His BP is 95/60 mmHg, with pulse 105/min and regular. His respiratory rate is 35/min. Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 129 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 8.9 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 200 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 132 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 15 mmol/l 22 - 20 mmol/l Chloride (Cl-) 105 mmol/l 98 - 106 mmol/l Glucose 4.9 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely cause of his acidosis?
explanation: D Metformin This man has a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis. As such, the most likely cause of his overdose is metformin excess. Treatment is supportive, although in severe cases prolonged haemodialysis can be considered. Mortality is considerable, particularly in patients with underlying cardiovascular disease. C Ramipril Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor overdose leads to profound hypotension and acute kidney disease rather than the picture seen here. A Paracetamol Metabolic acidosis in paracetamol overdose is a late presentation, associated with oliguria and acute kidney disease. B Atenolol Atenolol is associated with bradycardia and hypotension rather than the clinical picture seen here. E Sitagliptin Experience with respect to sitagliptin overdose is minimal, although up to 800 mg was given as a regular dose in early studies without any signiﬁcant adverse consequences.

stem: You review the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of a new agent for the treatment of epilepsy, and are aware that other agents used for the treatment of epilepsy may require therapeutic drug monitoring. Which of the following is likely to drive a requirement for pharmacokinetic monitoring?
options: Complementary mode of action to other antiepileptics
explanation: A Zero-order kinetics With drugs that obey zero-order kinetics, such as phenytoin and ethanol, their enzyme metabolism is saturable, which means only a certain amount of the drug can be eliminated over a period of time. This means that for relatively small increases in administered 773-555 THERAPE drug, relatively large increases in plasma concentration may occur, leading to potential drug toxicity. This makes zero-order kinetics a key driver for therapeutic drug monitoring. E Inhibition of CYP3A4 Inhibition of CYP3A4 may require drug interaction studies looking at the effect of this drug on the metabolism of others, rather than studies looking at the concentration of the drug itself. B First-order kinetics Where drugs display ﬁrst-order kinetics, the rate at which a drug is metabolised and eliminated is generally proportional to the dose given, with an exponential reduction in plasma concentration over time. Each half-life of a drug displaying ﬁrst-order kinetics is associated with a 50% reduction in plasma concentration, and drugs may be considered eliminated after 3–5 half-lives. This predictable PK is associated with less need for therapeutic drug monitoring. C High ﬁrst pass metabolism High ﬁrst pass metabolism does not stratify a need for therapeutic drug monitoring; evaluation of active metabolites in this case is more important with respect to the need for monitoring or not. D Complementary mode of action to other antiepileptics This drives a requirement for Parkinson's disease interaction studies rather than for therapeutic drug monitoring.

stem: A 39-year-old patient with Huntington’s disease is admitted by ambulance to the Emergency Department, having taken an overdose of tricyclic antidepressants. He left a suicide note stating that he did not wish to be resuscitated. The antidepressants were prescribed by the General Practitioner (GP) some three weeks earlier because of increasing symptoms of endogenous depression. On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 8. His blood pressure is 80/60 mmHg. His peripheral pulse is barely palpable and the monitor reveals a broad complex tachycardia with a ventricular rate of 210 bpm. His pH is measured at 7.12 on a venous blood gas. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
B Direct current (DC) cardioversion

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com A suicide note does not constitute a properly executed expression of wishes with respect to end-of-life care. Given the recent diagnosis of depression, you cannot assume that the decision to take the overdose was made when he was of sound mind. This means that appropriate intervention is essential; given the signiﬁcant circulatory compromise, DC cardioversion is the most appropriate next step. Apart from DC cardioversion, given the pH, sodium bicarbonate should also be considered. E IV Lignocaine Lidocaine is negatively inotropic and will drive a further fall in blood pressure, with a lower chance of achieving sinus rhythm than with electrical cardioversion. A Consult the hospital solicitor In this case, by the time the solicitor reviews the case, it will be too late for the patient. It is up to you at this point to make a decision in his best interests. C Give no intervention Choosing not to intervene here is inappropriate. There is no evidence the patient was of sound mind/competent at the time he took the overdose. As such, to act in the patient’s best interests, you should intervene with cardioversion. D Intravenous (IV) Amiodarone IV amiodarone is likely to be less effective than DC cardioversion and no time is to be lost, given that the patient’s systolic blood pressure is 80 mmHg and the ventricular rate is 210 bpm.

stem: You are reviewing a patient with hepatitis B and evidence of chronic active hepatitis, and you plan to instigate therapy with entecavir. Which of the following correctly describes the mode of action of entecavir?
explanation: D Nucleoside analogue Entecavir is a pro-drug and requires phosphorylation to the triphosphate form before it becomes active. It works by inhibiting the priming of HBV polymerase, blocking reverse transcription of the negative-strand DNA and synthesis of the positive-strand DNA of the virus. Clinical trials suggest increased viral clearance versus lamivudine; it is now recommended as an option for initial treatment of hepatitis B by NICE. E Protease inhibitor Protease inhibitors are used in the treatment of hepatitis C and HIV, boceprevir being an example of an NS3/4A protease inhibitor used in the treatment of hepatitis C. A Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) NNRTIs are used in the treatment of HIV, with nevirapine being an example of a ﬁrst-generation NNRTI that works by inhibiting HIV reverse transcriptase. B M2 proton pump inhbitor Amantadine is an M2 proton pump inhibitor that was developed for the treatment of inﬂuenza, and has been used in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease (although its mechanism of action in Parkinson’s is unknown). C Interferon alpha-2a agonist Interferon alpha-2a is used in pegylated form for intermittent administration in the treatment of some patients with hepatitis B and C.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presented to the clinic with symptoms of inﬂammatory bowel disease. Rectal biopsy was consistent with a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis and she is commenced on treatment. Other past history of note included mild epilepsy which is managed with lamotrigine, and hypertension, managed with amlodipine. She next presents to the Emergency room with severe acute epigastric pain and vomiting. On examination, she is pyrexial 37.8 °C and has severe epigastric pain. Her blood pressure (BP) is 100/60 mmHg and her pulse is 105/min. Investigations: Investigations: Normal Values 773-555 THERAPE Hb 119 g/l WCC 13.1 × 109/l PLT 209 × 109/l Na+ 140 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l Creatinine 141 μmol/l Amylase 1230 u/l 60/180 Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: D Mesalazine 5-ASA compounds are associated with the development of acute pancreatitis, as are azathioprine, sodium valproate, furosemide, oestrogens, corticosteroids and octreotide. Other drugs thought to be associated include metronidazole, thiazide diuretics, cimetidine and cisplatin. In this case it is likely that she was started on mesalazine in conjunction with her diagnosis of ulcerative colitis, and this precipitated her presentation with pancreatitis. C Paracetamol Paracetamol is associated with hepatotoxicity when used to excess, not with pancreatitis. A Amlodipine Although cases of pancreatitis in association with amlodipine therapy have been reported, the risk is thought to be less than that for 5-ASA compounds. B Lamotrigine Sodium valproate, not lamotrigine, is associated with increased risk of acute pancreatitis. E Loperamide Loperamide is an opioid receptor agonist which does not signiﬁcantly impact on risk of pancreatitis.

stem: A 57-year-old man attends the outpatient clinic. He has a background of hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes, and gastroesophageal reﬂux disease. The patient has recently returned from a holiday in Europe. While on vacation, he suffered a heart attack and was admitted to hospital. He states his heart went into a ‘funny rhythm’ which re- 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com quired medication to control it.
