The patient remembers a particularly bad stay in the coronary care unit when he had symptoms of vomiting, vertigo, tinnitus, headache and blurred vision. What medication is most likely to have caused these symptoms?
explanation: C Quinidine Quinidine is a class 1A antiarrhythmic drug that slows the rapid depolarisation that occurs during phase 0 of the cardiac action potential. It is used for the treatment of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, and is related to the antimalarial quinine. The constellation of symptoms described are those of cinchonism. This can be brought on by both acute and chronic treatment with quinidine and quinine. It can also cause a prolonged QT interval on the electrocardiogram. (Cinchona is the name of the tree from which quinine can be obtained.) E Flecainide Flecainide is associated dizziness and blurred vision, but not with the vomiting and tinnitus seen here. A Amiodarone Amiodarone therapy is associated with both pulmonary ﬁbrosis and skin photosensitivity, rather than the symptoms seen here. B Digoxin Digoxin toxicity is associated with vomiting and visual disturbance, but it is more likely to be associated with yellowing of vision. D Lignocaine Lignocaine is not associated with symptoms of cinchonism, it is associated with sensation of dizziness and tunnel vision.

stem: A 61-year-old woman is being reviewed in the medical follow-up clinic. She received a renal transplant 6 months ago because of end-stage kidney disease. She has been ﬁne but complains that she feels embarrassed whenever she laughs because her gums have become very prominent. Her past medical history, apart from the renal transplant, includes long-standing hypertension. Ciclosporin was started after her renal transplant, and this is the only medication she is taking. On examination, she has a blood pressure of 140/80 mmHg, BMI of 27 kg/m2, gums are swollen, chest is clear, 773-555 THERAPE and non-tender renal transplant. Investigations show: Investigation Result Normal Values Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 12 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 250 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Haemoglobin (Hb) 87 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 6 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 213 × 109 /l 150 - 400 × 109/l What other complications of ciclosporin treatment should this patient be aware of?
explanation: B Hypertrichosis Ciclosporin was introduced in 1983 and led to great improvements in patients and graft survivals in organ transplantation. It is metabolised through the cytochrome P450 system in the liver. Drugs affecting this enzyme system affect the blood levels of ciclosporin. Recognised side effects include: hypertension, hypertrichosis, diabetes mellitus, infection, tumours, gingival hyperplasia, nephrotoxicity, headache, hyperkalaemia, hyperuricaemia, gout, hypercholesterolaemia and pancreatitis. D Purpura Warfarin may have the side effect of purpura. A Alopecia Alopecia is a known side-effect of another renal transplant immunosuppressant – tacrolimus. C Pigmentation Ciclosporin does not affect pigmentation of the skin. Any change in pigmentation of moles in renal transplant should be taken seriously because there is an increased chance of malignancy whilst taking immunosuppression. Renal transplant patients are often advised to wear sun block when exposed to the sun. E Staining of the teeth Minocycline and doxycycline may have the side effects of dental staining.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents to the clinic as she has been feeling 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com low since her husband died and has started taking St John’s wort. She has a background of chronic atrial ﬁbrillation and diabetes. She is taking digoxin, warfarin and metformin. What is the patient at increased risk from?
explanation: A Embolic stroke St John’s wort is a herbal remedy that is used by many for depression, anxiety or sleep disturbance. It is an enzyme inducer and will result in decreased prothrombin time in patients taking warfarin. Hence the patient is at increased risk of embolic stroke. It can also cause photosensitivity and gastrointestinal upset. Young female patients who are also taking the combined oral contraceptive pill should be warned that St John’s wort will interfere with their contraception. D Increased blood glucose Metformin is not metabolised via the P450 system, and St John’s wort therefore has no effect with respect to increasing blood glucose. B Bleeding St John’s wort is an enzyme inducer rather than inhibitor, and therefore results in a decrease rather than an increase in INR. C Pancreatitis Diabetes mellitus per se is associated with an increased risk of pancreatitis, and the use of St John’s wort has no further impact on this level of risk. E Hypomania St John’s wort is as effective as an SSRI in treating depression and does not increase the risk of hypomania in patients who take it.

stem: You are asked to review a 73-year-old man who complains of failure to maintain his erection during sexual intercourse over the past two months. He has a history of psychiatric disorder, for which he is treated with lithium, type 2 diabetes diagnosed some three years earlier, managed with diet and metformin, and angina, for which atenolol was recently added, and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)-inhibition for blood pressure and renoprotection. Blood pressure is 145/85 mmHg; recent haemoglobin A1c 773-555 THERAPE (HbA1c) was measured at 75.96 mmol/mol (9.1%). Which of the following would represent the most likely cause of his deteriorating sexual function over the past two months?
explanation: C Beta-blocker therapy It is likely that he has some pre-existing vascular disease affecting the blood supply to the penis, but the acute cause of his deteriorating sexual function is likely to be the beta-blocker therapy. Switching the atenolol to a cardioselective beta blocker such as nebivolol and bisoprolol, or a non-beta blocker therapy for his angina, should result in an improvement in his erectile function. E ACE inhibitor therapy ACE inhibitors are protective against micro- and macrovascular disease in diabetes, and are not associated with erectile dysfunction. A Vascular disease Given he has only been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes for 3 years, signiﬁcant vascular disease leading to erectile dysfunction is unlikely. B Lithium therapy Lithium therapy is associated with diabetes insipidus, not with erectile dysfunction. D Metformin therapy Metformin therapy is not associated with vascular dysfunction and may indeed be associated with improvement in vasoreactivity.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is admitted after taking an overdose of 30 × 300 mg aspirin tablets. She begins to suffer from severe tinnitus, feels light-headed and starts to vomit about 1 h after her overdose and attends the Emergency Department. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 130/70 mmHg, her pulse is 85/min regular. She is very anxious and complains of a continuous ringing in her ears. Her respiratory rate is 36/min. Which of the following sets of arterial blood gas results would ﬁt best with her clinical picture?
options: pH 7.1; pCO2 4.8 kPa; pO2 7.1 kPa 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com
explanation: B pH 7.5; pCO2 2.9 kPa; pO2 12.1 kPa The early period of aspirin overdose is associated with respiratory alkalosis, as characterised by raised pH and hypocapnia. Late complications include encephalopathy and seizures, pancreatitis and acute kidney disease. Thankfully, however, the mortality rate associated with aspirin overdose is only around 1%. We are not given the results of other metabolic parameters, but given that the CO2 values are low, the high pH represents respiratory alkalosis. E pH 7.4; pCO2 6.7 kPa; pO2 8.1 kPa The CO2 is elevated here, meaning that the blood gas picture, including a normal pH, ﬁts best with a compensated respiratory acidosis. A pH 7.1; pCO2 4.8 kPa; pO2 7.1 kPa Given the CO2 is in the normal range, the pH is consistent with a metabolic acidosis, which is seen only in the later stages of aspirin overdose. C pH 7.1; pCO2 5.1 kPa; pO2 13.1 kPa Given the CO2 is only 5.1, this blood gas result is also consistent with a metabolic acidosis, only seen in the later stages of aspirin overdose. D pH 7.3; pCO2 4.5 kPa; pO2 12.1 kPa The pH is only slightly below the normal range at 7.3, and represents a metabolic acidosis given the CO is 4.5.

stem: A 34-year-old woman, who is eight weeks pregnant, comes in after an overdose of white tablets and is unable to remember how many she took. She refuses to wait for the results of her initial blood tests and leaves hospital, only to come back after a few hours complaining of feeling faint. At this point, her investigations are repeated. Salicylate levels are 4 mmol/l on the initial sample and 1.2 mmol/l on the subsequent one. Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFT Normal Initial ABG pH 7.6 pa(CO ) 2.0 kPa 773-555 THERAPE HCO 24 mmol/l Repeat arterial blood gas (ABG) following return: pH 7.35 pa(CO ) 3.0 kPa HCO 22 mmol/l What metabolic abnormality is seen on ﬁrst presentation?
explanation: D Respiratory alkalosis The elevated pH with low CO2 and normal HCO3 seen here is consistent with a respiratory alkalosis, the initial presentation of aspirin overdose. A Metabolic acidosis By the time the patient re-presents, the second blood gas illustrates a metabolic acidosis with partial compensation, commonly known as the third stage of aspirin overdose. B Metabolic alkalosis The bicarbonate in the normal range effectively rules out a metabolic alkalosis here. C Respiratory acidosis A respiratory acidosis is associated with an elevated CO2, which isn’t seen here. An isolated respiratory acidosis is seen in respiratory failure due to COPD or acute lower respiratory tract infection, and in overdose of opiates or benzodiazepines. E Mixed Metabolic and respiratory acidosis In a mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis, the bicarbonate is low and the CO2 is elevated, which isn’t the picture reported here. A mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis may be seen after events such as a myocardial infarction, where there is cardiac failure and co-existent decreased tissue perfusion.

stem: A 47-year-old woman presents following a self-terminating tonic-clonic seizure. She admits to regularly abusing benzodiazepines and opiates. She recently changed her GP, as her previous one refused to prescribe her the 60 mg diazepam and 180 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com mg of dihydrocodeine she takes a day. She does not drink alcohol and has not been known to abuse other prescription medications. Examination in the Emergency Department is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation: D iv diazepam This patient has suffered a seizure, most likely as a result of benzodiazepine withdrawal. Management of choice would be with a long acting benzodiazepine, such as diazepam, given intravenously initially and titrated to effect. It could then be switched to the oral preparation and a reducing dose regime established. In patients who have been using diazepam for a number of years, this may need to occur over as long a period as 8–12 weeks. Patients may well have to attend the pharmacy to collect a script on a number of occasions per week to prevent stock-piling or overdosing intentionally on the medication. E Oral methadone Oral methadone is used in addiction programs to allow withdrawal from diamorphine and other opiates of addiction. Opiate withdrawal does not, however, lead to seizures. A Intravenous (iv) Lorazepam iv lorazepam is usually reserved for refractory seizures associated with acute benzodiazepine withdrawal, and for patients suffering seizures who are withdrawing from alcohol. B Oral carbamazepine There is no indication for conventional anti-epileptic medication here, with a reducing dose of benzodiazepines the more appropriate option. C iv Naloxone iv Naloxone is used for acute opiate reversal in situations of respiratory arrest where airway support is not possible or not indicated.

stem: A 21-year-old man is admitted unconscious. There is no history available. On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 3/15, blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg, pulse is 75 bpm and regular, respiratory rate is 14. There are stigmata of previous self-harm. He is intubated and sent to the ITU. A toxicity screen is sent and shows a paracetamol level of 330 μg/ml. N-acetylcysteine is commenced. On day 2, he is extubated. His progress is monitored over the next few days. Which of the following is the most important determinant of liver transplant in paracetamol overdose?
explanation: B pH The King's College Hospital criteria for liver transplantation in paracetamol-induced acute liver failure are what drive the answer to this question. They state that a patient should be listed for transplantation if arterial pH <7.3 or arterial lactate >3.0 mmol/l after adequate ﬂuid resuscitation. D Bicarbonate 773-555 THERAPE Although low bicarbonate is a pointer to metabolic acidosis, it is decompensated metabolic acidosis with low pH which drives referral for transplantation. A ALT Elevated transaminases are not considered a criterion for liver transplantation. Although elevated transaminases may demonstrate hepatocellular damage, it is impaired hepatic synthetic function which most affects outcomes. C PT PT is one of three other criteria apart from pH which may drive transplantation; all three should be satisﬁed in a 24-hour period:  Creatinine >300 µmol/l  PT >100 (INR >6.5)  Grade III/IV encephalopathy. E Alkaline phosphatase Like ALT, alkaline phosphatase may be elevated in paracetamolrelated liver failure, but it is not strongly associated with outcomes.

stem: A 45-year-old civil engineer is brought to the Emergency Department with a decreased level of consciousness and slurred speech. His past medical history includes a diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder, which has remained quiescent of late due to his regular medications. Two weeks previously, he had developed a painful left knee, and had taken ibuprofen regularly since. His blood pressure is 122/82, pulse is 85 and regular. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13. Bloods on admission reveal an elevated sodium of 148 mmol/l, creatinine of 152 μmol/l and a lithium level of 4.8. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
C Haemodialysis Lithium (usually given in the carbonate form) is prescribed for the prophylaxis and treatment of mania, bipolar affective disorder and occasionally unipolar depression. It has a narrow therapeutic ratio and, therefore, careful therapeutic drug monitoring is mandatory. Toxicity may be precipitated by sodium depletion and, therefore,

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com diuretics should be avoided. Non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) impair the renal excretion of lithium, also leading to potential toxicity. In this case, with a lithium level of 4.8, potentially severe toxicity is indicated. The treatment is, therefore, haemodialysis, which may be repeated as blood levels of lithium can rebound due to widespread tissue distribution. E Sodium bicarbonate Sodium bicarbonate is indicated for the treatment of tricyclic antidepressant overdose where there is QRS prolongation (>100 ms). A Multiple-dose activated charcoal There is no evidence that activated charcoal is effective at adsorbing lithium. Gastric lavage may be considered within the ﬁrst hour of a potential overdose. B Forced alkaline diuresis This was formerly indicated in aspirin overdose, although it’s now not used because of the risk of exacerbating pulmonary oedema. D Flumazenil Flumazenil is used as a reversal agent for patients with acute benzodiazepine overdose associated with short- term use.

stem: A 32-year-old man is arrested after a ﬂight from Jamaica and brought to the hospital for assessment as he becomes increasingly agitated. Abdominal X-ray reveals evidence of ingestion of a number of packets of drugs, presumed to be cocaine. What is the management of choice in this case?
explanation: B Urgent surgical referral As this patient is symptomatic, following the royal college of Emergency medicine guidelines they should have an urgent surgical referral. E Laxative administration This practice is known as ‘body packing’ and is particularly associated with the smuggling of cocaine. The risk of toxicity from rupture or leakage of the package is not insigniﬁcant. Body packers and body stuffers may be asymptomatic when brought in by po- 773-555 THERAPE lice. The body packers, also called mules, pack their gastrointestinal tract with bags of cocaine (or other illicit drugs) in order to smuggle the drug from one country to another. In contrast, body stuffers hastily insert packages into the mouth, rectum, or vagina in order to conceal the evidence from police at the time of their arrest. Following the Royal College of Emergency Medicine guidance, if the patient is asymptomatic then laxatives can be considered, but if they have developed symptoms either drug to package rupture or bowel obstruction then they require surgical referral. A Gastric lavage and activated charcoal Institution of ﬂuid and charcoal potentially increases the risk of package rupture and should therefore be avoided. C Observation Given one of the packages at least appears to be leaking, observation risks waiting too long for them to exit the body. D Colonic wash-out Colonic washout utilises quite large volumes of water, increasing the risk of packet rupture.

stem: A 61-year-old man, known to the Neurology Clinic with poorly controlled epilepsy, presents unscheduled to the Outpatient Department. He has defaulted from neurology follow-up, but tells you he has been seizure-free on his present medication. Attendance was prompted by recent optometrist assessment and the unexpected ﬁnding of reduced peripheral vision. Past medical history is of epilepsy, substance abuse and tuberculosis. Current medication: sodium valproate, vigabatrin, lamotrigine and Rifater™ (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide), and ethambutol. On examination, he has severe constriction of visual ﬁelds; however, acuity, colour vision and fundoscopy are normal. What change must you make to his medication?
explanation:
E Stop vigabatrin The anticonvulsant vigabatrin is now recognised to cause irreversible visual-ﬁeld defects in up to 30% of users. The defect is often asymptomatic in the early stages, affecting only peripheral ﬁelds

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com with no alteration in acuity. Changes can occur as early as one month into treatment. This side-effect was ﬁrst noted in 1997 and, in recent years, the drug has been used only in cases of severe, treatment-resistant epilepsy, and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome in children. In cases where therapy is initiated, regular visual ﬁeld screening is required. Other side- effects include depression, psychosis and sedation. A Add pyridoxine Pyridoxine is used to prevent peripheral neuropathy associated with isoniazid therapy. B Stop sodium valproate Sodium valproate leads to weight gain, a polycystic ovarian syndrome-like picture and teratogenicity in young women. It is not associated with signiﬁcant ocular adverse effects. C Stop ethambutol The antituberculous agent ethambutol causes optic neuritis and regular monitoring of acuity is required, particularly in patients with impaired renal function. D Start thiamine supplements Thiamine is primarily utilised in patients with alcoholism and in pregnant women with hyperemesis gravidarum to prevent the development of Wernicke’s encephalopathy.

stem: A 61-year-old man presents to the Neurology Clinic with a 2week history of double vision and increased lethargy. He denies photophobia and does not wear prescription glasses. His past medical history includes glaucoma, urinary frequency and occasional leg cramps. On examination, there is visible ptosis of both his eyelids. He has a normal range of eye movements but complains of diplopia towards the end of the examination. His reﬂexes are preserved and there is no motor or sensory deﬁcit in his upper or lower limbs. Which of the following medications is it safe to continue?
explanation: B Pilocarpine This patient has myasthenia gravis, demonstrated by his ocular signs and muscle fatiguability. It is common in women under 40 773-555 THERAPE years and men above 60 years. The ﬁrst-line medication to start is pyridostigmine, an anticholinesterase that prolongs the duration of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. Drugs that reduce acetylcholine levels are, therefore, contraindicated in myasthenia gravis. Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist used to cause pupillary constriction to decrease intraocular pressure. It does not deplete acetylcholine release and is safe to continue in myasthenia gravis. E Tolterodine Tolterodine is a muscarinic antagonist used in the treatment of urinary frequency. Antimuscarinic drugs are contraindicated in myasthenia gravis due to reducing cholinergic transmission. A Erythromycin Some antibiotics have been reported to exacerbate myasthenia gravis, including aminoglycosides, tetracyclines and macrolides. Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic. Mechanisms of worsening myasthenia gravis include impairing neuromuscular transmission. If possible, they should be avoided and alternative antibiotics should be commenced. C Quinine Antimalarial drugs, such as quinine, can exacerbate symptoms of myasthenia gravis and should be avoided. D Timolol Timolol is a beta-blocker. Beta-blockers, including propranolol, atenolol and timolol, can increase muscle fatiguability in myasthenia gravis. Propranolol is most likely to cause increased fatigue.

stem: A top premier-league football manager recently expressed concern that some of the players had abnormally high red cell counts – a sign of using erythropoietin (EPO). He bemoaned the fact that EPO had been administered to some players by their former clubs outside the UK and they actually took the drug unknowingly. What is the best way of detecting EPO abuse?
options: It can be detected in urine for a few weeks following the most recent injection
It can be detected in saliva for a few days after the most recent injection
It can be detected in blood up to a week after the most recent injection
It can be detected by reticulocyte count for a few days after recent injection
explanation:
A It can be detected in urine for a few weeks following the most recent injection

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Drug taking has become a big problem in all high-level sports: EPO was ﬁrst introduced into the world of cycling in the late 1980s. By increasing the red cell mass, and hence the oxygencarrying capacity of the blood, EPO should increase performance during an all-out exercise. Currently, EPO testing has been greatly reﬁned, and levels may be detected in urine for some time after administration. It can lead to a dose-dependent increase in blood pressure or aggravation of hypertension; isolated patients have suffered a hypertensive crisis with encephalopathy-like symptoms and generalised tonic–clonic seizures. There is also a risk of thrombosis, and deaths have been reported from its use. E It can be detected by reticulocyte count for a few days after recent injection Although EPO may increase reticulocyte count, this in itself is not diagnostic of EPO use, particularly as many athletes may engage in high-altitude training, also recognised to increase red blood cell count. B It increases muscle bulk EPO has a positive effect on the oxygen carrying capacity of the blood, not muscle bulk. C It can be detected in saliva for a few days after the most recent injection EPO testing from saliva is under development, although currently urine testing is more reliable. D It can be detected in blood up to a week after the most recent injection Although EPO can be detected via blood sampling, urine testing is preferred because of infection risks associated with blood sampling.

stem: A 20-year-old man from Italy, previously ﬁt and well, is admitted to hospital with jaundice. He had recently been commenced on antibiotics by a general practitioner (GP) for a presumed urinary tract infection. Examination reveals jaundice, and a spleen tip is just palpable under the left costal margin. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 93 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 14 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 290 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 147 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 85 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 7.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Bilirubin 72 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALP 80 IU/l 30–130 IU/l ALT 28 IU/l 5–30 IU/l 773-555 THERAPE Albumin 39 g/dl 35–55 g/dl Blood ﬁlm Heinz bodies Urine dipstick Positive for urobilinogen and leukocyte esterase What antibiotic is most appropriate for treating this patient?
explanation: D Co-amoxiclav The patient has glucose-6-phoshate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deﬁciency, and Heinz bodies are the give-away here. The enzyme is required in the body for the conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to 6- phosphogluconolactone. This step is part of the hexose monophosphate pathway, needed for the generation of NADPH (reduced nicotinamide dinucleotide phosphate). NADPH maintains glutathione in a reduced form, which is required for the removal of oxidative metabolites. Deﬁciency of this enzyme shows X-linked inheritance and results in haemolysis when the patient is exposed to oxidants. A Chloramphenicol Chloramphenicol leads to haemolysis in G6PD deﬁciency and should be avoided. It is now mainly used for infections such as Salmonella that are resistant to multiple other antibiotics. B Nitrofurantoin Although nitrofurantoin is effective in treating UTIs, it should be avoided in patients with G6PD deﬁciency. C Ciproﬂoxacin Urinary pathogens are exhibiting signiﬁcant levels of resistance to quinolones, and they are a class that should be avoided in patients with G6PD deﬁciency. Recent recommendations also advise that ciproﬂoxacin or levoﬂoxacin should no longer be used in the treatment of uncomplicated cystitis unless other commonly recommended antibiotics are unsuitable. E Co-trimoxazole Co-trimoxazole is usually reserved for treatment of pneumocystis pneumonia, and is avoided in patients with G6PD deﬁciency.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is admitted in a comatose state. She was found lying unconscious on the ﬂoor of her apartment by her boy- 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com friend. She had recently been ﬁred by her employer for below-standard behaviour at work. She was taking regular amitriptyline at night, prescribed by her GP for low mood and trouble with sleeping. On examination, she is comatose and receiving oxygen by mask. Her pulse is 130/min and blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. Her pupils are 8 mm and unreactive to light. The fundi are normal. Her eyes are divergent and the oculocephalic reﬂex is sluggish. Painful stimuli lead to decortication of the upper limbs. Tendon reﬂexes are brisk and plantar responses are extensor on both sides. The bladder is full and she is catheterised. ECG reveals QRS widening. While she is being examined she has a generalised seizure. An urgent computed tomography (CT) of the head is normal and cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) study reveals 5 lymphocytes, 0.3 g/l protein and 5.5 mmol of glucose with a random blood glucose of 6.5 mmol/l. Blood gases were abnormal, showing metabolic acidosis. Her ECG is shown below. What one of the following represents the most important intervention for her?
explanation: B Sodium bicarbonate The QRS widening and seizure dictate sodium bicarbonate as the most important pharmacological intervention for her. Airway protection, delivery of oxygen and cardiac monitoring are of course also a priority. Where refractory arrhythmia is seen, both phenytoin and lignocaine are potential interventions. Gastric lavage is an option, but only where patients present in the ﬁrst hour. A Dimercaprol Dimercaprol is used to treat acute heavy metal poisoning, and is administered by IM injection. C Amiodarone 773-555 THERAPE Amiodarone can lead to further QRS prolongation and may actually exacerbate the risk of arrhythmia. D Physostigmine Physostigmine is used as a treatment for anti-cholinergic overdose/poisoning, and is also used as a pre- treatment to protect against organophosphate poisoning. E Charcoal haemoperfusion A systematic review has concluded that there is limited evidence to support the use of charcoal haemoperfusion in the treatment of tricyclic antidepressant overdose.

stem: A 38-year-old man has been rushed into the Emergency Department with vomiting. He describes his vomit as being dark brown in colour and resembling coffee grounds. On examination, he is afebrile. He is cool peripherally. His pulse is 124 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is stable at 133/90 mmHg. His chest is clear and heart sounds are normal. He is tender and guarding in the epigastrium, but the remainder of his abdomen is soft. He has melaena on digital rectal examination. He has a background of psoriasis, depression and hypothyroidism and is recovering from suprascapular tendinopathy. He is otherwise well and his medical conditions are well controlled. Which drug is most likely to be contributing to this patient’s symptoms?
explanation:
A Citalopram The presence of coffee ground vomiting and melaena is very suggestive of an upper gastrointestinal bleed. Of the drugs listed, citalopram and other serotonin-selective reuptake inhibitors can cause gastrointestinal bleeding, especially when taken in excess or with other medications that can cause similar symptoms. For example, this patient also has suprascapular tendinopathy and is likely to be taking non-steroidal anti- inﬂammatories to alleviate pain and swelling. E Paracetamol Paracetamol on its own does not cause gastrointestinal bleeding. A paracetamol overdose can cause hepatic toxicity and ultimately hepatic failure. Nausea and vomiting and abdominal pain are com-

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com mon early features that are followed by symptoms of hepatic failure. Hepatic failure may cause derangements in clotting that may, in turn, increase the risk of bleeding. However, this is less common and the absence of other signs of hepatic failure, such as jaundice, makes paracetamol overdose less likely. B Dithranol Dithranol is a topical agent used in the treatment of psoriasis. Sideeffects include local skin reactions. However, it does not cause gastrointestinal symptoms. C Hydrocortisone cream 1% Steroids can cause gastrointestinal bleeding. However, this is usually with systemic treatment, rather than with topical therapy. Therefore, the more likely causative drug is citalopram. D Levothyroxine Levothyroxine can cause vomiting. However, it does not cause gastrointestinal bleeding.

stem: A 59-year-old man with long-standing type I diabetes comes to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. He has intermittent and unpredictable vomiting of often undigested or partially digested food. He also has peripheral neuropathy and erectile dysfunction. On examination, his blood pressure is 130/84 mmHg and has a fall of 20 mmHg on standing. His body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m2. His abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no masses. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 121 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 10.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 203 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 145 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for his vomiting?
explanation: A Domperidone This patient has diabetic autonomic neuropathy, and has diabetic 773-555 THERAPE gastroparesis, which is associated with often unpredictable vomiting of undigested or partially digested food. Patients try varying the carbohydrate, fat, and ﬁbre content of their meals to try to reduce vomiting and indigestion, often with little success. Domperidone is the initial intervention of choice, with erythromycin a potential alternative. It can result in elevated prolactin which is rarely associated with galactorrhoea. In the event that monotherapy is ineffective, the missing agent can be added, and if dual therapy with domperidone and erythromycin is not effective in managing the condition, other interventions such as a gastric pacemaker could be considered. D Ondansetron Ondansetron is an effective, centrally acting anti-emetic, useful particularly in managing nausea and vomiting related to cancer chemotherapy agents. In this case, a prokinetic agent such as domperidone or erythromycin are much more effective. B Metoclopramide Metoclopramide is an effective prokinetic agent for the treatment of gastroparesis, although concerns about long-term neurological side-effects associated with its use now limit its use. Use of metoclopramide in younger patients, and women, in particular, can precipitate acute oculogyric crisis. Long-term use can lead to the development of drug-induced parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesias which may persist even on withdrawal of the drug. It is these latter factors that have limited use of metoclopramide. C Omeprazole Proton pump inhibitors are ineffective in managing diabetic gastroparesis. The defect which causes vomiting is not excess acid reﬂux but is dysmotility related to autonomic dysfunction. For this reason, a prokinetic anti- emetic is preferred. E Ranitidine Ranitidine is less effective as an acid suppressant than a proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole. It is not effective in managing diabetic gastroparesis, where a prokinetic agent such as domperidone is a more appropriate intervention. Ranitidine is mostly now sold as a supermarket purchase for indigestion relief.

stem: A 26-year-old man with a history of psoriasis returns from a 3week holiday to India with rapidly worsening psoriasis. He took antimalarials and antibiotics with him. His condition is normally mild and managed with topical therapies only. On examination, he has widespread psoriasis, which is contiguous in many areas. 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
explanation: C Chloroquine Whilst it is difﬁcult to establish the link between antimalarials and psoriasis from clinical trials, case reports of psoriasis associated with antimalarial therapy have stimulated original discussion about drug-induced psoriasis. One paper from 1997 postulated that the effect of antimalarials on trans-glutaminase activity leads to stimulation of epidermal proliferation, and thus chloroquine is the appropriate answer here. D Amoxicillin Penicillins are not associated with increased risk of psoriasis, but are associated with pruritis and urticaria. Some case reports link amoxicillin to psoriasis, although it may well be the infection rather than the antibiotic which is the cause of the rash. A Ciproﬂoxacin Quinolones are not recognised as a cause of worsening psoriasis - they are associated with tendonopathy, which precludes their use in pregnant women. Recent advice is to avoid quinolone use wherever possible if an effective alternative is available. B Metronidazole Metronidazole is not a cause of psoriasis but is linked to the development of pustular skin rashes. E Oxytetracycline Although oxytetracycline may increase the risk of psoriasis, the impact on risk is not thought to be as great as that seen for antimalarials.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue and shortness of breath over the past few weeks. Her history includes rheumatoid arthritis, for which she has been taking methotrexate and folic acid. Blood tests reveal pancytopenia, and her bone marrow biopsy shows megaloblastic changes. Upon further review, the patient admits to non-compliance with her folic acid supplementation. What is the mechanism of action of methotrexate that explains its role in causing these ﬁndings?
options: Inhibition of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase 773-555 THERAPE
explanation: B Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, an enzyme necessary for converting dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate. Tetrahydrofolate is essential for DNA synthesis, particularly in rapidly dividing cells. The inhibition leads to megaloblastic changes and can cause pancytopenia, especially in the absence of folic acid supplementation. E Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase Drugs such as hydroxyurea target this enzyme in DNA synthesis. Methotrexate does not act via this pathway. A Inhibition of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase This mechanism is seen with drugs such as mycophenolate mofetil, used as immunosuppressants. It does not apply to methotrexate. C Inhibition of xanthine oxidase This mechanism is associated with drugs such as allopurinol, used in the treatment of gout. It is unrelated to methotrexate. D Inhibition of purine synthesis While methotrexate indirectly affects purine and pyrimidine synthesis by limiting folate availability, the primary action is through dihydrofolate reductase inhibition.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with a history of chronic atrial ﬁbrillation has collapsed at home and has been admitted through Accident & Emergency. She is taking digoxin. She has no history of ischaemic heart disease. Other medication of note includes ketoconazole for a chronic fungal infection, and an antibiotic started by the duty general practitioner (GP) for a lower respiratory tract infection. On examination, her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg, pulse is 63 bpm and regular. Her heart sounds are normal and there are coarse breath sounds at the right base on auscultation. Investigations: ECG: sinus rhythm, a heart rate of 65 bpm, axis 30 °, PR interval 120 ms, QRS interval of 107 ms and QTc of 510 ms. Which antibiotic is most likely to have been started in this 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com patient?
explanation: D Clarithromycin This woman has an abnormal ECG and presented with a collapse. Her QTc is prolonged. Both ketoconazole and clarithromycin are known to prolong the QT interval, and clarithromycin is therefore the correct answer here. The antibiotic should be stopped, as should the ketoconazole if possible, and the patient monitored for episodes of torsades. In the event that there is hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia, then these electrolyte abnormalities should be corrected. E Co-amoxiclav This is amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid. Clavulanic does not have signiﬁcant effects on the cardiac action potential. A Amoxicillin Penicillin-based antibiotics are not associated with QT prolongation. B Doxycycline Tetracycline-based antibiotics are not associated with QT prolongation; a main concern of their use is that they can cause symptomatic gastro-oesophageal reﬂux. C Cefalexin Cephalosporins, like penicillins, do not cause prolonged QT.

stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department with probable Lyme disease. She has been on holiday with her husband and 3-month-old baby and is currently breastfeeding the child. You have read that doxycycline should be avoided in this situation. What is the main concern for the infant with respect to doxycycline use in breastfeeding women?
explanation: E Teeth staining Tetracyclines lead to teeth staining and may impair bone growth. Although doxycycline appears to bind calcium less avidly than other tetracyclines in the class, risk of accumulation in teeth or bones of breastfeeding infants cannot be excluded. For this reason, the class should be avoided if alternatives are available. A Elevated serum creatinine Trimethoprim inhibits tubular creatinine secretion. This phenomenon is seen in adults and in children where trimethoprim is prescribed, leading to a rise in serum creatinine in the absence of renal impairment. Creatine normalises once the course of antibiotics is complete. B Folate deﬁciency Folate deﬁciency is a rare consequence of trimethoprim therapy. This has led to avoidance of its use in pregnancy, particularly where there are alternatives, and in the ﬁrst trimester. Trimethoprim is safe in breastfeeding; it is only secreted in very small amounts into breast milk. C Neuropathy Neuropathy is a concern associated with quinolone therapy; it is not associated with the use of tetracyclines. With respect to quinolones, both neuropathy and musculoskeletal adverse events have prompted a Common Safety Method (CSM) warning to avoid their use if at all possible when alternative antibiotic regimens are available. D Tendon rupture Like neuropathy, tendon rupture is a concern with quinolone therapy. Arthropathy and joint pains are also a feature of quinolone use, as well as neuropathy and psychiatric disturbance in some patients. They should not be used in children or adults unless no alternative is available.

stem: A 30-year-old man is admitted one evening by the local out-ofhours general practitioner (GP). Although not his patient, he is able to tell you that the man has a history of schizophrenia, and has recently had his medications altered. 773-555 THERAPE Clinically, he has evidence of a lower respiratory tract infection, and bloods taken earlier that day indicate a neutropenic picture. What is the most likely causative agent?
explanation: B Clozapine Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic used in the treatment of schizophrenia, and in patients who are intolerant to, or unresponsive to, other antipsychotics. Many antipsychotic drugs can cause bone marrow depression, but agranulocytosis is particularly associated with clozapine. The patient’s leucocyte count and differential should be taken prior to its commencement, and at regular intervals thereafter. Agranulocytosis is seen in up to 32/100,000 weeks of observation within the ﬁrst 18 weeks of therapy for patients treated with the drug. E Prochlorperazine This is a phenothiazine, but it is used for the treatment of nausea and vomiting rather than for the treatment of psychotic disorder. A Olanzapine Although decreases in white cell count are reported as common, reports of agranulocytosis exist as case reports only versus the quantiﬁed risk versus exposure identiﬁed for clozapine. C Risperidone Like olanazapine, agranulocytosis was not reported in clinical trials for risperidone but was reported in post- marketing case reports. D Sulpiride Like other anti-psychotics, agranulocytosis is reported but not commonly enough to estimate an exposure– response relationship.

stem: A 70-year-old man is admitted to the Elderly Care Ward with urosepsis. He is treated with intravenous (IV) ﬂuids and gentamicin. On examination, his heart rate is 90 bpm and regular, with a blood pressure of 121/79 mmHg. His respiratory rate is 22 breaths/minute, with saturations of 94% on room air. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. He has suprapubic tenderness, but there is no guarding or peritonism. There is a urinary catheter in situ, which is draining cloudy urine. 5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 137 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 14.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 12.1 × 109/l 2.5–7.5 × 109/l Lymphocytes 1.9 × 109/l 0.8–5.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 265 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 7.0 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l EGFR 51 ml/min/1.73 m2 60+ ml/min/1.73 m2 CRP 155 mg/l < 10 mg/l Gentamicin trough level: 2.2 mg/ml (0.5–2 µg/ml) Urine culture: Escherichia coli growth. Sensitivities: gentamicin, ciproﬂoxacin. Resistance: amoxicillin, trimethoprim, nitrofurantoin What is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?
options: Continue with the same gentamicin dose
Switch to an alternative antibiotic regime
explanation: B Increase the gentamicin dose interval This patient has had an accidental overdose of the aminoglycoside antibiotic gentamicin. Patients on gentamicin require daily dosing levels for the ﬁrst 3–4 days, including a peak level taken one hour after administration and trough levels taken just before the next dose. This patient has a raised trough level which indicates the need to increase the gentamicin dosing interval to prevent toxicity. A Continue with the same gentamicin dose Continuing with the same dose of gentamicin increases the risk of aminoglycoside toxicity, including acute kidney injury and ototoxicity. C Intravenous (IV) ﬂuids Intravenous ﬂuids are an appropriate step in the management of this patient, particularly in the treatment of sepsis. However, this patient is not currently shocked and received IV ﬂuids on admission. The patient is about to receive his next dose of gentamicin and with a raised trough level, the most appropriate next step is to increase the dosage interval. D Reduce the gentamicin dose Patients who receive gentamicin routinely have their gentamicin levels monitored. If the peak level is high, then a reduction in the gentamicin dose is needed. However, in this patient, the trough 773-555 THERAPE level is raised, which indicates the need to increase the gentamicin dosage interval. E Switch to an alternative antibiotic regime Urine culture sensitivities conﬁrm that gentamicin is an appropriate antibiotic to initiate. Changing gentamicin to another antibiotic is not the recommended action to take when there is an increased trough level. Furthermore, frequently changing antibiotics and failing to complete antibiotic courses increase the risk of antimicrobial resistance and should be practised cautiously.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to his Primary Care Physician for a routine check-up. He reports no symptoms such as chest pain, syncope or palpitations. His medical history includes hypertension, for which he takes amlodipine. On physical examination, his heart rate is 58 bpm and his BP is 140/85 mmHg. His physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. An ECG is performed and is shown below: What is the most appropriate interpretation of this patient’s ECG ﬁndings?
options: Second-degree Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) atrioventricular block
explanation:
B First-degree atrioventricular block A PR interval greater than 200 ms (as seen in this patient’s ECG with a PR interval of 220 ms) without any dropped beats is characteristic of ﬁrst-degree atrioventricular (AV) block. E Left bundle branch block Left bundle branch block is characterised by a widened QRS complex, typically greater than 120 ms, with speciﬁc morphology changes in the QRS complex. This patient has a normal QRS duration, hence ruling out this option.

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com A Normal ECG for age While slight PR interval prolongation can occur with age, a PR interval that is over 200 ms is considered abnormal and indicates ﬁrst-degree AV block, regardless of age. C Second-degree Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) atrioventricular block Mobitz type I is characterised by progressive PR interval lengthening until a beat is dropped. In this case, the PR interval is consistently prolonged without any dropped beats, which is consistent with ﬁrst-degree AV block. D Sinus bradycardia Sinus bradycardia is deﬁned by a heart rate below 60 bpm, but it is not characterised by a prolonged PR interval. Although this patient’s heart rate is on the low end of normal, the prolonged PR interval indicates an AV conduction delay rather than just a slow heart rate.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is reviewed on the Acute Medical Unit. She was referred by her General Practitioner after the District Nurses checked her INR in the community. She has a past medical history of stroke and AF, and takes 3 mg of warfarin daily. She was recently commenced on clarithromycin. She is well and does not report any bleeding symptoms. On examination, she does not appear to have any bruising or bleeding gums. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 136 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 162 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l INR 8.2 Combined with repeat INR testing, what is the most appropriate management step?
options: Stop warfarin and give 5 mg IV vitamin K
Stop warfarin and give 5 mg PO vitamin K
Stop warfarin and give 50 IU/kg IV prothrombin complex concentrate
explanation:
B Stop warfarin and give 5 mg PO vitamin K This patient has warfarin toxicity due to the addition of clarithromycin to her usual medications, resulting in the inhibition of cytochrome P450. The British National Formulary (BNF) guidelines indicate that for patients with an INR of more than 8.0 and no bleeding, stopping warfarin and giving the preparation of vitamin

5-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com K PO, rather than IV, is appropriate. Warfarin can be restarted gradually once INR is less than 5.0. C Stop warfarin and give 50 IU/kg IV prothrombin complex concentrate IV prothrombin complex concentrate, such as Beriplex®, would be suitable in major bleeding alongside IV vitamin K. In the absence of any bleeding symptoms, it is not required here. A Stop warfarin and give 5 mg IV vitamin K IV vitamin K is indicated for minor bleeding where the INR is more than 5.0. It may result in rapid correction and can result in achieving the target range on restarting warfarin more difﬁcult. It is not required here in the absence of bleeding. D Omit warfarin dose In cases where the INR is between 5 and 8, without bleeding, it would be suitable for one or two doses of warfarin to be withheld, followed by a reduction in the maintenance dose and ongoing INR monitoring. Here, there is a high risk of possible future bleeding, necessitating the use of PO vitamin K. E Reduce warfarin to 2 mg daily A reduction in the normal maintenance dose would be appropriate for minor elevations in the INR (usually less than 5.0) without associated bleeding. Here, there is a greater risk of bleeding, and as per BNF guidelines, warfarin should be withheld and PO vitamin K administered.
